News.title: Shocking moment mechanic is crushed against car & left seriously injured after row with disgruntled customer at garage
News.content:
Next

THIS is the shocking moment a mechanic is crushed against a car and left seriously injured after a row with a disgruntled customer.

The 50-year-old worker suffered a broken pelvis and leg injuries after the angry driver sped away from Somerset Auto and MOT Centre in Handsworth Wood, Birmingham.



Shocking CCTV shows the dad-of-three being pinned against a parked vehicle and dragged to the ground on October 20 this year.

The motorist then smashed into another motor as the victim lay stricken on the forecourt before making his getaway – narrowly avoiding running over the man again.



The employee has been left bedbound by his injuries and will be unable to work for a number of months while he recovers.

The garage owner, who did not want to be named, said the driver had told his worker “people like you deserve this” as he drove away.



He said the horror unfolded after the customer turned up at the garage unannounced and wanted work done on his Vauxhall Corsa.

“The driver just turned up asking for work to be done,” he recalled.



“My employee said there was no point changing the brake pads until the calliper was replaced.

“He wanted the calliper taken off anyway and said he would buy his own but the mechanic said it wouldn’t be safe to drive off as he’d have no brakes essentially.

“He was moaning a bit but not ranting or raving that much. But he must have been frustrated or angry.

“Then he got back in his and then just drove at the mechanic. He could have been killed.

“Before he drove off, he shouted: ‘People like you deserve this.’



“He will be off work for months – he is just bedbound and can’t do anything. He has four fractures to his pelvis and leg injuries too.”

The business owner said police initially treated the incident as an accident despite it being caught on CCTV.

He added: “They said it wasn’t a crime and we really had to push to get it looked into further. We couldn’t believe it.

“They have now reopened an investigation now and so they should as this is a serious matter. The suspect still hasn’t been caught.

“We just want whoever did this to be found and held accountable but it’s getting frustrating as nothing seems to be happening.”



West Midlands Police said officers are investigating the crime as an assault but no arrests had yet been made.

A spokesperson for the force said: “We are investigating reports of an assault at a premises on Somerset Road, Birmingham.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“A man was injured by a vehicle on Tuesday, October 20, and we are carrying out further enquiries to establish the full circumstances around what happened.

“Anyone with information should contact us via 101 or Live Chat on our website quoting crime reference 20/446932/26.”

News.title: ‘Show off’ driver who raced along major motorway ‘like a nutter’ before killing pal in horror fireball smash is jailed
News.content:
MOTORING MANIAC ‘Show off’ driver who raced along major motorway ‘like a nutter’ before killing pal in horror fireball smash is jailed







Next

A “SHOW-OFF” driver who sped along a major motorway “like a nutter” before killing his friend in a horror fireball smash has been jailed.

Aadil Sabir, 31, suddenly “shot off like a rocket” along the M4 before the vehicle collided with a barrier and exploded, killing the rear passenger William Bailey, 28.



He was jailed for nine years at the Old Bailey on Monday, having previously pleaded guilty to causing death by dangerous driving and causing serious injury.

Sabir, from Cardiff, hit eye-watering speeds of 90mph, causing the car to plane and crash, erupting in flames on October 29, 2023.



Footage from the aftermath shows debris strewn across the road and the gutted shell of the car still smouldering after the blaze.

Passengers Azfur Khan and Hamad Zaman managed to escaped but sustained life-threatening injuries.

Sabir got out of the wreckage with only a few burns to his hands and fingers.

Addressing the defendant in the dock on Monday, Judge Katz KC said: “Aadil Sabir, you were the dangerous driver who caused all this damage, pain and misery.

“William Bailey was 28 years old when he was killed by the dangerous driving of a show-off. His death was entirely avoidable.”

His sister Brooke Bailey told the court: “There are no words to describe the pain of losing Will.



“We have re-lived the horror of losing him repeatedly. The trauma has affected every aspect of our lives.”

The court heard how Sabir and his friends had been driving eastwards on the M4 towards London to pick up something to eat after a car show.

Traffic officers had installed a roadblock at around 11.25am following a crash.

Just before it was lifted, wardens advised the defendant and other drivers to “take it easy” as they continued with their journeys.

Reflecting on CCTV footage of the crash, Judge Katz said: “No sensible driver would have seen the lifting of the roadblock as an opportunity to show off your car’s six-litre, V8 engine.



“You did. You put your foot down hard and, in the words of another driver who was also in a high-performance car, you ‘shot off like a rocket’.

“He even flashed his lights at you, in case you hadn’t noticed the speed limit.

“He described what he saw as like the start of a track event.”

Rainfall from earlier in the morning likely contributed to the crash, causing it to aquaplane and lose control before exploding.

The judge called Sabir out as a “show off” who was “racing ahead of the pack”.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

The judge acknowledged the defendant was of “previous good character”, was a “hard-working” family man and had expressed remorse.

News.title: Scots gran dies on bathroom floor in front of husband after 15-hour ambulance wait as 999 call ignored
News.content:
'HORRIBLE & TRAUMATIC' Scots gran dies on bathroom floor in front of husband after 15-hour ambulance wait as 999 call ignored







Next

A GRAN died on her bathroom floor in front of her distraught husband 15 hours after a 999 call was ignored.

Ambulance crews failed to turn up to help Janet Wigfield, 81, when she collapsed at home. She then passed away after a second fall.



Hubby Alexander, 83, who tried to revive her before medics finally arrived at their flat in Dennistoun, Glasgow, said: “It was too late. It was horrible.”

The grieving husband whose wife died 15 hours after his 999 call was ignored has slammed John Swinney’s talk about sorting NHS waiting times as “disgraceful”.



Alexander also called for answers over the loss of great-gran Janet, 81, who passed away on the bathroom floor of their Glasgow home.

He’d first phoned for an ambulance at 3pm on Saturday, November 7, when his spouse, who had Alzheimer’s, took a nasty tumble in the house.

But despite their flat in Dennistoun being just a five-minute drive from the city’s Royal Infirmary, no paramedics were dispatched to treat Janet.

A mercy crew was only sent out after a second 999 call from Alexander at 6am the next morning.



But they arrived too late to save the tragic pensioner, despite her hubby’s desperate attempts to resuscitate her.

Last night dad-of-two Alexander told The Scottish Sun: “She was pronounced dead lying on a cold bathroom floor.

“It was horrible and traumatic. But I honestly believe if that first ambulance had come she’d have been in intensive care and still living today.”

Hitting out at the First Minister and Scottish Government, he added: “I want answers and to make sure this doesn’t happen to anyone else.

“I think it’s absolutely disgraceful when people like John Swinney and the Health Secretary talk about waiting times. What a lot of rubbish.”



Alexander told how the emergency began after Janet collapsed in the afternoon.

The retired social work driver said: “I dialled 999 but the ambulance didn’t turn up. In the back of my mind I thought there was no point in pestering them if people are waiting in corridors.

“But as the time went by, I realised no ambulance was coming. Janet was knackered and the two of us went to bed.



“Around six on the Sunday morning Janet got up to go to the toilet. But she collapsed in a heap again.

“I called an ambulance and it turned up within minutes as I was doing CPR.

“But the paramedics told me they couldn’t find a pulse. It was too late.”

Tory health spokesman Miles Briggs said: “Janet’s tragic death should be a source of shame for John Swinney and the SNP government.

“It is indefensible that an ambulance was unable to turn up. Her family now deserve urgent answers.”



A spokesman for the Scottish Ambulance Service said: “We are very sorry for Mr Wigfield’s loss.

“We can confirm we received a call on November 7 that, after assessment, was triaged as non-life-threatening.

“Due to demand and lengthy turnaround times at the Glasgow Queen Elizabeth University Hospital, including delays of four hours, we were unable to dispatch an ambulance at that time.

“A second call was received the following morning, which was upgraded, and an ambulance responded within seven minutes.”

Health Secretary Angela Constance said: “The circumstances described are unacceptable and I expect the Scottish Ambulance Service to investigate.



“Ambulances must be able to respond as quickly as possible to emergencies.

“That’s why we are investing in hundreds of new paramedics and frailty units for every A&E.”

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Four days after Janet’s death Mr Swinney told MSPs: “People are waiting too long in A&E.

“The Government is focused on ensuring that we have a range of interventions in place to minimise that.”

News.title: Burnham should stop spinning yarns about a non-existent EU-topia and start tackling our real-world problems
News.content:
No EU-topia







Next

ANDY Burnham refuses to heed six former Prime Ministers’ advice not to re-open the Brexit debate.

They’re “stuck in the past” he declares.



That’s rich coming from a misty-eyed socialist who hankers after the good old days of the 1970s when Britain suffered economic turmoil and industrial unrest.

And he wants us back inside the EU — despite the fact it will mean UK tax-payers once again being drained of cash.



Unsurprisingly, his idyllic daydream of surrendering power back to Brussels is already unravelling.

His claim that a Brexit “reset” deal would slash food prices has been laughed off by producers as pure wishful thinking.



In fact, the weekly shop is likely to cost MORE once Eurocrats impose new checks on goods that currently flow freely into the UK.

Burnham should stop spinning yarns about a non-existent EU-topia and start tackling our real-world problems.

Tiking the mick

DOWNING Street is supposed to be the beating heart of British democracy, not a film set for fame-hungry TikTokers.

Yet since he became PM, Andy Burnham has rolled out the red carpet for at least 30 social media influencers, turning No10 into a playground of cringeworthy skits and cosy chats.



Nobody is saying politicians should ignore online creators.

British adults spend an average of 90 minutes a day scrolling on their phones so it makes sense to talk to people where they are.

The real gripe is that Burnham welcomes only the tame and agreeable — dodging scrutiny from everybody else.

Last week one digital creator was ushered through the famous black door to recreate Hugh Grant’s Love Actually dance routine before filming a chummy chat with the PM.

Yet when it came to explaining his Brexit deal, Burnham managed just two questions from actual journalists.



Britain needs a leader prepared to answer difficult questions — not one desperately fishing for “likes”.

It’s a disservice

THE NHS is drowning in taxpayers’ cash — yet patients are waiting longer, while productivity goes into reverse.

The health service gobbles up a massive 20p in every pound of ALL Government spending.

Shockingly, hospitals handed the biggest cash windfalls have suffered some of the biggest productivity drops.

Millions vanished straight into a whopping 28.9 per cent pay hike for junior doctors.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Waste is rife across the board, with clueless hospital trusts paying widely different prices for the exact same everyday supplies.

What happened to all Labour’s grand talk of NHS “reform”?

News.title: Millionaire hotel owner & sister cleared of murdering their mum, 100, with morphine overdose
News.content:
TRAGIC TRIAL Millionaire hotel owner & sister cleared of murdering their mum, 100, with morphine overdose







Next

A MILLIONAIRE hotel owner and his sister have been cleared of murdering their 100-year-old mum with a morphine overdose.

Jeremy Mogford, 79, and his sister Sarah Pickering, 72, remain on trial for the alleged murder of Pamela Mogford.



Their mother died at her home in Bledlow Ridge, Buckinghamshire, in February 2022.

Mr Justice Jay directed the jury to return a not guilty verdict for both defendants on the charges of murder at Oxford Crown Court on Monday.



Closing the Crown’s case, prosecution barrister Julian Christopher KC said it would no longer seek a conviction on the murder charges.

Judge Jay told jurors: “You have heard what the prosecution said. It’s up to you to work it out, but it follows that on my direction the only proper verdict you can reach on count one is not guilty.”

The defence case is due to begin on Tuesday and both defendants are expected to give evidence in their trial.

The court previously heard experts cannot conclude that the level of morphine given to Mrs Mogford was enough to kill her.



It was said the defendants gave their mother the equivalent of “at least four times” as much morphine as her GP had given her the evening before she died in an effort to “speed up” her death.

The court previously heard the GP, Dr Thomas Neale, had told Mrs Mogford’s children not to give her any further pain-killing medication.

Dr Neale said he left three further ampules of morphine in Mrs Mogford’s home in case of need, which could be administered by a medic called to her home.

Mogford and Pickering accept giving their mother morphine after the GP had left, but deny intending to quicken her death, rather maintaining they did so because she was in pain.

The siblings were arrested in June 2023 after texts were discovered from Pickering on the evening of her mother’s death.



One of the messages read “I am actually killing her”.

Another said: “I shall wait until Foyle is over then I can go to my grave knowing I have topped someone. It’s certainly on my bucket list”.

In a statement to police on October 16 2023, Mogford said he “emphatically refuted” the criminal allegations and found them “very hurtful”.

His barrister Trevor Burke KC told the court he and Pickering had “acted out of love” when they administered the morphine.

Mogford is known for founding various independent hotels and restaurants in Oxford.



His portfolio includes the Old Bank Hotel and Old Parsonage Hotel, Quod Restaurant, Parsonage Grill and Gee’s Restaurant.

The hotelier also founded the restaurant chain Browns, which he sold in 1996 for a reported £35million.

His mother Pamela married war hero Maj Peter Mogford in 1946 when he was decommissioned from the Army after service at Dunkirk and in North Africa, Cyprus, Italy and India.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

The couple was married for 70 years until his death in 2015.

The trial continues.

News.title: Moment hero pet dog saves drowning toddler in family swimming pool jumping in after girl’s head goes under
News.content:
Next

THIS is the moment a heroic dog saves toddler from drowning in her family pool.

Dramatic footage shows the courageous canine leap into the pool as Maite, 2, struggled to keep her head above the water.



The little girl managed to cling to Tereza the golden retriever, who kept her afloat – ultimately saving her life.

Spotting the chaos, two female family members raced to the pool, dove in and pulled the little girl and dog to safety.



The nail-biting scene unfolded in Cuiaba in central-west Brazil on Friday.

Maite’s mother Gladissa later said the terrifying incident happened while the family were holidaying at sister-in-law’s home, where the heroic dog lives.



She said she had briefly stepped away to get a slice of cake while her older daughter had gone to collect the dog’s bathtub.

In just a few seconds Maite unexpectedly decided to enter the swimming pool alone.



The footage captures the tot slowly waddling down the steps of her pool before losing her footing.

Gladissa said her young daughter had previously been swimming but never on her own.

She said: ” She always waits for someone to get in with her.

“She simply got into the pool. According to her, she was going to dive in. In the innocence of a child.”

Gladissa descided to share the terrifying footage as a warning to other parents.



She said: “In two seconds, a tragedy can happen.

“Today, once again, I thank God for His goodness and mercy towards my daughters and my family.

“You can never be too careful.”

The mother praised Tereza as a hero and credited the animal with saving her beloved daughters life.

Gladissa later shared further footage showing the little girl happily playing with her four-legged rescuer.



It comes as another hero dog saved a six-year-old boy from being mauled by a bear.

Bella, a husky mix, pounced on the beast just in time to protect young Colton who was playing outside his Connecticut home at the time of the terrifying near-miss.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Terrifying video captured by the Tazzara family’s security camera shows the brave dog charge at the grizzly before biting at its tail and chasing it out the yard.

Local politicians praised the pooch for her “incredible bravery” in chasing down the black bear.

News.title: I’ll END Labour’s early prison release scheme and keep up to 80k criminals in jail for longer, vows Kemi
News.content:
Next

UP TO 80,000 criminals a year would be kept behind bars for longer under Tory plans.

Kemi Badenoch will today vow to end Labour’s early release schemes and stop offenders walking free after serving just a third of their sentences.



The Tory leader wants criminals to serve at least half their jail terms instead.

She will also pledge to tear up new rules that spare offenders jail for sentences of 12 months or less.



Mrs Badenoch said: “Labour seems more concerned about getting criminals out of prison than making them face up to the crimes they choose to commit.

“Sentences must actually mean something in order to keep law-abiding people safe.”



Labour has cut the time most prisoners spend behind bars to just a third of their sentence to tackle overcrowding, while introducing a presumption against jail terms of 12 months or less.

The Tories claim their plans would see up to 80,000 criminals spend longer in jail every year and they have promised to build 50,000 new prison places to make room for them.

Shadow Justice Secretary Nick Timothy will launch an expert review into how to deliver the prison-building blitz.

It comes as figures show more than 1,100 thieves with over 75 previous convictions escaped jail last year.

News.title: Influencer stunts, cosy podcasts and a £700k bill… inside Andy Burnham’s toe-curling bid to become a social media star
News.content:
Next

IS TikTok-obsessed Andy Burnham in the last dance saloon – after inviting an influencer to show off his moves in No10?

The social media star, in chinos and a T-shirt, pranced upstairs and down as he recreated Hugh Grant’s dance from 2003 romcom Love Actually where the floppy-haired actor played a fictional Prime Minister.



The toe-curling stunt is the latest in a relentless publicity drive that has turned No10 into something resembling a celebrity PR agency.

A quick scroll through social media reveals Mr Burnham has found time to film with at least 30 influencers in just four months.



From comedy sketches to cosy podcasts, he seems determined to become Britain’s next big internet sensation.

But how much of it is about explaining Government policy? And how much is simply promoting Andy Burnham?



He has spared no effort making his new online pals feel special.

Earlier this month, Downing Street threw open its doors for an evening reception attended by TikTok and Instagram stars with a combined 470million followers.

Guests at the November 9 bash were treated to handwritten letters, professional photos outside No10 and the chance to meet the PM.

Software giant Adobe helped to arrange the photography, with more than 50 portraits taken, while Mr Burnham even had a turn on DJ decks set up for the party, one of the revellers revealed.



But it was TikTok trend-setter Luke Hamnett who was centre stage as he did his Hugh Grant dance — albeit warned not to bash into the furniture worth hundreds of thousands.

Lucky Luke, who boasts 1.3million followers, even got to interview the PM and, during a 20-minute podcast, was predictably chummy.

Hardly in the Jeremy Paxman tradition of grand political inquisition, he told Mr Burnham he was doing a “really good job”, before their chat turned to music, tattoos and Larry the Downing Street cat.



Comedian Maddy Lucy Dann also got a chat with the PM and opened with: “Do you agree the NHS is pretty slay?”

The event’s organiser, TikTok fav-ourite Max Balegde, posted a clip of himself outside No10 miming to a song featuring the lyrics: “Bomboclaat pussywagon chicken nuggets.”

For anyone baffled by that, it is part of TikTok trend “brainrot” — celebrating absurd internet slang.

Other guests included influencers Big Manny, Stu Pidman and Grace Beverley as well as artist Sophie Tea — who showed off a letter from the PM thanking her for “inspiring us to do things a bit differently in Downing Street”.

But Tory leader Kemi Badenoch led a backlash, posting: “When I was a new MP, we had to hand in our phones as we stepped into 10 Downing St, so it’s jarring to see a Labour PM turn it into a bit of a joke.



“Hugh Grant could dance through No10 in Love Actually because he was pretending to be Prime Minister. Andy Burnham IS Prime Minister.

“At a time when Trump, Xi and Putin are projecting power on the world stage, and people across Britain are anxious about the future, this looks extremely unserious.

“Being relatable doesn’t mean treating the public as though they are children who need entertaining.”



Indeed, the PM has been far keener of late to court influencers than be grilled by serious journalists.

At the Brexit summit in Brussels on Friday, he took just two questions from British reporters after signing his new deal cosying up to the EU.

The travelling Press were expecting another chance to quiz him afterwards, only for Downing Street to announce he had run out of time.



Curiously, there was room in his diary for Instagram creator and Celebrity Traitors star Freddie Fraser, who travelled to Brussels to interview the PM.

And at the Commonwealth summit earlier this month, Burnham again snubbed the Press as he took just seven-and-a-half minutes of media questioning across three days.

He also shut out journalists when at COP31 climate summit in Turkey.

But meanwhile the publicity stunts have come thick and fast.

Since entering No10, Mr Burnham has gone jogging with Olympic great Sir Mo Farah, ranked pub snacks with Chancellor John Healey and appeared on influencer Max Klymenko’s Career Ladder video series.



Another content creator asked him if he had a dream, while one wanted to know how many cups of tea he drinks each day.

The clips may look spontaneous but belie a slick publicity machine.

Just days before the November reception, more than 20 personal finance influencers were invited into Downing Street to share their pearls of wisdom about the Budget.



No10 also advertised five digital communication jobs in August — the most senior paying almost £70,000.

Official figures show Government departments have spent at least £2.4million working with social media influencers since July 2024 — and Mr Burnham has kept that up with a vengeance since taking office in the summer.

Ministers have also declined to name 22 influencers used in Cabinet Office campaigns, while citing commercial confidentiality.

Meanwhile, the bill for November’s bash — including the catering, photography and entertainment — remains unclear.

Perhaps somebody could ask at the next influencer brunch?



To be fair, Mr Burnham does have a perfectly reasonable argument for embracing social media.

'WRONG TO DODGE SCRUTINY' By Jack Elsom HOW come you’re such a normal and likeable bloke, Prime Minister?

This was the zinger lobbed at Andy Burnham by Luke Hamnett on the TikTok star’s Live Laugh Luke podcast.

It seemed lost on the interrogator that, after graduating from Cambridge University, the PM became a Labour adviser, an MP and then a Cabinet minister before landing the top job. But Mr Burnham promised to remain a man of the people, independent of the Westminster bubble.

Luke then pitched another curveball – not – by telling the PM: “I really, really do think you’re doing a good job.”

Not all interviews have to be combative, and sometimes you do get more from a politician with honey than vinegar. Also, nobody is denying content creators are now part of the media ecosystem and should be engaged by politicians.

But there is something wrong with consistently courting tame and biddable influencers as a substitute for real scrutiny and tricky questions.

Would Luke have been given free rein to prance around Downing Street if he had given the PM a good roughing up over the small boats?

Governments already wield enormous resources to communicate with the public, and the Press has always been a bulwark against unfettered propaganda.

Influencers should do better than prostrate themselves as useful idiots in Burnham’s PR machine

Millions of young people get their news online and politicians cannot expect everyone to sit down with a newspaper or watch the News At Ten on the box of an evening.

There is nothing wrong with a PM trying to reach out to them.

But there is a world of difference between explaining Government policy and turning the Prime Minister into a social media celebrity.



A flattering podcast about Larry the Cat might rack up the views.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

It is rather less likely to explain the finer points of a Brexit agreement or why families are struggling to pay their monthly bills.

And there is something distinctly odd about a PM who can find time to pose, dance and chat with internet stars but runs out of minutes when reporters want to question him about one of the biggest moments of his premiership.

News.title: Nvidia reinstates CEO Jensen Huang after affair with alleged spy as Trump says 'I made the deal'
News.content:
Nvidia has reinstated CEO Jensen Huang just days after rejecting his offer to return to the AI chipmaker - and less than two weeks after he was forced to resign over reports of an affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

The company had come under pressure from Donald Trump to reappoint Huang - and on Monday, the US president said he "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to reverse course and bring Huang back.

But Democrats have accused the Trump administration of selling out national security for financial gain. Huang is due to testify before Congress in early December.

His comeback helped end a week-long losing streak in US stocks that had left the S&P 500 in correction territory.

Stock prices for Nvidia fell sharply after Huang stepped down, but jumped by 31% after he was reappointed on Monday - adding about $1tn to the company's market value.

But Nvidia's closing price was still down slightly from its Friday morning opening price.

News.title: My approach to EU is pragmatic, says Burnham
News.content:
The prime minister has said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything", as he outlined his agreement with the bloc to MPs.

Andy Burnham told the Commons there was "no fixed destination" on talks to explore closer ties with the European Union, adding it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

After several former prime ministers urged him to not reopen the Brexit debate, Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" - and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

At a summit on Friday, Burnham agreed a new deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

He also finalised the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU and said both sides will "brainstorm" options for their long-term relationship.

He has previously suggested potential options for the future could include rejoining the customs union, the single market or a fresh referendum on full EU membership.

However, he has ruled out major changes to the UK-EU relationship before the next general election, saying he will stick to Labour's 2024 manifesto pledge not to return to the single market, customs union or freedom of movement.

Speaking in the Commons on Monday, Conservative MP Sir Edward Leigh said the "reset" with the EU is "a prelude to the prime minister's sincere desire to rejoin the EU and have another referendum" and risked leading to another Scottish independence referendum.

Burnham replied to the Gainsborough MP: "It's not a prelude to anything. It's a pragmatic approach and it will continue to be a pragmatic approach.

"If it's in Britain's national interest, I will recommend it to this House. If it is not, then I won't. There is no fixed opinion here. There is no fixed destination.

"Europe could change again in the next year, 18 months, and we'll have to obviously watch how life changes. But where Britain can make progress, surely we should make progress."

News.title: US rapper Don Toliver postpones two arena shows after Manchester evacuation
News.content:
The Wembley show has been rescheduled to 14 December, while Monday night's O2 gig has been moved to 15 December.

"I'm very sad to sit here and say I have to reschedule The O2 London show to December 15th due to (the) unfortunate incident last night," Don Toliver wrote on Instagram.

Greater Manchester Police (GMP) declared a major incident on Sunday and said 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena.

One woman was taken to Manchester Royal Infirmary for further assessment and treatment after the incident, which happened at about 22:00 GMT, the force said.

A further 88 people "underwent dry decontamination at the scene and were subsequently accommodated within the Etihad Stadium while the incident was managed", according to GMP.

Leon Douzi said he was right next to where the substance was released, and described someone holding a can and "this gas coming out".

"It just hit me in the throat," he said, adding that it felt like "burning".

There was "a bit of panic", Douzi said: "Everybody was having the same feeling and trying to get out."

Some fans reported eye and respiratory symptoms, according to the North West Ambulance Service.

Hannah Baxter, who went to the concert with her partner, said the first thing she noticed was a burning feeling in her throat.

"[We] were just coughing and coughing... there was a guy next to us who had vomited. There were people with red eyes and... tears everywhere," she told the BBC.

Joey Howe, a football journalist at the gig, told BBC Radio Manchester there was a "horrible smell" and added: "People were coming through in wheelchairs choking â it was really distressing."

Police launched an investigation and are continuing to carry out tests on items at the venue to try to identify the substance. No arrests have been made.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "Enquiries remain ongoing to establish the nature of the substance, where it came from and any associated risk. Testing will take place throughout the day as the investigation into the cause of this incident progresses.

"We are trying to establish whether any criminality has occurred in relation to this incident."

Some fans complained about security and a lack of searches as people went into the Manchester concert.

Jessica Moult-Boffey, of Wigan, said people were "crying and screaming in pain" as they left the venue, adding she felt "confused on how something like that got into a venue of that size".

Malachi Clarke also claimed security was "not good at all", adding: "They weren't checking bags, to the point where I had to ask them if they needed to check mine."

Co-op Live said on its website there were a range of security measures, and while "some of these are visible, others you won't be able to see".

It said the arena used a "frictionless security screening that detects prohibited items without you needing to empty your pockets".

Figen Murray, the mother of a Manchester Arena attack victim who led the campaign for a new law to prevent terrorist attacks at public venues, said people should feel "assured" about security measures.

"A lot of the big venues use mass screening technology, where you don't even know you've been checked," she told the BBC. They also have staff observing CCTV, security guards and plain-clothed officers on site.

Murray said that while the current technology is "good enough", it needed improvement over the next few years to become "more sophisticated".

Venues are currently focused on keeping out items â such as explosives â that could cause mass casualties, she added.

News.title: 'Life is not infinite': Catherine talks about 'mortality' in new documentary clip
News.content:
The Princess of Wales has said cancer made her confront her own vulnerabilities, in a new clip from her upcoming documentary, Heal.

"When you're faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite," Catherine says.

In March 2024, Catherine revealed that she had a cancer diagnosis and was receiving chemotherapy.

In a previously released trailer for the documentary, Catherine is seen hugging her children and her husband, the Prince of Wales, as she completed the Three Peaks Challenge earlier this year.

Heal will air on BBC One on Sunday, 29 November.

News.title: UK to host 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa confirms
News.content:
The participation of women and girls in football has risen by 2.3m since the Women's European Championship was held in England in 2022.

However, women remain significantly underrepresented in leadership positions.

Only a quarter of chief executive, chair or performance director roles in major UK sports are held by women and only 12% of sports federations are led by a female.

Noel Mooney, the chief executive of the Football Association of Wales, said: "This is a proud day for Welsh football.

"We've put forward Wrexham and Cardiff as host cities, and it's exciting to think what a World Cup could bring to both cities and the communities around them.

"In Llunio Cymru - our 10-year strategy - we've set ourselves the ambition of reaching the knockout stages in 2035. Some of the players who could take us there are learning the game at clubs across Wales today. Our job is to make sure that wherever a girl grows up in Wales, she can find a team close to home, have a coach who helps her develop and see a route to the Cymru shirt."

Irish Football Association chief executive Patrick Nelson said the event "would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country".

"Our young players would grow up having watched the best in the world play at home, and there is no substitute for that," he added.

Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell said hosting the tournament would be "the most significant thing to happen to the women's and girls' game in Scotland".

He added: "The impact would go far beyond just the matches themselves. The level of investment into coaching, facilities and player pathways in the years beforehand will shape the future of the game for the generations to come."

Fifa's evaluation, published earlier this month, rated the bid 4.3 out of five. Its contractual framework was rated 'medium risk', and the document claimed "certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security".

That is thought to refer to a lack of agreement over a request by Fifa for tax-free status for all football-related activities.

The bid evaluation said: "The bidder has submitted an extensive set of government support documents and contractual hosting agreements, demonstrating the commitment of the relevant authorities and stakeholders.

"However, certain government guarantees, particularly those relating to safety and security and tax, contain certain qualifications which have been duly noted in the legal evaluation.

"While certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion, the bidder's proactive engagement with Fifa and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding issues."

News.title: Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor received £750,000 from Turkish millionaire, court told
News.content:
A Turkish millionaire has told the High Court she was misled over a Â£750,000 payment she made to Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor in 2019.

Nebahat Isbilen is alleging her former business adviser, Selman Turk, misappropriated Â£38m of her assets, including a payment to the then-Duke of York which she believed was for help with her passport.

Turk has rejected the allegations, saying the 81-year-old Isbilen knew the money was actually being paid in the hope that Mountbatten-Windsor could help her husband, a politician who is in prison in Turkey.

Mountbatten-Windsor repaid the Â£750,000 and is expected to give evidence to the High Court in December. He is not accused of any wrongdoing.

Isbilen's lawyers also told the court on Monday that Turk had instructed a separate Â£15,000 payment to Mountbatten-Windsor's ex-wife, Sarah Ferguson, purportedly for the former Duchess of York's 60th birthday party in 2019, and an unquantified "wedding gift" payment for their daughter Princess Beatrice.

Isbilen's family founded a major soap and cosmetics firm in Turkey.

But when her husband, Ilhan, a former member of the Turkish parliament, was arrested in 2015, she wanted help moving her assets out of Turkey. Her lawyers said the charges were "politically motivated" and that in 2017 she was facing "political persecution".

She left Turkey for Greece in 2017 and moved to London in 2018.

Simon Colton KC, representing Isbilen, said she met Turk in January 2017 and gave him control of most of her financial assets.

But Turk "deliberately and systematically abused" her trust and transferred the money to companies he owned or controlled, Colton added.

Colton added that Isbilen approved the Â£750,000 payment to Andrew, but that Turk "lied to her" about its purpose, which was "a further example of his dishonesty".

The court heard that Isbilen had a private dinner with the then Duke and Duchess of York at Turk's flat in December 2019 where she discussed her husband's case.

Turk's lawyers told the court that Isbilen understood and directed the management of her own affairs.

Joshua Hitchens, representing Turk, said in written submissions: "In circumstances where the claimant dined with the duke and duchess and discussed her husband with them, she cannot have believed that the Â£750,000 was a disguised fee for help with a passport, or with a visa."

The trial before Mr Justice Adam Johnson is due to conclude in March, with a written judgment at a later date.

News.title: Teenage girl stabbed multiple times by 14-year-old boy, murder trial told
News.content:
Warning: This article contains details readers may find distressing

A teenage girl was stabbed "around 55 times" by a 14-year-old boy, a murder trial has been told.

Lilly Jones, from Blaina, in Blaenau Gwent, left home at about 18:30 on 20 June, telling her father she was "popping out for a bit".

Her body was discovered face down in woodland close to Duffryn Park two days later.

A 14-year-old boy, who cannot be named because he is under 18, denies her murder.

He and Lilly shared an interest in PokÃ©mon and were "in some kind of relationship", the court heard.

The boy was dressed in a white short-sleeved shirt and tie as he sat in the dock at Newport Crown Court on Monday.

Anna Pope KC, prosecuting, told the jury a camping knife containing a complete DNA profile had been found in the boy's bedroom drawer.

"It was calculated to be a billion times more likely if this DNA had come from Lilly Jones than if it had come from someone else," she said.

Pope said the boy had not given an explanation as to why Lilly's DNA was on the knife.

She added scratch marks were discovered on the inside of his arm and forensic swabs taken from Lilly's fingernails identified his DNA.

She had been stabbed in the heart, both lungs and an artery in her neck. There were 17 stab wounds to her neck, and knife wounds were found on her face, jaw, chest and bottom.

Lilly's phone has never been found.

Newport Crown Court was told Lilly and the boy became friends in March this year after a chance meeting in the street.

They were captured on CCTV cameras in Blaina and were last seen together at 18:50 as they walked towards a footbridge leading to the park, near to where her body was later found.

At 22:19 that evening, Lilly's family contacted the police to report her missing. It was the day after her 14th birthday.

Police searching for Lilly spoke to the teenager the following day. He told officers he was supposed to meet up with Lilly at the Red Lion pub in Blaina, but she never arrived.

He later told police they had been together for part of the previous night, before they separated. He said he came home after she told him she was going to meet up with someone else.

In a further conversation with police on the day Lilly's body was found, he said she had told him she wanted to show him a disused park, before leaving.

When he was arrested he told police he did not murder Lilly and did not know where her phone was.

The trial heard that, when a phone belonging to the defendant was examined, he was found to have searched for Gwent Police, and similar terms, about 30 times the morning after Lilly disappeared, between 05:49 and 10:02.

Pope added: "The phone also showed that photographs had been taken by someone using [the defendant's] phone, we say that's [the defendant]."

She added it was "of note" that one of the photographs "is looking back towards the scene where we say Lilly's body was later found".

Addressing the jury, Pope said: "We will ask you to consider why it is that [the defendant] would take a photograph of some distance, of the area where we know Lilly to have died that night? Particularly if, as he suggests, he left her alive, when she was going to meet a friend."

The trial continues.

News.title: Gisèle Pelicot 'humiliated' after nude photos sent to media to promote book
News.content:
GisÃ¨le Pelicot has said she has been "once again humiliated" after nude images of her were sent to the media to promote a book about coercive control.

The 73-year-old told French broadcaster BFM TV she would take legal action against the publisher and author of the essay.

Pelicot made headlines across the world when she waived her right to anonymity in the trial of her then-husband Dominique, who was jailed for 20 years for drugging and raping her, as well as allowing other men to rape her while she was unconscious.

The publisher apologised, saying it would no longer print or promote the work after "an unfortunate and inappropriate communication".

Pelicot told BFM: "I am deeply shocked that images from the most intimate part of my private life are being displayed and exploited for commercial purposes."

"Today I find myself once again humiliated, exposed and hurt, as if the ordeal of the trial had not been enough," she said.

The essay was written by Sabine Prokhoris, a philosopher and psychoanalyst, who has previously criticised the Me Too movement.

French media reported that Tinbad, a small Paris publishing house, emailed nude photos of Pelicot taken by her ex-husband to some media outlets in order to promote the essay.

In a statement on its website, Tinbad said that no further print runs of the book would be produced beyond the 280 copies already in circulation.

"We offer our sincerest apologies to Ms GisÃ¨le Pelicot," it said. The company also apologised to the author.

Tinbad said "no images of rape or pornographic videos" were sent to the media.

French news agency AFP quoted the blurb of the book as saying coercive control was "a cornerstone of #MeToo orthodoxy".

"These psychological situations, fundamentally ambiguous in nature, involve each of the parties in an equally responsible, though not symmetrical, way," it said.

Pelicot's lawyer Christophe Bigot told BFM the book "calls into question her status as a victim".

Prokhoris told AFP that she placed "full responsibility" for the "inappropriate" promotional campaign on her publisher.

Fifty men were convicted alongside Pelicot's ex-husband in 2024, in a case that made her a global feminist icon.

After her husband was arrested for secretly filming underneath women's skirts in a supermarket, she discovered she had been repeatedly raped by dozens of men, including her husband, while unconscious, over a period of nearly a decade.

Pelicot said she decided to waive her right to anonymity to show how "shame has to change sides" from victims to perpetrators.

If you have been affected by the issues in this story help and support can be found at BBC Action Line.

News.title: Pip assessments need 'fundamental overhaul', report to say
News.content:
A review into the personal independence payment (Pip) will call for a "fundamental overhaul" of the assessment process to "better recognise people's varying costs and needs", the disability minister has said.

Sir Stephen Timms has been looking into disability benefits in England and Wales for the past year and found the set up was "no longer fit for purpose".

Writing in the Times, external, he said his review, to be published on Tuesday, would recommend people with the most severe conditions have a "fast track" process which is "less burdensome".

It comes after a separate review into young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) recommended Pip be scrapped and replaced for under-25s.

Sir Stephen, who produced his report alongside disability groups, carers, clinicians and MPs, said that while Pip had the "right aims" when it was created, there have been "marked shifts in the nature of disability and ill health" in the 13 years since.

He said there had been "substantial growth in claims for mental health and neurodiverse conditions as well as changes to wider society and the workplace".

"For those with the most severe conditions and end of life care, the review recommends a fast track which is less burdensome, with assessment capacity freed up for other cases.

"Where claimants do not have additional costs or care needs, we should be signposting them to services and support."

He added: "Someone with a lifelong or degenerative illness should not need regular reassessments which feel adversarial and unnecessary.

"Disabled people must have the chance to participate fully in everyday life, including in work, and need a more personalised, flexible system that supports them to do so, rather than itself being a barrier."

The Timms review was commissioned after a U-turn from former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer's government on a plan for major benefit reform, which attempted to reduce the welfare bill by Â£5bn a year.

More than 130 MPs, including 120 from Labour, signed an amendment to reject plans to cut disability and sickness-related benefit payments in 2025.

The rebels said they opposed the plans because of the number of people expected to be pushed into relative poverty and a lack of consultation at the time.

News.title: Jury out in train stabbing attempted murder trial
News.content:
Jurors have been sent out to begin considering their verdicts in the trial of a knifeman accused of attempting to murder 10 people on a London-bound train.

Anthony Williams, 33, stabbed 10 passengers between Peterborough and Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, on 1 November 2025.

He has also pleaded not guilty to the attempted murders of three people in Peterborough and a boy in London prior to the stabbings.

After summing up the evidence in the case at Cambridge Crown Court, the judge, Mr Justice Calver KC, sent the jury out to start its deliberations. It will resume on Tuesday.

"You are under no time pressure whatsoever," he told jurors.

Williams has admitted wounding with intent to cause really serious bodily harm in respect of 12 victims and attempting to do so to two others.

Ten of the victims were stabbed on an LNER service from Doncaster to London King's Cross.

Williams is also accused of trying to murder three people in Peterborough the day before, as well as attempting to murder a boy in the early hours of 1 November on a train in east London.

News.title: Mild Atlantic air collides with cold air across the UK, a recipe for some snow
News.content:
The UK is in the grip of the coldest spell of autumn so far.

Yellow cold health alerts from the UK Health Security Agency remain in force until 09:00 GMT on Tuesday, warning of possible impacts to health services and vulnerable people.

The cold Arctic air is clashing with mild Atlantic air that arrived in the south-west of the UK over the weekend - a meteorological setup that provides the ingredients for possible snow.

However, there remains uncertainty in where the boundary between the cold and mild air masses will sit.

Even small shifts in temperature could make a significant difference to what falls from the sky and, crucially, the chances of snow.

News.title: Two men admit sex offences in drugged wife case
News.content:
Warning: This article contains distressing content

Two men have pleaded guilty to sexual offences against a woman who was drugged and raped by her husband without her knowledge.

Robert Stewart, 70, from Stockport admitted rape and conspiracy to administer a substance with intent at Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court.

In a separate hearing at Manchester Magistrates' Court, Tommy Golden, 59, pleaded guilty to sexual assault involving the same woman in June 2025.

Golden appeared via video link from HMP Risley, where he is serving a prison sentence.

District Judge Simon Blakebrough said his offending was too serious to be dealt with by magistrates. His case was sent to Manchester Minshull Street Crown Court, where he is due to appear in December.

During the hearing, Golden said that he had not spoken to a solicitor before entering a guilty plea.

News.title: Can AI spot breast cancer earlier? NHS launches world's largest trial to find out
News.content:
Nearly 700,000 women across the UK are to be invited to join the world's largest trial of how artificial intelligence can help in breast cancer screening.

AI will be used to review mammograms to see if it can improve early cancer detection and ease the workload of clinical staff, while not over-diagnosing women unnecessarily.

Recruitment to the EDITH trial , externalhas already begun at Cambridge University Hospitals, the first of 30 sites across the UK.

Women aged 50 to 71 are invited for routine breast screening every three years in the UK, and more than two million attend annually.

At present two NHS experts look at each breast X-ray, known as a mammogram, but in the trial, one of the human readers will be replaced by AI.

Several smaller studies have already shown that AI can improve breast cancer detection rates, but researchers running this trial say they need to be sure it won't cause harm by leading to women being recalled unnecessarily for further tests.

Sian Taylor-Phillips, professor of population health at the University of Warwick, and co-chief investigator said: "AI-assisted technology could help improve early cancer detection but we want to avoid the overdiagnosis of milder disease that would never have caused symptoms."

Breast cancer is the most common cancer among women in the UK, with around 59,000 cases diagnosed each year.

About a third of these are picked up by routine mammograms, usually at an early stage when they can be more easily treated.

It's estimated the screening programme helps prevent around 1,300 deaths a year.

News.title: Burnham does not view Wales as an equal nation, claims first minister
News.content:
The first minister says he wants an urgent meeting with the prime minister after Andy Burnham rejected calls to give more powers to the Welsh government.

Rhun ap Iorwerth said he was "deeply disappointed" and that Burnham "does not view Wales as an equal nation".

Meanwhile, Welsh Labour leader Ken Skates urged Burnham to "negotiate around a table" with ap Iorwerth.

In a letter to ap Iorwerth last week, the prime minister said he was "not persuaded" by the case to devolve policing and justice, the Crown Estate and rail infrastructure to Wales.

Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock said the UK government believed "devolution must be about more than transferring powers from one government to another".

Trade union body TUC Cymru said it was disappointing calls for further devolution had been "dismissed without any discussion".

In a written statement to Senedd members, the first minister said: "The refusal to even explore the devolution of the crown estate, justice and policing, and rail infrastructure proves that the prime minister does not view Wales as an equal nation.

"The case in favour of Wales having control over these areas of responsibility â just like Scotland â is compelling. Several commissions have argued for the devolution of justice and policing, yet the UK government seemingly prefers to put unionist ideology before hard evidence.

"This government is not interested in more powers for power's sake. The current settlement is unfair, unjust and unsustainable."

News.title: Mother and son riot ringleaders jailed for 'disgraceful' acts
News.content:
A mother and son described as ringleaders of rioting that targeted ethnic minorities have been jailed for what a judge called their "disgraceful activities".

Kelvin Kane, 32, of HMP Maghaberry, was jailed for four years on Monday after admitting 17 charges connected with rioting in Ballymena in the summer of 2025.

His mother Tracy Kane, 51, of Galgorm Street in the town, was jailed for two years after admitting two counts including encouraging and assisting her son's crimes.

Kelvin Kane's crimes included setting fire to a flat, which forced a family including a pregnant woman to be rescued.

Antrim Crown Court was told Kelvin Kane was both an instigator and organiser of the first night of violent disorder in Ballymena on 9 June 2025, which the judge called "an orgy of violence".

Kelvin Kane's offences included one count of riot, seven of criminal damage and one of arson being reckless as to whether life was endangered.

CCTV and police body-worn camera footage covering almost two hours was shown to the court at an earlier hearing on Thursday.

It showed Kelvin Kane helping to build a barricade on the junction of Clonavon Road and Clonavon Terrace, throwing missiles including paint and bricks at police, kicking in or attempting to kick in the doors of houses and smashing the windows of properties.

The court was also shown footage taken on a mobile phone from inside the ground floor flat of a property after Kane set fire to the kitchen.

Judge Peter Irvine KC said a family from Bulgaria had to be rescued from the upstairs flat including a pregnant woman suffering from smoke inhalation and a young child.

News.title: Capita shares plunge 70% as boss quits after civil service pensions failure
News.content:
Shares in outsourcing business Capita have sunk 70% after its boss stepped down as the saga over public sector pensions drags on.

Chief executive Adolfo Hernandez has agreed with the firm's board to leave with "immediate effect", admitting that the company had "not delivered" for members of the UK's Civil Service pension scheme.

The scheme, which manages the pensions of 1.7 million public sector workers in the UK, has been mired in controversy, with tens of thousands of retiring civil servants having faced delays receiving their pension payments.

Capita has cut its profit forecast, partly due to the problems surrounding the scheme, and says it plans to raise Â£190m to bolster its finances.

Capita took over the administration of the Civil Service Pension Scheme in December last year.

One Cabinet Office minister last month labelled the company's progress in improving how it runs the scheme as "abysmal".

Hernandez, who will be replaced by current chief financial officer Pablo Andres, said: "I am proud of the groundwork we have laid and the progress we have made under my leadership.

"Of course, within that I recognise that we have not delivered the service that members of the Civil Service pension scheme deserve."

News.title: Trump, victims’ families rail against Newsom’s death row clemency decision: ‘shocking act of injustice’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump and the relatives of several high-profile California murder victims condemned Governor Gavin Newsom on Monday during an event at the Justice Department, attacking the Democrat’s decision to grant clemency to hundreds of death row inmates.

Speaking at the department with Attorney General Todd Blanche, Trump joined family members who lost loved ones in decades-old murder cases to criticize Newsom's move commuting 548 death sentences to life without parole.

Early in the event, several relatives spoke in graphic detail about their loved ones’ slayings in an effort to highlight how unjust they felt Newsom’s move was.

Trump accused the governor of siding with convicted killers over grieving relatives, telling the audience that Newsom “stole away the only closure those families might ever have” and that the administration is “working as hard as they can to get this travesty overturned in some form.”

The president invited several relatives to the podium to speak about their cases, beginning with Sandy Fern, the mother of eight-year-old Michael Lyons, who was abducted, tortured and murdered in Yuba City, California, in 1996. Fern said Newsom erased the death sentence of her son's killer, Robert Boyd Rhodes, “with a swipe of a pen, without notifying the families.”

open image in gallery President Donald Trump joined the grieving relatives of several California murder victims at the Justice Department on Monday to denounce Governor Gavin Newsom’s decision to commute the death sentences of 548 inmates, calling the move a ‘shocking act of injustice’ ( Getty )

Addressing the governor directly during her remarks, she added: “Face me, Governor Newsom. Tell me, Michael’s life doesn't matter.”

Mark Klaas also addressed the gathering regarding the 1993 abduction and murder of his 12-year-old daughter, Polly. He stated that for three decades his family believed the jury’s sentence would remain intact, and said he stood before the crowd “outraged that Governor Gavin Newsom unilaterally erased that sentence and 547 more and commuted them to life without parole, without the consent of victims' families or the people of California.”

“This decision was not made by a jury,” Klaas said. “It was not approved by the voters. It was made by one politician acting alone.”

He argued that the pursuit of justice “should not become a political exercise.”

open image in gallery California Governor Gavin Newsom announced plans earlier this month to commute all 548 California death row sentences to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole, a move that still requires approval from the California Supreme Court before taking effect ( Getty )

Trump later recognized the relatives of Placer County Detective Michael Davis and Sacramento County Deputy Sheriff Danny Oliver, who were fatally shot in 2014 by Luis Bracamontes during a multi-county crime spree. Davis’s brother, Placer County Sheriff’s Lieutenant Jason Davis, told attendees that his family had begun to heal before Newsom “single-handedly ripped that bandaid off and opened that wound again.”

“And Governor Newsom, under the cloak of darkness, unilaterally makes a decision to commute the sentences of the most heinous criminals in our society,” Davis said. “I am disgusted and frustrated. My brother did not die in vain.”

The president also heard from Gloria Vega, whose father, Palm Springs Police Officer Jose Gil Vega, was fatally shot in 2016 just months before his planned retirement, and acknowledged several other families whose relatives were killed by inmates on California’s death row.

Trump characterized the clemency grants as a “shocking act of injustice” and argued that Newsom and “the radical left look at these heinous acts, and their sympathy is not for the children and their parents, but for the monsters who extinguished innocent young lives.”

He pledged that his administration would “bring justice for American families.”

open image in gallery Trump called the clemency grants a ‘shocking act of injustice’ and later pledged that his administration would ‘bring American families their justice’ ( Getty )

“Law enforcement is not the enemy. The enemy are those who rape and murder our citizens, and they deserve no mercy,” Trump said, later adding, “And the ultimate crimes deserve the ultimate punishment.”

During the event, Trump announced a new presidential directive instructing the Justice Department to seek capital punishment for child murderers, as well as rapists and human traffickers who kill their victims, while ordering the attorney general to speed up federal executions.

“Once jurors have spoken, capital punishment will be swift and certain,” he said.

The president announced nearly $150 million in new Justice Department public safety grants to hire more than 1,000 law enforcement officers, directed housing officials to tighten tenant screenings in public housing and endorsed newly introduced legislation from Republican Congressman Brandon Gill that would mandate the death penalty for undocumented immigrants convicted of murder.

open image in gallery The event follows heavy Republican losses in the recent midterm elections, which handed Democrats control of Congress and raised the prospect of new legislative oversight and investigations into the Justice Department’s operation ( Getty Images )

Monday's appearance marked Trump’s second speech at the Justice Department in less than two years. During his prior visit in March 2025, the president focused largely on grievances tied to past federal investigations into his conduct and vowed retribution, though several attempts by the administration to prosecute political adversaries have encountered legal setbacks in court.

The event also follows sweeping Republican losses in the recent midterm elections, which handed Democrats control of Congress and raised the prospect of new legislative oversight and investigations into the Justice Department’s operations.

Critics have argued that the department’s traditional independence has eroded during Trump’s second term, pointing to Blanche — Trump's former personal defense attorney, who succeeded Pam Bondi as attorney general in April and supports broad presidential authority over the agency — as well as symbolic changes such as a large banner bearing Trump’s portrait hung on the exterior of the Justice Department building.

News.title: Here's what's next after climate talks collapse: Reform, individual action, hope and more heat
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Just because the U.N. climate talks in Turkey imploded, it doesn't mean that hope for rescuing an ever-warming world is gone, experts say. But the road ahead will be tougher, require changes to negotiations and may be more about individual efforts by nations and companies instead of joint action.

And the planet will just keep getting hotter.

The climate talks, called COP31, ended Sunday in division and finger-pointing, without the hoped-for overarching agreement on fighting climate change that the world could follow. The main reason for the collapse was disagreement over mentioning the need to transition away from fossil fuels, the chief cause of global warming.

“The world cannot afford a repeat of this moment,” United Nations climate chief Simon Stiell said as the negotiations fell apart. “The fight continues. We will never give up.”

The Associated Press asked numerous experts to outline what's next for the U.N. climate process, which reconvenes next year in Ethiopia, and the fight to reduce emissions of heat-trapping gases from the burning of fossil fuels.

Most of the experts found positives from the collapse, mostly in how it appears to be galvanizing many countries to do something about phasing out coal, oil and natural gas.

“This leads to a crisis. It is a climate and political crisis,” said Johan Rockström, director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impacts Research in Germany. “But it will hopefully result in taking COP reform more seriously as well as ‘truly getting serious’ in delivery of the Paris Agreement.” That 2015 pact requires countries to ratchet up plans to cut carbon emissions and aims to keep global average temperatures out of the danger zone.

The climate doesn't 'care about politics'

The Paris deal set goals of limiting long-term warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius (3.6 degrees Fahrenheit) and preferably below 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) above pre-industrial times. Earlier this year the U.N. conceded that it's inevitable that the world will blow past that long-term 1.5 degree mark, probably in a year or two.

Exceeding it over the long term means “danger in terms of billions of people suffering from droughts, floods, fire, heat waves, disease and human-reinforced storms," Rockström warned.

But the temperature climb isn't stopping there.

Six times this month, the average global daily temperature was more than 2 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels, according to the European climate service Copernicus.

“This is yet another sign that the climate doesn't really care about our politics — either in the U.S. or COP,” said Berkeley Earth climate scientist Zeke Hausfather. Heat-trapping gases keep increasing in the air. The November temperature spikes show that the world is not only passing the 1.5 mark over the long term, but isn't too far away from the 2 degree threshold, he said.

But University of Pennsylvania climate scientist Michael Mann argues against making too much of these November heat spikes because they were influenced by the El Niño weather pattern, which is a phenomenon separate from climate change.

What happened after past talks failed

Given the need to address suffering from increasing extreme climate events such as the deadly Nepal flood, environmental advocates Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa and Tasneem Essop of Climate Action Network International called it “the worst COP ever.”

Because expectations were low and there wasn't a big deal needed, this isn't quite the worst climate talk failure, said climate negotiations historian Joanna DePledge of the University of Cambridge. That belongs to 2000 in The Hague — which had to be continued six months later in Germany — and 2009 in Copenhagen, where a hoped-for deal collapsed, she said.

She blamed the joint Turkey-Australia leadership of COP31 — as did many experts — for handling the negotiations poorly. She said there was no need for an overarching final agreement because the purpose of this round of talks was more about implementing past goals. Insisting on something big, and then not delivering it, was a mistake, she said.

Six years after the failure in Copenhagen, the world agreed to the landmark Paris pact.

Climate Analytics CEO Bill Hare said the failure of Copenhagen led the countries of the world to realize just how important it is to work together. And this failure will remind them to “stop running after the fossil fuel producers and companies and begin to deal seriously with the climate change problem,” Hare said.

Experts urge a reform of the climate talks

For years, experts have said the world needs to change the entire process of COP, a giant two-week climate Super Bowl that attracts 100,000 people to a closed-in campus. Many of the outside experts said the key thing is to ditch the requirement for near-unanimous consensus in big final agreements, and make it majority or super-majority rule.

Mann would also like to apply financial penalties such as embargoes and tariffs to countries that fail to fulfill climate commitments. He also thinks the talks should not be located in fossil fuel-exporting states — like four of the last five host countries.

“We can no longer continue with this charade where a small number of bad petrostate actors stand in the way of planetary sustainability,” Mann said. “The U.N. must change the rules now.”

Hope lies in countries' individual actions

While much of the focus in climate talks is on the overarching agreements, side deals that don't require consensus are thriving.

About 80 countries signed on to Turkey's plan to have 35% of the world's energy use — including transportation such as cars and planes — come from electricity. That could reduce emissions by at least 8 billion metric tons, said International Energy Agency chief Fatih Birol.

Just before the conference started, Brazil offered countries specific “road maps” for how they could transition away from fossil fuels — and several have already adopted them. Nearly 60 countries are part of a separate conference devoted entirely to phasing out fossil fuels.

“The true test of climate action will be what happens beyond the negotiating halls," U.N. Secretary-General António Guterres said.

His message to young people, scientists and those vulnerable to climate disasters is “keep demanding action. Keep turning up the heat,” Guterres said. “Hold governments and companies to account.”
