Sports.title: Inside the gymnastics lore of Bengals superstar Ja'Marr Chase
Sports.content:
Open Extended Reactions

CINCINNATI -- It was a move that looked so improbable that the majority of the 70,747 in attendance inside NRG Stadium didn't seem to process it in real time.

When the Cincinnati Bengals visited the Houston Texans in Week 2, quarterback Joe Burrow heaved a deep ball toward wide receiver Ja'Marr Chase ("F--- it, Ja'Marr's down there somewhere"). As Chase stumbled toward the near right corner of the end zone, he twisted his body, somehow located the ball to make the catch and then dragged both of his feet inbounds to complete a touchdown.

While the crowd in Houston reacted in disbelief as the replay on the videoboards confirmed it was a catch, TV announcer Kevin Harlan extolled the All-Pro receiver while watching the catch in slow motion.

"Oh, the contortion!," Harlan exclaimed. "The body control! The concentration!"

It was almost as if Harlan was talking about a gymnast. Instead, he was talking about a 6-foot, 205-pound dynamic route runner who is one of the best wide receivers in the NFL.

Over the years, Chase has spoken about how he took up gymnastics as a kid, once adding that it was something that never leaves his spirit. Given how well he controls his body and can still backflip from a standstill position, it could seem as if those skills might have helped him become an All-Pro player. But with a bit more digging, the reality isn't that linear.

Ja'Marr Chase's body control resembles that of a gymnast, and it has helped make him one of the best receivers in the league. Sam Navarro-Imagn Images

"In gymnastics, you got to stick the landing," Bengals wide receivers coach Troy Walters told ESPN. "And in football, the more times you stick the landing and not go to the ground and fall down, probably the more successful you're going to be.

"I could definitely see that [connection]."

Chase was a child with energy that needed to be expended. Sometimes, that manifested in activities outside of football, such as skateboarding. But that also meant leaping off things such as a house, garage or garbage can.

Toleah Chase decided that if her son, who was around 9 at the time, was doing all that, it would be done correctly. Chase's older brother, Terell Smith, spearheaded the mission.

"My brother knew somebody [who had access to a gym], and we met there when it was closed, and he taught me how to backflip," Ja'Marr told ESPN earlier this year. "My mom only made me do it so I wouldn't hurt myself."

After Chase came back from learning the backflips, he would call Toleah into a doorway in their home to showcase his new skill.

"He was very excited about it," Toleah told ESPN. "And I was a nervous wreck.

"I always used to tell him, 'Please be careful.' Don't hurt yourself. He was like, 'No, no, I got it, Mom. I know how to do it right.'"

Joe Burrow REACTS & Ja'Marr Chase explains his OUT OF THIS WORLD touchdown catch in the Bengals' win over the Texans https://t.co/qG9Wn0Mx1C — James Rapien (@JamesRapien) September 20, 2026

He wasn't exaggerating. In 2019, Chase racked up 1,780 receiving yards in 14 games, and along with Burrow, led the Tigers to a national title. Two years later, Burrow and Chase were reunited in Cincinnati, where Chase has made catches that look straight out of a floor routine.

Teaching gymnastics concepts to football players isn't new. Jay Clark, who led LSU's women's gymnastics team to an NCAA runner-up finish this year, is a proponent of having athletes do some form of gymnastics at a young age because of the foundational skills that translate to other sports

"It's control due to the spatial awareness that they have -- the aerial sense, knowing where the ground is and being able to feel that innately," Clark said. "Some people can be born with it, but the reality is that our sport probably combines every part of athleticism better than any other, whether that's strength, power, quickness, spatial awareness, balance, all of it."

Occasionally, Chase will showcase his "gymnastics" skills in fun ways. The first example was against the San Francisco 49ers in 2023, when he celebrated a touchdown with a backflip in the end zone.

"I just wanted to have some fun," Chase said after that game. "I did gymnastics when I was young."

Two years later, it came up again when asked if he did things to grab his parents' attention while he was growing up.

"I did gymnastics, y'all," Chase said in September 2025. "It can't leave my spirit."

This year, those incredible catches have highlighted another strong season. Along with his catch against Houston, he had a leaping, twisting touchdown grab against the Miami Dolphins when he secured the ball with his shoulder pad before landing back on the field.

After a slow start, Chase is on pace for one of his best seasons. He's coming off a game in which he had 11 catches for 231 yards against the Pittsburgh Steelers in the Bengals' fifth straight win. It was Chase's third career game with at least 225 receiving yards, tying Jerry Rice, Calvin Johnson and Julio Jones for the most in NFL history.

Chase will lead the Bengals against the Washington Commanders on "Monday Night Football" (8:15, ET, ESPN), and it should be no surprise that he excels in primetime. He has 110.5 receiving yards per game in 17 primetime games, the NFL's highest mark since the 1970 merger.

Ja'Marr Flippin' Chase. #CINatSF | 📺 CBS https://t.co/bQtUoO4ttI — Cincinnati Bengals (@Bengals) October 29, 2023

"The way Ja'Marr is able to track the ball down the field and just catch it way off his body -- the hand strength, the tracking ability -- it's pretty special," said Bengals offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher.

Chase's body composition is one of the things that make him unique. Since he entered the league in 2021 as the fifth pick, coaches and teammates noted how Chase had all the tools of a wide receiver but was built similar to a running back. That enabled him to break tackles and pick up yards after the catch.

But as this year has displayed, one of Chase's greatest strengths is his ability to control his frame while making catches.

"A lot of times, guys go up, and when they come down, they're all out of whack," said Walters, who has been Chase's position coach since he entered the league. "They hit the ground hard, the ball bounces out.

"But he comes down where he's able to control his body or contort his body in the air to make an acrobatic catch."

Similar to Walters, Higgins can understand the comparisons to a gymnast, but Higgins sees something more basic: "Just a freak athlete at the end of the day [who] has God-given talents."

Sports.title: Sources: Packers' Parsons cleared to make season debut Wednesday vs. Rams
Sports.content:
Open Extended Reactions

GREEN BAY, Wis. -- Welcome back, Micah Parsons.

The Green Bay Packers' star pass rusher was cleared on Monday to return from last season's knee injury and is expected to make his 2026 debut on Wednesday night against the Los Angeles Rams, sources told NFL Network's Ian Rapoport.

Earlier on Monday, Parsons said he still needed final clearance from Dr. Neal ElAttrache, who performed the surgery.

Parsons, who injured his left knee in Week 15 last season, still needs to be officially activated off the physically unable to perform list. That move did not happen before the end of NFL business Monday.

Parsons' return to game action will come 347 days after he not only tore his ACL but also his meniscus in a noncontact injury against the Denver Broncos.

Parson first returned to practice on Nov. 4 and did only individual drills that week. The following week, he began to incorporate team (11-on-11) drills into his work. The Packers then had their bye following the Nov. 15 loss to the Minnesota Vikings, but it was not a full bye week because of the Thanksgiving eve game. The Packers resumed practice Saturday and practiced for three days before they depart for Los Angeles on Tuesday.

Micah Parsons' return to game action for the Packers will come 347 days after he not only tore his ACL but also his meniscus in a noncontact injury last season. Stacy Revere/Getty Images

"I would say I feel like I've done everything I possibly could to put myself in position to potentially play on Wednesday but for sure this season," Parsons said Tuesday. "And I'll be looking forward to returning to the field."

Parsons is expected to be on a snap count upon his return.

Despite having a winning record (6-4), the Packers sit in last place in the NFC North, where the Chicago Bears, Detroit Lions and Vikings are all 7-2.

"I'm so locked in on what's ahead of me and I understand what this game Wednesday means to the organization and I myself and what it means for playoffs," Parsons said. "And if I can be out there, I wanna be out there and I'm excited for any time. Because we only got seven more games left, so I wanna capitalize on all those if I can."

Parsons led the Packers with 12.5 sacks last season and led the entire league with 64 pressures, according to ESPN Analytics, despite playing in only 14 games. It was his first season in Green Bay after the Packers gave up two first-round picks plus defensive tackle Kenny Clark to acquire Parsons from the Dallas Cowboys just days before the start of last season.

But the Packers did not win a game after Parsons was injured last season. They were 9-3-1 heading into the Broncos game but lost five in a row, including an NFC wild-card playoff game against the Bears, to close the season. Without Parsons, the Packers have gone 6-9.

"The only thing I'm targeting in a sense of mindset is to win every week to try to uplift this season, change this season around, and do exactly what the Packers brought me here to do," Parsons said. "That's it. That's my only target and that's to make a run for the playoffs and make guys around me better. That's it."

"So I have no targets and outcomes," Parsons added. "I think I've achieved everything that I've wanted in my career except for the big one and I think that's kind of like my own mindset and through the [Nick] Saban documentary I learned just stay in the process of every day. Own my process my today, so I owned it today. I got another process tomorrow and God willing, I'll have another process Wednesday night and that'll be the start of this new journey."

Sports.title: 49ers release Aiyuk, ending WR's tumultuous tenure with team
Sports.content:
Open Extended Reactions

The tumultuous relationship between the San Francisco 49ers and Brandon Aiyuk has ended with the team releasing the wide receiver Monday.

The move ends Aiyuk's tenure with the 49ers after about 6½ years. Because his release is happening after the trade deadline, Aiyuk is subject to waivers. If he's unclaimed in the next 24 hours, he will become an unrestricted free agent who is able to sign anywhere.

Because the move is happening after June 1, the dead money remaining on his deal will be split into $12.35 million for 2026 and $19.29 million in 2027. The Niners will receive a cap credit of nearly $5 million in March and are also aiming to recoup additional bonus money from Aiyuk.

Aiyuk's release has been months in the making after Niners general manager John Lynch said Jan. 21 that the team would be moving on from him. It happened now only because Aiyuk hired agent Drew Rosenhaus in late October, applied for reinstatement with the NFL and reported to the team Nov. 6.

49ers releasing Aiyuk: What to know • Because this move comes after the trading deadline, Brandon Aiyuk will be subject to waivers. If he goes unclaimed, he will become an unrestricted free agent. • The NFL reinstated Aiyuk from the reserve/did not report list Nov. 9. The 49ers had a two-week roster exemption that expired Monday. • The 49ers will split a $31.64 million dead money charge over the next two seasons. San Francisco will receive a salary cap credit of nearly $5 million in March and is trying to recoup additional bonus money from Aiyuk. • Aiyuk signed a four-year, $120 million extension with the 49ers in 2024 but tore the ACL, MCL and meniscus in his right knee Oct. 20, 2024, in what would be the last game he played as a Niner. • Aiyuk told reporters Nov. 6 that he is now feeling "great" and "healthy." Agent Drew Rosenhaus, whom Aiyuk hired in October, has indicated several times that he has multiple interested teams in Aiyuk. • One of those teams could be the Commanders, who are quarterbacked by Jayden Daniels, Aiyuk's close friend from Arizona State. Aiyuk also posted photos of himself in a Commanders hat this summer. Aiyuk and Daniels had an apparent rift this summer, but the pair have since patched things up, ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported Nov. 18.

That day, Aiyuk, Rosenhaus and the Niners met for a little more than an hour with the receiver saying he is feeling "great" and "healthy."

"It was a long recovery process, a long rehab process," Aiyuk said then. "But I'm back to 100% and looking to get reinstated to the National Football League."

For their part, the Niners have sought repayment from Aiyuk for about $13 million in bonus money they previously paid him.

The NFL officially reinstated Aiyuk on Nov. 9 after he reported for a physical. The league provided the Niners a two-week roster exemption to sort through any remaining business with Monday as the day the exemption expired.

Because the exemption ended after the NFL trade deadline, the 49ers had just two options: release Aiyuk or keep him. Coach Kyle Shanahan and Lynch had remained adamant since January that Aiyuk was done as a Niner, which meant his release was always a matter of when, not if.

While Aiyuk's release always seemed inevitable, the Niners clung to hope that they could find a trade partner rather than releasing him. Along the way, Aiyuk repeatedly voiced his displeasure with how the Niners handled the situation as they continued to retain his contractual rights.

Despite a lack of interest and momentum toward a deal, San Francisco held on to Aiyuk through free agency, the draft and every other offseason benchmark. In early June, Aiyuk began to speak out publicly for the first time. In a pair of videos posted to Instagram, he called the 49ers "dumb" and "stupid" for paying him and suggested San Francisco was scared to release him because of how he might play for another team.

Just before that, on June 3, Aiyuk also dealt with the Santa Clara County District Attorney's Office issuing a warrant for him on the misdemeanor charge of exhibition of speeding. That warrant is in reference to video Aiyuk posted to YouTube in December in which he appears to tape himself from the driver's seat going well over the posted 40 mph speed limit on a road that runs past Levi's Stadium.

Brandon Aiyuk is being released by the 49ers, ending a soured relationship between the sides just two years after he signed a four-year, $120 million extension. AP Photo/Jed Jacobsohn, File

Through all that, rumors of Aiyuk's desire to play for the Washington Commanders and with quarterback Jayden Daniels (Aiyuk's close friend from Arizona State) persisted. He posted photos of himself in a Commanders hat, and Daniels and the Commanders were among the five accounts he followed on Instagram.

After an apparent rift with Daniels, Aiyuk and the Washington quarterback patched things up, ESPN's Jeremy Fowler reported Nov. 18. That could open the door for Aiyuk to land in Washington, though Rosenhaus has indicated several times that he has multiple interested teams in Aiyuk.

Though Aiyuk is now free to sign anywhere, his departure ends a confounding partnership between team and player that began to deteriorate when the sides started negotiating a contract extension in 2024.

The Niners and Aiyuk went back and forth on a potential contract early in 2024 and, as other receivers around the league got paid, the price for his services continued to climb. Finally, the stalemate that had Aiyuk holding in during that summer's training camp seemed to reach a conclusion when he signed a four-year, $120 million extension with $76 million in guarantees Aug. 29, 2024.

At the time, the 49ers hoped the new deal would put any built-up issues with Aiyuk in the past, but that vanished less than a month later. On Sept. 27, 2024, Aiyuk and Shanahan had an awkward exchange on the practice field when the receiver showed up wearing red shorts instead of the requisite black ones his teammates were wearing.

From there, the sides never seemed to get on the same page again with Aiyuk struggling early in the season as he averaged 58.5 receiving yards with no touchdowns in the first six games. He tore the ACL, MCL and meniscus in his right knee against the Kansas City Chiefs on Oct. 20, 2024, ending his season. It would be the last game he'd play as a Niner.

The 49ers also hoped to trade Aiyuk last offseason, sources told ESPN, but the injury made getting a good return in a potential deal unrealistic, and that never gained traction. Aiyuk's $24.935 million roster bonus for 2026 became guaranteed on April 1, 2025, effectively ensuring he'd be with the Niners for the 2025 season.

Hopes that Aiyuk would return and contribute existed for chunks of the offseason, but when he didn't show up for multiple in-house rehab sessions, the Niners voided the roughly $27 million in guarantees his contract held for 2026 in July of last year.

On Nov. 22, 2025, Shanahan said that in more than two decades coaching he'd never had a situation when a player's contract was voided. Around that time, Aiyuk stopped reporting to the Niners facility altogether and cut off communication with the franchise's leadership.

"It's something I've never seen in 22 years of coaching," Shanahan said at the time. "It's unfortunate and it's confusing because it's confusing for all of us, but it eventually becomes it is what it is."

On Dec. 13, the 49ers placed Aiyuk on the reserve/left team list, a designation that ended his season and any chance he would play for the team again. He did not report for or participate in the team's offseason program or training camp.

At his end-of-season news conference, Lynch said moving on from Aiyuk would allow for more salary cap flexibility, though most of that will come in future years. Lynch added he "wish I knew" why Aiyuk stopped communicating with the team.

Before his knee injury, Aiyuk had emerged as one of the league's most productive wideouts. He had 75 catches for 1,342 yards and seven touchdowns on his way to second-team All-Pro honors in 2023.

A first-round pick (No. 25) in the 2020 NFL draft, Aiyuk had 294 receptions for 4,305 yards and 25 touchdowns in 69 regular-season games for the 49ers.

Sports.title: Metcalf denies trying to poke DeJean in eye; NFL won't suspend Steelers WR
Sports.content:
PITTSBURGH -- Steelers wide receiver DK Metcalf said Monday that he "can't remember" what occurred in the interactions with Philadelphia Eagles cornerback Cooper DeJean that led to Metcalf's disqualification in Sunday's loss.

Speaking for the first time since his ejection, Metcalf said he didn't try to poke DeJean in the eye.

"I was just telling him, stop pushing me," Metcalf said. "That's all I said."

Metcalf will not be suspended, the NFL said Monday, but the league is reviewing his actions from Sunday's game and he could be fined.

After the game, coach Mike McCarthy said officials told him Metcalf was ejected for poking DeJean in the eye.

Footage from the broadcast also captured Metcalf appearing to reach into DeJean's face mask after a third-quarter play. DeJean, though, said Metcalf "just missed." Metcalf was also flagged for unnecessary roughness earlier in the third quarter when he continued to block DeJean long after the play ended.

Eagles cornerback Cooper DeJean points to his eyes as officials and players try to hold back Steelers wide receiver DK Metcalf on Sunday. Metcalf said Monday he didn't try to poke DeJean in the eye before he was ejected. AP Photo/Chris Szagola

Asked if he thought DeJean provoked him, Metcalf said, "You got to ask him."

McCarthy said he had a "productive" conversation with Metcalf on Monday to address Sunday's incident.

"We talked through everything that happened and how we're looking to move forward," McCarthy said in his weekly news conference. "And obviously the importance of always being available for your teammates, being the responsibility of the 48 and obviously the actual process and everything that went on.

"I'm very comfortable with that conversation."

McCarthy declined to share if the team was going to levy any internal punishment on the receiver.

"Like anything, life's about learning situations," McCarthy said. "I do believe in second chances, so I will judge him based on my personal interaction with him. I did appreciate the way he communicated today."

At the time of his ejection, Metcalf had just one catch for 2 yards on four targets. So far this season, the Steelers' top receiver has 36 receptions for 434 yards and two touchdowns. He's also the only qualified receiver in the NFL this season catching less than 50% of his targets.

Metcalf, who said he exited the locker room in Philadelphia before his team was even off the field because he wanted to avoid the media, has been disqualified three times in his career. Speaking with reporters Monday, he didn't take accountability for his pattern of behavior.

"I think you got to ask the people that seemingly do that to me," Metcalf said when asked why he has struggled to maintain his composure at times in his career.

Though DeJean said after the game that he wasn't aware beforehand of Metcalf's history of being ejected, Metcalf said Monday that he "wouldn't be surprised" if the Eagles had a plan to agitate him.

He later added, "San Fran has done it my whole career when I was in Seattle, so it was nothing new to me." Asked if he wished he had done anything differently in Sunday's game, Metcalf said, "I just wish I would've been there for my team."

When asked if he'd heard anything about internal discipline from the team, Metcalf said, "You got to ask [general manager] Omar [Khan] that or anybody else other than DK."

Metcalf, who signed a $132 million, four-year extension last year after being acquired by the Steelers in a trade with the Seattle Seahawks, was suspended by the NFL for the final two games of the 2025 season for an altercation with a Detroit Lions fan. Metcalf also tried to poke Green Bay Packers linebacker Quay Walker in the eye in November 2025. He was flagged for unsportsmanlike conduct in the moment and fined $12,172 for fighting.

Since being drafted in 2019, Metcalf has been flagged for 56 total penalties. That's the seventh most in the league in that span and most among all players who aren't offensive tackles.

Sports.title: U.S. to co-host Women's World Cup in 2031; U.K. wins bid for 2035
Sports.content:
Open Extended Reactions

The United States has been confirmed as co-hosts of the 2031 Women's World Cup, before the United Kingdom will host the tournament four years later.

The FIFA congress on Monday approved a joint bid from Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 World Cup.

The combined bid from England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland was the sole bidder for the 2035 competition. To date, 19 venues have been put forward as potential options to host the tournament, with 14 grounds across England, two in Scotland, two in Wales and one in Northern Ireland.

The winning candidates and FIFA president Gianni Infantino promised commercially successful tournaments -- the first editions with 48 teams and 104 games -- and to reinvest all that money in women's soccer.

"This will be the largest women's sporting event in history," the U.S. Soccer Federation president, Cindy Parlow Cone, told FIFA members in a pre-vote presentation at the governing body's headquarters in Zurich. "Which means we have to deliver."

The U.S.-led bid previously predicted tournament revenues of $4 billion, and Parlow Cone said after the FIFA decision that "if we do it right we probably will surpass that."

FIFA wanted these heavyweights of women's soccer to face no opposition without rival bids and host the first expanded tournaments. That will bring parity with the men's World Cup which expanded to 48 teams this year in the U.S., Canada and Mexico.

The 2027 Women's World Cup will have 32 teams in Brazil.

The U.S.-led 2031 project across the Concacaf regional soccer body bid offers FIFA a choice of stadiums in 20 cities: 14 in the U.S., four in Mexico plus San José in Costa Rica and Kingston, Jamaica.

Women's soccer in Jamaica already has a good reputation, with standout forward Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw starring for Manchester City and the national team finishing unbeaten above Brazil in their group at the 2023 World Cup.

Parlow Cone said "we have a responsibility to raise the boats of every country" in women's soccer.

"I know first hand what hosting a Women's World Cup can do, and I wanted the same for throughout our region. It's going to be transformative for us, but imagine what it will do for Jamaica for the 'Reggae Girlz' to play in their home stadium in a World Cup match," Parlow Cone said.

The pair of four-nation co-hosting bids had a clear run in the past 20 months and were approved Monday by acclamation in an online meeting of FIFA's 211 member federations.

The U.S. previously hosted the Women's World Cup alone in 1999 and 2003. The national team's tournament win in 1999 was the second of its four titles.

Spain won the most recent World Cup, beating England in the final. Marc Atkins/Getty Images

It will be the first time since 1966 the U.K. has hosted a World Cup. The U.K. will also host the men's European Championships in 2028, but had previously failed in bids to secure the 2006 and 2018 men's World Cups.

The English stadiums included in the bid are: Brighton's Amex, Bristol City's Ashton Gate, Nottingham Forest's City Ground, Leeds United's Elland Road, Arsenal's Emirates Stadium, Manchester City's Etihad Stadium, Everton's Hill Dickinson Stadium, Manchester United's Old Trafford, Newcastle United's St James' Park, Crystal Palace's Selhurst Park, Sunderland's Stadium of Light, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Villa Park and Wembley.

Chelsea's potential new stadium, Wrexham's redeveloped ground and Birmingham's new 62,000-capacity Powerhouse Stadium could also be added.

In Wales, the Principality Stadium and Cardiff City Stadium are on the list. A redeveloped Windsor Park in Northern Ireland is also on the list as are Edinburgh's Easter Road and Glasgow's Hampden Park in Scotland.

FIFA's evaluation of the bid gave it a rating of 4.3 out of five, with the contractual framework of the bid rated "medium risk."

FIFA's evaluation said: "The bidder has submitted an extensive set of government support documents and contractual hosting agreements, demonstrating the commitment of the relevant authorities and stakeholders.

"However, certain government guarantees, particularly those relating to safety and security and tax, contain certain qualifications which have been duly noted in the legal evaluation.

"While certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion, the bidder's proactive engagement with FIFA and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding issues."

English FA chair Debbie Hewitt addressed the congress after the bid's success had been confirmed.

"Thank you for your trust and confidence in awarding us the FIFA Women's World Cup 2035," Hewitt said.

"We're deeply honoured by your support and grateful for the opportunity to host the pinnacle of women's football on behalf of the global football family.

"As we said throughout our bid, we want this to be your FIFA Women's World Cup, a World Cup for everyone.

"Together, we will celebrate the power of women's football, inspire the next generation, and unite fans from every corner of the world. We look forward to welcoming you to the United Kingdom in 2035 and just as importantly, to working closely with you all in the years ahead to deliver an exceptional FIFA Women's World Cup that the entire football community can be proud of."

- 2027 FIFA Women's World Cup: Format, who has qualified ahead of playoffs?

- England World Cup playoff squad: Isobel Goodwin and Katie Cox named

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "The world is coming to the United Kingdom. In 2035 the biggest tournament in women's sport will be played in cities across England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, bringing visitors, investment and jobs to every part of the country.

"Our players have inspired a generation of girls. In 2035 that generation will watch the best in the world play on their doorstep -- and some of them will be on the pitch. But the impact of this World Cup will go much further. It will reach into communities across the country, bring more people into the game and leave a legacy that lasts long after the final whistle."

England forward Michelle Agyemang said it was "incredibly special" and added: "I've been lucky enough to know what it feels like to play for my country in a major tournament, and those are moments you dream about as a young girl playing football.

"The thought of another generation growing up knowing that the biggest stage in the game is coming to their home country is amazing. To have the chance to play in a home World Cup would be a dream, but even more exciting is thinking about all the girls watching who might see 2035 and believe they can be part of it one day."

Scotland captain Caroline Weir added: "The women's game in Scotland has so much potential and this tournament is a real opportunity to drive momentum and help take it to another level both nationally and internationally.

"We're so proud to play our part in welcoming the world in 2035 and I know I speak on behalf of all of the players and staff when I say that we are ready to rise to the challenge and help deliver a truly memorable, world-class tournament."

For the second time in less than two years, FIFA is confirming a double award of World Cup hosts without rival bids that gives clarity for the decade ahead.

In December 2024, FIFA member federations were asked to rubber-stamp the unprecedented six-nation, three-continent bid for the men's World Cup in 2030 from Spain, Portugal, Morocco, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay.

That cleared the way for FIFA to award also the 2034 World Cup to Saudi Arabia in a fast-track process that seemed designed to exclude other candidates.

Information from The Associated Press and PA contributed to this report.

Sports.title: As lockout looms, MLB raises minimum salary offer while union eyes media deals
Sports.content:
Open Extended Reactions

In a series of proposals aimed toward making up ground with a lockout looming, Major League Baseball suggested more measures Monday to get players paid earlier in their careers while the MLB Players Association agreed to share local media equally among the 30 teams.

League owners attempted to sweeten their cap-and-floor proposal by increasing the minimum salary to $1 million in 2027 -- a $220,000 bump from 2026 -- and providing centrally funded bonuses to arbitration-eligible players who settle without a hearing and veterans signing one-year contracts.

Those measures, though, are unlikely to create much momentum with a players' union that is categorically opposed to a salary cap and has vehemently turned one down at every juncture.

MLB spokesperson Glen Caplin refuted the rationale as part of his statement on Monday, saying: "The Union's claim that our proposal would negatively impact 'all categories of players' is not accurate. To the contrary, especially in light of today's new proposals to increase the minimum salary, provide an automatic signing bonus for arbitration-eligible players and offer a new veteran signing bonus, MLB's proposals on the table would provide benefits to most players in every stage of their career."

MLBPA interim executive director Bruce Meyer said the league's proposals "don't add a single dollar in overall player compensation," alluding to the fact that all of their concessions are being made within the same cap-and-floor system.

MLB made its initial offer on May 28, suggesting a $245.3 million cap and a $171.2 million floor beginning in 2027. On Nov. 3, MLB proposed pushing it back to 2028, with a projected cap of $258.2 million and a floor of $180.2 million.

The union has repeatedly referred to the cap-and-floor system as a "zero-sum game" in which players compete against one another for finite amounts of money, as opposed to the current free market.

"Any supposed benefits to certain classes of players are simply taken out of the pockets of other players and are vastly outweighed by the negative effects of the cap and MLB's other restrictions," Meyer said in a statement. "These negative effects include, but are not limited to, a drastic reduction in overall player compensation and benefits, the end of fully guaranteed contracts, and dramatic restrictions on players' career choices and freedom to contract."

The current collective bargaining agreement expires at 11:59 p.m. ET on Dec. 1, at which point owners are expected to impose a lockout that would freeze transactions and cut off all communication between teams and major league players.

The previous lockout occurred after the expiration of the last CBA in December of 2021 and lasted 99 days. MLB's insistence on a salary cap, which prompted the cancellation of the 1994 World Series, have people throughout the sport fearing that this lockout could last much longer.

MLB proposed equal distribution of local media as part of its initial cap proposal, adding that the concept would eliminate the territorial exclusivity of regional sports networks and thus do away with blackouts. The MLBPA formally agreed to that form of revenue sharing on Monday, albeit outside of a cap-and-floor system, while maintaining prior proposals aimed toward rewarding low-revenue teams that win.

Under its proposal, the MLBPA says low-revenue teams would receive an increase of more than $1 billion in assistance over the life of a new CBA.

On Monday, the MLBPA proposed an increase from roughly $700 million to more than $950 million for low-revenue markets from 2026 to 2027, while maintaining $20 million monetary rewards for revenue-sharing recipients that either qualify for the postseason or fail to qualify but finish with a better record than the worst playoff team. Revenue-sharing recipients who finish with a record above .500 would receive a $10 million reward under the MLBPA's revenue-sharing model, which originally allowed teams to keep more stadium-related revenue.

In addition to a $1 million minimum salary in 2027, MLB proposed a $100,000 bonus for players who receive a full year of service time and spend less than half the season on the injured list. The league also established a centrally funded signing bonus equal to 5% of an arbitration-eligible player's base salary if he agrees to terms without the need for a hearing. MLB said 93% of players settled their arbitration cases without a hearing under the current CBA.

Under the league's proposal, each team can reward a $500,000 bonus to a veteran player -- one with at least six years of service time -- who signs a one-year contract valued at $10 million or less. MLB once again agreed to increase the pre-arbitration bonus pool by 30%, from $50 million in 2026 to $65 million in 2027, and to reduce free agency to five years for 30-and-older players.

Those players can still be kept by their teams if offered a one-year contract equal to the average salary of the 125 highest-paid players, the same model used to determine qualifying offers under the current system. MLB agreed to eliminate the qualifying offer for six-year free agents.

To the union, though, it's all essentially window dressing at this point.

The overall pot of money for major league players would be fixed under MLB's proposal; the distribution of money is simply different. The league fully acknowledges that is the case. Its hope is to eventually sway a large enough percentage of the player population to attain the cap it so desperately desires. As part of a fact sheet distributed to media members Monday, the league included a chart noting when every player would qualify for free agency under its current proposal.

"Every other major U.S. sport has a salary cap and floor system to limit payroll disparity, and the fact remains that growth in player compensation has been slower in baseball than every one of those leagues," Caplin said in his statement. "MLB is trying to reach an agreement with the players by meeting their objectives on a number of important issues, including earlier access to free agency and increased compensation for players earlier in their careers."

Sports.title: Who has the most to gain -- or lose -- down the stretch? Barnwell on 11 NFL players under pressure
Sports.content:
Open Extended Reactions

Thanksgiving week is the start of the sprint to the end of the NFL's regular season. And while there are players who know their teams don't have much to play for between now and then, there are plenty more who have quite a bit riding on what happens over the rest of the 2026 campaign.

Those stakes can be different things. For some, it's money, especially for young players on rookie deals who haven't yet signed a potentially lucrative second contract. For others, it's opportunity. There are rotational players who want to establish themselves as starters and veterans hanging on who want to stick in the starting lineup for another season.

Subscribe: 'The Bill Barnwell Show'

I'll take a look at 11 of those players who have the most to gain or lose over the remainder of the season, inspired by what they did in Week 11 and what's to come over the rest of the year.

Jump to:

Cousins | Metcalf | Pickens

McCarthy | Lassiter | Rice

Branch | Shough | Andrews

Watson | Van Ness

Well, the honeymoon is over. Last week, Vikings fans who had witnessed two months of Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz struggling to move the ball welcomed Cousins back with open arms, and despite a few hiccups, the good outweighed the bad. Cousins threw for 207 yards and two touchdowns in a comfortable victory over the rival Packers.

On Sunday in what amounted to a de facto home game for the 49ers in Mexico City, the magic dissipated. A great outing from Cousins likely wouldn't have made the difference on a day when the vaunted Vikings defense allowed the 49ers to score touchdowns on three of their first four drives in a 35-10 loss, but coach Kevin O'Connell might have hoped to find out.

Instead, playing a pass defense that Dak Prescott and the Cowboys picked apart last week, the Vikings struggled. Cousins went 26-of-38 for 235 yards with a brutal pick-six on an underneath pass that Ji'Ayir Brown jumped and returned to the house without even needing to break stride. After a touchdown on their second drive of the game and a field goal on their third, the Vikings didn't score again the rest of the way, with Justin Jefferson losing a fumble and two fourth-quarter drives failing on downs.

Cousins bears the brunt of the blame for the interception, and I suspect he'll wish he played better. But the most notable clip of this game from a Vikings perspective will probably be Cousins shouting at his offensive linemen on the sideline; he was knocked down seven times in the loss. And the issues that plagued Minnesota during the collective stints of Murray and Wentz at quarterback are likely to create problems for it against good teams moving forward.

Again, they couldn't run the ball. Aaron Jones Sr. had a physically impressive finish to his touchdown run, but the Vikings turned 21 carries into 69 yards and five first downs. Jordan Mason had a 16-yard carry, but it came against San Francisco's backups in the fourth quarter with Wentz on the field. The run game was mostly hopeless with Cousins out there.

An absent run game and a trailing game script takes Cousins away from play-action, which is where he has been at his best as a pro, 2026 included. The Raiders couldn't run the ball, either, but Klint Kubiak is excellent at creating throws for his quarterback with play-fakes, run game be damned. Before his trade to the Vikings, Cousins was third in the NFL in QBR when using play-action and 14th in the league when he was dropping back as a pure passer. Seven of Cousins' eight interceptions with the Raiders came in those pure dropback situations.

On Sunday, Cousins was effective using play-action, going 7-of-12 for 91 yards, averaging 7.6 yards per throw. Without it? He went 19-of-26 for 144 yards, averaging 5.5 yards per attempt. That included the pick-six, too. With nothing threatening Brown downfield or any sort of run fake to throw off his read, the 49ers safety was able to come from the backside of the play and poach Cousins' attempted slant to Brown, all but deciding the contest late in the first half.

Cousins has made more than $333 million in his career and has a minimum of another $10 million on the way in 2027. While many players on this list might have significant money riding on their performance over the rest of this season, that's probably not as important for Cousins. What might matter, though, is opportunity. If Cousins thrives in his second stint with the Vikings, O'Connell & Co. will likely bring him back as their starter in 2027, especially given the regrets the organization has about letting everyone from Cousins to Sam Darnold to Daniel Jones (and now potentially J.J. McCarthy) walk out the door in years past. And even if the Vikings decide to go in a different direction, a successful second half from Cousins likely would earn the 38-year-old a starting opportunity somewhere else next season.

play 2:28 Stephen A.: The 49ers ramrodded the Vikings

There's still plenty of time for Cousins to get things right, and there won't be many teams capable of getting a multi-touchdown lead on Brian Flores' defense over the rest of the season. After mostly unbridled enthusiasm from all sides about Cousins returning to the Vikings, though, the blowout loss was the coming-back-to-Earth moment for everyone involved.

Let's start with two wideouts who were essentially part of a multi-deal trade of sorts. The Steelers didn't want to re-sign Pickens, who was one year from unrestricted free agency, and traded him to the Cowboys in 2025 for a third-round pick. That third-rounder became Drew Allar, who is playing behind Aaron Rodgers at quarterback. The Steelers filled their need for a top wideout by sending a second-rounder to the Seahawks for Metcalf. The Seahawks used that pick to move up and select a cornerstone safety in Nick Emmanwori.

This sure looks like a three-team trade where two teams won and the Steelers lost. And it's not ideal to see your top wideout finish the day with as many receiving yards as personal foul penalties, but that was the Steelers' situation Sunday. In a frustrating loss to the Eagles, Metcalf caught just one pass on four targets for 2 yards before being ejected late in the third quarter for attempting to poke cornerback Cooper DeJean in the eye. Rodgers dropped back 53 times and was sacked five times, but he spent most of the day targeting rookies Germie Bernard and Max Hurleman.

This was probably rock-bottom for Metcalf's very disappointing tenure in Pittsburgh. In addition to trading that second-round pick to the Seahawks for Metcalf, the Steelers gave their new wideout a four-year, $132 million extension. (Emmanwori will make less than $12 million combined over his four-year deal in Seattle.) Metcalf racked up a career-low 850 yards in his first season with the Steelers before a late-season suspension after getting into an altercation with a fan; he had just two catches in last season's playoff loss to the Texans.

Though Rodgers was optimistic about the blossoming connection with his training camp roommate this summer, Metcalf has looked even more detached from the offense this season. He's on pace to finish with just 738 receiving yards and three touchdowns, both of which would be career lows. His 1.3 yards per route run is also a career low, down from his 1.9 YPRR in Seattle and 1.8 YPRR a year ago.

At his best, Metcalf has shown the ability to win downfield and overwhelm smaller defensive backs in contested-catch situations. Rodgers didn't make that throw very often in 2025, as Metcalf was targeted just 14 times on deep shots all season. Seven of those throws came in two games, suggesting that the Steelers had it as a priority heading into the game a couple of times and then forgot about getting Metcalf the football for multiple weeks.

With Mike McCarthy in the fold in 2026, Rodgers has targeted Metcalf downfield more often, but it hasn't been effective. Metcalf has just five catches on 22 deep shots this season, and that is nearly half of the league's completion rate (39.2%) on those throws. On Sunday, Metcalf was blanketed on both of his deep shots, which occurred with the Steelers on the cusp of the red zone, by star Eagles cornerback Quinyon Mitchell.

Against the Browns earlier this season, Metcalf got open on a blown coverage for what should have been a 68-yard touchdown, but Rodgers' throw brought Metcalf to a complete stop, at which point the veteran wideout dropped the ball into Denzel Ward's hands for an interception. It didn't matter much in a Steelers blowout, but it was one of the worst reps of the year for the Pittsburgh offense, a unit not known for its aesthetic beauty.

If we assume Allar (or another inexperienced quarterback) takes over for Rodgers after the season, you could argue that the Steelers should want to surround their new quarterback with as many useful playmakers as possible. With Rico Dowdle and Jaylen Warren at running back, Bernard and Michael Pittman Jr. at wide receiver, and Pat Freiermuth and Darnell Washington at tight end, the Steelers should have a solid starting group of backs and pass catchers to go with a young, promising offensive line.

In the world the Steelers imagined when they traded for the two-time Pro Bowl wideout, Metcalf would be the No. 1 receiver who puts all of those pieces into favorable roles as secondary and tertiary options. But in this world, he is playing like a very expensive second or third wideout. And crucially, he's owed $26.5 million in cash next year, none of which is guaranteed.

Though Metcalf would appeal to teams as a potential cap casualty, it's tough to imagine the veteran wideout receiving that sort of salary if he hits free agency. Getting back to even his 2025 level of play might be enough to earn Metcalf another season on this contract, either from the Steelers or with a trade to another organization. It seems like a fresh start might be the best thing for all involved.

A fresh start helped kick Pickens' career into high gear, as the mercurial wideout produced a career year in 2025 after leaving the Steelers to join a pass-happy offense in Dallas. And though he was briefly benched for a game last year after missing the team's bus, he has generally been on the straight and narrow after joining the Cowboys. Though Metcalf was ejected from the loss to the Eagles, Pickens racked up seven catches for 102 yards and a touchdown in a 51-30 win over the Titans.

It's admittedly a little easier to score on a bereft Titans defense, but since the start of 2025, Pickens is 13th among wideouts in yards per route run and eighth in ESPN's receiver score. He was a massive bargain for the Cowboys last season, when Pickens made $3.7 million in the final year of his rookie deal. He has lived up to expectations on the franchise tag in 2026, too, making $27.3 million.

A second franchise tag for Pickens in 2027 would pay the 25-year-old $32.8 million, which could still be reasonable, considering the top of the wide receiver market is averaging north of $42 million per year. For the Cowboys, though, that might be difficult to justify given how much they're paying the other key players on their roster. Dak Prescott, Quinnen Williams and CeeDee Lamb are already making nearly $130 million per year combined on their three contracts. With Jerry Jones dreaming of a competent defense, would the Cowboys really budget another $33 million to their offense without securing a long-term commitment?

play 0:16 Dak Prescott increases Cowboys' lead with a TD pass to George Pickens

Pickens might be the rare legit No. 1 wideout in his prime to hit unrestricted free agency. And though there might have been teams eager to commit to Pickens a year ago after one significant season, a second Pro Bowl-caliber campaign might encourage previously skeptical organizations to make a more substantial investment. Pickens, who has 247 receiving yards and four touchdowns over the past two weeks, can go a long way to locking up that massive deal by keeping this up over the rest of the season.

It has gone better than I think anyone could have hoped. After trading for McCarthy in late September, the Giants gave him time in the second half of a loss to the Saints, with McCarthy throwing for 243 yards in what was mostly garbage time. That was enough to earn McCarthy the starting job for the following week's game against the Texans.

McCarthy won that game and has gone 3-1 as the starter, coming within a first down or two against the Commanders to begin his Giants career 4-0. After four starts, McCarthy has been solid under center. His 62.8 Total QBR since entering the lineup ranks 14th in the league. He has averaged 8.8 yards per attempt over that span while attacking teams downfield, averaging more than 10 air yards per throw, the most of any quarterback in the league.

After committing numerous negative plays for most of his time as the Vikings starter, McCarthy has toned down those problems so far with the Giants. His sack rate is still worse than league average at 7.0%, but that's down from 10% during his lone healthy-ish season in Minnesota. McCarthy has thrown only two interceptions in five games, and though he's lucky to have gotten away with at least one or two would-be picks that weren't caught, he has done a better job of protecting the football with the Giants so far.

Sunday was almost the polar opposite of the sort of game McCarthy has played over the previous month. Facing a Jaguars team that created consistent pressure, McCarthy didn't create much as a passer, but he kept the Giants alive by avoiding negative plays. Though he averaged only 4.6 yards per throw, he didn't throw any interceptions and was sacked only once. He ran four times for 38 yards, including a 22-yard scramble that set up a Malik Nabers touchdown. Another long McCarthy scramble was called back for holding on a day when the referees seemed to dominate the proceedings.

I'm not sure we've learned whether McCarthy will become a great quarterback. The sack rate is still too high. He's inconsistent and still struggles with his accuracy; he has a below-average completion percentage over expectation (CPOE) despite a better-than-expected drop rate, per NFL Next Gen Stats. The deep-passing emphasis is at least partially a product of the Giants structuring the offense to keep McCarthy from putting the ball in danger.

After a month, though, it is clear that he's at least qualified to be on an NFL roster, something that didn't seem to be the case after his disastrous 2025 season in Minnesota. And that will create a very interesting quandary for McCarthy and the Giants. Trading for McCarthy was a logical move for the Giants, who had hopes of competing this year, and at 6-3-1, they've been vindicated for that choice. Even if the Giants miss the postseason, shipping a fifth-round pick will look like a smart move for general manager Joe Schoen.

What happens when Jaxson Dart is healthy? The Giants are likely more committed to their 2025 first-round pick than to McCarthy, who won't want to spend the rest of his rookie contract sitting behind Dart. After this season, the Giants also have to decide whether to pick up McCarthy's fifth-year option, which would guarantee the 23-year-old $25.7 million in 2028. Both quarterbacks have flaws, and given their history, both are pretty significant injury risks.

The simplest solution might be a competition next offseason, but McCarthy should have some ability to influence the proceedings. If McCarthy continues to play well and the Giants continue to win, it'll be tough to take the job from the new starter. If the Giants really are committed to Dart and see him as a franchise quarterback in 2027, McCarthy would suddenly have some more significant trade value for teams that might see him as a starter in the short- or long-term.

Lassiter entered 2026 as one of the finer young cornerbacks in the NFL. Coming off a Pro Bowl appearance in his second season, Lassiter had earned a reputation as a solid cover cornerback who made a significant contribution with his physicality and tackling. He started Week 1 against the Bills by coming up with a fourth-down stop on Josh Allen on a designed run. And when Allen tossed up a prayer into coverage with 1:48 to go, Lassiter settled under what should have been the game-ending interception.

But he dropped it. On the next play, Lassiter allowed the winning touchdown on a deep post to Joshua Palmer.

I'm not sure Lassiter has really recovered from it. He has looked overwhelmed by teams that have challenged him vertically, with George Pickens, Parker Washington and Malik Nabers beating him downfield for big plays this season. The Texans moved Lassiter into the slot without much luck. He has also committed nine penalties for 95 yards, including three pass interference calls. Lassiter had just 10 penalties over his first two years combined.

His struggles might be a microcosm of the broader and stunning decline of the Texans' defense, which came into the season with a reputation as one of the best in football. The issues extend beyond Lassiter. The defense hasn't exerted the same level of physicality. It has made sloppy mistakes with tackling, and players have taken poor angles to ball carriers. Even as recently as the Week 10 loss to the Browns, the Texans' coverage defenders repeatedly lined up at the same depth in the secondary, allowing a Cleveland offense that relies heavily on rub routes to create easy picks for completions and big plays.
