I have no doubt that everyone will recognize its significance. This is no small matter, particularly given that the investigating judges had initially dismissed the racist dimension of the case.”

Rap artist Stomy Bugsy said “this is a victory for all victims. If it can help curb, reduce and ultimately put an end to this kind of police misconduct and abuse, then it is a victory.”

World.title: Blacklisted Chinese universities procured Nvidia chips, records show
World.content:
At least six Chinese universities blacklisted by the US government have reported purchasing restricted Nvidia computer chips in recent years, a CNN review of business records found – highlighting US difficulties in controlling access to the in-demand technology.

Two of those universities known for their ties to the Chinese military establishment reported buying the high-powered chips just in the last few months.

The number of universities involved and full scope of their Nvidia purchases have not been previously reported.

The purchases, made through obscure sellers in China, were for relatively small amounts of older chips, not the industrial, cutting-edge computing technology that researchers fear could enable China to overtake the US in the artificial intelligence race.

Still, they show how widely available restricted Nvidia chips remain inside China, and how difficult it is for the US to block the sale of the chips even to some of the most high-risk entities – a particularly sensitive concern following allegations linking Nvidia’s CEO to a potential Chinese intelligence asset.

“Once these chips are in China, it’s very hard for anyone to be able to stop their sale,” said Kate Koren, a former US export control official who now serves as a research director at the Center for Strategic and International Studies. “We know it happens, and it’s very difficult to stop.”

The issue is likely to be a major talking point in this week’s high-stakes meeting between President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping as the White House moves to close loopholes that have allowed sensitive, AI-powering computer chips into China.

Concerns spiked over Chinese access to the technology as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week following the revelation he had a romantic relationship with a woman whose former company is suspected of helping smuggle chips into the country.

President Donald Trump greets Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday. Iori Sagisawa/China Pool/Getty Images Jensen Huang, pictured in London in October, resigned as CEO of Nvidia last week after admitting to a marital affair. Jose Sarmento Matos/Bloomberg/Getty Images

Speaking to reporters last week, Mao Ning, a spokeswoman for China’s Foreign Ministry, said Beijing rejects US claims that restrictions on high-powered chips are necessary for US national security.

“China firmly opposes the US overstretching the concept of national security and formulating various types of discriminatory lists to go after Chinese institutions,” she said.

CNN’s review was based on procurement documents from Chinese universities collected in a commercial database. Under Chinese regulations, universities and other public entities are required to publish notices on their websites when they make certain purchases.

Among the nearly 300 records CNN obtained and examined, most show purchases of Nvidia technology under US export control, such as A100, A800, H100, H200, and H800 chips. Among the 90 buyers CNN examined, nearly 80% are universities, and nearly 14% are research institutes, while government agencies also bought some Nvidia chips.

CNN’s review excluded purchases of computing power from overseas data centers – one of the loopholes that the Trump administration moved to close this week with new regulations.

Most notable, experts said, was a procurement notice from September that Harbin Institute of Technology had purchased an A100 chip for about $7,000, and two notices in September and October that Northwestern Polytechnical University had bought four H200 chips for a total of about $240,000.

An aerial view of Harbin Institute of Technology in Harbin, China, in May 2021. VCG/Getty Images The campus of Northwestern Polytechnical University in Xi’an, China, in September 2022. CFOTO/Future Publishing/Getty Images

Both universities are part of a grouping known in China as the “Seven Sons of National Defense” because of their connections to China’s People’s Liberation Army.

“Those are the universities that have tight linkages to the Chinese military,” said Gregory Allen, the CEO of Decision Tree Research, a firm focusing on tech and geopolitical issues. “If you’re talking about who’s going to be investing in military AI capabilities in China, a lot of that would start at these universities.”

The purchase notices had scant details about the supply chains that took the chips from Nvidia to the universities, or how the chips may be used there. Both universities reported buying the chips not from Nvidia itself or a major supplier, but from little-known firms in China. Reuters previously reported on one of the Northwestern purchases.

Under a new policy put in place last year after lobbying from Nvidia and Huang, the US government does allow the tech giant to sell the less powerful H200 chip to entities in China on a case-by-case basis – but those sales come with strict requirements related to reporting the end user of the chips. Experts said US officials were highly unlikely to approve sales that would go to a blacklisted university.

Sales of the A100 chip to China are still banned – but before the US government put restrictions in place in 2022, the hardware was widely sold there.

“It’s possible those were coming from stockpiles there before the controls were in place,” said Koren, because “there was a fairly large window of time” when the chips weren’t controlled under US export law.

A third university that’s part of the “Seven Sons” group, Beihang University in Beijing, also reported making more than a dozen purchases of Nvidia chips between 2022 and 2024, according to the records, mostly buying A100 and A800 chips. The university has been blacklisted by the US since 2001.

Signage for Beihang University, also known as Beijing University of Aeronautics and Astronautics, on a building at its Shenzhen campus in September 2026. Cheng Xin/Getty Images

In addition to the universities with tighter military ties, three other universities on the US government’s “Entity List,” a blacklist of organizations that are banned from receiving shipments of controlled items without approval from federal officials, also reported purchases of high-end Nvidia chips in recent years.

The records CNN obtained are likely incomplete because while public institutes in China are required to publicize procurement decisions, many only publish the notices locally or internally or take them down quickly. The commercial aggregator CNN used also doesn’t include all notices published by Chinese institutions.

CNN was not able to verify whether the Nvidia hardware was delivered in each case described in the notices.

US regulations require Nvidia and other chip suppliers to determine the end user for chips they sell abroad, and to take various measures to avoid the chips getting into China.

It’s unclear how the universities’ suppliers acquired the chips. But in general, smuggling operations for these chips can be based on “very sophisticated shell companies, with shipments going from other countries to China, multiple hops, multiple currency changes, and falsified documents that make it much harder to detect,” Koren said.

Government officials trying to disrupt this pipeline are facing a “constant” struggle to enforce bans, she said, “but rationally you have to know that despite your best efforts, some will get through.”

World.title: Republicans mulling deal that would fund military, but limit operations in Iran
World.content:
In the final days of the GOP’s complete power in Washington, there’s a real chance the Pentagon might not get another dollar this year – unless Republican lawmakers strike a deal with Democrats to rein in Trump’s ability to attack Iran.

Top Senate Democrats and Republicans are engaged in high-stakes talks about cutting off funding for future offensive operations in the Iran war in exchange for replenishing the tens of billions that the Department of Defense has said is urgently needed, according to multiple lawmakers and aides in both parties.

The push faces enormous obstacles in a bitterly divided Congress, with Republicans largely wary of crossing President Donald Trump on the war – even after their midterm losses – and emboldened Democrats seeking big restrictions on his power.

But if no deal is reached, the Pentagon has almost no other chance of getting the money this year. And that means they’d have to ask Democrats for the money next year — an even tougher task, when every House Democrat voted to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth earlier this month.

“I think there’s a way for Democrats to make their point without tying the hands of the commander in chief and the defense of our country,” Senate Armed Services Chairman Roger Wicker told CNN on Friday when asked about the emerging proposal.

Talks are in the early stages, and there are still major questions about exactly what any restrictions would look like, and what else could be included, such as funding for Ukraine’s war against Russia. Sources in both parties have said it’s not yet clear if there’s a way for Republicans to accept Democrats’ demands without hampering the US military’s ability to keep troops safe – and without infuriating Trump.

“I think there is a room for negotiation there, and it would have to be something that the administration would find acceptable, too,” said GOP Sen. John Hoeven of North Dakota, who is in talks with both Democrats and the White House on the matter. “But again, we want to deal, we want to end the conflict from a position of strength, and we need to fund the military.”

Some Senate Democrats hope they can convince Trump and GOP leaders to put a proposal into next month’s stopgap funding bill. If that did not pass, it would mean a debilitating shutdown at a time when Republicans still control all of Washington.

US carriers Theodore Roosevelt and George Washington sailing at a location given as Arabian Sea, in this screen grab obtained from a video released on November 17. US Central Command/Handout/Reuters

But several Republicans said they fear the talks could shift yet again if and when Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer wins a contested leadership election on December 1. They believe the looming contest has led him to strike such a firm posture on defunding the Iran war. (Several noted that House Democrats have privately struck a different tone, very eager to avoid a shutdown and suggesting they’re willing to punt the Iran issue to 2027, according to multiple sources in both parties.)

Still, many Republicans believe they have no real options, other than striking a deal with Democrats on next month’s funding bill, since they don’t have the votes to do it on a party-line basis.

At least one Republican, Sen. Josh Hawley of Missouri, told CNN on Friday he is open to supporting a compromise.

More military funding has been a key priority for the White House. Top Pentagon officials have spent months lobbying Congress for more money in the middle of a war with Iran — including personal calls from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, countless closed-door briefings and treks to Camp David.

Privately, though, GOP lawmakers and aides say that Pentagon officials have hurt their own chances by repeatedly misleading lawmakers about the true need for the funds. Defense officials have sent over four separate funding requests — including one just this week — that have made it difficult to discern the most urgent priorities, according to multiple people familiar with the discussions.

“I can add up four numbers, so don’t think you’re tricking me by dividing it into different buckets, and so that is a frustration,” lamented Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia, who is on the Armed Services Committee, about the various funding requests.

CNN has reached out to the Defense Department for comment.

The administration has been making a stronger case in recent days, according to sources. Senate Republicans heard a strong pitch from Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg at a closed-door meeting this week, and House Republicans are expected to hear from him in the coming days.

Kaine, who’s been a vocal advocate of ending the war while supporting US troops, has made clear that Democrats are not opposed to all of the Pentagon’s funding requests. But he also doesn’t consider most of them to be urgent.

“Most of what they’re seeking is important and needed, but not needed tomorrow. Because like munitions replacement, you put money in, you’re not going to get to munitions for some time. So this isn’t necessarily about tomorrow,” Kaine said. “Some of those priorities in the $350 [billion request] are needed, and you would find an openness to some of our other side.”

World.title: The Ukraine-Russia war is seeping out across Europe and there are two reasons it will get worse
World.content:
Rather than peace, there is stark escalation.

That is the product of over six weeks of shuttling diplomacy, posturing, betrayal of Ukraine’s ability to defend itself, Russian intransigence and the US’ failed reframing of the process as about European security and participation.

Put aside the near-zero public results from the Shenzhen trilateral meeting between Russia, China and the US, and consider the violence of the past week alone.

Russia launched Friday what Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky called the most intense attack of the year – a six-hour crescendo of drones and missiles, after weeks of striking Kyiv’s bridges, and power infrastructure across the country. Dozens have died, and swaths of the country and capital are often in blackout.

Ukraine struck Vladimir Putin’s prized bridge to occupied Crimea three times, in the days around the trilateral. And compounding that display of technical prowess, Kyiv’s drones apparently struck both a Russian-military linked ship this weekend off the coast of Kaliningrad, and then Russian naval assets near the port of Benghazi, on the Libyan coast.

Damage to the Kerch Bridge seen in a satellite image.

Where Moscow parades its brutal, relentless intensity, Kyiv strikes back with unexpected reach and precision.

Widening theater of conflict

The geography of Ukrainian strikes is important. Kaliningrad is a Russian enclave between Lithuania and Poland , hitherto considered safe – an odd legacy of the Soviet era, territory marooned in the heart of some of NATO’s most anti-Russian members.

The apparent strike against a Russian-linked military ship – the Sparta 2, one of their notorious military-cargo Sparta fleet – was likely by Ukraine, and either involved a drone launched from another ship, or one flying through Russian territory to the Baltic Sea. Inevitably Russia chose to blame a third option – that Lithuania permitted the drone to fly through its airspace – NATO territory. The accusation feeds the long-standing fiction that Russia is at war with all of NATO. It also raises further the possibility of more Russian malfeasance and sabotage around the Baltics , and the risks of escalation with NATO this carries.

The Libya strikes – hitting a Russian naval ship and cargo vessel off the coast of Benghazi, according to Zelensky – further showcases the ability of Kyiv’s drones to embarrass the Kremlin, which had over the last decade paraded its might in Africa, yet whose ships now bring great risk of damage in whichever Mediterranean ports they may dock.

The uptick in violence – and where it has spread – was unthinkable five years ago; from being contained inside Ukrainian territory, it spread to Russia in 2024, then to NATO’s eastern borders, with Russia-linked sabotage across the military alliance. The frog is truly boiling, as this war is slowly spreading across the continent, and the months ahead look perilous for two reasons.

What a Democratic Congress means for Ukraine

Firstly: the Kremlin has a small window before Capitol Hill is taken over by pro-Ukrainian Democrats, and everything from past conduct, to current funding – from Elon Musk to minor Pentagon officials – falls under their scrutiny, if not regulation. The peculiar sympathies with which Donald Trump acts in Russia’s favor will likely be reeled in, in sheer practical terms, and the focus of his inner coterie may turn more to survival under a looming Democratic White House, than their personal priorities when dealing with Putin’s war of choice.

Moscow has palpably tried to set the negotiation clock backward, through persuading the US to reframe the talks as about wider “European security infrastructure.” This is something Moscow has long sought, a chance to rewrite the Ukraine conflict as the symptom of NATO’s enlargement eastward.

Putin himself has fortified his demands, his most recent appearance in Shenzhen stating Russia had no interest in negotiating a ceasefire – the only real immediate deliverable for diplomacy now. Then he added if the Europeans wanted to join the talks on a technical level (as the US president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner has said the Kremlin had consented to) they should travel to Moscow to make the case to him, and then he’ll think about it.

Russian President Vladimir Putin speaks at a press conference in Shenzhen, Guangdong province, China on November 19. Maxim Shemetov/Reuters

Putin has clearly determined his best negotiating stance is to rip up what’s in front of him, step many paces back , and make any possibility of compromise seem remote.

There is a gruesome logic to this: reality is partially on Russia’s side on the battlefield. Capturing the remainder of the Donbas is openly Putin’s main war goal. And while Ukraine has kept Russia from occupying a Donbas town like Kostyantynivka for whole two years, neighboring Kramatorsk and Slavyansk are close to uninhabitable, as Russian drone and airstrikes force civilians out and streets into rubble, ready for the months of gruesome urban warfare ahead. Putin said in Shenzhen that Ukraine’s hold over this remaining 10% of Donbas may slowly become untenable. The horrific cost of Putin’s slow grind forwards, of at least 40,000 dead and injured a month, does come with some tiny results – almost absurd as they are, given the casualties.

Perhaps this is the short-term objective the Kremlin sees: make the remainder of Donbas rubble, and then accept a political settlement later, where you can claim victory over the ruins.

Disagreement over reality hinders diplomacy

But it is the longer term danger that poses the greatest risk to diplomacy. Currently, few of the words spoken by either side relate to each other’s reality. European participation in future multilateral peace summits? Kushner says it’ll happen, the Kremlin says it won’t yet. Territorially, Putin says he controls Kostyantynivka, when he palpably does not. He said Thursday Ukraine started the war, when it did not.

Both sides’ demands seem to be moving away from each other. The Kremlin appears to want NATO to fall back and westward, according to some reporting. In turn, some reports suggest Ukraine’s membership of the alliance has even been floated by the US. These are two incompatible red lines.

This photograph shows birds flying past a partially collapsed building in Dymer, Kyiv region, on Monday following an overnight Russian air strike. Vladyslav Musiienko/AFP/Getty Images

The two sides’ parallel realities are getting further apart, rather than converging on a possible path forward. That is entirely Russia’s intention, and a textbook example of how they use diplomacy to advance their military objectives. But the impact is to create a fictional universe for diplomacy, in which a future restraint of reality on the battlefield becomes elusive. In short: you can’t expect nonsense talks to ever stop the real business of killing.

This is where the last year’s mess of failed talks, cosying up to Putin, belittling and bullying Ukraine, European panic and Russian savagery has led the biggest conflict in Europe since the 1940s. A place where Ukrainian drones seem to hit anywhere there’s a Russian ship. Where Russian drones, missiles and helicopters stray monthly into NATO territory without fear of a military retaliation. And where the peace process seems merely a process to please Trump, devoid of actual peace. It is a bleak moment whose only end in sight is the unsettling and even more destabilising collapse of either side.

World.title: Foreign Minister inspects Swiss-funded water project in Upper Egypt
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty on Sunday, November 22, 2026, inspected the Drinking Water Management Programme in Upper Egypt in Aswan Governorate to review implementation progress and assess development projects funded by international partners.

The visit took place on the sidelines of Abdelatty’s participation in the sixth edition of the Aswan Forum for Sustainable Peace and Development.

The project is funded by the Swiss Confederation under the Egyptian-Swiss development cooperation framework and implemented by the Ministry of Housing, Utilities and Urban Communities.

World.title: Egypt, Iraq FMs discuss bilateral ties ahead of Iraqi PM’s Cairo visit
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptian Expatriates Badr Abdelatty and his Iraqi counterpart Fuad Hussein discussed bilateral cooperation and regional developments, ahead of the Iraqi prime minister’s scheduled visit to Cairo on Monday.

The meeting took place on the sidelines of the sixth Aswan Forum for Sustainable Peace and Development.

Foreign Ministry Spokesperson Nader Zaki said Abdelatty expressed Egypt’s keenness to bolster economic, trade and investment cooperation with Iraq.

The two ministers discussed preparations for the Iraqi prime minister’s visit to Cairo on November 23 and the fourth session of the Egyptian-Iraqi Joint Higher Committee.

The ministers also exchanged views on developments as well as challenges to security and stability in the region.

Both sides called for political and diplomatic solutions to regional crises and agreed to continue consultations on issues of mutual concern.

World.title: COP31 Ends Without Political Deal as Disputes Over Fossil Fuels and Finance Persist
World.content:
Countries adopted decisions on adaptation and just transition in Antalya, but failed to agree on the conference’s overarching political outcome. Photo: UNFCCC

Summary

COP31 ended without agreement on the proposed Antalya Pact after disagreements over fossil fuels, climate finance and the direction of global climate action.

Governments adopted decisions on adaptation and just transition, but failed to agree on the Mitigation Work Programme and several other proposals.

Developing countries left Antalya without a clear pathway for delivering adaptation finance, while attention turns to Ethiopia’s hosting of COP32 in 2027.

By Aria Deemie

The United Nations climate conference in Antalya, Türkiye, ended on Sunday without agreement on its proposed overarching political deal, after nearly two extra days of negotiations exposed deep divisions over fossil fuels, climate finance and how governments should respond to rising global temperatures.



“I am deeply disappointed that COP31 has ended without consensus on an overarching outcome,” United Nations Secretary-General António Guterres said in a statement following the conference.

“There may be no consensus in the negotiating room. There is no ambiguity in the science.”

The failure to adopt the proposed Antalya Pact left the conference without a common political statement addressing some of the most contested questions in climate action. But it did not mean all negotiations failed. Governments adopted separate decisions on issues including the Global Goal on Adaptation and the Just Transition Work Programme , while other proposals, including the Mitigation Work Programme , did not secure agreement.

The proposed Antalya Pact consisted of two Presidency-led decisions, one under the United Nations climate convention and another under the Paris Agreement. Together, they were intended to provide an overarching political response to the climate crisis and set direction for the next phase of international climate action.



But countries could not agree on the language. A central dispute was whether the decisions should explicitly address the transition away from fossil fuels, the main source of greenhouse gas emissions. Countries also disagreed over the strength of the language on climate action and whether the proposed text adequately addressed the financing needs of developing countries.

The breakdown is not without precedent. At COP6 in The Hague, Netherlands, in November 2000, negotiations also collapsed after countries failed to resolve disputes over emissions reductions, carbon sinks, compliance and financial support for developing nations. Conference president Jan Pronk suspended the talks without an agreement. Negotiations resumed in Bonn the following year, where countries eventually reached a compromise.

The disputes were different, but both conferences exposed the difficulty of reaching consensus when countries have competing priorities over climate action, financing and responsibility.

At COP31, the European Union found itself at the center of a dispute over the conference’s political outcome, this time insisting that any agreement must explicitly address fossil fuels. Speaking on behalf of the bloc, Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, said: “We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.”

The EU’s position, however, drew criticism from climate campaigners who accused the bloc of applying pressure on fossil-fuel language while resisting financing commitments needed by developing countries. Mohamed Adow, director of Power Shift Africa, said the EU could not distance itself from the outcome of negotiations in which it had also played a role.

“Europe’s hypocrisy is staggering. Its governments demand fossil fuel roadmaps from others while expanding fossil fuels themselves and blocking the finance poorer countries need to make the transition,” Adow said in a response to the EU’s rejection of the final text.

Russia, meanwhile, opposed language on fossil fuels, warning that reducing supply faster than demand could cause price shocks and energy shortages. Saudi Arabia argued that all proposed solutions should remain available. The disagreement left governments unable to reach the consensus required to adopt the two decisions.

The dispute was not simply about whether fossil fuels should be mentioned. It was also about whether the conference would reaffirm commitments made at previous summits or weaken them through a new political text. More than 130 countries had called for stronger action on transitioning away from fossil fuels, following the commitment reached at COP28 in Dubai. The proposed Antalya Pact did not include that language, prompting objections from countries that said the text fell short of what science and previous agreements required.

Vanuatu’s delegation said the proposed decision was silent on “fossil fuels, the principal driver of the climate crisis.” It also warned: “Consensus must never come at the expense of our people’s survival, sovereignty and future generations.”

The conference nevertheless produced decisions in areas where governments were able to reach agreement. One of the most significant was the Global Goal on Adaptation, which seeks to measure whether countries are becoming better able to cope with the effects of climate change.

At COP30 in Brazil, countries agreed on 59 indicators intended to help track adaptation progress. But questions remained over how the indicators would be measured and whether countries had the technical capacity to use them. At COP31, governments agreed to establish a technical task force of national experts to refine the indicators and develop guidance for their use by October 2027.

The agreement is a step towards making adaptation progress more measurable, but it does not itself provide the money countries need to implement projects. That distinction is important for countries such as Liberia, where coastal erosion, flooding, extreme heat and pressure on agriculture require investments in infrastructure, public services and community protection.

An aerial view of flooding in Liberia after heavy rains left communities affected and families in need of food and other essential supplies. Photo:Mamadou Jallow/WFP.

Another decision was reached on the Just Transition Work Programme, which was extended for three years. The program provides a space for countries to discuss how the shift to lower-emission economies can protect workers, communities and people whose livelihoods depend on industries affected by climate policies.

However, governments did not settle the operational arrangements for the Just Transition Mechanism agreed at COP30. Disagreements over its governance and institutional arrangements meant those decisions were postponed until COP32 in 2027. The extension keeps discussions going, but countries have yet to agree on how the mechanism will provide practical support.

Other negotiations ended less successfully. Governments failed to reach agreement on the Mitigation Work Programme, which was due for renewal. The program provides a forum for countries to discuss ways to reduce greenhouse gas emissions. Russia and Saudi Arabia objected to the draft decision, leaving the program without an agreed continuation at COP31.

Draft decisions on response measures and the Global Environment Facility also failed to secure adoption. The closing-day negotiations report documented the rejection of these draft decisions, leaving several issues unresolved as countries prepare for the next round of negotiations.

Climate finance remained one of the most difficult issues, particularly for developing countries that need funding to prepare for climate impacts they have contributed relatively little to causing.

At COP30, countries had agreed to efforts to triple adaptation finance by 2035. But developing countries came to Antalya seeking clarity on how that increase would be measured and delivered, including a baseline for calculating progress, predictable funding and stronger accountability from developed countries.

The African Group of Negotiators had also pressed for finance that is concessional and grant-based, rather than loans that add to the debt burdens of countries already struggling to fund basic services.

“Ambition needs to be supported by ambitious levels of finance,” Debra-Lee Swanepoel, the African Group’s finance thematic lead, said during a November 19 briefing on the group’s priorities.

The proposed Antalya Pact included language on accelerating adaptation finance and addressing barriers such as high borrowing costs, limited fiscal space and unsustainable debt. But because the overarching decisions were not adopted, those proposals did not become agreed outcomes. The conference did not resolve developing countries’ demand for a clear pathway to deliver the adaptation-finance commitment.

The Climate Action Network, a global coalition of climate organizations, criticized the outcome, accusing wealthy countries of blocking measures intended to strengthen support for vulnerable nations.

“Simply recalling the COP30 commitment to triple adaptation finance means nothing without a baseline or delivery plan. It remains an empty promise,” said Pooja Dave, the network’s adaptation lead.

The network cited annual adaptation needs of $305 billion by 2035, rising to $420 billion when adjusted for inflation, and said the Adaptation Fund had raised barely $50 million against a $300 million annual target. In its statement on COP31 , the network said wealthy countries had obstructed measures that could have strengthened finance and accountability for climate action in developing countries.

Mohammed Kamal of the Global Alliance for Incinerator Alternatives, in an earlier interview , said the finance problem begins with the scale of the commitment itself. He argued that the $300 billion annual goal agreed at COP29 in Baku was far below the $1.3 trillion sought by African and other developing countries.

“Some African negotiators decided back then that it’s better to take something instead of nothing. And that’s quite problematic,” Kamal said.

He said the problem was not only the size of the target, but also how much of the money committed actually reaches projects and whether countries receive grants or loans. For countries such as Liberia, he argued, borrowing to protect forests, coastal communities and other resources can create repayment obligations for projects that do not generate income.

Kamal also questioned whether African countries were using their collective influence strongly enough in the negotiations. Although the continent has a common negotiating position through the African Group, he said governments needed stronger political coordination and should be more direct in challenging countries that fail to deliver promised support.

He offered a deliberately provocative example: African leaders could consider refusing to attend one future climate summit if their demands continued to be ignored.

“Imagine a COP where all 54 say we’re not joining the next COP. How would that be?” he said.

Kamal acknowledged that such a move would require political decisions beyond the conference itself, potentially through the African Union. His broader argument was that African governments should not continue attending the annual meetings without using their collective political weight to demand stronger outcomes.

The disappointment over the failed political deal was also expressed by Guterres, who called on developed countries to turn their adaptation-finance promises into concrete commitments.

“Put dates and dollars behind that pledge now. Lives depend on it,” he said, referring to the commitment to increase adaptation finance.

Simon Stiell, the United Nations climate change executive secretary, also acknowledged the failure to agree on the two Presidency-led decisions. But he cautioned against treating the entire conference as a failure.

“I share the deep disappointment of many: COP31 has been unable to agree on issues related to both Presidencies’ led decisions,” Stiell said in his closing remarks .

“At this COP, key negotiating decisions have been made including on a Just Transition. Fairness and inclusion in the climate fight is absolutely essential.”

He said the climate process needed to learn from the deadlock, adding that “consensus works best from the ground up,” with full transparency and time to listen to all views. He also pointed to progress outside the formal negotiations, including initiatives on electrification and resilience.

The conference ended after almost two days beyond its scheduled Friday closing, leaving governments with adopted decisions on adaptation and just transition, but unresolved disputes over fossil fuels, mitigation and the finance needed to implement climate commitments.

Attention now turns to Ethiopia, which will host COP32 in Addis Ababa in 2027. The country will inherit unresolved disputes over fossil fuels, climate finance and the implementation of commitments made at previous conferences.

Speaking at the closing plenary, Ethiopia’s Minister of Finance and Cop32 Chief Negotiator, Fitsum Assefa said the next summit would be an opportunity to rebuild cooperation despite the divisions exposed in Antalya.

“Today the world has been reminded that multilateralism requires determination,” she said.

“We are in difficult times but that difficulty is why COP matters most … The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change remains the place where every country has a voice and where we come together to confront that challenge.”

She promised that Addis Ababa would be a “COP of hope,” adding: “Hope that despite our differences we can still come together and have the most ambitious decision.”

This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership , a journalism fellowship organized by Internews’ Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

World.title: NaFAA Opens Fisheries Development Grants to Women Entrepreneurs
World.content:
Photo: Officials of NaFAA and implementing partners pose for a group photograph following the launch of the Liberian Women’s Sustainable Fisheries and Livelihoods Incubator.

Bushrod Island, Monrovia-The Government of Liberia has opened a US$680,000 grant facility for women-owned and women-led fisheries businesses across the country’s nine coastal counties, offering financial support ranging from US$5,000 to US$20,000 to help entrepreneurs expand their businesses and improve their livelihoods.

The initiative, known as the Liberian Women’s Sustainable Fisheries and Livelihoods Incubator (LWSFILI), was officially launched Wednesday, November 11, 2026, by the National Fisheries and Aquaculture Authority (NaFAA) in Monrovia. The application period runs from November 11 to November 25, 2026.

The 17-month programme is being implemented by NaFAA in partnership with the iCampus Liberia Consortium, with support from the OPEC Fund for International Development. It forms part of the broader Liberia Integrated Fisheries Sector Strengthening Project (LIFSSP).



Applications opened on November 11 and will close on November 25, 2026. The programme is expected to support approximately 6,200 women-led entrepreneurs and enterprises involved in fishing, fish processing, trading and other related activities.

In his brief remarks at the launch at NaFAA’s headquarters, Director General J. Cyrus Saygbe Sr. said the initiative was designed to address the financial challenges that prevent many women in the fisheries sector from growing their businesses.

He explained that many women work hard to sell fish but cannot expand because they lack the money to purchase sufficient quantities, improve packaging or introduce new products to meet customer demand.

Saygbe illustrated the situation with the story of a woman who regularly sold fish at the market and had established loyal customers but could not increase her business because of limited capital.



“At the end of each day, she went home having worked very hard, but her business remained at the same level. Two years, three years, four years, no growth, no progress,” he said.

“That woman represents thousands of our hardworking women and young women entrepreneurs across Liberia’s fisheries and aquaculture value chain. And that is why we are here today,” he added.

According to Saygbe, the government has listened to the concerns of women fishmongers and entrepreneurs and is responding through the new grant and business-support programme.

“The government of Liberia has heard your cry. And through the Liberian Women’s Sustainable Fisheries and Livelihoods Incubator Program, we are taking practical steps to respond to these concerns,” he said.

He explained that the programme would provide more than financial assistance. Beneficiaries would also receive business training, technical support, help with financial management, business planning, market access and business registration.

“This initiative is designed to do more than distribute money. It is about building businesses, unlocking opportunities, and creating a new generation of Liberian entrepreneurs,” Saygbe stated.

He encouraged women to submit innovative business proposals that could improve fish processing, packaging, storage and marketing instead of relying only on traditional fish-selling activities.

“We are not simply looking to finance the same traditional businesses we have always known. We are looking for innovation,” he said.

He identified fish oil production, fish powder, fish-based products, improved packaging, digital marketing, modern storage facilities and better transportation systems as areas that could create new business opportunities.

“We want to move simply from selling fish to building business around fish,” he added.

Saygbe said the government wants women to move from small-scale businesses into larger and more profitable enterprises that can create jobs and supply supermarkets, hotels, restaurants and other markets.

He, however, warned that beneficiaries must use the grants for the purposes stated in their approved business proposals.

“We will monitor you. We will track you. And if you use the grant funds for things that are not applicable, we will prosecute you,” he warned.

In a special remarks, Director of Research and Statistics and Project Manager of LIFSSP at NaFAA, Austin Saye said the initiative would provide women with greater opportunities to participate in the fisheries sector and improve their economic conditions.

“Today is more than the launch of a program, it is the launch of opportunity and inclusion and transformation for women across Liberia’s fisheries sector,” Saye said.

He disclosed that approximately 6,200 women-led entrepreneurs and enterprises were expected to benefit from the programme through business expansion, increased production, employment opportunities and improved household incomes.

Saye said the US$680,000 grant facility would help beneficiaries purchase equipment, improve fish-processing methods, establish storage facilities and strengthen transportation and other business operations.

He also said the programme recognizes that many women operate successful businesses without formal registration or extensive financial records.

“Potential should never be limited by paperwork,” he emphasized, explaining that the programme would consider business viability, commitment and potential impact in providing women with opportunities to access support.

Providing overview about the application process, Team Lead and Project Lead of the iCampus Liberia Consortium, Luther D. Jeke said applications were open to eligible women-owned and women-led enterprises operating in Bomi, Grand Cape Mount, Montserrado, Margibi, Grand Bassa, River Cess, Sinoe, Grand Kru and Maryland.

He said applicants must have operated their businesses for at least six months.

To qualify as a women-led enterprise, a business must have at least 51 percent women ownership, with women occupying at least 50 percent of management positions.

Jeke explained that applicants could request funding under three categories: Band A, ranging from US$5,000 to US$8,999; Band B, from US$9,000 to US$14,999; and Band C, from US$15,000 to US$20,000.

He said documentation requirements would depend on the amount requested and could include identification documents, evidence of business operations, sales records, financial projections, business plans and proof of matching contributions.

He encouraged interested women to obtain the official application form, carefully follow the instructions and submit their completed applications before the November 25 deadline.

Jeke also assured applicants that the selection process would be transparent and fair. He explained that field officers would assist applicants in completing and submitting forms but would not have the authority to reject or rank applications.

“Every completed form must be accepted and forwarded,” he said.

He added that NaFAA’s LIFSSP Project Implementation Unit would be responsible for determining eligibility, reviewing applications, conducting due diligence and selecting beneficiaries.

Also speaking at the launch, Assistant Commerce Minister for Small Business Administration Jekeh Forkoa Koiyan, representing Commerce Minister Stephen Maka-Yekerson, endorsed the initiative and described it as an important opportunity to strengthen women’s businesses and promote economic growth.

“For us at the Ministry of Commerce and Industry, empowering women economically goes beyond providing opportunity to participate in business. It means creating pathway for women to build sustainable enterprise, improve their competitiveness, access market, strengthen their business capacity, and contribute meaningfully to the national economic growth,” Koiyan said.

He encouraged eligible women-owned businesses, fisheries cooperatives and other enterprises to take advantage of the opportunity.

Koiyan urged NaFAA and its partners to ensure that the application and selection processes remained transparent, inclusive and based on merit.

He reaffirmed the Ministry of Commerce and Industry’s commitment to working with government institutions, development partners and the private sector to strengthen small businesses and promote women’s participation in Liberia’s economy.

The programme is expected to strengthen women’s participation in the fisheries sector, improve fish processing and marketing, create employment and increase income opportunities in coastal communities.

NaFAA has also established a call centre to provide information and respond to questions from prospective applicants. Interested women can call 6232 free of charge using any mobile network.

World.title: Inside the US$5.7 Billion Deal That Could Light Up and Link Up Liberia
World.content:
MONROVIA – For as long as most Liberians can remember, two problems have stood between this country and the prosperity its natural wealth promises: the lights go out, and the roads give way. A new agreement between the Government of Liberia and Bea Mountain Mining Corporation (BMMC) aims to fix both at once, on a scale the country has never attempted.

By Rodney D. Sieh

The Master Infrastructure Development Agreement (MIDA), valued at about US$5.7 billion, would build four power plants with 270 megawatts of generating capacity, three major transmission lines, a national grid upgrade and 14 road and bridge projects reaching nearly every region of the country.



After months of negotiations, the Inter-Ministerial Concessions Committee submitted the agreement to President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr. The formal signing is scheduled for Wednesday, November 25. The agreement then goes to the Legislature for ratification.

If it is delivered as designed, MIDA could be the most consequential development program since the end of the civil war. It would turn gold mined in Grand Cape Mount into electricity for homes, hospitals and factories, and into highways for farmers and traders.

More than doubling the nation’s power

The numbers explain the excitement. Liberia’s entire installed generating capacity stood at about 126 megawatts in 2024: 88 megawatts at the Mount Coffee Hydropower Plant and 38 megawatts at heavy fuel oil plants. A 20-megawatt solar park at Mount Coffee came online in June.



MIDA’s 270 megawatts would, on their own, more than double what the country has today. Officials have put national demand at roughly 400 megawatts. Only about a third of Liberians had access to electricity in 2023, according to World Bank data, with rural access below 10 percent.

The agreement provides for:

* Via River Hydropower Plant – 100 megawatts

* SP-3 Hydropower Plant on the St. Paul River – 100 megawatts

* SP-4 Hydropower Plant on the St. Paul River – 10 megawatts

* Biomass Power Plant near the Via dam – 60 megawatts

Hydropower would account for 210 megawatts. The biomass plant would diversify the sources feeding the grid, so the country is not betting everything on rainfall.

Ending the dry-season blackout

The deal’s most important feature may be the one that gets the least attention: storage. Mount Coffee loses more than three-quarters of its output every dry season, forcing the Liberia Electricity Corporation (LEC) to rely on imported power and diesel.

MIDA’s three planned reservoirs would hold a combined 10 billion cubic meters of water. Operators can store water when rivers run high during the rains and release it through the turbines when flows drop. That is how hydropower nations keep the lights on year-round.

Actual output will still depend on rainfall, river flows and how the reservoirs and plants are run. But for the first time, Liberia would have a buffer against the annual power crunch that shuts down businesses and frustrates households.

Taking power beyond Monrovia

Generating electricity is only half the job. MIDA also provides for the lines that carry it to the people who need it:

* Main Transmission Line – 150 kilometers, 300 MVA, connecting the new plants to the Mount Coffee substation

* Nimba Transmission Line – 150 kilometers, 100 MVA, from the Via plant to Nimba County, with a substation

* Bong Transmission Line – 5 kilometers, 60 MVA, serving Bong County, with a substation

* National Grid

* ⁠Reinforcement – US$230 million to upgrade substations, transformers and transmission across the grid

Nimba and Bong are two of the country’s busiest mining and farming counties. Reliable power there could help hospitals keep essential equipment running, help businesses cut costly interruptions and give investors a reason to set up outside the capital.

Roads as economic arteries

The second pillar is mobility. The flagship is the 146-kilometer Liberia Development Road, a highway corridor designed to link the power plants to key facility centers. A further US$1 billion is set aside for road networks across the country.

The list reads like a map of Liberia’s most stubborn bottlenecks: the Konia–Voinjama corridor in Lofa, the Saclepea–Bahn–Karnplay road in Nimba, coastal roads from Cestos to Greenville and from Pleebo to Barclayville, Grandcess and Big Suehn Junction, and the Gbarnga–Kokoyah–Buchanan road.

Monrovia gets 75 kilometers of concrete-paved roads, a Kesselly Boulevard bridge linking 12th Street to Barnersville Junction, and an expanded Tubman Boulevard with a new four-lane bridge.

For a farmer in the southeast whose produce rots during the rainy season because trucks cannot get through, these are not lines on a contract. They are the difference between a harvest sold and a harvest lost.

Paying for it without new borrowing

What sets MIDA apart is how it would be financed. Rather than taking on traditional public loans, the government plans to ring-fence additional revenue payable by BMMC, made possible by record gold prices, and dedicate it to the infrastructure program.

BMMC will continue its regular payments to the Consolidated Account, officials say, meaning the money for MIDA comes from new revenue rather than funds already in the budget. To get work moving, BMMC is pledging US$500 million in bridge financing.

The scale of the mine makes the plan credible. Liberia’s 16th EITI report shows BMMC exported about 12,146 kilograms of gold worth more than US$653 million in fiscal year 2023. Gold prices have climbed sharply since then.

The government says the approach will ease pressure on Liberia’s debt burden by funding major projects without new borrowing.

Jobs, skills and the ARREST Agenda

Construction and operation of the projects are expected to create thousands of jobs, directly and through suppliers. Liberians would gain skills in engineering, construction, power generation and infrastructure management, building a technical workforce the country will need for decades.

The program advances President Boakai’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development by directing mining revenue toward infrastructure that helps farmers reach more buyers, keeps businesses running and brings communities closer to health care and public services.

The timeline

The agreement targets full implementation over five years. The biomass plant and the transmission lines are set for completion within two years, meaning some Liberians could see results before the 2029 elections.

Making the vision real

The ambition is large, and so is the work ahead.

Lawmakers will want to know how much ring-fenced revenue is expected each year and what happens if gold prices fall. Liberians will want to know who will own and operate the new plants, how they will fit into LEC’s system and what electricity will cost.

Reservoirs on this scale also require careful

environmental planning and fair treatment of affected communities. Grand Cape Mount lawmakers, including Senator Dabah Varpilah, have long pressed for clearer community benefits from Bea Mountain’s operations. Publishing the agreement and building strong oversight into it would help MIDA win the public trust it needs.

If those pieces fall into place, MIDA offers something Liberia has rarely had: a single, coordinated plan to power and connect the whole country, paid for by its own resources.

Generations from now, Liberians may not remember the contract clauses or the megawatt figures. They will remember whether the lights stayed on and whether the roads reached their towns. MIDA is a bet that they will.

World.title: Behind the Austrian ‘State Printer’ at the Heart of Liberia’s Rejected US$54.7m ID Deal
World.content:
MONROVIA – When Integrity Watch Liberia’s Harold Aidoo asked in May, “Who is this company? What is their track record?”, the question went largely unanswered. Six months later, the House of Representatives has unanimously rejected the national identification concession President Joseph Nyuma Boakai sent to the Legislature – and most Liberians still know little about the firm that was poised to build, run and earn from the country’s most sensitive database for a decade.

By Rodney D Sieh

FrontPageAfrica pieced together the company’s profile from Austrian company registry filings, the firm’s own corporate disclosures, international arbitration records, media reports in Austria and West Africa, and a 24-page company presentation prepared for the National Identification Registry (NIR) and obtained by this newspaper.



What emerges is a picture of a genuine, long-established European security printer – but one whose Liberian pitch leaned heavily on a “state” pedigree it no longer has, on a parent company’s reputation rather than the contracting entity’s own balance sheet, and on a procurement path that regulators had explicitly closed.

Not one company, but three

The company that signed with Liberia is OeSD International GmbH – not the 222-year-old Austrian State Printing House itself.

According to Austria’s official business register, OeSD International GmbH was registered in Vienna on May 9, 2007, with share capital of just €35,000. Its sole shareholder is Österreichische Staatsdruckerei GmbH, and it is managed jointly by Claudia Schwendimann, its CEO, and Helmut Lackner, the group’s general director.



The group’s own website describes a three-tier structure: a holding company, Österreichische Staatsdruckerei Holding AG, owns 100 percent of the operating printer, Österreichische Staatsdruckerei GmbH, which in turn owns 100 percent of OeSD International.

The international arm, the company says, focuses on travel documents – e-passports, machine-readable passports and visa labels – for foreign customers, typically larger projects involving system integration and on-site personalisation centres, and is active in Africa, Asia and South America.

The distinction matters. A €35,000 limited-liability subsidiary was the party proposing to pre-finance some US$54.7 million of national infrastructure. Neither the President’s communication nor the NIR’s public statements have disclosed whether the parent company or the holding company has guaranteed that commitment, or where the money will actually come from. Biometric Update has reported that a May memorandum of understanding involving the government, OeSD and Ecobank Liberia carries the same revenue split found in the concession – suggesting a local bank was lined up in the financing chain.

The ‘State’ printer that the state sold

The name invites confusion. Österreichische Staatsdruckerei translates as “Austrian State Printing House”, and in Liberia the firm has repeatedly been described as the “global arm of the Austrian State Printing Company”. Some Liberian officials and commentators have spoken of it as though it were an arm of the Austrian government.

It is not. Austria privatised the printer more than two decades ago. In 2000 and 2002, under then-Finance Minister Karl-Heinz Grasser, it was sold in two tranches for a combined €31 million to the Vienna private equity firm E.C.P. Capital Partners, led by Robert Schächter and Johannes Strohmayer, according to the Austrian news agency APA.

Today, the same two men effectively control it through private foundations: Schächter’s GRT Privatstiftung holds 45.8 percent and Strohmayer’s G3 Industrie Privatstiftung 45.7 percent, with an employee foundation holding 4.9 percent.

Schächter is CEO of the holding company; Strohmayer chairs its supervisory board. The holding company left the Vienna Stock Exchange in 2020 after failing to meet the minimum free-float requirement.

The company presentation prepared for the NIR does not mention any of this. Its corporate timeline jumps from 1918 – when, it says, the firm “becomes the state-owned Österreichische Staatsdruckerei” – straight to 2014. The privatisation is absent. Its closing “Five reasons to ratify” describes OeSD as “a state printing house founded in 1804”.

The firm does still produce Austria’s passports, identity cards and driving licences under contract – a genuine credential in a field where few companies are trusted with national documents.

How big is it?

By global standards, it is a niche player. APA reported that the group’s revenue rose from €62.3 million to €77.2 million in the 2024/25 financial year ending in March, with net profit nearly doubling to €16.2 million on the strength of passport business.

Put differently: the US$54.7 million Liberia concession would amount to well over half of the entire group’s annual revenue – committed to a single country, through a subsidiary with €35,000 in share capital.

The presentation to the NIR says OeSD has more than 255 full-time employees plus 112 engineers “contracted exclusively” to its projects, serves “over 60 governments” and runs an Africa office in Accra, Ghana. FrontPageAfrica could not independently verify those figures. At the ID4Africa conference in Addis Ababa in 2025, the company listed Charles Boakye as its Director Africa.

What it has actually done in Africa

OeSD’s African portfolio is real but narrower than a national ID system of the kind Liberia needs.

* Ghana: The company’s strongest African reference. OeSD says it developed and implemented MyNHIS, the mobile app Ghana’s National Health Insurance Authority launched at the end of 2022 for membership registration and renewal. That app, however, runs on top of the Ghana Card – it relies on an ID system someone else built. The presentation also cites a Ministry of Education data dashboard and an e-visa platform for the Ghana Immigration Service.

* Nigeria: The presentation says OeSD’s personalisation software supports Nigeria’s ECOWAS National Biometric ID Card, launched in November 2025 – but it acknowledges this was supplied “through prime contractor Euphoria Press”. OeSD was a subcontractor, not the system builder.

* ECOWAS: It cites the 2016 ECOWAS biometric laissez-passer – a travel document for regional officials, produced and personalised at ECOWAS headquarters in Abuja.

Nowhere in the 24-page pitch does OeSD cite a completed, nationwide, population-scale biometric enrolment of the kind it proposed for Liberia – 3 million adults in 18 months, with 130 mobile enrolment kits in the field. Its largest-scale experience is in printing and personalising documents for Austria, the European Union, Liechtenstein and Andorra, where population registers already exist.

The Kosovo precedent

One past dispute is instructive. OeSD won Kosovo’s 2011 e-passport tender. Kosovo terminated the contract early, and in 2016 an arbitration tribunal of the International Chamber of Commerce in Paris ordered Kosovo to pay roughly €5 million in damages plus costs.

According to OeSD’s lawyers, Wolf Theiss, part of the money owed to the company had been transferred to other parties; Global Arbitration Review reported the tribunal found Kosovo had paid funds into an incorrect bank account, enabling a third-party fraudster to steal them.

OeSD won – and to its credit, the company discloses the case in its presentation. But it is a reminder that ID contracts in fragile administrations can go badly wrong for both sides, and that when they do, the dispute lands in Paris, not Monrovia.

How the deal slipped under the radar

The paper trail suggests OeSD did not win a tender – because there was no tender.

* March 2024: A Liberian delegation led by then-Foreign Minister Sara Beysolow Nyanti, including Senator Abraham Darius Dillon and Transport Minister Sirleaf Tyler, toured OeSD’s Vienna headquarters, according to The Liberian Investigator. An MoU between the government and OeSD followed that year.

* May 2025: The Public Procurement and Concessions Commission (PPCC) granted a conditional “no objection” for the NIR to engage OeSD, subject to a concession plan.

* June 10, 2025: The NIR sought clearance for restricted bidding, estimating the cost at US$9.85 million.

* July 5, 2025: President Boakai named National Security Advisor Samuel Kofi Woods to chair a 10-member steering committee. The presidential memo, as reported, both instructed the committee to finalise contractor selection and described the OeSD procurement as already complete.

* July 7, 2025: The PPCC rejected the NIR’s request and ordered international competitive bidding. PPCC spokesman Nathan Bengu later said there had been no communication reversing that decision.

* May 2026: NIR Executive Director Andrew Peters told Biometric Update that after OeSD’s demonstration, the President asked that “instead of a standard contract” the government enter a concession through a public-private partnership. The NIR later cited the amended PPCC Act of 2026, which allows sole-source arrangements on grounds of strategic national interest or security.

* October 15, 2026: The concession was submitted to the Legislature. Earlier copies lacked the signature of OeSD’s chief executive, prompting lawmakers to suspend their review until it was corrected.

* November 2026: A joint House committee chaired by Rep. Foday Fahnbulleh flagged more than 40 legal, financial, administrative and technical risks. The House unanimously rejected the deal and called for open, competitive bidding.

Along the way, the price moved from US$9.85 million, to US$39 million in some reports, to US$52 million in the President’s communication, to US$54.7 million in the NIR’s figures – a discrepancy lawmakers singled out.

The Liberian Investigator also reported in August 2025, citing an unnamed government source, that unnamed officials had demanded US$120,000 from OeSD after an agreement was signed, and that OeSD complained to the President. Those claims have not been independently verified, and no official has been named.

‘No cash’ – but who pays?

OeSD’s pitch frames the deal as free money: its comparison table says Ghana paid US$124 million upfront for the Ghana Card, while under the Liberian deal the government pays “no cash”.

The concession’s fine print tells a different story. Annex Five, as reported by The New Republic and Biometric Update, gives OeSD 65 percent of specified revenues from the ID system and the government 35 percent over a 10-year term. Projections cited in the media put total revenue at about US$107 million, with about US$69.5 million going to OeSD.

The pitch also promises a free card “for every adult citizen”. But in September, the NIR’s Peters clarified that free cards would go only to an estimated 3.5 million disadvantaged and unemployed Liberians; employed citizens and foreign residents would still pay, according to BudgIT Liberia. Fees paid by Liberians, in other words, are how OeSD gets its money back.

The system was also designed to hold up to 10 million biometric records – nearly double Liberia’s population – while Liberia still has no data protection law.

What lawmakers – and Liberians – still don’t know

The House vote ends this version of the deal, but not the questions:

* Did the parent company or holding company guarantee OeSD International’s US$54.7 million commitment, and what role does Ecobank play?

* Who negotiated the concession for Liberia, and who briefed the President that the procurement was complete when the PPCC had ordered open bidding?

* Why did the price quintuple between June 2025 and October 2026?

* Will OeSD compete in an open tender if one is called – and will the NIR run one?

FrontPageAfrica has contacted OeSD International CEO Claudia Schwendimann and NIR Executive Director Andrew Peters for comment.

World.title: Liberia: CDC Accuses VP Koung of Bankrolling MOVEE Faction to Oust Kemayah, Alleges US$50,000 Payoff
World.content:
MONROVIA – The Congress for Democratic Change (CDC) has accused Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung of allegedly financing a faction within the Movement for Economic Empowerment (MOVEE) to remove its Political Leader, former Foreign Minister Ambassador Dee-Maxwell Saah Kemayah Sr., escalating political tensions within the opposition and raising questions about alleged government interference in opposition party affairs.

By Willie N. Tokpah

In a statement released Saturday, November 21, in Monrovia, the CDC alleged that US$50,000 was provided to members of MOVEE’s executive structure to facilitate Kemayah’s suspension and ultimately push him out of the party’s leadership.



The opposition party described the alleged financial inducement as part of what it characterized as a broader strategy by the Unity Party-led government to weaken opposition institutions through internal divisions and political manipulation.

The allegations, which have not been independently substantiated, come amid growing tensions within MOVEE, where Kemayah faces internal disciplinary action as he challenges his criminal conviction.

The CDC portrayed the suspension as politically motivated, alleging that those behind the move acted in Vice President Koung’s interest after receiving financial inducements.

However, the party did not identify the alleged beneficiaries or provide documentary evidence, transaction records, or other independent proof to support its US$50,000 claim.



The US$50,000 Allegation

At the center of the controversy is MOVEE’s decision to suspend Kemayah, a former senior government official and prominent opposition figure who has maintained political ties with former President George Manneh Weah.

The CDC alleged that the suspension was not merely an internal disciplinary matter but an orchestrated effort to undermine Kemayah’s political influence and weaken his relationship with the former president.

According to the party, Vice President Koung is uncomfortable with the political alliance between Kemayah and Weah and is allegedly using financial inducements to influence the internal affairs of opposition parties.

The CDC also rejected allegations that Kemayah converted a MOVEE campaign vehicle to his personal use, insisting that the vehicle had been returned to the CDC in accordance with an agreement governing the 2023 electoral campaign.

“The vehicle in question was properly returned to the CDC under the campaign agreement, the agreement was fulfilled, full stop,” the statement declared.

The party further maintained that it currently has possession of the vehicle and its title documents, which it argued contradicts allegations being advanced by some MOVEE members against Kemayah.

However, the CDC did not attach a copy of the alleged campaign agreement or supporting vehicle documentation to substantiate its explanation.

Questions therefore remain about the specific terms of the agreement, when the vehicle was returned, and whether documentary evidence exists to establish the transfer.

Kemayah’s Legal Troubles and Party Suspension

The political dispute is unfolding against the backdrop of Kemayah’s legal troubles following his conviction in a criminal case, which the CDC characterized as politically motivated.

The party said Kemayah is challenging the conviction while simultaneously facing suspension from MOVEE, describing the developments as an attempt to weaken his political standing through both judicial and internal party processes.

However, the CDC’s characterization of the conviction and its allegations of political orchestration remain claims by the opposition party and have not been independently established.

The latest controversy also raises questions about MOVEE’s internal governance, particularly the authority of its executive committee to suspend its political leader and the procedures followed in reaching that decision.

It remains unclear what specific constitutional provisions MOVEE’s executive committee relied upon, whether Kemayah was afforded an opportunity to respond to the allegations against him, and whether an appeal mechanism has been activated.

These questions carry implications for internal party democracy, political representation, and the broader opposition landscape as political maneuvering ahead of the 2029 elections intensifies.

Broader Opposition Political Tensions

Beyond MOVEE, the CDC accused Vice President Koung of pursuing what it described as a wider campaign to influence the leadership structures of opposition parties.

The party cited alleged interference within the National Patriotic Party (NPP), claiming that US$175,000 in state resources was provided to sponsor the party’s convention scheduled for December 11–12 in Grand Bassa County.

According to the CDC, the alleged objective is to facilitate the emergence of Senator James Biney as the party’s Political Leader.

The opposition party also alleged that Vice President Koung offered US$30,000 to induce some of its executive members in Nimba County to resign.

The CDC characterized the alleged activities as a strategy of political infiltration and hostile takeovers, claiming that the government is seeking to weaken opposition leadership ahead of the next electoral cycle.

If substantiated, the allegations could raise serious questions about the use of public resources, political patronage, and the independence of opposition parties.

However, the CDC did not provide financial records, identify the alleged beneficiaries, or present independent evidence to substantiate the claims involving the NPP and its own county executives.

VP’s Office Previously Denied NPP Interference

While the Office of the Vice President has not responded to the latest allegations involving the alleged US$50,000 payment to influence MOVEE’s internal affairs, it previously rejected similar accusations concerning the National Patriotic Party.

In October, the office dismissed claims that Vice President Koung was maneuvering to take control of the NPP or financing efforts to remove former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor as the party’s Political Leader.

Taylor, who is facing prosecution on allegations of drug trafficking and money laundering, remains the NPP’s Political Leader. She is currently under house arrest as the legal proceedings continue.

In a written response to an inquiry from FrontPage Africa dated October 20, 2026, the Vice President’s Office said Koung had no interest in the internal politics of the NPP or any other political party.

The response, signed by the Vice President’s Chief of Staff, Prince Menkalo Gbieu, described the allegations as false and deliberately misleading.

“At no point has the Honorable Vice President sought to interfere in the internal affairs of the NPP or any political party. The allegation is not only false, it is deliberately misleading and designed to create unnecessary tension in our body politics,” Gbieu stated.

The office maintained that Koung was not interested in controlling political institutions or creating controversy, but was focused on supporting President Joseph Nyuma Boakai in implementing the government’s ARREST Agenda.

“His sole focus remains clear: to stand firmly beside President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and ensure that the ARREST Agenda delivers real results — roads, jobs, education, healthcare, and opportunity to every Liberian,” the statement said.

Gbieu further emphasized that the Vice President would continue engaging Liberians across political, ethnic, and regional lines to preserve national peace and create an enabling environment for development.

“He will continue to work with all well-meaning Liberians, irrespective of parties, tribe or region, to maintain the peace we enjoy and to create the stable environment Liberia needs for development and progress,” he added.

The October response, however, addressed the allegations of interference in the NPP and did not specifically address the latest claims involving MOVEE or the alleged US$50,000 inducement.

Questions for the Vice President and MOVEE

The latest accusations place renewed attention on the relationship between the executive branch and the internal affairs of political parties, particularly whether public officials are using financial influence to shape opposition leadership.

The central issue remains whether there is credible evidence that money was offered to influence MOVEE’s disciplinary decision against Kemayah.

The CDC’s statement did not provide transaction records, names of alleged beneficiaries, dates of payment, or other independently verifiable evidence to support the US$50,000 allegation.

Although the Vice President’s Office has previously denied allegations of interference in the NPP, it has yet to publicly respond to the latest accusations involving MOVEE.

What began as an internal leadership dispute within MOVEE has now evolved into a wider political confrontation, with the CDC accusing the country’s second-highest elected official of using financial influence to reshape opposition politics.

Whether the allegations can be backed by verifiable evidence or are part of the intensifying political contest ahead of 2029 remains an open question.

World.title: Liberia: LCC President Reeves Calls for Scrutiny of MIDA Deal
World.content:
Monrovia – The President of the Liberia Council of Churches (LCC), Rev. Dr. Samuel B. Reeves, Jr., is urging the Legislature not to ratify the current version of a proposed infrastructure agreement with Bea Mountain Mining Corporation (BMMC). He warns that the deal could shortchange Liberia by trading billions in future mining revenue for projects whose cost, delivery and benefits are not guaranteed.

By Rodney D. Sieh

In an analysis of the draft Master Infrastructure Development Agreement (MIDA) obtained by FrontPageAfrica, Rev. Reeves said Liberia would receive roads, power plants and transmission lines, “but it would pay for them by redirecting future mining-related public revenue, with interest.”



“The central problem is that the draft gives BMMC a strong, long-lasting right to recover its costs while leaving Liberia with much weaker protections on price, delivery, operating performance and community compensation,” he wrote.

“My recommendation is to withhold ratification of this version,” Rev. Reeves said.

He noted that key parts of the deal are missing from the copy he reviewed. Annex C contains no payment milestone schedule. Annex E contains no detailed technical specifications. The engineering, procurement and construction (EPC) contracts are not available. Those gaps, he said, “prevent an independent assessment of what triggers payment, what the contractor must deliver, and whether the prices represent fair value.” He also cautioned that the draft’s execution and ratification status remain unverified.

The intervention comes days after the LCC issued its circular “Who Protects the People When Justice Fails?”, which called for “honest accounting” of public funds.



$500 Million Up Front, Billions at Stake

Under the draft, BMMC is required to keep only US$500 million in financing available at any one time. The money revolves: as BMMC recovers costs through tax set-offs, the facility refills.

The projects themselves cost far more. According to Rev. Reeves’ analysis, the eight primary projects carry a base cost of US$4.4513 billion, including US$50 million for land and resettlement compensation. Another US$1.23 billion is allocated for additional public roads and grid reinforcement. That brings the total to US$5.6813 billion before interest, indexation, cost overruns and other charges.

Other projects could be added under a ceiling tied to 50 percent of the base cost, about US$2.23 billion. Crucially, Rev. Reeves said, “the draft does not establish a single all-in ceiling on what Liberia ultimately pays.”

Revenue on Paper, No Cash in the Treasury

Under Article 9, BMMC could offset its corporate income tax, royalties, withholding tax on dividends and any surtax against its infrastructure costs. It could also offset dividends due on Liberia’s 5 percent stake in the company and even the PAYE income tax it withholds from its employees.

Rev. Reeves warned that no minimum share of these payments is guaranteed to reach the Treasury in cash. “The budget could record both revenue and infrastructure expenditure on paper while receiving no cash from the amounts offset,” he wrote. That would leave less money for health, education and other priorities. The Finance Ministry can also designate additional payments for offsetting, and the draft makes those designations irrevocable.

Paying Interest Before the Contractor Is Paid

Interest begins the moment BMMC approves a contractor’s payment certificate. There is no requirement to show that BMMC has actually paid the invoice. The interest rate applies regardless of BMMC’s real borrowing cost, including when an affiliate supplies the money. Unpaid interest is added to the balance every quarter, and repayments go to interest first.

As an illustration, Rev. Reeves calculated that at a 6 percent rate, a US$500 million balance left unpaid for a year would generate roughly US$31 million in interest. He said the Legislature needs a year-by-year forecast of set-offs, construction draws, interest and the cash left for the national budget before it can decide.

No Bidding, Limited Checks

Article 31.3 would exempt the contractor, MAPA, and all EPC contracts from Liberia’s public procurement and concessions law. MAPA is named as the exclusive initial contractor. BMMC approves the contractor’s bills, and the government generally has only 30 days to object. Claims of fraud or arithmetic error must be raised within six months, which Rev. Reeves called short for problems that may surface in later audits.

The General Auditing Commission (GAC) may inspect payment certificates and set-off records, but not the actual costs incurred by BMMC and its contractor. And while the draft requires several annexes to be published, the payment milestones in Annex C are not among them.

Rev. Reeves singled out the SP-4 hydropower plant. It is priced at US$634.44 million for 10 megawatts, about US$63.4 million per megawatt.
