He acknowledged that the project includes reservoir and water-transfer works, so that figure alone “cannot establish overpricing.” But he said it justifies an independent review before Liberia commits public revenue.

Plants Without Power in Homes

Only three projects have stated two-year completion periods: the public biomass plant, the Main Line and the Bong Line. Even those clocks start only after certain conditions are met. The timelines of the other projects depend on how much tax BMMC has available to offset. If the agreement is terminated, Liberia could inherit unfinished works and still owe the costs already accrued.

“A finished plant does not guarantee electricity in homes,” Rev. Reeves wrote. Liberia must pay for distribution, connections and metering, and it carries the operating and collection risk. The draft sets no binding target for household connections or affordable power. If LEC chooses to have BMMC operate the public biomass plant, the US$0.03 per kWh operating fee could apply even to power never generated, when output is curtailed for specified reasons outside BMMC’s control.

Works can also be “deemed accepted” if a government authority misses a deadline to object, or if the government starts using them early. The contractor’s overall liability is capped at 10 percent of the contract price, subject to exceptions. The draft includes no express performance bond, parent company guarantee or retention requirement.

Communities Bear the Burden

Annex A lists at least 446.42 square kilometers for the three main reservoir and permanent-works sites. The draft does not say how many people would be displaced or how many livelihoods would be affected. Only US$50 million is set aside for compensation on the primary projects. Any additional compensation would be recovered through set-offs, so a low estimate could mean both delayed payments to communities and a bigger claim on public revenue.

Rev. Reeves called for independently costed resettlement plans, prompt compensation and accessible grievance procedures before anyone is displaced. He noted that Article 24 of the Constitution protects just compensation, and that the Land Rights Act recognizes customary land.

He also flagged a private benefit. BMMC pays for its own 60-megawatt biomass plant, but it receives half of the wood cleared from public project sites, free of government charges, while the cost of cutting and stacking that wood falls under public project costs. He also questioned the draft’s classification of reservoir clearing as something other than natural forest conversion.

Liberian workers get few guarantees. There are no enforceable minimums for Liberian jobs, apprenticeships or contracts for Liberian-owned firms, and missing a local-content objective carries no consequence. Meanwhile, eligible foreign contractor employees would be exempt from PAYE, pay half-price work permits and be exempt from employee NASSCORP contributions. Liberian employees would keep paying PAYE.

Binding Future Governments

The agreement caps BMMC’s corporate income tax at 25 percent for the covered entitlement and protects its fiscal terms until all costs and interest are recovered. Set-off rights can survive termination and, in some circumstances, pass to an affiliate or buyer. If government default makes recovery impossible, Liberia could owe cash instalments with interest.

Rev. Reeves also raised a constitutional concern. The draft seeks advance legislative approval for set-offs and spending, removes the need for further budget authorization, and would override conflicting laws, while the Constitution gives the Legislature the power to tax and appropriate. He urged lawmakers to obtain an independent Liberian legal opinion before ratification.

What Reeves Wants Before Ratification

Rev. Reeves listed five conditions:

• publish the full deal, including Annexes C and E and the EPC contracts, and independently verify the prices;

• cap total exposure and annual set-offs, guarantee a minimum cash payment to the Treasury, and exclude employee PAYE;

• tie payment to independently certified, usable infrastructure, backed by performance security;

• give the GAC full access to the underlying cost records;

• make compensation, livelihood restoration and Liberian jobs commitments funded and binding.

“The Legislature’s central question should be: How much cash revenue will Liberia give up each year, and what completed, independently verified public service will Liberians receive in return?” he wrote. “The draft gives BMMC a mechanism to collect. Liberia should insist on equally enforceable answers about price, delivery and public benefit before approving it.”

World.title: Liberia: 300-Plus Students Learn Under Leaking Roofs as Pedebo Public School Crumbles
World.content:
HARPER, Maryland County – More than 300 students attending Pedebo Public School in Harper District, Maryland County, are struggling to access education in a deteriorating school building marked by leaking roofs, broken walls, inadequate classroom furniture and a complete lack of toilet facilities.

By Peter P. Toe, Jr.

The government-run institution, which serves children from several surrounding villages, offers classes from Kindergarten One (K1) through sixth grade. However, its worsening physical condition continues to undermine teaching and learning activities.



A visit to the school by FrontPage Africa reporters on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, found that classes were ongoing despite the deplorable condition of the facility.

The school’s zinc roofing is severely damaged, while sections of the classroom walls are broken. Inside the classrooms, reporters observed broken pieces of chairs, with students reportedly bringing their own benches to school because of the shortage of seating furniture.

Steven Nyemah, Township Commissioner and a classroom teacher who has served the institution as a volunteer for more than 20 years, described the situation as embarrassing, disclosing that rainfall frequently disrupts classes and forces students to return home.

“When rain falls, we send the children home. We have no offices, we have no seating chairs and no desks. Students bring their own benches to school for sitting. This is seriously embarrassing. We complained to the DEO office several times, but nothing has been done,” Nyemah told journalists.



Beyond the deteriorating classrooms, the school has no toilet facilities for either students or teachers, creating additional sanitation and hygiene challenges for the more than 300 children enrolled at the institution.

Despite these conditions, students continue attending the school because many come from surrounding villages, where traveling to Harper City to access alternative educational facilities requires considerable time and distance.

The school’s staffing situation is equally concerning. Although Pedebo Public School has five teachers, only two are reportedly receiving government salaries, leaving the remaining three to provide instructional services without government compensation.

Nyemah, who has spent more than two decades teaching at the institution, also disclosed that his efforts to secure government employment through the Ministry of Education have not yielded results.

He said his name and relevant documents were submitted to the Ministry, but he was not among those eventually placed on the government’s payroll.

Education Authorities Acknowledge Neglect

Meanwhile, the District Education Officer for Harper Education District #1, Augustine Doblah, has acknowledged the school’s deteriorating condition, saying education authorities have repeatedly reported the situation to the government without receiving any intervention.

Speaking to FrontPage Africa by telephone on Wednesday afternoon, Doblah confirmed that the government was aware of the school’s condition.

“Yes, I am aware of the situation, and government is aware. We have made a lot of reports on this school building.” he said.

Doblah disclosed that the district was recently requested to submit another report documenting the school’s condition, which has since been completed.

According to him, the County Education Officer was preparing to travel to Monrovia with the latest report, and expressed optimism that something will be done to address the problem.

FrontPage Africa also contacted the Ministry of Education through WhatsApp and email to obtain its response regarding the school’s condition and the repeated reports submitted by local education authorities. However, the Ministry had not provided an official response up to the time of publication.

With more than 300 students depending on the institution for their elementary education, Pedebo Public School continues to operate despite the deteriorating infrastructure, inadequate classroom furniture, lack of sanitation facilities and shortage of teachers receiving government salaries.

The school community is appealing to the Ministry of Education and other relevant government authorities to urgently rehabilitate the building, provide adequate classroom furniture, construct toilet facilities and address the shortage of teachers on the government payroll.

World.title: Liberia: ‘Cape Mount Is Home’ – Wantoe Launches Nationwide Tour, Eyes CDC Vice Chair for International Affairs
World.content:
Robertsport, Grand Cape Mount County – Wantoe Teah Wantoe, the Oxford-trained public policy graduate and outspoken social media voice of the opposition Congress for Democratic Change (CDC), has formally launched a nationwide political engagement tour, choosing his maternal home of Grand Cape Mount County as the starting point for his bid to become the party’s Vice Chair for International Affairs.

In a statement posted on his social media pages, Wantoe said he was received by “hundreds of CDC partisans, independent citizens, young people, and community leaders” as he moved from Gedema, across the border in Sierra Leone, to Bo Waterside and Tewor District.

The launch carried a personal note for the young politician. His late mother, he said, was a lifelong resident of Bo Waterside, and his maternal family, the Sambola family, has deep roots across the county.



“Cape Mount is not simply a place I visit; it is my home, my heritage, and an important part of who I am,” Wantoe wrote. “Returning to the communities that shaped my family’s history, particularly after losing my mother, made this occasion profoundly personal and emotional.”

‘No Individual Is Bigger Than This Institution’

Addressing partisans, Wantoe cast the CDC as “the party of ordinary Liberians,” built on the sacrifices of market women, motorcyclists, farmers, students and working citizens.

“No individual is bigger than this institution, and our greatest strength remains our grassroots,” he said, adding that unity, reconciliation and institutional reform must guide the party’s future.



The remarks come as the former ruling party, now in opposition, works to rebuild ahead of the 2029 presidential and legislative elections, while managing internal rifts, including disputes that have rocked its U.S. chapter over its convention this year.

Five-Point Agenda

Wantoe outlined five priorities he says he will pursue if elected Vice Chair for International Affairs:

* An international engagement strategy to strengthen the CDC’s ties with political institutions, international partners and diplomatic stakeholders across Africa, Europe, the Americas, Asia and the Middle East.

* A diaspora engagement framework to strengthen the party’s overseas chapters and give Liberians abroad a structured role in the party’s institutional development.

* Partnerships for education and leadership training, linking young Liberians to scholarships, mentorship and international opportunities.

* International fundraising and resource mobilization, with what he described as transparent mechanisms to support the party’s long-term sustainability.

* Greater youth participation in international political engagement.

“Young people must not simply be celebrated as the leaders of tomorrow while being excluded from the decisions of today,” he said. “Our generation must be given the opportunity to serve, contribute, and lead.”

From Oxford to the Campaign Trail

Wantoe, 31, holds a Master of Public Policy from the University of Oxford’s Blavatnik School of Government and studied public policy and sociology at the College of Mount Saint Vincent in New York. He has built a sizable following online, where he is a frequent commentator on national affairs and a vocal defender of the CDC.

His pitch on diaspora engagement and fundraising touches a sensitive nerve for the party, whose overseas chapters, a key source of money and mobilization, have been dogged by leadership disputes and boycotts in recent months.

Wantoe closed his statement with a nod to the road ahead: “From Cape Mount to every mountain ahead, our responsibility is to build bridges, strengthen our institutions, and remain connected to the ordinary people who are the foundation of our political movement.”

“Cape Mount is home. Cape Mount is family. Cape Mount will always have a special place in my heart,” he said.

World.title: Three months in Mukobeko, one indictment, and the questions nobody has answered
World.content:
Have you heard? For weeks, it seemed the President and his supporters had gone quiet on the militia story. The other day, President Hakainde Hichilema warned that anyone who declares himself the winner of an election will go to jail. I could not help asking what happened to the earlier warning, the one that said if you run a militia, you will go to jail.

It seemed to me that Director of Public Prosecutions Mr Gilbert A. Phiri SC was stuck between a rock and a hard place. The State had spent years telling us it investigates thoroughly. Yet Brian Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and the others had spent three months behind bars before any indictment was put on the table.

On Monday morning, journalist Augustine Mukoka published a report that put that question at the front of the queue. He described the 18 detainees held at Mukobeko Maximum Security Prison as political prisoners and called the treason case bogus. He claimed that the DPP had arranged an abrupt sitting at the Subordinate Court in Lusaka in order to enter a nolle prosequi for some or all of them.

Mr Mukoka reported that the detainees, who had been due in Lusaka a day later, were moved from Kabwe in the early hours without their lawyers or families being told. In his account, the sudden sitting was meant to get ahead of a constitutional bail hearing before the Lusaka High Court, a petition he says the court had already found to be properly before it.

He went further. Citing an unnamed source, Mr Mukoka claimed that while some detainees might be freed, the State wanted Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu kept away from public life, and was preparing to re-arrest their security personnel. He named them as Jackson Mutyoka, Brazil Soko and Bernard Chanda Chewe, whom he described as retired Zambia Army Special Forces servicemen, and Richard Banda, whom he described as Mr Mundubile’s bodyguard and a former police officer.

“They are planning to re-arrest the security guys because it might be difficult to stop the constitutional bail,” the source told Mr Mukoka.

Mr Mukoka also tied the case to the wider fight over the Constitution. In his view, keeping the opposition leaders confined suits a Government that wants to remove presidential term limits, at a time when, he says, Zambians and the international community are pressing for the detainees’ release.

By Monday afternoon, things had gone differently. There was no nolle prosequi for the main group. Lusaka Chief Resident Magistrate Nthandose Chabala told the accused that she had received a certificate from the DPP, and 14 of them were committed to the High Court for summary trial on a charge of treason.

Four of the original 18, including former Anglican Bishop Trevor Mwamba, are not on the indictment. Whatever the reason for that, Mr Mukoka’s claim that some detainees would walk free has partly come true.

As for the militia story I thought had been quietly dropped, it is back, and this time it is written down. The indictment alleges that Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu engaged a serving colonel to recruit serving and retired soldiers, that money was found for military training in Russia, and that offensive weapons were held for the operation.

All four men Mr Mukoka named as the security detail, Mr Mutyoka, Mr Soko, Mr Chewe and Mr Banda, appear in the indictment’s weapons count. The State does not need to re-arrest men it has already sent for trial.

So the questions change. They no longer start with “where is the charge?” They start with “where is the evidence?” An indictment is an allegation, not a verdict. Every one of the 14 is presumed innocent until the High Court says otherwise, and the State must now prove in open court what it has alleged on paper.

Three months is a long time to hold people before setting out the case against them. Zambians are entitled to ask why it took that long. They are also entitled to know whether the constitutional bail petition will still be heard, and when.

Then there is the question that has hung over this whole affair since August. Mutotwe Kafwaya, a former cabinet minister, died during the security operation of 14 August. His family and the country are still waiting for a full account of how that happened. Treason trials do not make that question go away. If anything, the State now owes the answer more urgently than ever.

The 14 accused will next appear before a High Court judge to take plea. That courtroom, not Facebook and not State House, is where this matter must now be settled.

By Linda Banks

Source: A Collection of Voices

Editor’s note: The views expressed in this column are the author’s own. Claims attributed to Augustine Mukoka’s unnamed source have not been independently verified by Lusaka Times. All accused persons are presumed innocent until proven guilty.

World.title: Mundubile, Makebi Zulu and 12 Others Committed to High Court Over Alleged Plot to Topple Government
World.content:
Brian Mundubile, his running mate Makebi Zulu and 12 co-accused have been committed to the High Court for summary trial on a charge of treason. The State alleges that the group tried to overthrow the Government by recruiting serving and retired soldiers, paying for military training in Russia and keeping offensive weapons for the operation.

Lusaka Chief Resident Magistrate Nthandose Chabala told the 14 accused that she had received a committal certificate from the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions. The group was before the Lusaka Magistrates’ Court for mention and explanation of the charge. The case now moves to the High Court, where they will take plea.

Mr Mundubile stood in this year’s presidential election as the candidate of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) and belongs to the Tonse Pamodzi Alliance. Mr Zulu, a legal practitioner, was his running mate. Both now face the most serious charge in the Penal Code.

Director of Public Prosecutions Mr Gilbert A. Phiri SC signed the certificate under Section 254 of the Criminal Procedure Code, Chapter 88 of the Laws of Zambia. Dated 23 November 2026, it states that this is a proper case for trial by the High Court as a summary procedure case.

The indictment brings one count of treason under Section 43(1)(a) of the Penal Code, Chapter 87. It alleges that between 1 April and 14 August 2026, in Lusaka, the 14 men, acting jointly and with others still at large, prepared or endeavoured to overthrow by unlawful means the Government of the Republic of Zambia as by law established.

Not everyone who first appeared in the case made it onto the indictment. Former Anglican Bishop Trevor Mwamba and three other people, who had appeared before the magistrates’ court with the group, were left off. That leaves 14 of the original 18 accused heading to the High Court.

With Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu in the dock are Harry Valden Findlay, Brazil Soko, Jackson Mutyoka, Bernard Chanda Chewe, Richard Banda, Simon Phiri, Ezra Gideon Tolopa, Dickson Tembo, Victor Muzyamba, George Kangwa Chisanga, Patrick Bwalya Mwansa and Davies Chisopa. The charge sheet lists them as politicians, legal practitioners, businessmen, a retired soldier, a farmer, a police reserve officer, a bodyguard, a salesman and an entrepreneur. They are aged between 30 and 63, and the document records that they were arrested without a warrant.

The prosecution sets out nine overt acts. The first alleges that Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu engaged Colonel Mundubile Mwamba and other unknown people to recruit serving and retired defence and security personnel to carry out the overthrow.

Colonel Mwamba is not one of the accused, but the indictment names him as the main recruiter. It alleges that he recruited Brigadier General George Mumbi (Rtd), Major John Siwila, Brigadier General Blackson Nyoni (Rtd), Lieutenant Colonel Quincy Mwansa (Rtd), Warrant Officer Class One Mutungulu Sifuniso and Warrant Officer Class One Stephen Phiri, along with others unknown. None of the six officers is charged in the case.

In a separate overt act, Mr Chisopa is accused of working with Colonel Mwamba to recruit Warrant Officer Class Two Kelvin Mungoni Munachaka and others. Warrant Officer Munachaka is not on the indictment either.

The State also alleges that Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu and Mr Chisanga gave logistical and financial support to serving and retired military personnel. Mr Mundubile, Mr Zulu and Colonel Mwamba are accused of holding meetings with other people to advance the plot.

The indictment’s international thread runs to Russia. Mr Mundubile and Mr Tembo are alleged to have recruited Mr Tolopa and Mr Muzyamba for the operation.

Mr Mundubile and Mr Findlay are then accused of paying for military training in Russia for Mr Tolopa, Mr Tembo and Mr Muzyamba, as well as Enock Mwanza, Susan Chileshe and Richard N’guni, who are not on the indictment. The two are also alleged to have bought international airline tickets and arranged transport so the six could travel from Zambia to Russia for that training.

The ninth overt act deals with weapons. It alleges that Mr Mundubile, Mr Soko, Mr Mutyoka, Mr Chewe, Mr Banda, Mr Simon Phiri and Mr Patrick Bwalya Mwansa had offensive weapons meant for the operation. The indictment does not say what weapons they were or where they were found.

Three of the accused also face an alternative charge. Mr Zulu, Mr Chisanga and Mr Patrick Mwansa are charged with misprision of treason under Section 44(b) of the Penal Code.

The prosecution alleges that the three knew that Mr Mundubile, Mr Findlay, Mr Soko, Mr Mutyoka, Mr Chewe, Mr Banda, Mr Simon Phiri, Mr Tolopa, Mr Tembo and Mr Muzyamba intended to commit treason. It says they failed to tell the President, the Vice-President, a minister, a deputy minister, an administrative officer or a police officer with all reasonable despatch, and did nothing else reasonable to stop the offence.

This leaves Mr Zulu facing two alternatives in the same trial: that he helped plan the overthrow, or that he knew about it and kept quiet. The period covered by the indictment covers the whole campaign season and ends on 14 August, the day after the national vote.

The same magistrate committed a separate treason case to the High Court on the same day. Cindy Mutale, a farmer, is accused of conspiring with Patrick Tembo between 1 and 25 August 2026 in Lusaka to overthrow the Government and kill the Head of State.

The 14 accused in the main case will now appear before a High Court judge to plead to the treason count and, for three of them, the alternative charge. No date for plea had been set when the matter left the magistrates’ court.

World.title: Ref Michelo under spotlight after MUZA-Nkana match
World.content:
Chipata-based Super Division referee Jimmy Michelo has come under scrutiny following his handling of the Week 8 MTN Super League match between FC MUZA and Nkana at Nakambala Stadium in Mazabuka.

Michelo took charge as MUZA beat Nkana 2-0 on Saturday, 21st November 2026.

Debate online has centred on three disputed moments: the penalty awarded to MUZA in the 49th minute, converted by Lewis Kasono; the second MUZA goal in the 74th minute scored by Bridger Ng’andu; and the red card shown to Nkana coach Elijah Tana.

The claims are from fans and analysts on social media, and do not represent an official FAZ verdict.

Retired Kamfinsa referee Patrick Tembo has described Michelo’s handling of the match as questionable.

“Ordinarily, as a former match commissioner and committee member of the FAZ referees committee, I am not supposed to openly criticise referees, but surely Saturday’s questionable refereeing at Nakambala cannot be ignored,” Tembo said in a written statement.

“The penalty that Nkana conceded was questionable and there was a clear foul before MUZA’s second goal was scored. Make no mistake, MUZA played well and deserved to score, but the referee clearly spoiled what would have been a wonderful contest between the two youthful sides,” he said.

Tembo has urged FAZ to sanction referees who make obvious mistakes.

“I advise FAZ to continue what we introduced last time, where we were suspending forthwith referees who were making obvious mistakes. Then, referees manager Kafuli was closely monitoring the referees’ performance and was not shy to raise his whip when it was needed,” he said.

World.title: PS Kalusa calls for strong public sector collaborations
World.content:
Government says it recognises the crucial role that the private sector plays in advancing the country’s economic growth, food security and national development.

Lusaka Province Permanent Secretary Joe Kalusa says enhanced collaboration with the private sector and other partners compliments government’s efforts to grow the economy through strengthened agriculture production and increased national food security.

Mr Kalusa has stressed that the Grow Zambia Agenda calls for increased participation from all productive sectors of the economy, and commitment from citizens and other relevant players across the country.

He was speaking when a team from SEEDCO paid a courtesy call on him in Lusaka.

Mr Kalusa commended SEEDCO for seeking to strengthen its collaboration with government through initiatives to empower government departmental heads in the province with seed, to encourage maize production.

He reiterated that the move speaks to President Hakainde Hichilema’s aspiration to achieve the 10 million metric tonnes of maize by 2031.

“Achieving such an ambition requires collective effort , improved farming practices, access to quality seed and technologies, timely planting and effective crop management from all players, and so we do not want the Grow Zambia Agenda to just be a slogan but to swing into action,” he said.

The PS further appealed to the team to explore further areas of collaboration in agriculture development beyond Lusaka Province.

SEEDCO Head of Sales Jasper Simanego said strengthened collaboration with government institutions in Lusaka province will promote agriculture production and ultimately contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Mr Samanego said the institution’s initiative to empower heads of departments with seed, was aimed at encouraging more civil servants to venture into maize production to enable them contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda.

He however, explained that other initiatives aimed at bridging the knowledge gap in technical farming knowledge were already being implemented across the country.

“We also have initiatives where one farmer is trained and given a target to train 100 other farmers to help bridge the Knowledge gap that we have noticed among farmers and civil servants ” he said.

World.title: Kasenengwa civic centre construction commences
World.content:
The Kasenengwa Town Council has started phase one of the construction of the civic centre.

Director of Engineering Services George Syansingu says the works were being done at a cost of K2.5 million using the Constituency Development Funds (CDF).

Mr Syansingu said the works which are being done at the Central Business District (CBD) started last month and are expected to be complete by May next year.

“Works involve putting up a foundation box upto the completion of the superstructure,” he said.

He said the offices will accommodate all council workers including those from the devolved departments.

Kasenengwa was declared a district in 2018 by late former President Edgar Lungu and most government departments have been facing serious accommodation challenges.

World.title: Cholera cases rise to 3,584
World.content:
Government has recorded 3,584 cholera cases and 81 deaths across seven provinces, warning that transmission remains very high.

Addressing the media, Minister of Information and Media Elvis Nkandu says 69 new cases were being recorded daily on average over the past seven days, compared with the 72 cases per day recorded two weeks ago.

Mr Nkandu said 60 new cases have been recorded in the last 24hours, with Lusaka Province accounting for the largest share.

Of the new cases, 49 were recorded in Lusaka Province, 7 on the Copperbelt, 2 in Southern Province and 2 in Northern Province.

The Minister explained that Lusaka Province remains the epicentre of the outbreak, accounting for 2,652 of the 3,584 cases recorded nationally.

The Minister said 3,004 patients have since recovered and have been discharged, while 81 people have died since the outbreak was declared on September 30, 2026.

He expressed concern that 57 of the 81 deaths have occurred within communities rather than health facilities, suggesting that patients were delaying seeking medical attention.

“This is an indication that there is delay in seeking healthcare among our community members,” he said.

And the Minister raised concern over infections at a nursing college in Kafue, where 11 cases have been recorded since November 21, including four in the latest 24 hour period.

He said the government was encouraging vaccination in communities reporting new infections, noting that 78 percent of recorded cases involved unvaccinated individuals.

To strengthen the response, the Minister said the government has activated the Public Health Emergency Operations Centre and deployed rapid response and emergency medical teams to affected areas.

He added that treatment capacity remained adequate, with 200 beds available at treatment centres across the country, of which 69 were occupied.

He said the government has also installed emergency water tanks and handwashing facilities in affected districts as part of its efforts to improve access to safe water and sanitation.

As part of strengthened measures, Mr Nkandu has further directed the Ministry of Health and the Zambia National Public Health Institute to intensify disease surveillance, case management, vaccination and emergency coordination.

And the Ministry of Local Government and Rural Development has also been directed to strengthen waste collection, inspect markets and bus stations and close unsafe food premises in accordance with relevant public health laws.

The Minister has directed the Ministry of Water and Sanitation to ensure safe water supply and sanitation, while the Ministry of Education has been tasked with strengthening cholera awareness and screening in schools, colleges and universities.

The Disaster Risk Management Division has also been directed to coordinate the national response and mobilise resources, while the Ministry of Information and Media will intensify public communication by providing regular and accurate updates on the outbreak.

Meanwhile, the Minister urged members of the public to seek medical attention immediately at the first signs of diarrhoea or vomiting, instead of attempting to manage the illness at home.

He also urged eligible members of the public to accept the oral cholera vaccine when offered, while calling on cooperating partners and other stakeholders to support the response.

World.title: 19 Vubwi households left homeless
World.content:
-Nineteen households have been left homeless after a heavy downpour accompanied by strong winds destroyed houses in Sindemisale Ward of Vubwi district in Eastern Province.

The disaster also resulted in the destruction of household property, food supplies including mealie meal, maize, groundnuts and farming inputs including fertiliser.

Some houses had their roofs completely blown off, while others sustained partial damage to their walls, with no lives lost and no injuries recorded during the incident, despite leaving affected families facing difficulties in rebuilding their homes and restoring their livelihoods.

One of the affected residents, Damalesi Mwale said she was distressed by the loss of essential household items and the uncertainty of where she could find alternative shelter with her children.

Ms Mwale said the disaster has also affected her farming arrangements following the destroyed fertiliser and other farming inputs.

“I have nowhere to sleep with my children, and I do not know how I will manage my farming activities after losing my essential items,” she said.

Another victim, Alex Phiri said rebuilding his damaged house will be a major challenge because he was already experiencing financial difficulties.

Mr Phiri, however, expressed gratitude that his family escaped the disaster unharmed.

Acting District Commissioner Musinda Lunkuntwe who visited the affected families alongside the Council Chairperson, sympathised with the victims, acknowledging the difficulties caused by the disaster and its impact on family security and national development.

Mr Lunkuntwe said the government understood the challenges facing the affected households and would engage relevant higher offices to explore possible assistance.

He disclosed that an assessment of the affected areas had already been conducted, with only the compilation of the findings remaining before the report can be submitted to the relevant authorities.

“We understand the challenges these families are going through, and following the assessment, we will engage the higher offices to see how assistance can be provided,” he said.

And Vubwi Council Chairperson Debby Zulu has appealed to the government to urgently intervene by providing temporary shelter to the affected households.

Mr Zulu said the immediate provision of tents would help families find shelter as they begin recovering from the disaster.

He also appealed to well-wishers and other stakeholders to come on board and assist the affected families with essential supplies.

The Council Chairperson further urged residents to revisit and strengthen their rooftops to minimise similar destruction during heavy rains and strong winds.

He emphasised the importance of planting trees as windbreaks, to help protect communities against strong winds, particularly amid changing climatic conditions.

The disaster has left the affected households facing the difficult task of rebuilding their homes and restoring their livelihoods as they await possible government intervention.
