World.title: South Sudan: MSF Suspends All Activities in Yei River County Following Abduction
World.content:
press release

Juba — Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders (MSF) suspended all its activities for a minimum of three months starting Tuesday 17 November, in South Sudan’s Yei River County, Central Equatoria State, after armed assailants abducted an MSF staff member and a Ministry of Health midwife on Thursday 12 November. Although both staff members were released unharmed on Saturday 14 November, this incident highlights the continuation of violence against healthcare workers in South Sudan.

MSF denounces in the strongest terms the abduction of humanitarian and medical workers as utterly unacceptable. MSF calls upon authorities and other actors to take responsibility and act decisively to put an end to these incidents.

"The suspension of services was a painful and uneasy decision, given the people's needs in the area, particularly among vulnerable groups, such as pregnant and lactating women, children and the elderly," says Dr Ferdinand Atte, MSF's Head of Mission in South Sudan. "In addition, we had to suspend MSF’s support to the Ebola preparedness, in particular for the management of the isolation facility, which could have dramatic consequences in case of the outbreak in the area."

Only a substantial, sustained and verifiable improvement in the security environment, together with concrete measures to prevent and actively combat abduction crimes would allow MSF to restart activities. At present, no such conditions are in place. "MSF cannot continue operating in Yei area while abductions are now taking place even within the town. The safety and security of our staff comes first," adds Dr Atte.



In August 2025, MSF was forced to temporarily suspend all activities in the same county following two abductions in just over a week. "Following last year's abductions, we received verbal assurances from authorities that medical staff and patients would be safe and protected within the 5-mile radius around Yei," adds Dr Atte. However, on 17 November, armed assailants stopped the MSF ambulance approximately 3 miles from the town.

The MSF driver and Ministry of Health midwife were abducted after an MSF ambulance was stopped at gunpoint by unknown armed assailants while heading back to Jansuk from the Yei Civil Hospital, after referring patients. The incident took place 500 metres from the Jansuk primary healthcare facility.

This was the fifth abduction affecting MSF in Yei River County since 2024, following a period of bombardments, attacks, looting and vandalism of MSF facilities throughout South Sudan. All actors must fulfil their obligations to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure, including healthcare workers, patients, and medical facilities. Healthcare workers must never be targeted.

MSF was supporting Yei Civil Hospital and Jansuk clinic, performing community-based care for gender-based violence, as well as establishing the Ebola Isolation Unit with 10-beds capacity, the only such facility in the County.

Close 

MSF provides medical care to people affected by conflict, displacement and disease outbreaks across six states and two administrative areas in South Sudan, including in areas where hospitals are difficult to reach. MSF has been present in what is today South Sudan since 1983 and remains one of the largest medical humanitarian agencies in the country. From January to October 2026, MSF provided more than 719,349 outpatient consultations (including for children under 5), inpatient care for over 99,658 patients (including 8,771 surgeries), and screened 303,063 children for malnutrition.

World.title: Congo-Kinshasa: Have Drones Given M23 a Regular Army's Reach in Eastern DR Congo?
World.content:
analysis

As government forces also expand their aerial arsenal, the strategic value of these systems complicates prospects for de-escalation.

The eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is rapidly emerging as a key theatre of drone warfare. State militaries and non-state actors alike are exploiting technological advances, a thriving military drone market and cheaper access to commercial aerial vehicles that can be adapted for conflict.

Since 2022 both the Armed Forces of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (FARDC) and rebel groups like M23 have been ramping up drone acquisition and use. The Rwanda-backed rebels captured Goma in North Kivu in January 2025 and Bukavu in South Kivu a month later. Many experts believe these gains would have been impossible without an extensive arsenal of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).



UAVs are used for intelligence, reconnaissance, surveillance and, increasingly, attack missions. Armed Conflict Location & Event Data's John Ngono notes that 'since July we have seen [increased drone use] by M23 during its counter-offensive to prevent the FARDC from gaining control of Minembwe, a strategic headquarters for M23 in South Kivu.'

Recent shifts in the DRC's political landscape may have contributed to this growing trend. In early October former president Joseph Kabila declared himself leader of the M23-aligned Front for the Refoundation of the Nation.

Fierce fighting followed between M23 and the FARDC and its allied Wazalendo militias. The key focus was an aerial bombing campaign around Uvira - a strategic stronghold near the Burundi border. M23 briefly took the city in December 2025 before the FARDC regained control.

Multiple sources, including the United States (US) Representative to the United Nations (UN), Ambassador Mike Waltz, said M23 used attack drones and Rwanda-supplied artillery during that initial seizure. Several reports suggest the drones were Turkish-made YIHA-IIIs - long-range precision-strike loitering drones.

DRC government-aligned media claim the FARDC shot down three powerful M23 drones during the October offensive, which they claim are Rwanda-supplied long-endurance kamikaze YIHA-III OWA (one-way attack) drones. Rwanda is accused of violating the December 2025 Washington Accords, and numerous senior Rwandan officials face US sanctions.

'We have also seen M23 using civilian or commercial drones and modifying them for their use,' says Ngono. Such drones often require less on-the-ground support and are easier to adapt.

The FARDC's accelerated drone use is also extensively documented. The UN Group of Experts' final report, released in June 2026, says the army has used Turkish long-endurance drones (with 'external technical or operational assistance') and Chinese CH-4 and CH-5 drones. And Burundi has reportedly purchased drones for use in the DRC.

Media reports also suggest the FARDC's capabilities have been enhanced with support from Blackwater founder Erik Prince, a private US military contractor who is part of a DRC military support mission.

All this points to growing drone use, which the International Committee of the Red Cross warns 'drastically' increases the risk of civilian harm. '[More] drones have been used in this past year than in all the previous years' since the military started using drones in the DRC in 2022, says Ngono.

Two main drivers are the terrain and availability. The DRC is vast, and UAVs have given both sides a commanding presence in the skies.

M23's capture of airports and an airstrip has given it the infrastructure to launch larger military-grade drones. It has also enabled the M23 rebels to project power beyond the conflict zone and level the playing field between armed groups and the state.

The UN report says M23 used kamikaze drones in its February 2026 attack on Kisangani airport, some 400 km from the frontline. The rebels claimed the FARDC was using the airport as a military drone command centre.

The attack significantly damaged the control tower and runway. Peter Sereko, a former South African Army brigadier general who commanded an infantry unit in the DRC as part of a stabilisation force, told ISS Today that 'it was just small calibre weapons' a decade ago, 'but ... when I returned to DRC in 2024 ... the M23 had the capability of a regular army.'

UAV advances have also enabled each side to target economic assets. According to FARDC sources, the army has mounted drone strikes on key rebel-held mining sites such as Rubaya, which Ngono says 'produces around 15% of the global coltan supply.' UN experts estimate the site earns M23 US$800 000 a month - revenue that helps the rebels stockpile weapons.

Both sides have relied on external help to restock their drone arsenals, but Ngono believes M23 is depending less on Rwandan trainers and on-the-ground support. Although the rebels may still receive intelligence support and access to mobile air defence systems from Rwanda, technical operations are largely driven by M23 coalition fighters themselves, he says.

Rwanda justifies its military presence in the DRC as protection against the Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Rwanda (FDLR) militia. As recently as December 2025, UN estimates put the number of Rwanda Defence Force troops at up to 10 000 in South Kivu and 8 000 in North Kivu.

Given drones' strategic, tactical and psychological value, their rapid proliferation in the DRC could complicate military de-escalation and lasting peace. There is mounting evidence that simply possessing UAV capability has significant strategic value, including as a propaganda tool.

Close 

A recent Africa Center for Strategic Studies (ACSS) report notes that 80% of Africa's major armed non-state actors 'have now used small unmanned systems to drop mortars or conduct Kamikaze attacks.' Drones are also growing more sophisticated, with 'capabilities such as fibre-optic controls and AI enabled targeting' that make them harder to detect and neutralise.

The ACSS echoes earlier calls by the Institute for Security Studies (ISS) and others for African governments to consider a more risk-based approach to importing drones and drone parts, and to invest more in anti-drone technologies.

However, an African drone arms race is already underway, with unconfirmed reports that Ukraine is becoming a player in this space - including in the DRC. If so, it would join global and regional powers such as China, Turkey and the United Arab Emirates - all with a stake in the DRC conflict.

For permission to re-publish ISS Today articles, please email us. In South Africa, News24 has exclusive rights to republish ISS Today articles. In Nigeria, Premium Times has exclusive rights to republish ISS Today articles.

Karen Allen, ISS Consultant, independent researcher and former BBC foreign correspondent

World.title: Ethiopia: COP31 Ends in Deadlock, Leaving Ethiopia to Pick Up the Pieces
World.content:
Around the venue at COP31.

Antalya, TÃ¼rkiye — There is no final cover decision at this year's United Nations climate summit after countries did not agree on a text that explicitly mentions moving away from fossil fuels.

The deadlock, which has happened only once before, comes after a record 44 hours of overtime.

Several other issues, including climate science, energy policy and climate finance for developing nations, remain unresolved.

Ethiopia, which is hosting COP32 in Addis Ababa next year, must revive the talks and address the deep divisions sown in Antalya, Turkey.



This is a major setback not only for international climate diplomacy but also for Africa.

But the continent has made some progress, and it can use its hosting role next year to build on that momentum and push for stronger commitments on climate finance and adaptation.

Africa's setbacks Fossil Fuels

A major tension at the annual two-week conference was the move away from coal, oil and gas.

African negotiators and campaigners were pushing for a cover decision that explicitly mentions the transition away from fossil fuels.

But fossil fuel-dependent countries, like Saudi Arabia, pushed back, arguing that countries should retain flexibility in how they choose to reduce emissions.

Fossil fuels are the primary driver of the climate crisis.

A cover decision, an agreement led by the COP31 President and Turkish Environment Minister Murat Kurum, summarises the summit's political commitments and guides future climate action.

Kurum clashed with UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell during the closing plenary.

Stiell tried to intervene during proceedings, and Kurum asked him to go back to his seat.

Kurum also clashed with Nana Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, the Chair of the African Group of Negotiators (AGN), after the COP31 president interrupted Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, Ghana's minister of environment, who was speaking on behalf of the African Group at the closing plenary.

Agyeman-Rawlings reiterated the need for an inclusive, transparent and respectful process in the international climate negotiations.

The European Union also rejected the cover decision.

People from all over the world gathered in Antalya, Turkey for the two-week climate conference. Credit: Farai Shawn Matiashe/IPS

Adaptation Finance

The AGN was pushing for adaptation finance at COP31. After Parties agreed to triple adaptation finance at COP30 in Belém, with a target year of 2035, African countries wanted the summit to agree on a baseline from which the figure is being tripled. But that is still not clear. If developed countries triple adaptation finance from the $40bn agreed at COP26 in Glasgow, they will provide $120bn annually by 2035.

This is important because African countries lose an average of 2% to 5% of their Gross Domestic Product (GDP) every year because of climate extremes. Yet governments in Africa spend up to 9% of their annual budgets on unplanned disaster relief and climate response.

Jiwoh Abdulai, Minister of Environment and Climate of Sierra Leone, said it is deeply disappointing that COP31 failed to make meaningful progress on climate issues that have devastating effects on the most vulnerable people.

"Farmers are losing their harvests, children unable to learn in extreme heat, and communities losing lives and livelihoods to devastating floods and droughts," he said.

"We came to COP to make progress, in particular on adaptation finance. This is an urgent need. We remain committed to the multilateral process - global cooperation is critical and urgent."

Members of the African Group huddle in the corridors during the COP31 negotiations. Credit: UN Climate Change/Kiara Worth

Just Transition Mechanism (BAM)

Africa was pushing for an institution that can coordinate and support a just transition for workers and vulnerable communities as the world shifts to a low-carbon economy.

But wealthy nations wanted the already overstretched UN climate secretariat and external institutions, including development banks, to take responsibility.

Africa does not want another bureaucratic process.

This year's collapse of the COP deal has reversed the gains made at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, where they agreed to BAM.

Mohamed Adow, a director of a Nairobi-based think tank, Power Shift Africa, said it is disappointing that rich countries blocked the creation of a just transition mechanism.

"Agreeing to do so was one of the most promising outcomes from last year's meeting in Brazil. And yet countries could not even achieve that modest goal in Antalya," he said.

"We need decisive action to accelerate the much-needed just transition, not more evasion."

Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, Ghana, gesticulates during the closing plenary of COP31. Credit: Kiara Worth/UN Climate Change

IPCC Reports

Another dispute among countries at COP31 included the timetable for assessments by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN-backed authority on climate science.

Fossil fuel-dependent countries like Saudi Arabia and India were pushing to delay the next reports to 2029. Kenya also wants the report to be delayed, citing lack of capacity.

But dozens of European, African and Pacific nations wanted to publish them ahead of the 2028 global stocktake.

The IPCC reports will measure international progress on reducing emissions and inform countries on their future climate commitments.

Electrification

COP31 President was pushing to increase renewable electricity from the current 20% to 35% by 2035.

Despite concerns from several African countries regarding the financing of the proposed electrification, a handful of countries backed the initiative.

Ethiopia, Kenya, Togo, Uganda, and Zambia publicly announced support for the COP31 Presidency's voluntary "35 by 35" global electrification pledge in Antalya.

This was in the cover decision, which COP31 did not adopt.

COP31 President Murat Kurum and President of Negotiations Chris Bowen confer at the final plenary. Credit: Kiara Worth/UN Climate Change

Africa's wins Loss and Damage Fund

There is hope for developing countries, including African nations, as developed countries convert their pledges into contributions to the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage.

As of July 31, 2026, developed countries have pledged about USD822m to the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage, operationalised at COP28 in Dubai.

About half of this amount turned into contributions before the end of COP31.

The European Union is also among the countries that converted their contributions.

Close 

In the resort city of Antalya, Spain also committed USD16.4m to the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage.

More Pledges to GEF

Denmark, South Korea, Belgium and Germany pledged a combined USD200m in funding managed by the Global Environment Facility (GEF).

Germany pledged EUR 18m (USD 19.7m) to the GEF's Least Developed Countries Fund (LDCF).

The offers bring pledges to more than USD 4.5 billion for 2026-2030, according to the GEF.

The GEF facility supports countries' efforts to tackle the root causes of environmental degradation by providing financing primarily as grants.

Carbon Credits

During COP31, the Leaf Coalition, a public-private global initiative designed to halt tropical deforestation by mobilising large-scale financial support for forest-protecting jurisdictions, announced that Ghana would be the first country to access finance for a carbon credit project.

Ghana will get millions of dollars as buyers transact credits. The REDD+ program covers approximately 2.5 million hectares of forest across 10 regions in southern and central Ghana where forests are threatened by agricultural expansion, illegal logging and mining.

But Adow said promoting unproven and "eye-wateringly" expensive carbon removal technologies is a lifeline to the fossil fuel industry.

"These climate summits should be about accelerating the demise of fossil fuels, not letting them tout far-fetched schemes that act as get-out-of-jail-free cards," he said.

Parties will now carry the outstanding disagreements to COP32 in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, in 2027.

IPS UN Bureau Report

World.title: Mozambique: Mondlane to Be Questioned By Revimo During Fifth Day of His Trial
World.content:
Maputo — During fifth day of his trial, Venâncio Mondlane, a former presidential candidate and leader of the National Alliance for a Free and Autonomous Mozambique (Anamola), will be questioned by the lawyer Rodrigo Rocha, who acts as an assistant to the Attorney General's Office (PGR) on behalf of the controversial state-owned company Revimo (Mozambique Road Network).

Mondlane is standing trial for allegedly committing five crimes related to 2024 post-election mass demonstrations, namely: public apology for a crime; incitement to collective disobedience; public instigation to crime; instigation and incitement to terrorism. The mass demonstration he called to protest started peacefully but then degenerated into rioting.

Revimo is basically a state-owned company. 70 percent of its shares are held by the government's Road Fund, 15 per cent by the Bank of Mozambique Pension Fund, and 15 per cent by the National Social Security Institute (INSS).

Among the roads operated by Revimo are the Maputo Ring Road (71.4 kilometers long), the Maputo-KaTembe bridge, and the connecting roads to the border with the South African province of Kwazulu-Natal (187 kilometres), and the Beira-Zimbabwe highway (287 kilometres).

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Rioting and destruction halted the collection of tolls in December 2024. Rioters who infiltrated the demonstrations utterly destroyed some of the tollgates.

Rocha is expected to question the defendant regarding his role in the destruction of REVIMO's toll plazas. During the trial, Rocha has once requested the court to sanction Mondlane and other individuals who provide statements to the press, arguing that they do so without proper decorum or with a lack of respect for public institutions. To date, none of his requests have been granted by the Court.

On Friday, during the fourth day of the trial, President of the Supreme Court's Criminal Section, Luís Mondlane, authorized Mondlane's defender Shamir Mendes to remain in the courtroom, but without the right to speak.

World.title: South Africa: Is South Africa Losing Ground Against HIV? These Four Graphs Offer a Warning
World.content:
Lenacapavir, the six-monthly anti-HIV jab, which prevents HIV through sex, is now stocked for free at 360 government clinics in six of South Africaâs provinces.

Findings from one of the world's largest ongoing population surveys tracking HIV, in rural KwaZulu-Natal, are "a sobering warning", researchers say.

All four indicators they analysed show that the momentum in bringing the HIV epidemic under control has been lost — which could mean it could start growing again.

It's a pivotal moment, experts say. South Africa will have to get smart about testing people and getting them on to treatment or prevention if the country were to end HIV as a public health threat.

We unpack the numbers.

Findings from one of the world's largest ongoing population surveys tracking HIV, in rural KwaZulu-Natal, are "a sobering warning" that progress towards getting the HIV epidemic under control has stalled. We unpack what the data means for the future.

In 2002, a large HIV survey from South Africa made the world sit up.



Field workers from the Human Sciences Research Council (HSRC) knocked on thousands of doors across the country to ask people to complete a questionnaire and give a small blood sample.

The results were alarming: 11 out of 100 people in South Africa tested positive for the virus at a time when politicians were in denial about the link between HIV and Aids — a stance that cost an estimated 330 000 lives between 2001 and 2005.

Knowing the true size of the epidemic set the wheels in motion for a public health response that would — over the next 25 years — grow to the world's biggest HIV treatment and prevention programmes.

Today, just under 6.2-million of the estimated 7.9-million people with HIV in the country are on treatment, and the health department says that by the end of September, around 2.43-million HIV-negative people had used HIV prevention medicine, or PrEP (short for pre-exposure prophylaxis) since it became available in the public health sector .

And now findings from another door-to-door study — this time run by the Africa Health Research Institute (Ahri) in the uMkhanyakude district in KwaZulu-Natal and in which close to 30 000 people have been tested for HIV every year over 20 years — are again sounding what researchers say is "a sobering warning".

Studies like this, which track an entire population over a long time in a community with high levels of HIV, puts "a very sensitive finger on the pulse of the epidemic", says Frank Tanser, the senior author on the paper. Because the data is not biased by researchers only studying people who visit clinics, results give a true reflection of what's happening in real life. This is different from models, which give a projected view of the situation based on input values that usually come from national surveys that happen only every few years, clinic reports and (albeit rigorous) mathematical assumptions.

Researchers looked at four indicators in the study: the number of new infections ( incidence ) in the community; the ratio of incidence to prevalence (how many people already have HIV in the community); the lifetime chance of someone getting infected; and viral load (how much HIV someone has in their blood; if someone uses their treatment correctly, their viral load becomes so low that they can't transmit the virus ).

Progress towards getting the epidemic under control is "faltering in KwaZulu-Natal" , the authors wrote, which is something "we should definitely be worried about", Helen Rees, executive director at Wits RHI, told Bhekisisa last week in a podcast.

South Africa's success in rolling out antiretrovirals to millions of people through the public health system may have led us to believe the epidemic is more under control than it really is, the findings suggest.

Here's what the numbers mean — and why experts say South Africa is at a turning point in its fight against HIV.

A lifetime of risk

Imagine you're a teacher in this community and there are 100 fifteen-year-old girls at your school. In 2004, chances were that 75 of them could have HIV by the time they turned 55, assuming that the rate at which new infections occurred remained the same and that everyone survived for 40 years.

Two decades on, the prospect is not looking much better: today, the projected chance of a 15-year-old girl having HIV by age 55 sits at 50 out of 100. It's worse than what boys' future outlook was 10 years ago.

Although the chance of someone getting HIV over their lifetime has declined among both men and women, it remains stubbornly high among women — and more so than in men.

Nationally, one in nine young people are likely to have had sex by the time they turn 15. For girls, early sexual debut could mean a higher risk of HIV, not simply because of biological reasons (developing tissues in the cervix and vagina may be easier targets for the virus ), but also because of the unequal position of women in society . Girls may have little power to negotiate when or who they have sex with, especially in relationships with older men, who are often at least five years older and may have more than one partner at once.

Findings from the study are "in many ways an 'action agenda' of what needs to be done to get back on track", says Mitchell Warren, head of the international HIV advocacy organisation Avac , including scaling up the roll-out of new prevention medicines like lenacapavir, a six-monthly injection, fast and smart .

'Staying still is not good enough'

Fifteen years ago, about four new infections were recorded among 100 women each year and about two among every 100 men. Then the rate dropped markedly, with incidence among men down to half of what it was before and about two-thirds in women by 2019.

And then progress stalled.

Although the rates of new infections aren't picking up, they're not dropping either, meaning that the big gains from before have stopped.

"Staying still is not good enough," says Warren.

Many people in uMkhanyakude have HIV and money from Pepfar (the US President's Fund for Aids Relief) has helped to set up programmes to get people tested and on treatment . The stagnating incidence trend could be a worrying sign of what could happen in other areas also with high HIV burdens — especially when Pepfar money is pulled out of South Africa for good from early next year , without strategic plans being in place for relying solely on government money .

"There's limited time to ensure that we don't see declines in resources and programmes being set back even further," says Warren. "Although we can't go back to January 2025 [when US foreign aid was abruptly frozen and later withdrawn ], we also can't stand still. In the wake of the US mid-term elections, I hope that this new Congress will push the Administration to articulate much clearer and more strategic plans to transition and that we aren't doing this at breakneck speed with recklessness and without a plan."

Down but not yet out

In the early 2000s, there were about four new infections on average over the lifespan of a person living with HIV in this community. It dropped sharply in the following years, coming close to a value of one by 2019.

Since then, the number has been hovering around the same level.

The incidence-to-prevalence ratio is one way for researchers to track progress towards epidemic control . It compares the number of new HIV infections each year with the total number of people who already have HIV, taking into account the average survival time (around 33 years) . If the ratio is bigger than 1, the epidemic is growing. If the ratio is smaller than 1, the epidemic is shrinking. If the ratio is equal to 1, the epidemic is broadly stable, suggesting that progress towards epidemic control has stalled. If more new infections are recorded than the number of people already infected — in other words, if the ratio is bigger than 1 — the epidemic is growing. If the number is smaller than 1, the epidemic is shrinking. If the ratio is equal to 1, the epidemic is broadly stable, which means progress towards stamping it out has stalled.

The data from this study "provides an important baseline for how we need to do monitoring in the future", says Warren. If things carry on in this way, getting 95% of people with HIV on treatment and 95% of those to be virally suppressed — the second and third targets in a cascading series set by UNAids to end the epidemic — will not be possible.

But, says Warren, we have to get the first target in the series — getting 95% of people tested — right to start with. "We often say we need treatment and we need prevention. But we also need testing at massive levels, because that's how we're going to find more people living with HIV who are not yet on treatment, and it's how we're going to find people who are not living with HIV and who can benefit from PrEP."

Close 

Says Warren: "We talk about antiretroviral treatment. We talk about PrEP. We need to talk about testing as the gateway to both of those."

A growing burden

Fifteen years ago, 70–80% of people with HIV had more than 1 550 copies of the virus per millilitre of blood. The proportion halved in less than 10 years.

But the trend has reversed over the past six years, and now at least 44% of people again have high viral loads, suggesting that more people either are not on treatment yet (or not on the right plan) or have stopped taking their medicine .

At a viral load of >1000 copies/mL, the virus is not suppressed , which means that the infection can spread through unprotected sex.

The numbers seen here are roughly 30 percentage points away from the UN's cascade-implied target of close to 86% of HIV-positive people on treatment having to be virally suppressed to end the HIV epidemic. (To work this out, consider a population of 100 people. The target series says that 95% of people have to have been tested. Of those 95 that have been tested, 95% who tested positive have to be on treatment, which means 90 people out of the original group of 100. And then 95% of those — in other words 86 people out of the original 100 — must have suppressed viral loads.)

When many people in a community have high viral loads, there's a bigger chance that the epidemic will start growing again.

This means we have to get smart about testing people and closing the treatment gap . For this, says Warren, we have to build programmes "not around an individual pathogen or disease, but around the individual person", not only in South Africa but also globally.

To build on the success of the past, "we have to be ambitious and we've got to be smarter and more strategic than the virus itself, and that means thinking differently about how we work with communities.

Warren concludes: "That may be the most important shift in our thinking."

This story was produced by the Bhekisisa Centre for Health Journalism .

World.title: Cape Verde: Cape Verde's Elections Were Loud. Its Voters Are Increasingly Silent
World.content:
analysis

On the 29th of October, before 10 o'clock in the morning, a car with speakers has already driven twice through my neighbourhood in Mindelo, the city of Cesária Évora and of Cape Verde's best-known Carnival, blasting MpD (Movimento para a Democracia, Movement for Democracy) viewpoints and a jingle. I notice I'm immediately annoyed, because I'm trying to conduct an interview from home and the noise keeps interrupting the conversation. The same car passes twice more that day. Three days later, on Sunday 1 November, a whole procession of floats drives along the beach, honking, accompanied by Cape Verdean and PAICV (Partido Africano da Independência de Cabo Verde, African Party for the Independence of Cape Verde) flags, candidate headshots and more jingles, while my boyfriend and I are trying to get onto the road in the car. Election season in Cape Verde has begun: a very loud time, and a disruptive one. As an outsider, I wonder whether it has the desired effect, people voting for a certain party, or the opposite: abstention.

The noise is meant to bring people to the polls. In May's parliamentary election, most of them stayed home. Just 46.5 percent of the 416,096 registered voters cast a ballot, down from 57.4 percent in 2021 and 66 percent in 2016. Yet Cape Verde is often held up as one of Africa's most stable democracies, and in May the PAICV, which grew out of the independence movement, returned to power after ten years in opposition. It was the loudest election I've ever witnessed, with central roads closed for concerts and rallies, pickups with speakers crawling through town, and people handing out partisan t-shirts. Six months later, the country was campaigning again, this time for the presidential election on 15 November.

On 12 November at 8pm, the band Corda do Sol plays on Rua Lisboa, ahead of a speech by President José Maria Neves, backed by the PAICV. At the same time, Joana Rosa, the MpD's candidate and former justice minister, is holding a concert with the band Pendrive in Monte Sossego, another neighbourhood. While I'm standing in the crowd, I hear people behind me say: 'Come on, the concert's almost over and the speech starts after this. Let's go to the other concert now.' With street vendors with drinks and food around the corner as part of the rival political campaigns, it's a night out for many people: they run into acquaintances and catch up over the music.



There are two kinds of people in the crowd. Some wear party t-shirts and make it very clear who they're here for and who they'll vote for. The others come for the music and would rather not talk about their political preference. They tell me they're afraid of repercussions. 'If I say I'm voting for this one and the other party gets wind of it, I'm afraid they'll obstruct me in other matters,' one person says. That fear isn't unusual: in a 2024 Afrobarometer survey, more than one in five Cape Verdeans said it was likely that powerful people could find out how they voted, despite the secret ballot. A few people at the concert tell me they won't vote. Others are still undecided, but say it matters to them to use their vote. A few more say they'll cast a blank ballot.

When I asked António Tavares to describe election season, he started much further back, before independence. A choreographer, dancer and researcher, Tavares is the artistic director of the Mindelo Cultural Centre and a co-founder of Bombu Mininu, a cultural space in São Vicente. He was a child when Cape Verde gained independence in 1975, and he says he has never belonged to a political party. According to Tavares, music once carried the dream of independence. Musicians, poets and thinkers imagined the country through lyrics before it existed. 'Music is the material,' he says. 'It's our way of communicating. We are a sonic entity. Why music? Because we knew we were going to leave here. If we had to leave, we had to come up with a Morse code.'

To this day, music is one of the main ways Cape Verdeans communicate. Cape Verde's historic World Cup debut this year came with its own anthem, Nôs Óra Dja Txiga, bringing together artists from across the islands. While the World Cup gave Cape Verdeans a song to unite behind, election season brings a different soundtrack: songs meant to win them over to competing parties. In May, the MpD campaigned with Ulisses na Frente and Cabo Verde pa frente and the PAICV with Francisco Carvalho and Tchico ki nu kre. Behind the songs were competing programmes. Prime Minister Ulisses Correia e Silva's MpD asked for 'one more term to consolidate the gains,' pointing to growth and tourism, and promised more ships, planes and higher wages. The PAICV promised cheaper inter-island ferries and flights, free public university, a higher minimum wage and fewer government posts and agencies. The MpD offered more scholarships instead of free university, and said the PAICV's fares would make inter-island transport unviable.

Whether it wins votes is another matter. People go to the rallies, Tavares says, and 'they take the t-shirts from one side, they take the t-shirts from the other [...]. But that doesn't mean they belong to that party. It's a shirt. They need a shirt. '

And while the campaign music blasts through the streets, the political parties go quiet afterwards. 'The elections end, they leave, they never show up again for four years, then they come back, ' Tavares says.." To him the songs are jingles, 'propaganda of feelings,' and as a way to involve people in politics, this style of campaigning is over: 'For me, it died.' Taking office should be an oath, not a celebration, he argues.

On 15 November, six candidates were on the presidential ballot: President José Maria Neves from PAICV, MpD's Joana Rosa, and four without a party: Antero Tavares, Casimiro de Pina, Gilson Alves, and Loisito de Sousa. Emigration and jobs were central to the campaign: Neves promised a youth convention on employment, while Rosa, the first woman to run for president, argued that young people need reasons to stay and called for a balance of power instead of 'total control by PAICV.' Neves was re-elected in the first round. With 99 percent of polling stations counted, he had 64 percent of the vote, against 31.5 percent for Rosa. But the bigger number was abstention. According to the provisional results, 68.3 percent of the 419,448 registered voters did not vote, a record for Cape Verdean presidential elections. Neves called for a study into why voters are withdrawing and proposed modernising the voting process with electronic voting, as the National Electoral Commission had already proposed after May. Rosa called the abstention a 'ponto negro', a black mark, on Cape Verdean democracy.

Part of the figure may be arithmetic. More than 76,000 registered voters, 18 percent of the roll, live abroad, against 14 percent in 2021, partly because Cape Verdeans abroad are now often registered automatically when applying for a passport. But the declining turnout cannot be explained by registration figures alone.

A 2020 thesis at the University of Mindelo, covering elections from 1991 to 2016, linked rising abstention in Cape Verdemainly to low interest in politics among citizens who don't see their problems being solved. Staying home, it argued, is also a way of punishing politicians.

On paper, there seems little reason for distrust: Transparency International's 2025 Corruption Perceptions Index ranks Cape Verde 35th of 182 countries. Its citizens are less sure. In the Afrobarometer survey, half of Cape Verdeans said corruption had increased over the past year and two-thirds said the government was handling it badly.

Close 

That is what I hear in Mindelo, too. Nelson stopped voting when he was about 25. He no longer believes in politicians. As far as he's concerned, they are only in it for themselves.

Jorge, a Cape Verdean teacher, says the same thing: politicians do the job for the money. He points to the corruption and money-laundering allegations the country has seen involving political figures from both major parties.

Lúcia does vote. There is always so much noise to persuade people to vote, she says. In the last election, young people showed they no longer took it seriously by staying home. She is also careful about discussing politics and never says who she votes for. She votes, she says, for the development of Cape Verde, and leaves it at that.

Still, Tavares doesn't think Cape Verdean democracy is failing. He sees May's change of government as proof that voters have learned to judge parties on what they deliver. 'It's a learning process,' he says. It's the politicians who haven't kept up: 'The Cape Verdean politician is a politician of discourse, not a politician who makes things happen.'

After three elections in less than two years, Tavares believes people have grown tired of the spectacle. 'If we asked people today whether they want elections in this form, nobody does. We're tired.'

Some names have been changed to protect people's privacy.

Carmen Esselink is an independent journalist living and working in Cape Verde. She previously worked for eight years as a TV editor and online content strategist at Dutch public broadcaster BNNVARA. She produces human-interest stories that connect culture, travel, politics, and sustainability for Dutch and international outlets, such as Condé Nast Traveller, Business Insider, Minority Africa, and soon Wander With Wonder and AFAR.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 23, 2026
World.content:
COP31 Ends Without Global Climate Agreement

The COP31 in Türkiye closed without an overarching climate deal after almost 200 countries could not agree on a consensus after two days of extended talks. The European Union, UK, Panama and others rejected the proposed Antalya Pact, which was marred by deep divisions on fossil fuels, climate finance and the 1.5C warming threshold. UN Secretary-General António Guterres expressed disappointment, and climate advocates denounced the failure to secure a clear commitment to move away from fossil fuels and to boost adaptation funding for vulnerable countries. The result leaves major questions unresolved on climate finance, energy transitions and support for communities facing worsening climate impacts for Africa and other developing countries. The target was scrapped in the final draft, which would have seen adaptation funding for developing countries ramped up to at least $120 billion a year by 2035. Despite the setback, separate initiatives on electrification and ocean protection offered some progress, with more than 90 countries supporting an electrification initiative.

Nigerian President Urges Parliament to Decriminalise Attempted Suicide

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Nigerian President Bola Tinubu has asked parliament to decriminalise attempted suicide. He called for survivors to receive medical treatment and mental health support rather than face prosecution. The proposed reforms, contained in the National Suicide Prevention Bill and National Mental Health Amendment Bill, seek to replace criminal penalties with rehabilitation and care. Attempted suicide currently carries prison sentences of up to one year in most Nigerian states and five years in some northern states. The government aims to reduce suicide attempts and deaths by 15% by 2030. Mental health advocates said that criminalisation deepens stigma and discourages people from seeking help. They warned that the country's shortage of psychiatrists and limited access to mental healthcare must also be addressed. Nigeria records an estimated 300,000 suicide attempts and at least 7,000 deaths annually, according to figures cited by the health minister. The country has fewer than 1,000 psychiatrists serving a population of more than 200 million people.

Drug Investigation Uncovers South Africa-Brazil-Australia Cocaine Network

An international drug trafficking investigation involving South Africa, Brazil and Australia has uncovered links between a fatal aircraft crash, cocaine shipments and an alleged transnational criminal network. Australian pilot Timothy Clark died in September 2025 when his small aircraft, which had flown from South Africa to Brazil, crashed in a sugarcane field carrying 202kg of cocaine. The investigation has since led to a major crackdown in Brazil, where police arrested five people and seized about 660kg of cocaine, alongside other drugs. Brazilian and Australian authorities say the network used small aircraft to transport drugs internationally. Investigators have also identified alleged links between the pilot and individuals arrested in Australia in 2024, including a German national reportedly based in South Africa, with possible connections to the Kinahan cartel. Australian authorities said the arrests in 2024 followed the seizure of about 200kg of cocaine, aviation equipment and other items. The latest developments underscore the international nature of drug trafficking networks and growing concerns about South Africa's links to the trade.

Kenya and DR Congo Move to Restore Diplomatic Relations

Kenyan President William Ruto and Democratic Republic of Congo President Félix Tshisekedi have agreed to restore full diplomatic relations following talks in the Republic of Congo. The two leaders committed to restoring ambassador-level representation, resuming the Joint Grand Commission for Cooperation and strengthening diplomatic consultations. Their agreement also seeks to expand cooperation in trade, economic development, security and cultural exchanges, while promoting regional peace and stability. The talks were facilitated by Republic of Congo President Denis Sassou N'Guesso, with Togo's President of the Council of Ministers, Faure Gnassingbé, participating as the African Union mediator. The deal comes after years of a turbulent relationship between Nairobi and Kinshasa. Ruto thanked the mediators for the talks, and said Kenya's commitment to diplomatic dialog and African-led solutions remained. The resumption of engagement is expected to provide a framework for the rebuilding of trust and strengthening of economic and security ties between the two countries.

Search Continues After Boat Carrying Mourners Capsizes in Nigeria

At least 24 people have died after a boat carrying mourners to a burial ceremony capsized in Nigeria's southern Bayelsa State. The vessel was travelling from Ayama to Ukubie on Friday when it sank, with preliminary reports suggesting a mechanical failure. Nigeria's National Emergency Management Agency confirmed that 24 bodies had been recovered as search and rescue operations continued. Authorities initially rescued four people, including two children, but have yet to establish the total number of passengers on board. President Bola Tinubu expressed his condolences to the affected families. Boat accidents are frequent in Nigeria and are usually linked to overloading, poor maintenance, and failure to comply with safety rules. The latest tragedy comes after several other deadly incidents, including a boat accident in Sokoto State in August that killed at least 51 people. Authorities have called for improved safety measures as rescue teams continue searching for survivors.

Suspected Drone Attack Sinks Russian Ship in Libya

Libya's eastern government said that a suspected drone attack caused an explosion aboard a Russian naval ship docked at Benghazi port, leaving the vessel reportedly capsized and sunk. The incident happened while the ship was reportedly stopping for fuel and supplies on its return journey to Russia. No casualties were reported, although a separate commercial vessel was also reportedly targeted, leaving several people with minor injuries. The United Nations called for an independent and transparent investigation, warning against Libya becoming a battleground for foreign conflicts. Neither Moscow nor the authorities have confirmed who was behind the suspected attack, although a Libya specialist suggested Ukraine could be responsible. The eastern government said the Russian vessel was operating under an existing maritime agreement and condemned the incident as a violation of Libya's sovereignty. The attack comes amid concerns that the country's ports and infrastructure could become entangled in the wider Russia-Ukraine conflict.

Close 

UN Building Damaged in Drone Attack on Sudan's Khartoum

The United Nations has reported a drone attack on a residential area in Sudan's capital, Khartoum, which damaged a UN building in a civilian neighbourhood. Explosions were heard near Khartoum Airport and other parts of the city in the early hours of Sunday, with reports that a residential house was destroyed. No casualties were immediately confirmed. A Sudanese army source alleged that the drones were launched from Ethiopia, an accusation Addis Ababa has previously denied. The strike comes amid a surge in drone attacks in Sudan's civil war, which has been raging since April 2023 between the army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF). The conflict has killed tens of thousands and displaced more than 14 million people, while UN figures indicate that drone attacks killed more than 1,100 people in the first six months of this year. The UN's Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Sudan, Denise Brown, condemned the risks posed to humanitarian personnel and facilities. The latest incident follows another drone strike in West Kordofan that killed 15 people, including four children. Local Government MEC Anton Bredell expressed sympathy for affected residents. He described the destruction as particularly heartbreaking. Authorities have appointed an investigator to determine the cause of the fire.

World.title: Mozambique: OMR fined $27,400 for Making Documentary Film About Post-election Protests Without Permission
World.content:
The 2024 audiovisual and cinema decree apparently gives pre-filming censorship power to Mozambique’s National Institute of Cultural and Creative Industries (INICC). The law requires authorisation before the production of any film, according to INICC director Roberto Dove. Thus OMR (Rural Environment Observatory) has been fined $27,400 for filming its documentary Não é nosso país este aqui? (Isn't This Our Country?) without a licence. The documentary was coordinated by researcher João Feijó examines the social and economic causes of the 2024–2025 post-election protests. (Savana 20 Nov)

“The timing and scale of the penalty raise questions about whether audiovisual licensing rules are being used to restrict politically sensitive expression. The documentary addresses the same protests now under examination in Venâncio Mondlane's trial” writes Zitamar. (20 Nov) The fine is unprecedented and comes after Cinema Scala in Maputo was forced to cancel a screening on 20 October.

The trial by five Supreme Court judges is in a small courtroom. It is not being broadcast and journalists and others present are not allowed to record or photograph the proceeding, and thus depend on taking notes. Discussion is largely on television and social media, and there is increasing attempt to restrict this. OMR is one of the most important research institutes in Mozambique, but is a civil society organisation dependent on donations, so the fine will hit hard.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Mozambican Bar Association (OAM) Friday (21 Nov) prohibited lawyers and trainee lawyers from publicly commenting on ongoing trials without prior authorisation from the organisation. “Lawyers must not make public statements, or discuss or contribute to public or media discussions, on professional matters pending or to be brought before courts or other State bodies. They must refrain from any conduct intended to influence the outcome of pending cases,” reads an OAM statement.

Meanwhile President Daniel Chapo has been touring Zambezia province with five ministers in a highly publicised tour of government buildings such as police stations damaged in the post-election demonstrations. In a rally in Namacurra Thursday, he linked the destruction of public infrastructure to the actions of “enemies of the people”. (Lusa 19 Nov) He did not mention the killing of demonstrators by the police, which triggered the violence.

World.title: Americans don’t have to choose between our AI future and ripping off copyright owners
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

One of the biggest court battles over artificial intelligence (AI) is putting an age-old legal principle to the test — and raising important questions about the Trump administration's AI policy.

Several news organizations, including The New York Times, are suing OpenAI and Microsoft for using millions of newspaper articles to train AI systems. The newspapers argue that the tech firms violated basic copyright protections. The tech firms contend that training their models on those articles qualifies as "fair use," a longstanding principle that allows copyrighted material to be used in certain ways without permission from or compensation to the copyright owner.

The Department of Justice (DOJ) has sided squarely with OpenAI's position — breaking with the administration's previously more balanced stance on the issue. The DOJ filed a statement of interest embracing an extreme vision of fair use that would grant AI companies virtually unfettered access to copyrighted material for commercial training, without obtaining permission from or compensating the creators whose works fuel these systems.

MIKE DAVIS: THE TRUMP DOJ SHOULD WITHDRAW ITS STATEMENT OF INTEREST IN THE OPENAI LAWSUIT

This expansive interpretation threatens to turn a narrow copyright exception into a blanket exemption for the world's most powerful and profitable industries.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

FOX NEWS POLL: VOTERS SEE AI REGULATION AS URGENT, RANK SAFEGUARDS AHEAD OF INNOVATION

Those concerns deserve consideration. But the DOJ's aggressive arguments in the brief depart from more measured guidance elsewhere in the administration. The White House's official AI framework acknowledges valid arguments on both sides of the copyright debate.

Likewise, the Carolina Principles for Emerging Technologies, adopted by G20 ministers at the Commerce Department's recent Innovation Ministerial, recognize that the intersection of AI and copyright poses "complex legal and policy questions." The principles note the "essential role" of copyright protections in supporting creators and call for respecting IP as a pillar of G20 AI policy.

MUSIC INDUSTRY FENDS OFF FLOOD OF AI MUSIC 'STEALING' THE CHARTS

The DOJ statement also overlooks how its stance could favor larger AI companies over smaller firms and startups. Several AI startups have argued that paying for the material they use provides more reliable access to training material, reduces legal uncertainty and improves models. Other companies have emerged to aggregate copyrights and make licensing easier.

It's particularly problematic for large AI companies to complain about paying for access to copyrighted materials. They are among the best positioned to pay for those materials, and doing so would help develop the kind of licensing markets they claim are lacking.

OBAMA CRITICIZES TRUMP ON APPROACH TO AI, ESCALATES WARNING FOR STRONGER REGULATION

And even if national security were a legitimate justification, the government could not simply disregard property rights. The Constitution and other laws require just compensation when private property is taken for public use, and intellectual property rights are still property rights. Letting AI firms appropriate creators' IP without permission or compensation would be akin to letting data center builders seize private land without paying fair value.

If courts adopt the DOJ's position that fair use protects AI developers in virtually all circumstances, it would reduce incentives to create new works. Copyrights encourage creative work by assuring writers, artists and other creators that their work can't be easily stolen or copied. Licensing those rights allows creators to earn a living and underpins over $1 trillion in U.S. economic activity.

Weaker copyrights could result in fewer human-created books, articles, research papers, films and songs. Ironically, that could eventually leave AI systems with fewer and lower-quality materials to train on – a scenario that serves no one's interests.

All of this is why the Trump administration would be wise to follow its own AI framework and let the court system evaluate AI copyright disputes case by case, rather than arguing for unfettered fair use exceptions.

The DOJ's reasoning is that requiring a copyright license for material used in AI training would impose high costs on AI developers. It claims those costs could make it harder for small companies to compete and hamper U.S. AI leadership and national security.

Policymakers also have a role to play. One promising bill is the bipartisan CLEAR Act. Introduced in February by California Democrat Sen. Adam Schiff and Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis, the CLEAR Act would require AI developers to publicly disclose the copyrighted works used in each new generative-AI model's training dataset.

The proposal would not settle whether any particular training practice qualifies as fair use. But it would give creators more information about whether their work helped train an AI system, enabling them to pursue appropriate compensation or other remedies when they believe their rights have been violated.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

That kind of targeted reform offers a useful model for copyright enforcement in the age of AI. Rather than treating licensing as an obstacle to innovation, policymakers should foster a market where AI developers can efficiently license copyrighted material while respecting creators' rights.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

AI innovation is vital to America's future. But America's creative industries still depend on strong copyright protections. Policymakers need to promote both.

World.title: Hunting, fishing and outdoor recreation fuel $704 billion American industry, new data reveals
World.content:
Turns out, spending a Saturday on the lake or a weekend in the deer stand isn't just good for the soul. It's pretty good for the American economy, too.

According to new data released by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, outdoor recreation contributed a whopping $704.2 billion to the U.S. economy in 2025, accounting for 2.3% of the nation's gross domestic product.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

And while that figure includes everything from hiking and camping to RVing and outdoor concerts, fishing and hunting are doing plenty of heavy lifting.

Boating and fishing led all traditional outdoor recreation activities, generating $39.1 billion in economic value added. In fact, it was the largest category across 35 states and Washington, D.C., with Florida ($4.5 billion), California ($3.3 billion) and Texas ($3 billion) leading the way.

FISHING IS BIG BUSINESS, AND FXR FOUNDER SAYS THE SPORT'S GROWTH IS ONLY GETTING STARTED.

Hunting, shooting and trapping weren't far behind, ranking third nationally at $15.1 billion. Texas topped that list with $1.8 billion, followed by California ($849.8 million) and Florida ($831.3 million)

RVing, for those keeping score, came in second at $26.8 billion.

Hunting and fishing support more than just hunters and anglers

Of course, anyone who's ever walked out of a tackle shop $200 poorer than they intended probably isn't shocked that outdoor recreation is a big business.

But the economic impact goes well beyond fishing rods, rifles and bass boats.

Those dollars help support jobs, local businesses and rural communities that depend on visitors coming to hunt, fish and explore the outdoors.

And as the Theodore Roosevelt Conservation Partnership pointed out in its response to the new figures, none of that happens without healthy wildlife populations, accessible public lands and conservation efforts that keep those opportunities available.

The organization cited a National Fish and Wildlife Foundation report finding that conservation spending generates $115.8 billion in economic activity and supports more than 575,000 jobs nationwide.

Meanwhile, the broader outdoor recreation economy continued to grow in 2025, with inflation-adjusted GDP increasing 1.9% and employment climbing 1.7%.

Not bad for a bunch of people who supposedly just want to get away from work.



The bottom line is that hunting, fishing and outdoor recreation aren't just hobbies. They're major economic drivers, and protecting the natural resources that make them possible is an investment that pays off well beyond the woods and water.

World.title: Former Navy SEAL says New Jersey’s Islamophobia bill puts protected speech in the crosshairs
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A New Jersey proposal aimed at combating anti-Muslim discrimination could make Americans think twice before criticizing religious and political ideas, a lawyer and former Navy SEAL warned.

Bill Brown, a partner at Parlatore Law Group, told Fox News Digital that Assembly Bill 1146 contains language broad enough to discourage public debate, even though the legislation expressly preserves First Amendment rights.

"The mere threat of state scrutiny is a direct assault on public debate," Brown said.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

The proposal would establish a state definition of Islamophobia and require public officials and law enforcement officers to consider it when determining whether alleged discriminatory acts were motivated by anti-Muslim bias.

Brown argued that requiring officials to use a definition that includes harsh criticism and other speech could make people afraid to speak openly.

CHRISTIAN GROUPS AND PASTORS SAY NEW CALIFORNIA LGBT HATE SPEECH LAW IS DISGUISED AS INDOCTRINATION

"The First Amendment guarantees that no religion or theology is immune to criticism," he said.

Democratic Assemblyman Joe Danielsen sponsors the bill, which is co-sponsored by fellow Democrats Assemblywomen Verlina Reynolds-Jackson and Mitchelle Drulis and Assemblyman Roy Freiman. The legislation describes a uniform definition as a tool to help officials identify and investigate anti-Muslim crime, harassment and discrimination."

Fox News Digital made multiple attempts to contact Danielsen and all three co-sponsors for comment but did not receive a response.

Its definition includes "hatred or severe disparagement towards Muslim persons or their culture," as well as "rhetorical, violent, or physical anti-Muslim manifestations."

Other examples include pulling hijabs from Muslim women, discriminatory treatment and blaming Muslims collectively for wrongdoing committed by an individual or group.

CONNECTICUT BARS NATIVITY DISPLAY IN STATE CAPITOL BECAUSE IT'S 'RELIGIOUS,' LAWSUIT THREAT SAYS

The bill would create no standalone criminal offense for criticizing Islam. It directs officials to consider the definition when reviewing an alleged violation of an existing policy, law or regulation prohibiting discriminatory acts.

It also explicitly says nothing in the legislation should diminish or infringe on rights protected by the First Amendment or New Jersey’s Constitution.

AMERICA'S FIRST MUSLIM SENATOR EXPOSES A POLITICAL BLIND SPOT

Asked about that safeguard, Brown maintained that the prospect of scrutiny itself could discourage people from speaking, regardless of whether a case ultimately succeeds.

He also singled out a provision in the bill’s legislative findings that lists "anti-Islamism" among terms that may describe the same characteristics as Islamophobia. Brown argued that the wording risks blurring the distinction between prejudice against Muslim people and criticism of a political movement.

JONATHAN TURLEY: FRANCE'S FREE SPEECH CRACKDOWN SHOWS WHAT HAPPENS WHEN POLITICIANS DEFINE TRUTH

"Islamism is a distinct geopolitical movement," he said. "It’s not just a religious faith."

Brown described the proposal as a "backdoor blasphemy law," arguing that government should protect people’s rights while allowing their religious beliefs to face public scrutiny.

PASTOR UNLEASHES ON DEARBORN AS RELIGIOUS TENSIONS ERUPT AT CITY COUNCIL MEETING: 'ENOUGH IS ENOUGH'

The legislation excludes criticism of Muslim-majority countries comparable to criticism directed at other countries. Brown argued that criticism of religious and political ideology also needs protection.

Brown said his concerns are informed in part by his military service. He recalled responding to two suicide bombings in Iraq and said he remains committed to speaking out against jihadist ideology.

He also recalled studying Arabic at Rutgers after leaving the military, where Muslim American classmates helped him when he struggled with the language.

For Brown, the broader concern is whether Americans will feel free to challenge ideas they oppose.

"True diversity is diversity of thought," he said.

World.title: With Skubal signing, the New York Mets should have bought themselves the 2027 World Series title | Ian Miller
World.content:
Cancel the 2027 Major League Baseball season. Why even bother playing the games? We don't need a World Series, just hand the trophy to the New York Mets right now.

Sounds a bit ridiculous, doesn't it? Except those exact phrases were repeatedly used ahead of the 2026 MLB season to describe the Los Angeles Dodgers. Because they signed Kyle Tucker and Edwin Diaz after winning the 2025 World Series over the Toronto Blue Jays.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Now though? The Dodgers are on the outside looking in, thanks to the Mets' stunning, 9-year, $450 million deal with superstar starting pitcher Tarik Skubal. Who we were told just a few months ago was going to bring about the end of baseball after being traded to those same Dodgers at the deadline.

METS, TARIK SKUBAL AGREE TO RECORD CONTRACT AS MLB LOCKOUT LOOMS OVER OFFSEASON

First, some background on Skubal. He just turned 30, meaning he'll play all of 2027 in his age-30 season. He's been one of the best handful of pitchers in baseball for the past four seasons, with ERAs under 2.80 in each. His command and consistency is second to none, with walk rates from 2023–2026 of 1.57 per nine innings, 1.64, 1.52, and 1.53. Hard to be more consistent than that.

He's been worth, per Fangraphs WAR calculations, 3.3 wins above replacement in 2023 in just 15 starts, 6.0 in 2024, 6.7 in 2025, and 5.2 in 2026, despite making only 26 starts. Skubal is a two-time Cy Young Award winner, and if you made a list of pitchers you'd want taking the ball in a postseason game, he'd be at or near the top, along with Jacob Misiorowski, Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Chris Sale or Paul Skenes.

NEW STATEMENTS FROM ROB MANFRED, MLBPA, GUARANTEE BASEBALL IS SHUT DOWN INDEFINITELY IN TWO WEEKS

He was widely expected to get the largest free agency contract for a pitcher ever handed out, and that's exactly what he got from Mets owner Steve Cohen and a beleaguered front office. At least three other teams, the Dodgers, Blue Jays and San Diego Padres, met with Skubal. But only New York was willing to get to a whopping $50 million per year for the remainder of his career.

Now though, it's worth evaluating what this actually means, the fan reaction, and how this impacts New York's chances of winning their first World Series since 1986.

The short version? Fans don't seem to be bothered by the fact that the Mets have now guaranteed over $1.2 billion to just two players: Skubal and Juan Soto. Yes, there's been some complaining about big markets, but there's little of the wailing and gnashing of teeth that explode when the Dodgers make an acquisition or signing. The implication here is that fans don't care when bad teams try to improve, only good teams. An interesting sentiment.

What does it actually mean for baseball, for free agency, and for the Mets? Well, there's plenty to dig into. For baseball, it once again means that money is flowing into the sport at a record pace. The Mets do not have the Dodgers' television deal that's caused such misplaced consternation among fans. They are conclusively the second team in their media market, although New York obviously is not your average market, and they ranked No. 12 out of 30 teams in attendance in 2025.

In fact, they sold 1.3 million fewer tickets than the Dodgers and 600,000 fewer than the Padres.

So how are they raking in enough money to afford $1.2 billion on two players? On top of that, they have to pay the rest of the roster while also paying tens of millions for the luxury tax, scouting, research and development and so on.

Maybe, just maybe, there's more money coming into baseball teams than they're willing to let on. That might have raised some interesting possibilities, wouldn't it?

As for what it means for free agency, again, this is why the players don't want a salary cap. Clearly, teams can afford these types of contracts. Clearly, the interest is there for a pitcher with a lengthy and recent injury history to make $50 million per year. It's not the players' problem that some owners are cheap, or some are more concerned with increasing their franchise valuations or raking in another $50 million in profits, than they are with fielding a competitive baseball team. That's on the owners to figure out. So why should players take a massive cut in both total income and potential peak income, just to make ownership richer?

But what about competitive balance? Doesn't this, as the headline suggests, guarantee the Mets a championship? Shouldn't we just cancel the season now?

MILWAUKEE BREWERS BROKE BASEBALL ON THEIR WAY TO REMARKABLY DOMINANT WORLD SERIES RUN

Of course not. It's ridiculous to even suggest that it guarantees anything. Just as it was ridiculous to suggest that the Dodgers bought their title, or would ruin baseball by trading for Skubal in the first place. We just saw, with the Milwaukee Brewers, how postseason baseball actually works.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

The Dodgers entered October with arguably the greatest playoff rotation in modern memory. Skubal, Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow. It was better than their rotation in 2024 or 2025, and significantly better than any that the competition brought to the postseason. How'd it work out for them?

Well, all four of those pitchers started the four games of the NLCS. And the Dodgers lost all four. Brewers' Robert Gasser (who is not a Cy Young contender), was one of the best pitchers in the postseason. Despite a woeful strikeout rate and thanks to incredible luck on balls put in play, Gasser had a 0.60 ERA in the playoffs. He gave up one run in over 15 innings. Skubal gave up three in 11 innings.

Aaron Ashby was the most valuable pitcher of the playoffs, with just five hits allowed in 18 innings, only three walks, literally zero runs, and 20 strikeouts. He was making $5.5 million, compared to Skubal's upcoming $50 million salary. Drew Rasmussen also earned $5.5 million and was brilliant over 28 playoff innings, with just a 2.20 ERA. Gavin Williams was dominant too, making $822,000. Should Skubal make 30 starts in 2027, he will take home $1.67 million per start. More than double Williams' yearly salary. And Williams outpitched him in October.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

This is the problem with fans trying to say you can "buy" a title. You cannot. Because the small sample sizes of playoff baseball mean that players like Williams, Rasmussen, Ashby and Gasser can outpitch Skubal, Yamamoto or Chris Sale over a few weeks' span. It's not even remotely surprising that it happens! In fact, it happens all the time during the regular season, though nobody notices, or cares.

Gasser, who nobody outside of Brewers fans or hardcore baseball diehards had even heard of, threw the best start by a left-handed pitcher in a World Series since Sandy Koufax. Skubal's never made the World Series. That's how baseball works.

For the Mets in particular, they're still not very good! They were 74-88 in 2026, and assuming Skubal puts up another Cy Young-caliber six WAR season, and all other things remain equal, they'd be an 80-win team in 2027. That's still bad. They were bad at everything in 2026. Here's how they ranked in some important statistical categories last season:

No. 20 in runs per game offensively

No. 24 in batting WAR

No. 23 in baserunning

No. 18 in runs allowed per game defensively

No. 21 in team weighted runs created plus

No. 23 in weighted on base average

No. 25 in outs above average

No. 23 in rotation ERA

No. 27 in team OBP

No. 23 in team slugging percentage



Skubal will help some, but one player ain't fixing that mess. Even with spending as much or more than any team in baseball over the past five seasons. And over $400 million in commitments for next year. Lindor had the worst season of his career and is now 33 years old. Bichette made over $40 million to be a below-average hitter. Former top prospect Brett Baty has looked awful. A.J. Ewing was a below average hitter. Juan Soto missed time and while still outstanding, was far below his 2024 peaks. Carson Benge was the lone bright spot, but used some BABIP luck to boost his numbers.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Their rotation looks solid, but the back half is still shaky at best. And as usual, there's no depth. Devin Williams was mediocre, and Freddy Peralta and Clay Holmes are now free agents.

This is the problem fans ignore when talking about free agency; teams paying for players in their 30s are paying for the declining phase of their careers. Especially with pitchers, there's added injury risk, and the valuation of these contracts makes it, so there's little margin for error.

Even if the Mets were good, signing Skubal wouldn't guarantee anything. And that's what makes baseball so beautiful. It's unpredictable, always. New York might win 100 games, or it would be equally unsurprising if they lost 100. Skubal might win a Cy Young, or get booed off the mound in August.

That's baseball.

World.title: DK Metcalf avoids NFL and club suspension from the Pittsburgh Steelers following his ejection from Sunday game
World.content:
DK Metcalf lost his composure but he didn't lose his ability to play for the Pittsburgh Steelers because the NFL has decided not to suspend the wide receiver despite him being ejected from Sunday's game against the Philadelphia Eagles.

The league has instead opted to review Metcalf's conduct during the game and decide if fines are in order, a source confirmed.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

And the sound you hear coming from Western Pennsylvania is a sigh of relief.

DK METCALF DISQUALIFIED FROM STEELERS GAME FOR UNSPORTSMANLIKE PENALTIES INCLUDING TRYING TO POKE OPPONENT'S EYES

Earlier on Monday, Metcalf talked with Mike McCarthy, and the Steelers' coach said he was comfortable with the receiver's accountability and approach and indicated there would be no team discipline that is public.

So Metcalf is in the clear to continue playing.

NEW NFL FINE SCHEDULE IS GOING TO A POINT SYSTEM THAT COULD LEAD TO SUSPENSIONS BUT ALSO REFUNDS

Metcalf was ejected from the Eagles game because NFL rules stipulate any player flagged twice for unsportsmanlike conduct related to taunting, abusive conduct or striking another player, is automatically disqualified.

Sunday's disqualification marks the third time in Metcalf's career he is removed from a game. Metcalf has been suspended by the NFL previously, that coming last year when he got into an argument with a fan.

So what happened in this game that led to Metcalf getting ejected?

"I can't remember," Metcalf told reporters on Monday after leaving the locker room on Sunday without speaking. "I just wish I had been there for my team."

Metcalf didn't think himself responsible for what happened and, hey, that's possible because in football it is sometimes the reacting party that gets caught instead of the offending party.

So, yeah, that's what Metcalf is going with.

"You got to ask the people that seemingly do that to me," Metcalf said when asked about his temper issues on the field.

It is fair to say something set off Metcalf and that something almost definitely was personified by Eagles defensive back Cooper DeJean.

RAMS OL ALARIC JACKSON EXPECTING TWO-GAME SUSPENSION AFTER PUNCHING BILLS DEFENDER BRADLEY CHUBB

The two players got into a fracas in the third quarter on a play in which Metcalf was blocking DeJean. The blocking turned into something else when Metcalf grabbed DeJean by the collar, DeJean grabbed back, one pushed the other and then other players surrounded the pair.

It was basically a routine football fight and that's when Metcalf picked up his first flag. On the next offensive series for the Steelers, Metcalf was caught on camera poking at DeJean's facemask.

"I mean, we were just competing," DeJean said. "Things like that happen in football. It wasn't anything crazy. Just two guys going at it. He was trying to block me, I was trying to get him off me. And it carried over to whatever that was at the end."

Metcalf said nothing happened at the end. He denied poking DeJean at all.

"I wasn't trying to poke him in the eye," Metcalf said. "I was just telling him."

None of this washes away the question of Metcalf's long term prospects with the Steelers.

He is turning 29 years old next month and has three years remaining on his contract after this season at a cost of $90 million. But all of that money is unsecured by guaranteed money.

The Steelers must pay Metcalf a $6.5 million roster bonus on March 13 to retain his rights. The club can decline to pay the bonus and move on from the volatile player, and while that will carry nearly $70 million in dead cap money through 2029, it also comes with a salary cap savings of around $54 million over that time.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

So Metcalf's future is not secured with the Steelers by his contract and its salary cap implications. But is he worth keeping based on his talent?

Well, that talent is undeniable. He's 6-4 and fast as the wind. He should be great and has been in the past.

But that was around 2020-2023 with the Seattle Seahawks. The numbers – yards, receptions, touchdowns – have been in steady decline since 2024, including the past two seasons with the Steelers.

Metcalf's production, in other words, exposes him to being released in the offseason.
