World.title: $25 minimum wage backers frame midterms as 'blue-collar wave,' 'mandate' to raise pay
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Democrats' huge wins in the 2026 midterms represent a "blue-collar wave" mandate for a $25 federal minimum wage, an advocate for the wage hike tells Fox News Digital.

One Fair Wage President Saru Jayaraman joined House Democrats and restaurant workers on Capitol Hill on Nov. 18 to urge the incoming 120th Congress "to answer the affordability election with a $25 living wage and to make the Living Wage for All Act a Day One priority."

"We're saying it's actually not a blue wave, it's a blue-collar wave. It's working people who didn't necessarily turn into Democrats but are demanding change so that they can meet the cost of living," Jayaraman said in an interview.

DEMOCRATS SEIZE ON MIDTERM WINS TO PUSH MASSIVE MINIMUM WAGE HIKES, BUT ECONOMISTS SEE TROUBLE AHEAD

"I don't care what their political affiliation [is], people are looking for help and change and relief because the cost of living is out of control," she added. "Nobody can live on the wages. Most people's pay doesn't meet the cost of living in America right now."

One Fair Wage co-leads the Living Wage for All coalition — a group of more than 100 organizations, including major teachers unions and progressive advocacy groups — pushing to more than triple the federal minimum wage, which has sat at $7.25 an hour since 2009.

SANDERS-AOC BACKED PROGRESSIVE DEBUTS FEDERAL $25 MINIMUM WAGE BILL WITH COALITION OF 100+ ORGANIZATIONS

Introduced in April by Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., and backed by 35 House cosponsors alongside a Senate companion from Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., the Living Wage for All Act would phase in a $25 hourly floor by 2031 for large employers and by 2038 for smaller businesses. The legislation would also eliminate the $2.13 federal subminimum wage for tipped workers and index future increases to the national median wage.

One of the bill's House co-leads is Rep. Analilia Mejia, D-N.J., a progressive who won an April special election before securing a full term on Nov. 3. Mejia, who was backed by Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., has campaigned on progressive priorities including Medicare for All, a wealth tax and abolishing U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

'CRAZY': MODERATES FEAR DEM LEADERSHIP PROMISED FAR-LEFT REPARATIONS AND ICE DEMANDS IN TURN OF VOTES

Small-business advocates and restaurant industry groups have repeatedly warned that steep federal wage mandates could force employers to cut staff, raise menu prices or close altogether — particularly in rural states with significantly lower living costs than major coastal cities.

Rep. Everton Blair Jr., D-Ga., who attended the Nov. 18 Capitol Hill press conference, dismissed arguments that a $25 floor would hurt lower-cost states, arguing the rate should serve as a nationwide baseline.

PROGRESSIVES UNVEIL $25 MINIMUM WAGE PUSH TO SOLVE AFFORDABILITY CRISIS DESPITE ECONOMIST INFLATION WARNING

"We should be rallying around $25 at minimum, and it should be cost-adjusted for inflation, so that people can have a job that enables them to survive and thrive," Blair told Fox News Digital. He added that $25 an hour should be "the floor" and "should be higher in places with a higher cost of living."

While Blair acknowledged concerns that higher wage mandates could fuel inflation, he argued lawmakers must find a way to boost earnings while "keeping people afloat."

AOC-BACKED $25 MINIMUM WAGE PLAN SOUNDS GREAT — BUT AT WHAT COST?

The renewed push comes after Democrats swept into majorities in both the House and Senate in the Nov. 3 midterms. However, when the new Congress convenes in January, Democrats will remain well short of the two-thirds supermajorities needed in each chamber to override a presidential veto — setting the stage for messaging bills aimed at forcing President Donald Trump to reject progressive economic proposals.

Still, Jayaraman insisted voters delivered an unmistakable verdict on wages as "people are overwhelmingly" demanding action quickly.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"There's a mandate from working people based on this election to deliver on raising wages closer to the cost of living," she said, adding, "Most people do not care about parties. Most people care about results. They want to see electeds deliver on the cost of living, and that means raising wages to the least you need to live anywhere in the U.S."

World.title: Bessent gave Iran weeks before it had ‘nothing left to trade.’ New sanctions expose what survived
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent warned in September that Iran would have "nothing left to trade" within two weeks.

Nearly two months later, the Trump administration is still targeting the overseas financial networks Tehran has used to keep money moving despite sweeping U.S. sanctions in the midst of ongoing war.

On Monday, Treasury announced another round of sanctions targeting more than two dozen individuals and companies accused of helping Iran move billions of dollars through financial networks spanning Dubai, Hong Kong and Turkey.

Bessent has repeatedly warned that Iran is nearing economic collapse, describing successive crackdowns as steps toward cutting off the regime's remaining financial lifelines. Yet each new round of sanctions has exposed more of the networks Tehran has used to keep doing business abroad — even as mounting economic pressure has failed to produce a diplomatic breakthrough.

COULD IRAN’S REGIME COLLAPSE? EXPERTS ASSESS BESSENT’S BID TO SEVER FINANCIAL LIFELINES

While the administration says its blockade has largely stopped Iranian oil exports, Monday's sanctions detail how Tehran has relied on currency dealers, trading companies and middlemen to conduct business abroad.

Treasury identified approximately $14.7 billion in financial activity potentially linked to Iranian shadow banking between January 2025 and August 2026, underscoring the scale of the networks Washington is now targeting.

Just three days earlier, Treasury declared that Iran had exhausted its seaborne oil supply outside the U.S. blockade, saying no new oil had been loaded onto vessels since the launch of Operation Economic Outcast in August.

"The regime has exhausted its seaborne oil supply, and it may never see the revenue from the oil it has already sold. The ship is sinking," Bessent said Friday.

In a response to Fox News Digital, Treasury said Iran has not loaded a single barrel of oil onto vessels since Aug. 25, 2026, and claimed Tehran is struggling to access foreign currency and recover proceeds from previous oil sales.

The department also provided a report showing the Iranian rial has lost roughly 25% of its value since August, while inflation reached 90% in September. Treasury said it is continuing to target alternative financial channels, including cryptocurrency exchanges, as Tehran looks for ways around U.S. restrictions.

BESSENT SAYS IRAN WILL HAVE 'NOTHING LEFT TO TRADE' WITHIN TWO WEEKS AS OIL LIFELINE DRIES UP

But even as the administration claims success in cutting off new oil shipments, Treasury is still pursuing Iranian operatives accused of collecting billions of dollars from previous sales. Friday's sanctions targeted four individuals involved in recovering oil revenues held overseas, some of which Treasury said had been diverted by middlemen for personal gain.

Bessent's September prediction was hardly his first warning that Tehran was approaching an economic breaking point.

Months earlier, he said U.S. sanctions were "asphyxiating" Iran's economy and warned that the country could soon be forced to shut down oil wells as storage facilities filled up.

By late August, Bessent was predicting Iran's economy could collapse within "weeks or months," as the administration launched Operation Economic Outcast, a campaign aimed at cutting off the regime's remaining revenue.

The warnings continued in October, when Bessent projected Iran's economy could shrink by more than 25% over the year ending in March 2027. Earlier this month, he described the country as experiencing one of the fastest economic collapses in history.

BESSENT WARNS IRAN'S OUTSIDE BACKERS TO 'STAY AWAY' AS TRUMP SEEKS TO 'ASPHYXIATE' TEHRAN'S ECONOMY

The administration had increasingly turned to economic pressure after months of military strikes failed to force Tehran into an agreement. Washington reimposed its naval blockade in July after an interim deal collapsed, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in September that the price Iran would pay going forward would be primarily economic, although military action remained an option.

But neither the military campaign nor the mounting economic pressure has produced a broader agreement. Iran continues to demand sanctions relief, access to frozen assets and an end to the blockade, while Washington is pressing Tehran for concessions on its nuclear program and regional activities.

Despite months of escalating pressure, Treasury is still identifying overseas financial networks that have allowed Iran to conduct business outside traditional banking channels.

Iran has spent decades developing ways around American financial restrictions, relying on middlemen, shell companies and foreign currency exchanges to keep trade flowing even as Washington moves to cut off its access to international markets.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Monday's announcement detailed some of those channels, including exchange houses and trading companies operating across Iran, the United Arab Emirates, Turkey and Hong Kong.

Among the newly sanctioned entities was an Iranian currency exchange center that Treasury says facilitates tens of billions of dollars in annual trade, connecting exporters holding foreign currency with importers seeking to purchase goods abroad.

World.title: Democratic Rep. Jimmy Gomez to resign after Ethics Committee finds he engaged in sexual misconduct
World.content:
Rep. Jimmy Gomez, D-Calif., said Monday he will resign next week after the House Ethics Committee found that he engaged in sexual misconduct with a House staffer and said that his behavior could constitute “criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse.”

“I recognize the seriousness of the Ethics Committee’s report, and as I previously stated I take full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage,” Gomez said in a statement.

He said he cooperated with the Ethics investigation but added he has “strong disagreements with the Committee’s report and its conclusions.”

Gomez said that although he disagrees with the conclusions of the House Ethics Committee, he sees “no other alternative than to resign, effective December 1, to allow for my staff to close out important constituent casework and needs.” Heather Diehl / Getty Images

“Among other significant deficiencies and omissions, the report does not include key portions of my testimony that are essential to a full and fair understanding of what occurred,” Gomez said in his statement. “I also have serious concerns about the process. In my interview, I answered the Committee’s questions only to see my statements selectively quoted, disparaged, and disregarded throughout the final report, to which I was given no opportunity to respond.

“With this in mind, I see no other alternative than to resign, effective December 1, to allow for my staff to close out important constituent casework and needs,” he said.

His resignation will speed up his departure from Congress by about one month. Earlier this month, Democratic socialist Angela Gonzales-Torres defeated Gomez in California’s 34th District, as he faced the ethics investigation.

The development comes months after Gomez’s close friend, former Rep. Eric Swalwell, D-Calif., dropped his bid for governor and resigned from office following sexual assault allegations from multiple women, including a House staffer.

The Ethics panel had launched an investigation into Gomez in the wake of the Swalwell saga after news reports that the married Gomez was observed at a party kissing a House staffer.

Gomez disclosed to the Ethics panel he had interactions with two women, including “consensual kissing.” But one of the women, identified as “Witness 1” in the new Ethics report, described the interactions with Gomez as unwanted sexual advances. Witness 1 was in her mid-20s and worked for a House leadership office and not for Gomez, according to the committee. She left her job as a House staffer in 2025.

During the first incident, while celebrating an unidentified member of Congress’ birthday in 2024, the woman told the committee that Gomez groped and sexually assaulted her at Rocket Bar in Washington, D.C., according to the report. When they went outside, she told investigators he pushed her against the wall and began kissing her.

The congressman told the committee that he did kiss the woman outside the bar and that there was sexual contact but that she gave him consent. Witness 1 later told another person her account, that second witness told investigators.

During a second incident, Witness 1 said she went to Gomez’s congressional office during late votes and that he tried to kiss her and was “forceful” with her; she said his actions were nonconsensual, according to the report. Gomez, speaking to the Ethics panel, rejected that characterization and said there was no indication she was uncomfortable and that he did not try to prevent her from leaving.

The Ethics panel did not issue a recommendation for the full House, such as censure or expulsion, presumably because Gomez was slated to leave Congress in January. But the panel said it issued its report as a warning to the entire House of Representatives.

“There must be zero tolerance for unwanted sexual advances toward House staff. The Committee is tasked with investigating alleged misconduct and, where appropriate, holding Members accountable for conduct that does not reflect creditably on the House or puts other Members and staff in danger,” the Ethics panel wrote in its report.

“Having determined that Representative Gomez made unwanted sexual advances toward a House staffer, the Committee adopted this Report to hold Representative Gomez accountable and to serve as a warning to the entire House community that this conduct will not be tolerated,” the committee added.

Responding to Gomez’s resignation, the top three House Democrats, Hakeem Jeffries, Katherine Clark and Pete Aguilar, said in a joint statement: “The report of wrongdoing and abuse of power by Rep. Gomez is serious and deeply troubling. It is appropriate that he is stepping down. Decisive action to set a new standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats.”

The Gomez report comes just days after the Ethics Committee formally adopted six changes to its procedures aimed at speeding up investigations and increasing transparency, particularly in cases involving sexual misconduct.

All six proposed changes were adopted without amendment following a rare public meeting, a source familiar with the matter confirmed to NBC News.

The changes include formally requiring public disclosure of substantiated sexual misconduct findings while protecting victims’ identities; allowing the chairman and ranking member to jointly issue subpoenas without a full committee vote; and streamlining disciplinary proceedings.

The reforms follow longstanding scrutiny over the pace and secrecy of congressional misconduct investigations, including cases in which lawmakers resign before investigations conclude. The changes come amid a separate bipartisan congressional workplace reform effort announced earlier this year.

Rep. Mark DeSaulnier, D-Calif., the top Democrat on the Ethics panel, said the reforms followed bipartisan deliberations and collaboration with the Congressional Women’s Caucus.

“The House of Representatives must have a zero-tolerance policy for sexual harassment and misconduct and the Committee on Ethics is committed to ensuring that its practices and processes sufficiently hold perpetrators accountable and deliver justice for survivors,” DeSaulnier said.

World.title: Court allows Army to go forward with planned detonation of toxic drums in Iowa
World.content:
A U.S. appeals court said Monday that it would allow the Trump administration and the Army to move forward with the detonation of lead azide in Iowa, denying an emergency request by environmental groups to halt the Army’s permit.

It is not clear when the detonation, which was most recently set for Wednesday, will happen.

“We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army’s planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide,” the order from the 8th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals said. “However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place.”

The court said that the Environmental Protection Agency had adequately incorporated safeguards to minimize the dispersal of lead and that the Army had considered a full range of alternatives.

“A controlled detonation with attendant safety measures better alleviates the risk of irreparable harm than the risk of an uncontrolled explosion,” the court said in lifting an administrative stay on the permit.

The detonation, which had been planned for Wednesday, would send a plume of lead dust across Iowa and likely into neighboring states and has raised fear and concern from residents who said they had not had enough time to prepare.

Earlier Monday, President Donald Trump ordered the Army to pause its planned detonation until the court weighed in.

“I feel the proper course is to get rid of this longterm problem but, at the same time, have ordered the Military not to do so until such time as the Eighth Circuit agrees that we can go forward, and am further making this decision fully subject to the incoming Governor Elect, Rob Sand, agreeing to the operation,” Trump said in a Truth Social post.

The detonation was initially scheduled for Friday. After public outcry and a lawsuit from environmental groups last week, the Army delayed the detonation until Monday and then later pushed it again to Wednesday. The court last week gave an administrative stay in the case, putting the Army’s environmental permit to detonate on hold. But the Army told the court it could go forward with a detonation in an emergency without the court’s ruling. The Eighth Circuit ruling, released on Monday afternoon, will clear the way for the Army to go forward with the court’s blessing.

The outcry over the federal government’s handling of the situation and the decision of whether to detonate had become something of a political football earlier on Monday afternoon. In his Truth Social post before the appeals court ruling, Trump seemed intent on deferring responsibility to Sand, who has not taken office yet.

“If he or the Courts do not agree,” Trump said of Sand, “we will have no choice but to not proceed with the controlled removal of these hazardous materials, and be forced to hold the incoming Governor responsible for any and all death or destruction caused by this very unfortunate, and longterm, situation.”

Middletown sits on the edge of the Iowa Army ammunition plant. Scott Olson / Getty

Trump said military leaders had advised him that detonating the material soon was the safest option and that the weather forecast for Wednesday was optimal.

“The Experts, who know it well, and have been studying it for many years, feel there is a substantial chance that this material will explode of its own volition, perhaps sometime in the near future,” Trump wrote. “The weather, right now, is optimal for this planned response to take place.”

The Army has said it must detonate the 68 drums of deteriorating, toxic lead azide — a chemical used to make bomb triggers — at the Iowa ammunition plant because the chemical has undergone a process of “recrystallization” that has made it highly unstable and dangerous. The Army has said that it is unsafe to move the drums and that cold weather will further destabilize the material and could cause a spontaneous explosion.

The Army had told Middletown residents that the blast could break windows and shake their homes. But residents elsewhere in Iowa — and in the plume’s potential path outside the state — said they didn’t learn about it until last week and were concerned for their families’ well-being, crops and pets.

Windows are covered to reduce the chance of shattering at a home near the plant in Middletown. Scott Olson / Getty

Lead is a potent neurotoxin for which there is no safe level of exposure. Airborne lead is an acute health risk, experts said, and once the metal gets deposited in soil or on surfaces, it can remain there forever unless it’s physically removed.

Exposure to lead is associated with learning disabilities, reproductive problems, mental health issues and increased risk of hearing loss, among other effects. The long-term risks are particularly pronounced for young children.

The Army said it had covered the bunker with two stories of sand in collapsible, modular barriers to dampen the effects of the explosion. Meanwhile, scientists, politicians and residents have been trying to figure out how the situation got so sideways and why the Army feels its only choice is a detonation, whether planned or unplanned.

In a statement on X before the court’s ruling, Sand said the administration should make its decision “based on the information they have from the people they brought in to do the job months ago” and who have been in Middletown for weeks. Sand implied that the administration might have information about the urgency of the situation that is not known publicly.

“Everyday Iowans are entitled to know how Middletown came to this situation, and learn why the administration believes this is the best path forward,” Sand said. “That means they should have the same access to the information I’ve received in briefings from the administration, straight from the source. I’ve asked the federal government to share that information with the public as soon as possible.”

An Army spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Iowa residents said they were growing frustrated with the twists and turns of the detonation saga.

Debra Ott, who works at Fat Annie’s August Tap, which is about a quarter-mile from a gate that leads into the ammunition plant, said she was planning to stay inside for a full day if and when the detonation takes place.

“I have some heart issues, and I have a hard enough time breathing anyway. So whenever they do it, I plan on staying in the house 24 hours because I don’t want to be out,” Ott said. “The bean dust and corn dust around here is bad enough without lead.”

Ott, who lives in Augusta, Iowa, about 5 miles from Middletown, said she was growing tired of the scheduling changes for detonation and increasingly concerned about a spontaneous explosion.

“I don’t want to be sitting at home at midnight and have it go off and not have a clue what’s going on without anybody up there to try to control it. If they’re going to do it, I wish they just do it and quit changing it every day,” she said.

Ott lives with her granddaughter and her granddaughter’s three young children, who are 13, 4 and 2.

“We’ll hose down all the outside stuff and wipe off, you know, wipe down the doorknobs and anything the vehicles, anything the kids can touch with their hands, where they could get it in their mouth,” Ott said. “We just don’t know what to expect because we don’t know when they’re going to do it.”

The trajectory of the dust plume depends on the direction and strength of the wind, so each delay puts a new group of people in the path of the expected hazard.

“It’s just very frustrating,” said Jill Holler, who lives about 50 miles from Middletown, in Muscatine, Iowa, which could be in the path of the lead dust plume, depending on the wind.

Holler, whose family has a farm about 20 miles west of Middletown where they raise cattle and grow soybeans and corn, said she was racing to gather soil samples ahead of the blast Sunday night. Understanding the lead content present in soil before the blast could help determine if a property is affected and what remediation might be needed.

“We thought it would be tomorrow. So I was down in the dark getting the soil samples and it just, it’s frustrating,” Holler said on Monday. “It’s just strange, and you just never know what the next day is going to bring, and so you never. You’re, you’re pretty confident there’s going to be something else changing, and we can’t really believe what the next thing they say is going to happen.”

Holler said she was most sympathetic to the people of Middletown, who are essentially living with a threat in their backyards that the Army has indicated could spontaneously explode.

“If there really is an imminent threat and it’s very dangerous to explode at any time,” Holler said. “But it seems like they’re delaying, so it just isn’t adding up. It doesn’t make sense. So I think there’s going to have to be some explanation of what’s been going on.”

World.title: How will voters respond to divided government?: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into how an electorate that is hungry for results may collide withe the realities of divided government. Plus, we look ahead to the governor’s races on the ballot in the South next year.

— Adam Wollner

Which party is expected to deliver in divided government? The last 3 presidential elections provide clues.

Analysis by Sahil Kapur

With Democrats poised to claim historic majorities in the House and Senate come January, the biggest substantive question is what they’ll be able to accomplish with President Donald Trump in the White House over the next two years.

And the biggest political question: If little is done, who will pay the price?

A common theory after midterm elections is that the party that just won needs to prove it can govern — and deliver tangible results — in order to be successful in the next presidential election.

But is that actually true? History says no — voters tend to punish the president’s party, not the party that captured one or both chambers of Congress in the previous midterm, when they’re unhappy with the status quo.

Let’s review what happened after the last three midterms.

2014: Republicans flipped the Senate and expanded their House majority for President Barack Obama’s final two years in office.

But what happened next? Not much. Congress passed 172 substantive bills (not including ceremonial ones like renaming federal buildings), according to the Pew Research Center, well below the average of 236 substantive bills over the last four decades. Highlights included a surface transportation bill, unwinding “No Child Left Behind” and a Medicare bookkeeping resolution known as the “doc fix.” There was plenty of fighting, including the rebellion that led to Speaker John Boehner’s resignation and countless Affordable Care Act repeal show votes.

So, did voters punish Republicans? No. They won the trifecta in 2016, with Trump becoming president for the first time.

2018: Two years later, Democrats flipped about 40 House seats and took control of the chamber, although Republicans kept the Senate.

Just 150 substantive bills passed in the next session of Congress, the Pew Research Center found. Key pieces of legislation included the United States–Mexico–Canada Agreement and several emergency Covid relief measures once the pandemic hit. But as was the case after the 2014 midterms, divided government led to several high-profile clashes, including a 35-day government shutdown and Trump’s first impeachment.

Were Democrats punished for the lack of productivity? No. They won full control of Washington in 2020, with Joe Biden taking the White House.

2022: Biden’s first midterm saw Republicans regain control of the House while falling short in the Senate.

But it was a similar story as the previous two midterms, with just 84 substantive bills passing during the next congressional session, according to Pew. That included a spending agreement following a debt ceiling fight that spooked the markets and led to a downgrade of the U.S. credit rating. Republicans also fought bitterly with each other, eventually deposing Speaker Kevin McCarthy mid-session.

But did Republicans pay a political price? Not quite. The GOP again won a trifecta in the 2024 election, with Trump returning to the White House.

2026: And two years later, voters ushered in huge Democratic majorities after deciding, according to NBC News exit polling, that Trump failed to fulfill his promises to make life more affordable.

Will Democrats deliver on that? And if they don’t, will they suffer politically for it in the 2028 presidential election?

Based on the lessons of the last dozen years, the onus is on the president and his party to work with the new majorities in Congress, because voters have shown that they’ll punish the party in the White House for dysfunction and paralysis in Washington.

📺 Related: Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich., said on “Meet the Press” that he’s open to working with Trump to bring down costs and improve healthcare for Americans. Read more →

Democrats look to 2027 races for governor to build on gains in the South

By Bridget Bowman, Alexandra Marquez and Adam Edelman

Democrats calling on their party to invest in the South after historic victories this year won’t have to wait until 2028, with races for governor in Mississippi, Louisiana and Kentucky ahead in 2027.

These contests will come just one year after Democrats flipped Senate seats in Mississippi and South Carolina, governorships in Texas and Georgia and House districts across the South for the first time in decades. And Southern Democrats are confident their party has taken notice.

“The South is competitive for Democrats,” Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, who chaired the Democratic Governors Association this year, told NBC News. “As a Southern Democrat, we were often overlooked, underfunded, sometimes even looked down upon. But we have scrapped our way back to the table.”

Beshear, a possible presidential candidate, won a second term by 5 points two years ago and cannot run again due to term limits. In 2023, Democrat Brandon Presley lost in Mississippi to GOP Gov. Tate Reeves, who is term-limited, by 3 points. And former Democratic Gov. John Bel Edwards won two terms in Louisiana in 2015 and 2019 before Republican Gov. Jeff Landry won the office in 2023.

This year, Democrat Scott Colom notched a historic Senate victory in Mississippi and Democrat Jamie Davis came close to winning Louisiana.

Read more →

World.title: Appeals court gives Trump another chance to move his hush money conviction case to a federal venue
World.content:
An appeals court on Monday opened the door to moving to federal court President Donald Trump’s New York state criminal case that resulted in a felony conviction.

In a brief two-page order, the 2nd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals found that a lower court judge had “erred” when he ruled Trump’s legal team had waited too long to raise a presidential immunity defense.

“We disagree with the district court,” the three-judge panel said, directing a lower court judge to reconsider Trump’s motion to move the case from state court.

U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein in August had denied Trump’s request to consider moving the case, finding his arguments were not “legally sufficient.”

A spokesperson for Trump’s legal team praised the appeals court’s “prompt and correct ruling.”

“As today’s order highlights, the Supreme Court’s historic decision on Immunity, the Federal Constitution, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan DA be removed to federal court, and immediately overturned and dismissed,” his statement said.

“President Trump will keep defeating the Liberal Hoaxes at every turn,” it added.

A spokesperson for the Manhattan district attorney’s office, which prosecuted the case, declined to comment.

Trump was convicted on 34 felony counts of falsifying business records in 2024 as part of a scheme to cover up a hush money payment that his attorney had paid to an adult film star during the 2016 presidential campaign.

Trump managed the repayment to his attorney while he was president, and his lawyers have contended that a 2024 Supreme Court ruling that expanded the parameters of presidential immunity after he’d already been convicted should have resulted in the conviction being overturned.

Trump, who has denied any wrongdoing, had been separately appealing the conviction in state court, but Monday’s order effectively freezes that case while it’s being decided in federal court.

“In order to preserve the status quo, the district court shall also respectfully request that no further proceedings occur in the state courts while the removal question is pending,” the judges wrote.

Judges Raymond Lohier, John Walker and Jose Cabranes also found that if the lower court decides the case should be moved to a federal venue, the “court should adopt the state court judgement.”

That would allow Trump to make his case for the conviction to be tossed out by the 2nd Circuit.

It’s unclear who will hear the case at the lower federal court level. Hellerstein died last month at age 92, and the case has yet to be reassigned.

Hellerstein had previously rejected other attempts by Trump to move the case, finding “hush money paid to an adult film star is not related to a President’s official acts.”

During arguments before the 2nd Circuit last week, Steven Wu of the district attorney’s office argued Trump had been prosecuted for falsifying business records, not for official presidential conduct, and that challenges to the conviction should go through the state courts.

Trump attorney Robert Giuffra acknowledged to the appeals court judges last week that it was unusual for a defendant to try to move a case after he’d already been convicted, but noted, “Everything about this case is unprecedented.”

Trump was sentenced to an unconditional discharge in the case 10 days before he was sworn in for his second term as president. The sentence meant that the conviction is on his record, but with no further penalties.

World.title: Huang's return at Nvidia puts spotlight on chipmaker's board
World.content:
Nvidia's stunning about-face on Monday to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO undermines the credibility of its board of directors and raises questions about its commitment to enforcing the company's own rules, according to corporate governance experts.

Huang resigned from Nvidia on Nov. 12 after revelations that he had an extramarital affair with a Chinese businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence suspects of spying for China. In announcing its decision to rehire Huang, the company's board said it had concluded that reinstating him "poses no national security risk," citing input it had received from senior U.S. officials.

Yet in reversing itself, Nvidia is undermining its own corporate code of conduct and could expose the company to potential legal liability, Charles Elson, founding director of the John L. Weinberg Center for Corporate Governance at the University of Delaware, told CBS News.

"It shows a weakness, and I think, frankly, a lack of courage to stand behind the correct decision they made to suggest he resign. That was the right decision," he said.

Nvidia's code of conduct stipulates that personal relationships can create a conflict of interest and instructs employees to ask themselves whether they could defend an action if it were made public on social media or known to colleagues. If not, the policy states, "do not proceed."

"A company culture that allows this sort of stuff to occur ultimately will kill the company itself," Elson said.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment. In announcing Huang's return, Nvidia Board Chairman Harvey Jones said the board "believes Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers."

Bowing to political pressure?

Technology industry leaders and President Trump celebrated Huang's return. Investors also cheered the return of the man who co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and whom many view as synonymous with the burgeoning artificial intelligence sector. The company's stock price surged more than 31% on Monday, quickly bolstering its market value by $1 trillion.

At the same time, the move drew swift condemnation from Democratic and Republican lawmakers, who said the board's decision could put America's national security at risk by undermining efforts to strengthen chip export controls to China.

Despite Nvidia's stock market gain on Monday, governance experts said Nvidia directors failed to live up to their fiduciary duty to act in the best interest of shareholders, including ensuring the company's long-term value.

"They are there for the difficult times. They are the shareholders' fiduciary and lifeboat pick to navigate through a crisis," said Betsy Atkins, who has served on dozens of private and public company boards. "That's their job — deliberate and make the right business judgment."

President Trump told CNBC in a phone interview on Monday that he spoke to Nvidia's board and convinced directors to reinstate Huang, raising questions about whether the board may have bowed to political pressure.

Shiva Rajgopal, a Columbia Business School professor who studies corporate governance, said Mr. Trump's move put Nvidia directors in a difficult position, given the U.S. government's importance as a stakeholder in the company.

"I don't know whether any board would have been able to say no to the president," he told CBS News.

Nvidia's 10-person board, which includes the former president of Taco Bell and a former vice chairman of Goldman Sachs, was lacking in critical ways even before bringing Huang back, Rajgopal added.

"I don't see a whole lot of expertise in, say, export controls, chip architecture, or foundry supply chain," he said.

Several high-profile CEOs have been ousted after their relationships with employees and customers came under scrutiny, such as former McDonald's CEO Steve Easterbrook. But it's rare for a CEO to exit under a cloud only for the board to swiftly bring them back.

The only other high-profile case cited by experts was in 2023, when OpenAI's board decided to rehire CEO Sam Altman just days after pushing him out over questions about his ability to lead the AI startup.

Huang's reinstatement is noteworthy given allegations that he violated Nvidia's code of conduct at least twice, Elson said. Huang allegedly had a relationship with Alice Huang, who U.S. intelligence has linked to China's Ministry of State Security. At the time, Alice Huang was an executive at an Nvidia customer, Singapore data center Megaspeed.

The Trump administration on Monday formally restricted Megaspeed from buying advanced semiconductor chips. Megaspeed has been accused of transferring high-tech Nvidia chips that power AI to China, a charge the company denies. China also denies targeting Jensen Huang in an intelligence operation.

Huang also had an extramarital affair with a subordinate at Nvidia, according to The New York Times, while Reuters reported that he had an intimate relationship with a second employee at the company. Huang's connections to Alice Huang (no relation) have raised concerns that Nvidia was providing its AI chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules.

World.title: Why the Army says it needs to detonate unstable explosives in Iowa
World.content:
The U.S. Army's plan to detonate several tons of unstable explosives at a munitions plant in Iowa has been delayed multiple times amid a court battle and community outcry about the risk of toxic lead particles spreading in a dust plume for miles.

The Army said the controlled detonation of lead azide is necessary due to the public safety risks associated with the possibility of the explosives detonating on their own.

"Officials have been meticulously planning for this event since March, and all agencies involved are prepared to take the most extreme mitigation measures available to ensure there is no risk to the public and any disruptions are minimized," the Army said in a statement.

President Trump said Monday that without the demolition, "a very dangerous situation exists," but ordered the Army to defer its plans until a ruling came down from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit. The court ruled Monday evening that it can go forward.

So why exactly does the Army need to detonate the chemicals and what are the risks to the public?

Why does the Army need to detonate lead azide in Iowa?

In March of this year, the Army said it discovered that 68 drums of lead azide at the site had started "recrystallization." The lead was stored in bunkers at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, a munitions plant built in 1941, which produces quality medium- and large-caliber munitions.

Lead azide is a highly sensitive primary initiating explosive. Due to its extreme sensitivity, even minor external triggers, such as sparks, open flames, friction or pinpricks, can detonate it.

The recrystallization of lead azide can have a high risk of spontaneous explosion, which the EPA said creates a highly unstable and dangerous situation.

Additionally, cold weather would further destabilize the explosive materials. Justine Barati, a public affairs specialist at Army Sustainment Command, told CBS News Chicago that the risk of accidental detonation increases in cold weather.

Military officials said it's not safe to relocate the explosive materials.

The Army said it modeled four different ways to try to neutralize the chemicals, and concluded that a controlled detonation was the best method available.

"It was determined that a controlled detonation was the option that posed the lowest risk to the public in the immediate and surrounding area," Acting Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in a statement.

Army officials said they connected with stakeholders and the public in Middletown and the surrounding area about the approved plan. Critics, however, contend they weren't made aware of the plan to detonate the lead azide until just days before the scheduled controlled explosion.

Local politicians said the decisions were made at the federal level, and poor communication contributed to the outcry and confusion from residents concerned about toxic chemicals.

"The safety of Iowans now and in the future should be the government's top concern. An unacceptable lack of communication and clarity has made Iowans understandably concerned and angry about this situation," Sand said.

What are the risks to residents?

One of the main concerns is that lead particles would be scattered in the dust plume created by the explosion. Lead in any amount is dangerous for humans, and in particular for young children.

"Lead is a really challenging contaminant," said David Cwiertny, a professor at the University of Iowa and director of its Environmental Policy Research Program.

He said there are essentially two ways the lead could be released: moving freely in the air and collecting on the ground.

"We do expect that air to dissipate fairly quickly as it moves with the wind," Cwiertny said.

Lead can enter the body through contaminated food, water or through dust or fumes, according to the U.S. National Institutes of Health, leading to health issues for adults and children. It can impede growth, contribute to learning disorders and damage the brain and nervous system. Children under age 6 are most susceptible to lead poisoning, the CDC says, as their bodies and brains are still developing.

Residents were told to evacuate the immediate area ahead of the planned explosion. But some are worried that afterward, lead would contaminate the environment and infiltrate their groundwater, rendering their communities unsafe.

Middletown resident Sean Byers, whose house is across from the munitions plant, pointed down the street and said, "There's a playground back over there where kids in the community play all the time."

Byers, who has three young children, said he's worried about contamination.

"It's going to linger probably for decades," he said. "It's going to affect everyone."

Are there any steps to reduce the risk?

The Army said it planned to take a number of steps to reduce the risk in a controlled detonation.

The lead azide drums would be detonated inside earth-covered magazines made of concrete, and surrounded with Hesco barriers full of sand, which are approximately two stories high. Before and during the detonation, explosive experts would saturate the soil above with water. Water misters would also be spraying, the Army said.

Residents would be asked to vacate the area at that time, as the controlled detonation "will cause temporary noise, ground vibrations, and a dust plume that will contain some lead," the Army said in a statement.

Byers said he found out about the planned explosion through his neighbor a few days before the planned explosions — not from the U.S. Army. He said he plans to evacuate with his family to Branson, Missouri, where they'd stay for three or four days.

He said the Army told them it would be safe to return to their homes after six hours, but he "highly doubts" that.

Notices were sent out by the Army saying residents' windows could potentially break, and if they do, they'd be replaced by the ammunition plant.

Byers said he got the notice, but says, "The damage at that point has already been done, because it's going to let all that lead enter the house. And the question is, are they going to come in and decontaminate that? Are they going to, you know, are they going to do that? Probably not."

The Army said that due to its mitigation efforts, while there will be some lead particles in the air after the detonation, the levels will be well below the level at which the EPA requires protective actions.

World.title: Rep. Jimmy Gomez resigning after panel finds evidence of misconduct
World.content:
Warning: This story contains graphic content.



Washington — Rep. Jimmy Gomez announced Monday that he will resign from Congress, with the announcement coming shortly after the House Ethics Committee released a report saying it found "substantial evidence" that the California Democrat engaged in sexual misconduct, including making unwanted sexual advances and sexual contact with a House staffer.

The committee said Gomez's behavior toward the House staffer "could constitute criminal misdemeanor sexual abuse," or sexual assault.

Gomez said he had "strong disagreements" with the findings, but saw "no other alternative than to resign." He said his resignation is effective Dec. 1 "to allow for my staff to close out important constituent casework and needs."

"I recognize the seriousness of the Ethics Committee's report and as I previously stated I take full responsibility for the personal mistakes I committed outside of my marriage," Gomez said in a statement.

Gomez was set to leave office in early January after losing his reelection bid.

The bipartisan committee announced in August that it was looking into allegations against Gomez.

As part of its investigation, the panel interviewed one woman who said Gomez made unwanted sexual advances toward her while she was a House staffer on two occasions, including one in which he made "sexual contact" with her in public and another where she described him as "forceful" with her in his congressional office, according to the report.

The woman, described as Witness 1 in the report, said she met Gomez at a birthday party hosted by another lawmaker at a bar near Capitol Hill in February 2024. Gomez and the woman eventually left the party with another woman and lawmaker to go to a bar in Chinatown.

According to the report, the woman told the committee that at the Chinatown bar Gomez started to touch her legs and then she said he penetrated her with his fingers. She described the incident as nonconsensual and said she was "mortified" that it had happened.

"I kind of just was really embarrassed by it. I didn't know how to react," she told the committee, adding that she "ran to the bathroom" and "started to cry."

Later outside the bar, the woman said Gomez pushed her against a wall and kissed her, and she said she "kissed him back because I just wanted to go home and I just, like, wanted it to end."

Gomez initially described the encounter outside the bar as "consensual kissing," but later acknowledged that "I put my hand down the top of her skirt." Gomez said the sexual contact happened outside the bar and he had asked her, "yes?"

"And she said yes," he said. He denied penetrating her, but also alleged that "she did not say no, she did not push me away."

The woman also told the committee about a second incident in July 2024 and alleged that Gomez invited her to his office after she had texted him. She said when she tried to leave his office, he grabbed her and pushed his body into hers and "tried to kiss me."

She alleged that she "said no" and that she needed to leave, and told the panel, "I was trying to push off of him, and he wouldn't let go. And, at some point I, like, succeeded in pushing him off of me, and then I just ran out."

Gomez described the incident, saying, "I walked her to the door, gave her a beso, a kiss on the cheek, a hug, and she left."

The committee called Gomez's actions "aggressive and inappropriate" and said his "conduct at various junctures suggests he knew that what he was doing was wrong." The report also said Gomez's conduct caused the woman "significant and ongoing distress" and contributed to her decision to leave her job.

The committee did not recommend any punishment for Gomez, such as censure or expulsion, noting that the California Democrat had lost his reelection campaign.

"[T]he Committee has observed that although there is not enough time for it to pursue an adequate House sanction, it remains essential that the Committee adopt and publish its Report so that the House is aware of Representative Gomez's misconduct and so that the House may determine, in its judgment, whether to sanction Representative Gomez," it said.

In a statement, the woman's lawyers claimed the committee's report "confirms that Representative Gomez sexually harassed and assaulted our client while she was a staffer on Capitol Hill."

Her attorneys, Lisa J. Banks and Sarah E. Nesbitt, said Gomez "abused the power given to him by the voters when he violated this young woman, effectively destroying her dreams of a career in public service," adding that he "seems to believe that the power he wields, both as a man and as a member of Congress, makes him untouchable."

They said that the committee's findings "are a meaningful step toward dismantling that belief."

House Democratic leaders called the report "serious and deeply troubling" and said it is "appropriate that he is stepping down."

"Decisive action to set a new standard for reform is an urgent priority for House Democrats," House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Minority Whip Katherine Clark and Democratic Caucus chairman Pete Aguilar said in a joint statement.

World.title: Nasdaq gains 6.5% after Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO
World.content:
U.S. stocks made a comeback on Monday, with Nvidia's decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO boosting financial markets after Friday's sell-off plunged the S&P 500 and Dow into correction territory.

The Nasdaq Composite jumped 1,472 points, or 6.5%, to close at 24,090, regaining ground after the tech-heavy index on Nov. 20 suffered its second-worst day of 2026. The S&P 500 rose 4.7%, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average added 3%.

Huang resigned less than two weeks ago amid scandal over an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of spying for China. On Monday, the board said it believes Huang is the "right person to lead Nvidia" and that it has "every confidence" in him as he resumes his leadership role at the company. Huang's reinstatement is "effective immediately," the board said.

"The company reported fantastic numbers last week, but the uncertainty of their leadership was like a huge overhang," eToro investment analyst Bret Kenwell told CBS News.

"Now that uncertainty suddenly is not only removed, but it's replaced with the very familiar leadership of Jensen," he added.

Nvidia shares surged more than 31% on Monday, adding roughly $1 trillion to its market value. Shares of CoreWeave, a cloud computing company and Nvidia customer, shot up 22%. The PHLX Semiconductor Sector Index, which tracks 30 of the largest companies involved in the design, distribution, manufacture and sale of chips, rose 14%.

"I believe the White House leaned hard on the board, and the message is crystal clear. America needs Jensen Huang leading Nvidia and, therefore, the wider AI industry," Nigel Green, CEO of investment advisory firm deVere Group, said in an email. "His return hands him more control than ever. He's got the backing of the board, the U.S. president and the market, and that's a phenomenal platform to take Nvidia to another level."

Not out of the woods

Despite Monday's market exuberance, some Wall Street analysts said investors remain on edge amid concerns that the artificial intelligence sector is unraveling.

"Stocks in the U.S. are staging a large rebound rally so far this morning, although, just to put things into context, the S&P futures aren't even reclaiming their loss from Friday, much less the entire week," Vital Knowledge analyst Adam Crisafulli said in a note to investors on Monday before Nvidia announced it was reinstating Huang.

"Sentiment remains pretty bleak — most people are looking at this [Monday] uptick as nothing more than technical in nature, a partial reversal of extremely oversold conditions," he added.

Financial markets tumbled Friday as concerns swelled about a possible slowdown in data center construction across the U.S. and tightening restrictions on chip exports, both of which could hurt corporate profits.

The losses were led by microchip companies like Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom, which shed 13.3% and 12.2%, respectively. Both recovered Monday, with AMD gaining 6.9% and Broadcom rising 3%. Anthropic, which made its public market debut on Thursday, sank 1.4%.

Kenwell said financial markets still face headwinds, including a more hawkish Fed, high inflation and investor uncertainty over the AI trade. However, corporate profits remain strong, he said, citing Nvidia's robust earnings last week and bullish financial markets.

"That's not a today story," Kenwell said. "That was true a week ago, true a month ago, and it'll be true at the start of next month."

World.title: California Democrat Rep. Gomez resigns following ethics report on sexual misconduct allegations
World.content:
California Democrat Rep. Gomez resigns following ethics report on sexual misconduct allegations

toggle caption i Heather Diehl/Getty Images North America

Rep. Jimmy Gomez (D-Calif) says he is resigning from Congress after a bipartisan investigation released Monday found "substantial evidence" he engaged in sexual misconduct toward a House staffer.

The House Ethics Committee concluded Gomez violated House rules by "making unwelcome sexual advances and engaging in unwelcome sexual conduct towards a House staffer and disregarding the power imbalance inherent in his relationship with House staffers."

The report also says the behavior could constitute criminal sexual assault.

Gomez has served in Congress since 2017 representing parts of Los Angeles. He lost reelection this fall to fellow Democrat Angela Gonzales-Torres. California uses a system where the top two vote-getters no matter the party advance to the general election. Gomez says his resignation will be effective Dec. 1.

Sponsor Message

Lisa Banks and Sarah Nesbitt, attorneys for the unnamed House staffer, wrote in a statement that their client testified to the committee truthfully and at personal risk.

"She sacrificed her own sense of safety and privacy to help reveal the ongoing misogyny and debauchery that permeates Capitol Hill," Banks and Nesbitt wrote. "Representative Gomez seems to believe that the power he wields, both as a man and as a member of Congress, makes him untouchable. Today's findings are a meaningful step toward dismantling that belief."

In a statement announcing his plan to resign, Gomez wrote that he cooperated with the investigation, but has strong disagreements with the report and its conclusions.

"Among other significant deficiencies and omissions, the report does not include key portions of my testimony that are essential to a full and fair understanding of what occurred," he wrote.

"I also have serious concerns about the process. In my interview, I answered the Committee's questions only to see my statements selectively quoted, disparaged, and disregarded throughout the final report, to which I was given no opportunity to respond."

The House Ethics Committee, which includes five Democrats and five Republicans, opened its investigation into Gomez in August following a press report of Gomez kissing a staffer from another Congressional office at a party. Gomez denied those allegations.

Sponsor Message

The committee asked Gomez to disclose whether he "ever engaged in a romantic or sexual relationship or made sexual contact with a congressional staffer." Gomez disclosed interactions with two women — telling the committee the encounters were all consensual. Both women spoke to the committee.

One denied "she had ever had a nonconsensual sexual encounter" with Gomez. The other, described as Witness 1 in the report, said she had more than one encounter with Gomez and she did not consider them consensual.

She told investigators that Gomez made sexual contact without her consent at a bar in February 2024 and then was forceful with her and tried to kiss her at his congressional office in July 2024.

Gomez denied the interactions were nonconsensual. The staffer, described as Witness 1 in the committee report, eventually left her job on Capitol Hill.

"Here, the House lost Witness 1 as a competent and able staffer because of Representative Gomez's misconduct and because of a broader culture of disrespect and toxic sexual behavior toward staff that permeates life on the Hill and is long overdue for correction," the committee wrote.

The report comes amid a broader conversation about how Congress deals with the behavior of its members, especially when it comes to sexual misconduct.

In April, Democrat Eric Swalwell of California resigned his House seat amid allegations of sexual assault and misconduct. He also denied the allegations. Rep. Tony Gonzales (R-Tex.) also resigned from the House after admitting to an affair with a former staff member.

Rep. Chuck Edwards (R-N.C.) dropped his reelection bid earlier this year after the House Ethics Committee recommended he face a censure vote for allegedly harassing two young female staffers. Edwards denied the allegations.

Republican Reps. Max Miller of Ohio and Cory Mills of Florida also face House Ethics investigations stemming from allegations of domestic violence. Both deny wrongdoing.

Sponsor Message

Miller lost his reelection bid this fall and Mills lost his GOP primary.
