World.title: The War of the Entire Cuban People
World.content:
Cuban president Miguel Diaz Canel in a meeting with top military officials.

By Francisco Acevedo

HAVANA TIMES – Cuba has spent nearly 70 years preparing for a military war with the United States, but the truth is that, after the 1960s, that possibility became increasingly remote.

The current US administration has said on more than one occasion that it does not rule out that option, but the reality is that adding yet another armed conflict to the financial burden borne by United States taxpayers would be extremely complicated, to mention only the economic aspect.

Beyond that—which remains a hypothetical scenario—what is actually happening in Cuba is that fear of war is being used to serve the interests of the dictatorship. At the same time, the regime wants Cubans to believe it could withstand a military confrontation, when we all know that would be impossible.

This week, President Miguel Di’z-Canel met with the country’s top military leadership to reiterate the decision to repel any aggression (it would be the height of absurdity if they surrendered at the first opportunity). But far from projecting an image of strength, he looked exhausted.

His words conveyed anything but determination, confidence, courage, or leadership. What we saw was someone badly in need of sleep, someone weakened. Someone repeating the same old rhetoric while seeming almost to beg the United States not to go so far as to invade and to let them live in peace, as he claims the rest of the world advocates—even if that means he can continue enjoying his privileges while the vast majority of Cubans endure hardship.

What we witnessed at the beginning of this year with the capture of Nicolas Maduro in Venezuela demonstrated the enormous military disparity between a superpower and a Third World nation, a gap that would be even greater in a confrontation between Cuba and the United States.

Perhaps the dictatorship’s only advantage in such a scenario would be its extensive infiltration of US government institutions with spies, an effort that has been underway for decades and has proven highly effective. But even if military secrets could not be adequately protected, everything would ultimately be decided on the battlefield. And there, it would be the classic fight between a lion and a monkey—with the monkey tied to a post.

The tyranny’s position is clear: it seeks to impress those who still believe in it and intimidate everyone else, attempting to prevent these threats from triggering another social uprising, which would actually be the perfect formula for change.

To that end, every so often they display their obsolete weapons, which must give US military intelligence a good laugh, while here only the ignorant could believe they would withstand an assault.

Since Fidel Castro’s time, the island’s strategy has been based on establishing pockets of resistance throughout the country, under what was officially called the “War of the Entire People.”

But there is one enormous difference between the Fidel Castro era and today, and it is the key to understanding how different the situation would be now: the vast majority of Cubans do not support their leaders.

I know there are no reliable statistics to substantiate this. That would require the referendum we have been demanding for years, which the dictatorship refuses to hold. But it is what I see every day: countless people tired of being used in this political confrontation while watching their own dreams, and those of their children and grandchildren, continually postponed, just as the dreams of their parents and grandparents were buried.

There is a weariness that makes no noise, that is not proclaimed in public squares or featured in headlines. Instead, it settles on the shoulders of someone returning home late, in the hands of someone counting coins before making a purchase, in the eyes of someone who has learned not to promise their children too much. It is the exhaustion of feeling used.

For years, far too many people have been called upon to defend flags that offered them no shelter, slogans that put no food on their tables, promises that evaporated as soon as the march ended or the ballot boxes closed. They were asked for patience, sacrifice, and loyalty. They were told of a bright future, an imminent victory, a higher cause. And they gave their days, their enthusiasm, even their resentments, while watching the present slip through their fingers.

They had been promised that education would open doors, that honest work would allow them to build a home, that perseverance would be rewarded. But many of those doors remain closed. Owning a home has become a distant aspiration. Young people pack their bags not out of a thirst for adventure, but because they feel that staying means giving up. Parents watch silently as their children inherit not only a surname and a history, but also frustrations and the obligation to start over somewhere else.

That is why the frustration keeps growing. Not necessarily because people have abandoned their ideals, but because they are beginning to distinguish between ideas and those who exploit them. They no longer want to be a crowd, fuel for someone else’s cause, or an argument to be used. They do not want their suffering invoked in speeches by people who live far removed from its consequences. They do not want to keep sacrificing the present in exchange for a future that is always postponed.

The truth is that the real “War of the Entire People” is the struggle for survival. What people want is something simpler and, for that very reason, more profound: to live.

To live without having to justify their children’s hunger. To work without feeling that every effort disappears into a labyrinth. To grow old knowing that their grandchildren will have more opportunities than they did, not fewer. To reclaim the right to dream without asking permission, without waiting for another promise, without turning every hope into an act of faith.

Perhaps the time has come to listen to that exhaustion. Because when a society stops believing in those who summon it to action, it does not always abandon its dreams. Sometimes, at long last, it begins to demand that they be fulfilled. And that is the real terror sweeping through the corridors of the Central Committee.

Read more from Cuba here at Havana Times.

World.title: Cuba’s Benchmark Hospital That Lost Its Greatness
World.content:
Photo of the exterior of the Hermanos Ameijeiras Hospital, taken from the hospital’s archives.

By Kamil Kenders

HAVANA TIMES – Some buildings are part of a city’s landscape, while others are also part of its memory. Hermanos Ameijeiras Hospital belongs to both categories.

Its tower, visible from different points along Havana’s Malecon, was for many years an image associated with the development of Cuban medicine. For thousands of people, that building represented something more than a hospital: it offered the possibility of receiving specialized care, obtaining a diagnosis for a complicated condition, or undergoing treatment that was not available at just any other institution in the country.

Inaugurated on December 3, 1982, Hermanos Ameijeiras was conceived as a national referral center. Its facilities, equipment, specialists, and the diversity of services it offered placed it among Cuba’s most prestigious hospitals.

Highly complex medical procedures, research, and professional training programs were carried out there. For decades, its name inspired confidence. For many Cubans, being referred to Ameijeiras meant reaching one of the best possible places to receive medical care. But the years have passed, and that image of excellence seems to have become trapped in memory.

Today, speaking of Hermanos Ameijeiras also means speaking of shortages, deterioration, limited services, and difficulties that ultimately affect both patients and their families.

The reality behind its doors is far removed from the institution that was once a source of pride. It is not simply a matter of the physical deterioration of certain areas. It goes much deeper. The scarcity of material resources, lack of supplies, difficulties keeping equipment operational, and loss of medical professionals have gradually weakened the capacity of an institution that needs precisely the opposite: resources, technology, and specialized personnel.

Many healthcare professionals have emigrated in search of better living and working conditions. Those who remain in the country try to practice their profession under increasingly difficult circumstances. And those who continue caring for patients must confront a reality in which they do not always have what they need to do their jobs. Because a doctor may possess all the knowledge in the world, but without the necessary medications, reagents, instruments, or equipment, their ability to provide adequate care is inevitably limited.

According to accounts I have heard, difficulties performing certain clinical tests because of a lack of reagents have become another obstacle for patients at this hospital. Sometimes, even when a patient manages to obtain an appointment or see a specialist, completing the necessary diagnostic tests remains an unresolved problem.

A CT scan can be crucial in determining how a disease is progressing. An MRI can provide essential information for establishing a diagnosis. These are not optional machines or luxuries reserved for those who can afford them. They are fundamental tools of modern medicine. Yet breakdowns and a lack of resources to maintain and repair this equipment have ended up compromising essential services.

In July 2026, Associated Press published a report on the state of healthcare in Cuba that specifically included Hermanos Ameijeiras Hospital. A patient with a history of cancer had been waiting seven months for a CT scan because the hospital’s machine was broken. Her story was a painful illustration of what it means to lack access to technology that can be decisive for a person’s life.

But some situations do not need to appear in a news report to reveal just how far the deterioration has gone. Not long ago, I witnessed a scene that I still find difficult to forget.

One of the hospital corridors. The cart with two blue tanks is used to transport water to the upper floors.

Family members accompanying hospitalized patients had to go down to the hospital basement to fetch water because the supply was not adequately reaching the upper floors. While patients remained hospitalized, their relatives had to take responsibility for obtaining something as basic as water. I am not talking about a bottle of drinking water out of personal preference or some additional comfort. I am talking about a basic necessity in any healthcare institution, especially in a place where there are sick people, some with mobility difficulties and others completely dependent on those caring for them.

I stopped to think about what it means for a family to have a loved one hospitalized and, on top of worrying about their health, have to go down to the basement to fetch water. How many other things must these family members manage on their own? How many needs end up becoming family responsibilities because the hospital cannot guarantee even the most basic conditions?

It is difficult not to feel disappointed. Because one can understand that a country is going through economic difficulties, that there are supply problems, or that certain resources are hard to obtain. But it is also impossible not to wonder how an institution of such importance has come to depend on such makeshift solutions for basic aspects of its operation.

And what is most troubling is that we are not talking about a small municipal hospital, a secondary facility, or a center that never had substantial resources. We are talking about Hermanos Ameijeiras.

That hospital which was once a national benchmark, which received patients from across the country, and which for years concentrated some of Cuba’s most specialized medical services.

I think about those who arrive there seeking answers about a serious illness. About those waiting for a diagnostic test that cannot be performed because the equipment is broken. About those who need laboratory tests and discover there are no reagents. About the family members who walk the corridors, climb up and down stairs, and end up taking care of needs that the institution itself should guarantee.

I also think about the doctors and other healthcare workers who remain there, trying to keep what still functions going, often under conditions that do not match the enormous responsibility resting on their shoulders.

Because the deterioration of a hospital is not measured solely by its walls, elevators, or facilities. It is measured, above all, by what it can no longer offer those who need its services.

And perhaps that is the saddest part of this story: the hospital’s name still carries the prestige of what it once was, but the everyday reality of many patients no longer seems to live up to that reputation.

The building is still standing. Its tower continues to dominate part of Havana’s skyline. It still bears the name “Hermanos Ameijeiras” and preserves the memory of an era when it represented the most advanced achievements of Cuban medicine.

But a hospital cannot live off its history. It cannot make diagnoses with memories of its former specialists, perform CT scans with broken equipment, or guarantee medical care by relying solely on the prestige of its name.

A hospital needs doctors, nurses, technicians, medications, reagents, water, electricity, and functioning technology. Above all, it needs to be able to care for its patients.

Hermanos Ameijeiras is still there. But I fear that, for many Cubans, its greatness is beginning to belong to the past. And that is much more than the deterioration of a building.

Read more from the diary of Kamil Kenders here on Havana Times.

World.title: Pneumonia complicates Jair Bolsonaro's hospital stay in Brasília
World.content:
Pneumonia complicates Jair Bolsonaro's hospital stay in Brasília

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 22:09 UTC Full article

Jair Bolsonaro, 71, remains in intensive care at the DF Star hospital.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro has been diagnosed with pneumonia at the Brasília hospital where he has been admitted since Friday with an intestinal obstruction, his doctors said on Monday, although they ruled out surgery after his intestinal condition improved.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro has been diagnosed with pneumonia at the Brasília hospital where he has been admitted since Friday with an intestinal obstruction, his doctors said on Monday, although they ruled out surgery after his intestinal condition improved.

Cardiologist Brasil Caiado told a press conference that Bolsonaro's health had improved since his admission, but that on Sunday afternoon he suffered chills, pain and vomiting. Tests detected bilateral aspiration pneumonia, although less serious than the one diagnosed during another hospital stay in March, according to the doctors.

Surgeon Cláudio Birolini said the intestinal obstruction, the reason for his admission, had improved, so doctors opted to continue clinical treatment rather than operate. The 71-year-old former president will remain in the intensive care unit of the DF Star hospital, and there is no forecast for his discharge.

Bolsonaro, who governed from 2019 to 2022, has had numerous hospital stays and operations since he was stabbed in the abdomen at a campaign event in September 2018. His fragile health was one of the arguments the Supreme Federal Court considered in allowing him to serve under house arrest the 27-year sentence imposed on him for plotting a coup. The court will vote between December 4 and 15 on the constitutionality of a law that reduces the sentences of those convicted in the coup plot.

World.title: UK expresses support for Pedro Alliana's government in Paraguay
World.content:
UK expresses support for Pedro Alliana's government in Paraguay

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 22:05 UTC Full article

Pedro Alliana is sworn in as president of Paraguay, next to his wife.

The United Kingdom has expressed its support for the government of Paraguayan President Pedro Alliana, who took office just over two weeks ago after the removal of Santiago Peña over the collapse of Ueno Bank, Paraguay's Foreign Ministry said on Monday.

The United Kingdom has expressed its support for the government of Paraguayan President Pedro Alliana, who took office just over two weeks ago after the removal of Santiago Peña over the collapse of Ueno Bank, Paraguay's Foreign Ministry said on Monday.

Paraguayan Foreign Minister Rubén Ramírez received a call from Chris Elmore, Parliamentary Under-Secretary of State at the UK Foreign Office, “who conveyed his country's support” for Alliana's administration, the ministry said in a statement. The two reviewed the main issues on the bilateral agenda and agreed on a round of political consultations for early 2027.

Since taking office, Alliana has received calls from Argentine President Javier Milei, Bolivian President Rodrigo Paz and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

Alliana, previously vice-president, was sworn in on November 6 amid the crisis over the takeover of Ueno Bank, a bank linked to Peña that received large deposits from public bodies during his term, including five pension funds. Peña remains in pre-trial detention at a military facility, charged with breach of trust, self-serving administration and criminal association. Former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, also in pre-trial detention, is charged in the same case.

World.title: Brazil's Supreme Court summons Flávio Bolsonaro by public notice over alleged slander of Lula
World.content:
Brazil's Supreme Court summons Flávio Bolsonaro by public notice over alleged slander of Lula

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 21:44 UTC Full article

Senator Flávio Bolsonaro at a public event.

Brazilian Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes on Monday ordered that Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who is in the United States, be summoned by public notice to submit within 15 days his defence against a charge of slandering President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the state news agency Agência Brasil reported.

Brazilian Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes on Monday ordered that Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who is in the United States, be summoned by public notice to submit within 15 days his defence against a charge of slandering President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the state news agency Agência Brasil reported.

The Prosecutor General's Office charged the senator, eldest son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, last week over a post on X on January 3, the day of the US military operation in Venezuela that removed Nicolás Maduro from power. “Lula will be informed on. It is the end of the São Paulo Forum: international drug and arms trafficking, money laundering, support for terrorists and dictatorships, rigged elections,” Flávio Bolsonaro wrote at the time. According to the charge, he linked the president to those crimes.

In his decision, Moraes recalled that the senator had been required to surrender his passports and that he left for the United States after the presidential election, so he must be summoned through a notice published online. “Supreme Federal Court case law holds that summons by public notice is valid when the defendant remains at an uncertain and unknown location, including abroad, with the evident purpose of frustrating the application of criminal law,” he said. If by the end of the period the senator has not appointed a lawyer, the judge may assign his defence to the Public Defender's Office.

Flávio Bolsonaro lost the October 25 presidential run-off to Lula, did not concede defeat and left Brazil via the border with Argentina — with valid documents, according to Argentine authorities — bound for the United States. He is also under investigation for money laundering. The senator denies the allegations and says he is the victim of political persecution.

His father, sentenced to 27 years in prison for plotting a coup, remains in intensive care in Brasília with an intestinal obstruction.

World.title: Brazil cuts its 2027 growth forecast to 1.8% and raises inflation to the top of its target
World.content:
Brazil cuts its 2027 growth forecast to 1.8% and raises inflation to the top of its target

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 21:40 UTC Full article

The Banco Central do Brasil headquarters in Brasília.

Brazil's Finance Ministry has cut its economic growth forecast for 2027 from 2.3% to 1.8% and raised its inflation forecast from 3.8% to 4.5%, the upper limit of the official target, according to its November Macrofiscal Bulletin. The government attributes the slowdown to high interest rates and more expensive credit.

Brazil's Finance Ministry has cut its economic growth forecast for 2027 from 2.3% to 1.8% and raised its inflation forecast from 3.8% to 4.5%, the upper limit of the official target, according to its November Macrofiscal Bulletin, published on Monday. The government attributes the slowdown to high interest rates and more expensive credit.

For this year, the growth forecast was lowered from 2% to 1.9%, and the inflation forecast raised from 4.9% to 5.3%, above the ceiling of the target, which is 3% with a tolerance band of 1.5 percentage points. These are government figures; the Central Bank's latest survey of analysts, published on November 16, is more pessimistic, forecasting growth of 1.7% this year and 1% in 2027.

Economic Policy Secretary Débora Freire said the slowdown is consistent with the Central Bank's tight monetary policy and that third-quarter data confirm it. The ministry expects gross domestic product to have held steady on the second quarter, although it does not rule out a slight decline. By sector, industry will grow 1.4% this year and services 1.7%, while agriculture, the only sector revised upwards, will grow 3.1% thanks to better soybean, maize and coffee harvests.

The report expects the benchmark Selic interest rate, now at 13.75%, to remain high for longer and fall gradually, which will continue to weigh on consumption and investment. Among factors that could push prices up, it cites a stronger dollar, higher state taxes on fuel and gas, tensions in the Middle East, the El Niño phenomenon and the effects of tax reform. The ministry raised its forecast for the price of Brent crude in 2027 from US$79.50 to US$95.20 a barrel.

Some factors could support activity, such as the income tax exemption for lower earners, debt renegotiation programmes and a resilient labour market.

The revision comes days after the Central Bank sold US$1 billion from its reserves to curb the rise of the dollar, amid market distrust of the fiscal adjustment by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's government, which the Chamber of Deputies will vote on this week.

World.title: Uruguay will not announce its CPTPP accession this year and will consult business and unions
World.content:
Uruguay will not announce its CPTPP accession this year and will consult business and unions

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 21:36 UTC Full article

Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin at a press conference in Montevideo.

Uruguay's Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin has ruled out the government announcing before the end of the year the country's accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), and said it will not move forward without consulting business and trade unions.

Uruguay's Foreign Minister Mario Lubetkin has ruled out the government announcing before the end of the year the country's accession to the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), which brings together 12 countries, and said it will not move forward without consulting business and trade unions, amid opposition from industrial unions to the terms under negotiation.

“We are in the phase of exchange and negotiation, of understanding the parameters, comparing them with our parameters and our laws,” Lubetkin said, according to Ámbito. “We will not do anything without permanent consultation with the different actors,” he added, referring to business and union organisations. The government aims to conclude the technical negotiations before the end of the year, but the political decision to join will not be announced in the coming weeks.

Deputy Foreign Minister Valeria Csukasi, who is leading the process, said meetings of the bloc's chief negotiators and trade ministers will be held in Vietnam next week and will be decisive in setting the timetable. The CPTPP brings together 12 countries, including Japan, Australia, Canada, Mexico, Chile, Peru, the United Kingdom and Vietnam.

The Confederation of Industrial Unions rejects accession under the current terms. It warns that opening up without tariffs would hurt sectors such as clothing, footwear, metalworking, plastics and auto parts, and questions possible restrictions on public procurement and the operation of state-owned companies UTE, Ancap, Antel and OSE, as well as the state's exposure to claims by foreign investors. It is calling for a sector-by-sector impact study and tariff phase-out periods of at least 15 years. The main business chambers, meanwhile, are awaiting information from the government on the terms being negotiated.

Uruguay is also focusing its December agenda on Mercosur. On December 2, Punta del Este will host the first Mercosur-European Union business forum; on December 3 the Trade Council of the interim agreement with the EU will meet for the first time, and on December 4 Montevideo will host the bloc's 69th summit of heads of state, at which Uruguay will hand over the pro tempore presidency.

The distribution among members of preferential-tariff export quotas to the EU remains unresolved. Paraguay favours an equal split; Uruguay and Argentina propose taking into account each country's trade with the EU, and Brazil, each partner's global trade. Lubetkin acknowledged that the political crisis in Paraguay and the expected cabinet change in Brazil are slowing the talks, so no decisions are expected at the summit.

World.title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after assurances from the US government
World.content:
Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after assurances from the US government

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 15:08 UTC Full article

The board voted unanimously for his reinstatement “following a series of conversations and meetings” with Huang and was “satisfied with his candour and ability to lead” the company

Nvidia's board on Monday reinstated founder Jensen Huang as chief executive and board member, weeks after his resignation, after receiving information from senior US government officials indicating that his return poses no risk to national security.

The board voted unanimously for his reinstatement “following a series of conversations and meetings” with Huang and was “satisfied with his candour and ability to lead” the company, according to a statement. The board “received information from senior officials of the United States government and, based on that information, is confident that Mr Huang's reinstatement does not represent any risk to national security”, the text adds.

“Jensen is the right person to lead Nvidia,” said Harvey Jones, who remains chairman of the board, thanking Colette Kress for her work as interim chief executive; Kress will continue as chief financial officer. “It is an honour for me to return to Nvidia and lead one of the world's most important technology companies at the dawn of a new industrial revolution. I take on this responsibility with the utmost humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said.

US President Donald Trump, who had publicly called for his return, welcomed the decision. “The Nvidia board has made the right and proper decision to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO. The country needs Jensen's leadership at Nvidia to ensure the success and prosperity not only of the company but of the American economy,” he wrote on his Truth Social network.

Huang resigned after it emerged that he had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom a US intelligence report links to Chinese espionage. According to Uruguay's El País, he had admitted “serious mistakes” and asked to return to the helm. The Justice Department is investigating Megaspeed over the possible diversion of Nvidia chips to China. There are no charges against Huang, and the statement does not clarify the status of the investigations.

World.title: Bolsonaro "clinically stable" in intensive care with an intestinal obstruction
World.content:
Bolsonaro “clinically stable” in intensive care with an intestinal obstruction

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 04:17 UTC Full article

Bolsonaro walking in the hospital corridor, connected to an IV line.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, in intensive care with an intestinal obstruction, is “clinically stable”, the DF Star hospital in Brasília said on Sunday. Bolsonaro, 71, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup, under house arrest.

Former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, in intensive care with an intestinal obstruction, is “clinically stable”, the DF Star hospital in Brasília, where he was admitted on Friday, said on Sunday. Bolsonaro, 71, is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup, under house arrest.

According to the hospital bulletin, the former president is continuing “clinical treatment, fasting and nutritional support”, and there is no forecast yet for his discharge. His wife, Michelle Bolsonaro, wrote on Instagram that he “spent the night without pain” and had been able to walk, and asked for prayers so that he “does not need to undergo a more invasive procedure”. His son Carlos, however, said on X on Saturday that his father had spent the previous night vomiting and in pain, and warned that he could face “the tenth surgery in less than eight years”.

The symptoms began on Friday morning with abdominal distension, and his doctor decided to take him to hospital as his condition worsened. Since he was stabbed in the abdomen during the 2018 election campaign, Bolsonaro has suffered recurrent episodes of intestinal obstruction and has undergone several operations.

Supreme Federal Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes authorised three of his sons to visit him during his hospital stay, banning phones, cameras and other recording devices. The Supreme Court will vote between December 4 and 15 on the constitutionality of a law that reduces the sentences of the former president and others convicted in the coup plot.

His eldest son, Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, had promised to pardon him if he won the election, but lost the October run-off to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva and left Brazil for the United States after becoming the target of a money laundering investigation, according to AFP and O Globo. Flávio denies the allegations and says he is the victim of political persecution.

World.title: COP31 ends without a major climate deal amid divisions over fossil fuels
World.content:
COP31 ends without a major climate deal amid divisions over fossil fuels

23rd Monday, November 2026 - 04:12 UTC Full article

COP31 President Murat Kurum (L) and Australian minister Chris Bowen at the summit in Antalya.

The UN COP31 climate summit in the Turkish city of Antalya ended on Sunday without a major political agreement, after deep divisions between countries over fossil fuels and finance for the poorest. It is the first time since the 2009 Copenhagen summit that the main declaration of one of these conferences has collapsed in this way.

The UN COP31 climate summit in the Turkish city of Antalya ended on Sunday without a major political agreement, after deep divisions between countries over fossil fuels and finance for the poorest. It is the first time since the 2009 Copenhagen summit that the main declaration of one of these conferences has collapsed in this way.

Negotiations, due to end on Friday, ran into Sunday, making COP31 the longest UN climate conference in history, according to the BBC. The final draft, presented in the early hours, did not mention “fossil fuels”, the main cause of global warming, and referred only indirectly to the commitment made at COP28 in 2023 to “transition away” from them in energy systems. An earlier draft mentioned them six times, which was unacceptable to oil-producing countries.

The European Union, Pacific island states and others rejected the text. “It is unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no mention of fossil fuels,” said the EU's representative, Irish minister Darragh O'Brien. Panama and the Marshall Islands also criticised its lack of ambition. At the other end, Saudi Arabia's delegate, Mohammad Ayoub, said Arab countries had negotiated “in good faith” and noted that they account for only a small share of historical emissions, while Russia warned that moving away from fossil fuels too quickly would cause “fuel poverty”.

Developing countries also objected to the absence of concrete figures to deliver on the commitment, agreed last year at COP30 in Brazil, to triple finance for adaptation to climate change. “Rich nations and polluting governments cannot keep arriving empty-handed,” said Mohamed Adow of the African think tank Power Shift Africa.

UN Secretary-General António Guterres, at his last climate summit before stepping down, said he was “deeply disappointed” and accused “powerful fossil fuel interests” of following “a page from Big Tobacco's playbook”. Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, whose government led the negotiations, blamed the failure on “difficult geopolitical times”. Australian minister Chris Bowen, president of the negotiations, spoke of “unbridgeable red lines”.

There was some progress, including on a “just transition mechanism” to support workers and communities affected by the energy shift, and more than 80 countries backed Turkey's proposed target for electricity to meet 35% of global energy use by 2035. UN climate chief Simon Stiell said he would seek advice on reforming a consensus-based process that “fell short” on Sunday. The next summit, COP32, will be held in Ethiopia in November 2027.

With current policies, the planet is heading for warming of about 2.8C by 2100, according to the UN, well above the 1.5C limit set in Paris in 2015, which will be exceeded in the next few years.

World.title: In Q3, Mexico’s economy grew 3.3% over 2025, its best showing since 2023
World.content:
Mexico’s economy grew 0.9% during the third quarter of 2026 compared to the previous three months and 3.3% compared to the same period of last year, according to final seasonally adjusted data published by the national statistics agency INEGI on Monday.

The quarter-over-quarter growth rate was unchanged from that reported in preliminary data in late October, while the year-over-year expansion was 0.1 percentage points higher.

The 3.3% year-over-year growth rate is the highest for any quarter since the second quarter of 2023, when Mexico’s economy also expanded 3.3%. The quarter-over-quarter growth rate is lower than the 1.4% expansion in Q2 of 2026, but a much better result than the 0.6% contraction in Q1.

INEGI also reported that Mexico’s economy grew 1.9% in the first nine months of 2026 compared to the same period of 2025.

Services sector drives growth

The tertiary or services sector outperformed the primary and secondary sectors in terms of growth in the third quarter of 2026 and in the first nine months of the year. The tertiary sector grew:

1.2% in Q3 compared to the April-June quarter.

3.6% in Q3 compared to the third quarter of last year.

2.5% between January and September compared to the first nine months of 2025.

The secondary sector, which includes manufacturing and construction, grew:

0.4% in Q3 compared to Q2.

2.7% in Q3 compared to the same period of last year.

1.1% year over year in the first nine months of 2026.

The primary sector, which includes agriculture and fishing, was Mexico’s worst-performing sector. It grew:

0.3% in Q3 compared to Q2.

1.5% in Q3 compared to the same period of last year.

In the first nine months of 2026, the primary sector contracted 0.9% compared to the same period of last year.

2026 growth forecasts for Mexico’s economy

The most recent Citi Mexico Expectations Survey yielded a median GDP growth projection of 1.8% for 2026, unchanged from the previous survey.

In a social media post after INEGI published its Q3 growth data on Monday morning, Gabriela Siller, director of economic analysis at Banco Base, predicted growth of 2.1% in 2026.

Mexico’s economy grew just 0.8% in 2025, the worst result since a sharp pandemic-induced contraction in 2020.

Other need-to-know economic data

The USD:MXN exchange rate was 19.12 at 1:30 p.m. Monday Mexico City time, according to Bloomberg.

Mexico’s annual headline inflation rate was 3.75% in October, up from 3.45% in September.

The Bank of Mexico’s benchmark interest rate is currently set at 6.25% after a 25-basis-point cut earlier this month.

Mexico received US $47.16 billion in remittances in the first nine months of 2026, an increase of 2.1% compared to the same period of last year.

With reports from Reuters and El CEO

World.title: A new WhatsApp chatbot in Mexico has a mission: protecting children from recruitment by organized crime
World.content:
A new WhatsApp chatbot named Fran is seeking to combat the recruitment of children by Mexico’s criminal groups.

Developed by the Mexican nonprofit Reinserta with support from Meta, the parent company of Facebook and WhatsApp, the chatbot provides free information to help young people and families spot the warning signs before an offer of friendship or work becomes a trap.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Reinserta, A.C. (@reinserta)

The automated chatbot also offers emotional support tools and options for those seeking help. It’s designed for adolescents, caregivers and frontline workers who may encounter children at risk.

Reinserta works with young people affected by violence, including children living with incarcerated mothers, and helps young offenders reintegrate into society.

The nonprofit presented Fran last week at its care center in Mexico City, noting that recruitment into cartels and criminal organizations can begin in schools, parks, families or online, including through video games.

Criminal groups exploit vulnerabilities through deception, coercion and promises of jobs or belonging, the organization added.

The danger often comes through someone familiar.

According to figures from a 2022 study Reinserta cited at the launch, half of the detained adolescents it studied who had been recruited by organized crime identified a friend as their recruiter.

Among those studied, eight in 10 had not belonged to gangs before joining a cartel, and seven in 10 reported receiving training within the criminal organization. The study used a nonrandom sample, so its findings are not nationally representative.

Fran grew out of messages from people worried about recruitment and unsure what to do, said Carmen Mari Suárez, Reinserta’s communications director. The organization, whose name means “reintegrate,” was founded in 2013 by psychologists Saskia Niño de Rivera and Mercedes Castañeda.

Reinserta developed the chatbot using its research, prevention guides, and experience supporting adolescents and families.

The goal is to put guidance within reach when concerns first emerge, rather than after recruitment has occurred.

Past cases show how those approaches can escalate.

Mexico News Daily reported in 2021 that three boys were rescued in Oaxaca after a cartel recruiter approached one through the online shooting game Free Fire and offered him work as a lookout.

Another report described a boy recruited as a lookout at 13 who later received hitman training.

The chatbot was inspired by Francisco, who experienced organized crime violence at 6 and became a hitman at 12, Uno TV reported.

Fran is available on WhatsApp by sending a message to “Chatbot Reinserta” at +52 (566) 984-8797.

With reports from Infobae, Uno TV, MVS Noticias and Linea Politica

World.title: Center for experimental sargassum solutions to open in Playa del Carmen
World.content:
Mexico’s first Experimental Center Sargassum Collection and Treatment (CEATS) will be developed in the Caribbean beach town of Playa del Carmen in Quintana Roo, with the aim of finding innovative ways to tackle increasing arrivals of sargassum in high-tourism-value areas.

Playa del Carmen’s mayor, Estefanía Mercado, announced that CEATS will be developed by the National Fund for Tourism Development (Fonatur), in coordination with the Quintana Roo State Government and the Playa del Carmen City Council, with operations expected to commence in the first half of 2027.

The federal government has earmarked more than 2.6 billion pesos (US $135.8 million) to confront the problem, with part of the funding going toward the development of the center. The investment follows a record season in which 162,226 metric tonnes of sargassum were cleared from Quintana Roo’s beaches between April and November, more than double the 85,000 tonnes recorded in 2025.

The center will study the collecting, separating and processing of the algae to explore alternative uses. Authorities say the goal is to limit environmental damage and prevent the loss of sand that results from conventional cleanup methods along the state’s coastline.

Mercado emphasized that the initiative was the result of coordination between President Sheinbaum and the Governor of Quintana Roo, María Lezama Espinosa. She said that if CEATS proves to be successful, the technologies and solutions could be deployed in other sargassum-prone areas.

This year, in Playa del Carmen alone, officials collected 55,378 tonnes of sargassum. Local media sources reported that around 4.3 billion pesos (US $231 million) were allocated to cleanup efforts across the state, carried out by hoteliers and all three levels of government.

“Protecting our beaches also means protecting the livelihoods of thousands of families and the future of Playa del Carmen,” Mercado wrote on her official social media pages on Nov. 16.

With reports from Quadratín Quintana Roo

World.title: Farmacias Guadalajara, the national drugstore chain, introduces robot technology in its customer service
World.content:
Farmacias Guadalajara — a nationwide drugstore and convenience chain — has incorporated robotic technology into one of its newest outlets in an effort to streamline customer service.

Located in the Plaza Las Américas in Zapopan, Jalisco, a northwestern suburb of Guadalajara, the new drugstore incorporates technology into sales and storage processes to reduce service times and facilitate medication purchases without eliminating counter service.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Farmacias Guadalajara (@farmaciasguadalajara)

The concept — the first of its kind in Mexico — features artificial intelligence platforms to expedite inquiries and inventories, a robot that can dispense medication and allows for cash or card payments.

Branch manager Griselda García told Mural newspaper that customers can search for medications using text, voice commands or by scanning their prescription to view available products.

Customers can also search for medications by brand name or active ingredient using voice or text commands.

To use the robot — named Rudy — shoppers have four options: dictate the name of the medication they need, enter the code of a prescription issued by PharmaClinic offices, type the name or active ingredient of the product or directly scan the prescription, even if handwritten.

Once the medication is identified, the system checks the branch’s inventory to display only available products and brands. If it’s an over-the-counter medication, the customer can select it and pay directly at the machine.

Rudy is programmed to locate and deliver the products requested (via a slide located next to the screen) and also conducts inventory control, recording the receipt and dispatch of merchandise, thus automating storage and order fulfillment tasks.

Artificial intelligence also plays a role in prescription interpretation by identifying medications and generating product suggestions, García said.

Although technology handles some operations, the branch maintains traditional checkout lanes and staff to assist those who prefer to shop directly with an employee.

In a statement, Farmacias Guadalajara said the new system is not designed to replace staff.

Workers continue to serve customers, especially when antibiotics or controlled medications are needed, as they require the review of the corresponding prescriptions.

Likewise, counter staff remain available to answer questions about medications and process payments for other items in the store, as is the case at conventional checkouts.

With reports from Mural and Informador

World.title: MND Local Guadalajara: A chocolate fair, Tame Impala, Navidalia and art contemplating longevity
World.content:
Holiday decorations are popping up all over town, and Navidalia will be opening shortly. For visitors and residents alike, Guadalajara delivers a packed December calendar with craft markets, a book fair, art exhibits, live concerts and more.

We’ll get into all of that in a minute. But first, let’s talk chocolate.

The Cacao and Chocolate Fair returns to Guadalajara in December

For that special someone on your holiday shopping list who’s especially difficult, the Cacao and Chocolate Fair arrives at just the right time.

Returning to Guadalajara for its 12th edition next month, the annual Cacao and Chocolate Fair brings together more than 40 chocolate brands and master chocolatiers from around Mexico, allowing locals to sample to their hearts’ delight.

Organized by the beloved Producers’ Fair, the event aims to promote high-quality Mexican chocolate as part of the country’s cultural and economic heritage. As in previous years, there will be a gastronomic area with single-origin chocolate bars, traditional beverages, one-of-a-kind desserts and whatever else these innovative chocolatiers have in mind.

In addition to tastings, there will be live music, workshops and talks focused on cacao cultivation and its myriad culinary applications. For the little ones, there will be chocolate-themed play areas and plenty of space for socializing.

It’s a perfect holiday outing for chocoholics, with activities for the whole family to enjoy. For more information, keep an eye on the organizers’ social media.

Dates: Dec. 18 and19 from noon to 7 p.m. Dec. 20 from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m.

Dec. 18 and19 from noon to 7 p.m. Dec. 20 from 10 a.m. to 7 p.m. Location : Club de Leones, Av. de los Leones #75, Colonia Tepeyac Casino, Zapopan

Cost: Free

Tame Impala is set to perform in Guadalajara next February

Tame Impala returns in early 2027 for its first live concert performances in Mexico since 2023.

Writer, producer, musician, performer, DJ and all-around creative force behind the band, Kevin Parker has had music critics and rock fans swooning since Tame Impala’s debut album, “Innerspeaker,” dropped 16 years ago. A self-described loner who prefers tinkering in his home music studio, Parker makes music that defies easy categorization.

Its lush, genre-bending oeuvre spans psych rock, indie, modern disco, electronic dance music and more recently, pop. For those who love to dance, check out the 2025 Grammy-winning “Neverender,” performed with Justice, and anyone looking to explore the band’s roots should stream the confessional “Solitude is Bliss.”

Over the past 15 years, Tame Impala has racked up numerous Grammy, ARIA and BRIT awards along the way, as well as billions of listens on music streaming platforms, cementing Parker’s rock legend status.

Touring in support of its fifth studio LP, “Deadbeat,” Tame Impala plans to make stops in Monterrey and Mexico City this winter in addition to Guadalajara, before headlining the Coachella Valley Music and Arts Festival in April.

Date: Feb. 23, 2027

Feb. 23, 2027 Location: Arena VFG on the Chapala Highway, Tlajomulco de Zúñiga

Arena VFG on the Chapala Highway, Tlajomulco de Zúñiga Cost: Sales to the general public began on Nov. 20 via Ticketmaster.

Navidalia stages its 7th edition in Guadalajara

There are some who consider the Christmas season to be the most wonderful time of the year. If you’re one of them, Navidalia 2026 in Guadalajara should be squeezed into your December to-do list.

Now in its seventh year, Navidalia is an immersive, nighttime Christmas-themed park designed by Altea Emotions, which is also the creative force behind the Día de Muertos-themed park Calaverandia.

This year’s Navidalia will span five hectares in Parque Ávila Camacho and feature four unique themes. Guests can expect a fairy-tale-like snowy forest ambiance with wintry decorations, ice skating, a huge evergreen tree, a European-style holiday market, nativity scenes, holiday carols, seasonal gastronomy, myriad family activities and more.

Dec. 4 to Dec. 30 (closed Dec. 7, 14 and 24) Location: Parque Ávila Camacho, across from Plaza Patria in Guadalajara

Parque Ávila Camacho, across from Plaza Patria in Guadalajara Cost: On sale at the park’s box office and online at Boletomovil.

Contemplate the keys to longevity at the new art exhibition ‘Everblue’

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Platino60. Nueva Longevidad (@platino_60)

The new art exhibition “Everblue” was inspired by the five blue zones across the globe, where humans frequently live to be 100 years old. The five blue zones are in Okinawa, Japan; Loma Linda, California; Nicoya, Costa Rica; Sardinia, Italy; and Icaria, Greece.

What explains this outsized number of centenarians in these seemingly dissimilar places?

Scientists have identified a handful of traits shared by the inhabitants of these blue zones, including strong community, daily rituals, plant-based diets, regular physical activity, connection to nature and having a clear purpose in life.

Drawing from this phenomenon, the art featured in “Everblue” invites us to reflect on our current lifestyles and what brings us joy, while questioning areas we may have long neglected.

The exhibition is a joint Chile-Mexico initiative organized through the Movimiento Internacional Arte Azul and the Chilean chapter of Ciudades Azules. Among the 20 artists participating in “Everblue” are Guadalajara natives Indira Castellón and Hiran Lomelí, Mexican Caribbean-born Edgar Bacalao and Freak Salazar of Durango.

Dates: Runs from Nov. 5 to Dec. 6

Runs from Nov. 5 to Dec. 6 Location: Manifesto Gallery in Colonia Americana

World.title: 49ers give their ample Mexican fan base something to cheer about, 35-10
World.content:
Mexico’s loud and proud San Francisco 49ers fan base roared with delight throughout Sunday night’s NFL game at Mexico City’s Estadio Banorte as the Niners demolished the Minnesota Vikings 35-10, in the NFL’s return to Mexico for a regular season game after a four-year absence.

In front of 85,612 spectators, San Francisco quarterback Brock Purdy threw three touchdown passes against the NFL’s stingiest team, while linebacker Fred Warner led a hard-hitting defense that forced two turnovers, including a pick six by Ji’Ayir Brown just before halftime.

Though hundreds of Vikings jerseys were visible in the stands, there was no doubt which was the “home team.”

Sports Illustrated wrote that “it was more than clear that this was a pro-49ers crowd at the historic venue in Mexico City.”

San Francisco tight end George Kittle was the recipient of two of Purdy’s TD passes and each time celebrated with the “Zero Fear” hand gesture popularized by Penta, a Mexican WWE wrestler who has been friends with Kittle for years. Kittle even donned a Penta mask before the game.

Warner is also a fan favorite in Mexico. The 30-year-old linebacker carried the Mexican flag onto the field before Sunday night’s game, just as he did four years ago when the 49ers last played in Mexico City. Warner’s maternal grandfather was born in Mexico and he attended several World Cup matches at Estadio Azteca proudly wearing an El Tri jersey this summer.

On the negative side, 49ers defensive end Nick Bosa was booed during pre-game warm-ups as thousands showed their displeasure at his comments last week criticizing the timing of Mexican fans’ cheering, though others took them as well-intentioned.

While the Niners took care of business inside the stadium, Mexico City authorities collaborated with NFL officials to safeguard the environment outside Estadio Banorte throughout the night.

Mexico City’s Security Ministry implemented its “Estadio Seguro” operation perfected during the World Cup, with approximately 5,000 officers carrying out perimeter screening, crowd control, transit/Park & Ride logistics and staff accompaniment, before and after the game.

With reports from ESPN, Esto, TUDN and El Financiero

World.title: 8 more arrested in Sinaloa after firefight with soldiers, bringing weekend total to 16
World.content:
Two days after the arrest of the cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro” and seven other suspects in the northern state of Sinaloa, the Mexican Army detained eight more alleged members of the same criminal organization.

Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, identified by Mexican authorities as the leader of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organization, and seven other alleged criminals were arrested in an operation in Guasave on Friday night, while Sunday’s arrests took place in the neighboring municipality of Sinaloa.

Derivado de la detención de Fausto N (a) “Chapo Isidro”; personal de Fuerzas Especiales del Ejército Mexicano, en coordinación con elementos de Fuerzas Especiales del Ejército comisionados en la Secretaría de Seguridad Pública del Estado de Sinaloa, durante reconocimientos a inmediaciones del poblado El Platanito, municipio de Sinaloa de Leyva, Sin., fueron agredidos con armas de fuego por integrantes de un grupo delictivo. Al repeler la agresión, se logró la detención de 8 integrantes, entre ellos un menor de edad, de la organización delictiva “Beltrán Leyva”, facción “Chapo Isidro”, quienes participaron en los bloqueos del día 20 de noviembre tras la detención de Fausto N; y el aseguramiento de 1 ametralladora Cal. .50”, 1 fusil Barrett Cal. .50”, 1 ametralladora Minimi Cal. 5.56 mm, 6 armas largas, 4 armas cortas, droga, cargadores y municiones de diferentes calibres, diverso equipo táctico y 6 vehículos, de los cuales 2 cuentan con blindaje artesanal y una torreta para el emplazamiento de ametralladoras. Los detenidos y lo asegurado serán puestos a disposición de la Fiscalía General de la República, con sede en Culiacán, Sin., para continuar con las investigaciones correspondientes. #NoticiadeÚltimaHora #ComunicadoDePrensa #EjércitoMexicano #FuerzaAéreaMx #GuardiaNacional — @Defensamx (@Defensamx1) November 23, 2026

The Ministry of National Defense (Defensa) announced the latest arrests in a social media post late Sunday night, saying that military personnel made them after they came under fire.

“Following the arrest of Fausto N, alias ‘Chapo Isidro,’ Mexican Army Special Forces personnel, in coordination with Army Special Forces personnel assigned to the Sinaloa State Public Security Ministry, were fired upon by members of a criminal group while conducting reconnaissance near the town of El Platanito in the municipality of Sinaloa de Leyva, Sinaloa,” Defensa said, using the name of the municipal seat rather than the municipality.

The ministry said that the military personnel fended off the attack and subsequently arrested eight members of the “Chapo Isidro faction” of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organization, including a minor. None of the suspects was identified by name, and no injuries from the gun battle were reported.

Defensa said that the suspects “took part” in the narco-blockades that were set up on major roads in Sinaloa after the arrest of Meza Flores on Friday night. Video footage included in the ministry’s post showed one handcuffed suspect being marched toward a helicopter by soldiers.

Defensa said that military personnel also seized 13 firearms, magazines, ammunition, drugs, tactical equipment and six vehicles, two of which were fitted with makeshift armor and machine gun turrets.

The ministry said that the eight detained suspects and seized property would be turned over to the Federal Attorney General’s Office in Culiacán “in order to continue the corresponding investigations.”

With reports from López-Dóriga Digital and El Financiero

Trevilla said Meza Flores was transferred to Culiacán and then flown to Mexico City, where he was placed in the custody of the Federal Attorney General’s Office early Saturday. He was wanted in Mexico on organized crime and drug trafficking charges and is subject to a U.S. extradition request. 👥 Cousin and brother-in-law also detained: Trevilla said Meza Flores’ cousin and alleged second-in-command and his brother-in-law and “financial operator” were also detained in Guasave.

Trevilla said Meza Flores’ cousin and alleged second-in-command and his brother-in-law and “financial operator” were also detained in Guasave. ⚠️ 16 “alleged criminals” killed in operation: Trevilla said seven deaths were initially reported in a Nov. 21 Defense Ministry press release. However, nine others’ bodies were located later, he said.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Monday morning press conference three days after Mexican special forces detained Fausto Isidro Meza Flores, a cartel leader known as “El Chapo Isidro,” who was one of the U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation’s 10 most-wanted fugitives.

Meza Flores, 44, was allegedly involved in drug trafficking for more than two decades, including as a leader of the Beltrán Leyva Organization and Los Mazatlecos, also known as the Guasave Cartel and the Meza Flores Transnational Criminal Organization. He was considered one of Mexico’s largest and most powerful drug traffickers, allegedly shipping huge quantities of narcotics, including fentanyl, to the United States.

His arrest at a home in the municipality of Guasave in the northern state of Sinaloa on Friday night was the central focus of today’s mañanera, at which Sheinbaum was accompanied by the federal government’s top security officials.

The arrest of Meza Flores and seven other alleged criminals in Guasave occurred during Operación Centella (Operation Lightning), a Mexican military operation for which U.S. authorities provided intelligence.

Sheinbaum laments deaths of 4 soldiers in Sinaloa

At the start of her press conference, Sheinbaum acknowledged the deaths of four soldiers in Sinaloa on Friday during the operation to capture Meza Flores.

“Our condolences, our affection, appreciation and admiration to the army troops who lost their lives,” she said.

“[They were] four very well-trained men with a lot of dedication to the country,” Sheinbaum said.

“Our condolences, our admiration not just to their families, but also to the entire army and Ministry of National Defense,” she added.

On behalf of the federal government’s Security Cabinet, Security Minister Omar García Harfuch expressed “our deepest respect, gratitude and solidarity” to the families of the deceased soldiers and their “comrades in arms.”

He also wished a speedy recovery to 10 troops who were injured in Friday’s operation.

Defense Minister highlights intelligence cooperation with US authorities

National Defense Minister Ricardo Trevilla Trejo said that Operación Centella, like all operations, had three stages: “One of intelligence, another stage of planning and then the execution.”

He said that in 2026, a lot of intelligence “analysts” were tasked with monitoring the movements of Meza Flores.

Trevilla said that the Defense Ministry shared “a lot of information” derived from that monitoring with the U.S. government.

In the past three months, there was “a very significant exchange of information” between Mexican and U.S. authorities, he said.

I commend Mexico’s security forces for their courage and professionalism in carrying out this operation. Strategic intelligence sharing between the United States and Mexico helped make this operation possible, leading to the arrest of Fausto Isidro “Chapo Isidro,” one of the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted fugitives, and two other key members of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organization. Results like these don’t happen overnight. They are built on sustained cooperation and trust. This is what partners can accomplish together. We will continue the hunt. Terrorist Cartels and criminals will be brought to justice. And together we will make both our nations safer. — Embajador Ronald Johnson (@USAmbMex) November 21, 2026

“The intention was to establish the [exact] location of this person, who we had already placed in the area of Guasave,” Trevilla said.

He noted that U.S. drones were used to monitor Meza Flores. He stressed that Mexico requested such assistance from the U.S. and asserted that the flying of U.S. drones in Mexico didn’t violate the Mexican Constitution or the National Security Law.

“This work was carried out [and] a lot of the information that was obtained was analyzed by the analysts … and we identified the location of this person … on November 20,” Trevilla said.

The New York Times reported on Saturday that “[w]henever the weather allowed, the United States flew drone reconnaissance missions, at the request and authorization of the Mexican government, over the area where Mr. Meza Flores was believed to be.”

“Mexican military analysts then pieced together his daily routines, intercepting his communications and studying him on live video feed from the drones,” the Times reported, citing an unnamed official.

How the operation unfolded

Trevilla said that 47 members of a Mexican Army special forces team called the “murciélagos” (bats) and a National Guard special forces team called the “lobos” (wolves) carried out the ground operation to detain Meza Flores.

He said that 128 paratroopers and 106 “regular troops,” among other military personnel, also participated in the operation, which was carried out with “stealth” and “surprise,” according to a Defense Ministry statement.

Trevilla said that six military helicopters provided air support for the operation. He added that seven military planes and an Air Force drone made up the “strategic reserve” for the operation.

Trevilla said that the military personnel arrived at the home where Meza Flores was detained at 7:50 p.m. on Friday and came under attack. Nevertheless, they entered the home and detained those inside, including “El Chapo Isidro.”

“The criminals who were inside the home surrendered,” Trevilla said.

“Afterward, the attacks aimed at rescuing El Chapo Isidro increased,” he said, explaining that narco-blockades were set up on various roads to “prevent his transfer.”

Trevilla said that military helicopters came under attack and returned fire.

“That is what was seen in the images,” he said, referring to video footage of helicopters firing at targets on the ground in Guasave.

Trevilla said that Meza Flores and other suspects detained in the operation were transferred by land to Culiacán late on Friday night. El Chapo Isidro and two other suspects were subsequently transported by air to Mexico City, where they were placed in the custody of the Federal Attorney General’s Office early Saturday.

“Speaking of the results of Operación Centella, the arrest of Fausto N, alias El Chapo Isidro, boss of the Beltrán Leyva criminal organization, was achieved,” Trevilla said.

He noted that Meza Flores was wanted in Mexico on organized crime and drug trafficking charges. Trevilla also acknowledged that he is subject to an extradition request from authorities in the United States, where he also faces drug trafficking charges.

He said that Meza Flores’ cousin and the alleged second-in-command of the Beltrán Leyva organization, a man identified as Germán N, as well as his brother-in-law and “financial operator,” a man identified as José Luis N, were also detained in Guasave on Friday.

Trevilla: 16 ‘alleged criminals’ were killed during the operation

Trevilla told reporters that a total of 16 “alleged criminals” were killed during the operation in Guasave.

“In the press release that the Ministry of National Defense issued on the morning of Nov. 21, [the deaths of] seven [alleged criminals] were mentioned. The rest [of the deceased alleged criminals] were located later,” he said.

Trevilla also conveyed his condolences to the families of the four soldiers who were killed.

“Today, funeral honors will be held for our brothers in arms,” he said.

World.title: Peru Ex-Mayor Says Lima Ban Is Vote Theft
World.content:
Peru's electoral court says a former mayor cannot return to City Hall by the back door. He calls the decision theft, and the fight now moves to other institutions.

The Municipal Palace, city hall of Lima, on the Plaza Mayor. Photo: Ovruni / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Peru · Lima Mayor Ruling

Peru’s electoral court, the Jurado Nacional de Elecciones (JNE), rejected a request for reconsideration on Thursday 19 November 2026 from the party of Rafael López Aliaga, the former mayor of Lima. The ruling closes the file and keeps him out of the capital’s mayoralty.

López Aliaga leads Renovación Popular, a conservative party, and was mayor of Lima from 2023 until he resigned on 13 October 2025 to run for president. In the regional and municipal elections of 4 October 2026, ONPE, the national electoral office that counts the votes, finished its Lima count with his party first, on 27.685% of valid votes.

The party’s mayoral candidate, Luis Rubio, withdrew in August 2026, and López Aliaga ran as first regidor, the first councillor, who normally steps up when a mayor cannot serve. Article 194 of Peru’s constitution bars the immediate re-election of mayors, and the JNE applied that rule to this route as well.

On 2 November 2026 the JNE’s full bench issued Resolution 4557-2026-JNE, whose point 3 says a first regidor who was mayor in the previous term cannot take over the mayoralty, not even by succession. The court’s five magistrates adopted it by majority, under its president, Roberto Burneo.

The credential for Lima mayor therefore goes to the second regidor on the list, Jeanette Alonzo. JNE secretary general Yessica Clavijo Chipoco said on 12 November 2026 that the law, given the supremacy of the Constitution, “clearly establishes that there is no re-election” (translated).

Lima is not the only case: Clavijo said about 20 winning lists nationwide have a former mayor as first regidor, and that the resolution corrects six of those cases. The same criterion therefore applies to those lists.

On 10 November 2026 the party’s legal representative, Fernando Sandoval Ruiz, filed a request for reconsideration. It argued that the JNE changed the rules after the vote.

On Thursday 19 November 2026 the plenary declared the request improcedente, meaning inadmissible, in a ruling that closed the file. The ruling carries the signatures of Burneo, Martha Maisch, Gunther Gonzales, Rubén Torres and Aarón Oyarce, and the JNE’s secretary general has said its plenary resolutions are final.

In the television interview reported on Monday 23 November 2026, he called the ruling a violation of the popular will. He argued there is a legal difference between running directly for re-election and taking over the mayoralty through succession, and cited Articles 195 and 139(9) of the Constitution.

He also said the JNE exceeded its powers by ruling on provisions of the Organic Law of Municipalities, the statute that governs local councils, and renewed his criticism of Burneo, the JNE president, alleging irregularities in earlier elections, including those of 2021 and 2026. These are his claims, and the interview report gives no evidence for them.

The party’s legal representative, Sandoval Ruiz, holds that the rules were changed after the vote. The JNE’s answer is its secretary general’s reading that the constitution leaves no room for re-election at this level.

If nothing changes, Alonzo takes over the mayoralty and López Aliaga becomes a regidor. He said that if his situation is not resolved before 1 January, the next person on the list must take office and he will serve as regidor, as the law requires.

López Aliaga announced he will go to the Constitutional Tribunal, and is weighing criminal actions, a competence conflict and a constitutional complaint in Congress. As of 23 November no filing at the Tribunal is confirmed.

It is not known whether the Tribunal will take a case. It is also not known whether the JNE will hand Alonzo the credential on a set date.

The ruling is mainly a domestic matter for Peru. For US readers the link is limited to investors who follow how Peru’s institutions handle disputed results.

On Sunday 6 December 2026, Peruvian regions where no ticket reached 30% of valid votes elect governors in a second round, convened by Supreme Decree 150-2026-PCM of 11 November 2026 in the official gazette. The new municipal term, 2027 to 2030, begins on 1 January 2027, the date López Aliaga himself cites.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why can López Aliaga not become mayor of Lima?

Peru’s constitution bars the immediate re-election of mayors, and the electoral court applies that rule to a former mayor who steps up as first councillor. It ruled that the ban holds even by succession.

Can the electoral court’s ruling still be appealed?

The electoral court has said its plenary resolutions are final. López Aliaga says he will go to the Constitutional Tribunal, but no filing there is confirmed.

Who becomes mayor of Lima instead?

World.title: Doctors Without Borders Halts Care in Yei
World.content:
Brief: South Sudan

Doctors Without Borders, known by its French initials MSF, suspended all its work in Yei River County in South Sudan for at least three months from Tuesday 17 November 2026. An MSF ambulance driver and a South Sudan Ministry of Health midwife had been abducted on Thursday 12 November.

Both were freed unharmed on Saturday 14 November, MSF said in a statement dated Monday 23 November 2026. The pause ends its support for Yei Civil Hospital and the Jansuk clinic near the town, and halts work on a 10-bed isolation ward for Ebola, a deadly viral disease, that MSF calls the only one in the county.

MSF says it will return only when security clearly improves. The statement carries no official response.

Dr Ferdinand Atte, MSF’s head of mission in South Sudan, called the decision “painful and uneasy” given the needs of pregnant and breastfeeding women, children and older people. He said MSF also had to suspend its Ebola preparedness support, which “could have dramatic consequences in case of the outbreak in the area”.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Doctors Without Borders Email address Follow

MSF says unknown armed assailants stopped its ambulance at gunpoint about three miles (five kilometres) from Yei, as it headed back to Jansuk from Yei Civil Hospital after referring patients. The stop happened 500 metres from the Jansuk health facility, according to the statement.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Libya's oil firm says a group shut a pipeline valve” Get the brief

“MSF cannot continue operating in Yei area while abductions are now taking place even within the town,” Dr Atte said. He added that after the 2025 abductions, authorities gave verbal assurances that staff and patients would be protected within a five-mile (eight-kilometre) radius around Yei.

MSF counts this as the fifth abduction affecting its staff in Yei River County since 2024. MSF says it already suspended all activities in the same county in August 2025, after two abductions in just over a week.

MSF says it has worked in what is now South Sudan since 1983, and that from January to October 2026 it gave more than 719,000 outpatient consultations in the country. It will restart only after a “substantial, sustained and verifiable improvement in the security environment”, it says, a condition it describes as not met today.

The statement gives no names for the two people, no motive and no ransom detail, and no police or government comment has been published with it. Our report on a separate abduction of three aid workers near Yei on 9 November has more.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Doctors Without Borders leave Yei?

It says staff safety comes first, because abductions now happen even within the town. It also says earlier verbal assurances from authorities did not hold.

Is there Ebola in Yei?

MSF’s statement does not report an outbreak there. It describes the suspended work as preparation in case one starts.

World.title: Buenos Aires Gas Blast Toll Rises to Four
World.content:
Four deaths, a pipe the mayor says was missing from the plans and a drilling machine in evidence: what is known ten days after the blast, and what remains open.

ARGENTINA · SECURITY

Two more workers have died, bringing the toll to four, after the gas explosion that ripped through a shopping street in Remedios de Escalada, a district of Lanús on the southern edge of Buenos Aires, on Friday 13 November 2026. Two of the dead worked for Metrogas, the gas distributor for the capital area, and two for Exgadet, the contractor that was renewing its pipes.

Investigators now ask why a gas pipe that was in service did not appear on the plans Metrogas gave the local authorities. Nobody has been charged, and the answer matters to US investors because YPF, the Argentine oil company listed in New York, has agreed to sell its 70% stake in Metrogas for US$780 million.

The inquiry No one is charged, and the drilling machine has been seized.

The chain of events began at 9:44 a.m. on 13 November, when a horizontal drilling machine owned by Exgadet struck a gas pipe at the corner of Coronel Beltrán and Del Valle Iberlucea, according to the municipality’s reconstruction of events. Metrogas said in a statement that a machine damaged a pipe of its network and that the explosion came while its crew was repairing the leak, at about 10:50 a.m.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Remedios de Escalada (Argentina) Email address Follow

Exgadet was working under a Metrogas contract for the renewal of the distribution network in the area, according to the company’s filing to the prosecutor. The company also handed the prosecutor its contracts and documents.

Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Julián Álvarez, the mayor of Lanús, says the crew worked from a map on which the pipe did not appear. He adds that the municipality does not supervise the gas network, which is regulated nationally.

More than an hour passed between the puncture of the pipe and the explosion. Judicial accounts of the case call the broken pipe medium pressure, so even its class is still to be settled.

The municipality accuses Metrogas of failing to follow emergency protocols, and the prosecutor, Yanina Estévez of Lanús prosecution unit 6, ordered two Metrogas executives detained for questioning. Metrogas has said only that a machine damaged its pipe and that the blast came during the repair.

Estévez has since seized the drilling machine, a Ditch Witch JT20 kept at Exgadet’s yard in Valentín Alsina, together with its control computer and the phones of workers at the site. Her office says it will determine whether emergency protocols were broken between the puncture of the pipe and the explosion.

Exgadet has asked to be told before any expert work on the machine, arguing that such tests cannot be repeated. After two of its operators died in a clinic in San Justo, the company said it “deeply regrets” the loss and will help clarify the circumstances.

Two of the dead were Metrogas workers, and two were Exgadet operators who had been in serious condition in hospital since the blast. The last two deaths were confirmed on Saturday 21 November, and the injured number about 30, though official counts have differed.

The national gas and electricity regulator, known as ENReGE, has opened its own examination and asked Metrogas for the network plan at the break, the work under way and the year’s incident history. Its technicians need the rubble cleared before they can inspect the excavation pits.

For US readers, the case tests how liability is split between a utility that owns the pipes and the contractors that dig near them. YPF, which trades in New York, agreed in August 2026 to sell its 70% of Metrogas to Edenor, an Argentine electricity distributor, and the sale needs regulatory approval that we found no sign of having been granted.

It is not known why the pipe was off the plans or whom it supplied. Argentine press reports, citing investigation sources and a worker, say it fed a depot of the supermarket chain Coto near the corner, but neither Metrogas nor the prosecutor has confirmed this, and nothing published says the connection was illegal.

No date has been set for the fire-brigade reports on how the machine broke the pipe. Until they arrive, no one has been charged, and the regulator’s own findings are also outstanding.

More: Argentina news in English, every day from The Rio Times. Earlier coverage: the Lanús blast and the Metrogas sale and Edenor on the Metrogas deal.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who Has Died in the Lanús Gas Explosion?

Two Metrogas workers and two operators of its contractor Exgadet have died. Many more people were hurt, and official counts of the injured have differed.

Who Is Responsible for the Blast?

No one has been charged yet. The prosecutor is examining the drilling machine and the emergency protocols, while the gas regulator runs its own review.

Does the Blast Affect the Sale of Metrogas?

The sale still needs regulatory approval, and the gas regulator is also examining the blast. We found no public statement on whether the inquiry will delay the deal.

World.title: Colombia Says Chile Will Reopen to Beef
World.content:
Chile's ban on Colombian beef is to be lifted, the Colombian minister says, but Chile has not published the change.

Photo: Alejandro Bayer Tamayo / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

Colombia · Brief

Colombia says Chile will reopen its beef market to Colombian meat, which Chile’s farm and livestock service, the SAG, closed with a resolution dated 23 June 2026, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond said over the weekend of 20 to 22 November. Colombian exporters expect to ship about 3,500 tonnes worth more than US$27 million to Chile in 2027.

Chile has not confirmed the reopening in a document we could find. Minerva Foods, a Brazilian meatpacker with plants in Colombia, is among the exporters that stand to gain.

World.title: Medellín Utility Takes Over Bogotá Lights
World.content:
Bogotá is handing its street lights to a Medellín public utility to modernise them with LED and sensors.
