Empresas Públicas de Medellín (EPM), the publicly owned utility of Colombia’s second city, will operate and maintain Bogotá’s street lighting for ten years from 1 December 2026. Bogotá Mayor Carlos Fernando Galán and EPM’s board chair, Medellín Mayor Federico Gutiérrez, presented the plan at a joint event reported on Monday 23 November.

World.title: Insurers Seek US$108,000 From Cencosud
World.content:
A dispute over insurance cover for an ex-executive's defence has turned into a counterclaim.

A Jumbo supermarket of Cencosud in Los Andes, Chile (Photo: Carlos yo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Chile · Brief

Two insurance companies that covered its executives, Southbridge and Starr, have asked a Santiago court to order Cencosud, the Chilean retail group, to repay 109.3 million pesos (about US$108,000) they advanced for the defence of its former chief executive, Matías Videla. Chile’s financial regulator, the CMF, fined Videla in 2023 for trading on inside information.

The counterclaim answers a suit Cencosud filed in June asking the court to confirm that the policy covered those costs. On 3 November the court rejected the insurers’ objection to how Cencosud had filed its suit.

World.title: Brazil Audit Court Probes Bank Tenders
World.content:
The audit court did not suspend the tenders, citing the safety of bank branches.

Brazil · Brief

Brazil’s federal audit court, the Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU), is examining two Banco do Brasil tenders worth R$105.7 million (about US$17.8 million) for metal-detecting security doors, according to Brazilian press reports on Monday 23 November 2026. Auditors suspect that four bidders coordinated their offers to fake a competition.

The audit unit found signs that the bidders’ papers had the same author, were finished on the same night and used a similar calculation base. It also found shared addresses and money transfers between the companies.

“The set shows coordinated action: the companies submitted proposals calculated from the same base and did not compete among themselves for first place,” the court’s specialised procurement audit unit (Unidade de Auditoria Especializada em Contratações) wrote, as quoted in the press reports. The inquiry began with a complaint from another company that took part in the tenders. On 7 November, the press reports say, Jorge Oliveira, a TCU minister (the court’s term for a member), gave the bank five working days to explain, calling the evidence “several, concordant and convergent” signs of a possible “simulation of competition”.

He did not suspend the tenders, because stopping them could affect the protection of people and property in branches where old equipment is due to be replaced. If the irregularities are proven, the companies can be declared unfit and barred from federal tenders for up to five years.

The bank says its review of the tender files found no irregularities, that it has given the court the explanations requested and that it follows governance, integrity and compliance rules. The names of the four companies and the court’s final decision are not known.

For readers abroad, the case concerns procurement at a state-controlled bank with branches across Brazil. Our report on the bank’s third-quarter results and the Brazil hub give context.

World.title: Refugees in Costa Rica Lose UN-Funded Health Coverage on Jan. 1
World.content:
A program that gave public health coverage to more than 14,000 refugees, asylum seekers and stateless people in Costa Rica over seven years will end on Dec. 31. Those still enrolled will have to find another way into the public health system from Jan. 1, 2027. The Costa Rican Social Security Fund, known as the Caja or CCSS and the United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR, said the collective insurance agreement is closing for lack of funding. UNHCR attributed the decision to budget limits it faces worldwide.

The agreement began in 2019 as a pilot for people in economic hardship with serious medical needs, four years before Costa Rica expanded the coverage to more asylum seekers and refugees. It paid for consultations, medicines, specialized treatment and follow-up for chronic illness. UNHCR put more than $11.5 million into it between 2020 and 2026.

About two-thirds of the beneficiaries were women and roughly 60% were between 18 and 50 years old with chronic or serious illnesses, according to figures released with the announcement. The two institutions have not said how many people are covered today. For 2025, UNHCR committed 1,048.2 million colones (about $2.3 million) to insure an estimated 4,330 people and the agency has said the program was running at reduced capacity this year.

Eithel Corea Baltodano, the Caja’s interim financial manager, said the agreement had a positive effect on more than 14,000 people in extreme vulnerability, many of whom needed continuous treatment for chronic disease. People whose coverage runs out on Dec. 31, along with those on waiting lists, must apply to the Caja directly for another form of insurance.

Enrollment is not automatic and each option has its own requirements and the Caja will assess applications case by case at the rights-validation desk, or Validación de Derechos, of each person’s assigned health center. The options include insurance paid by the state for those who qualify and an assessment by the Joint Social Welfare Institute (IMAS) for people living in poverty, which does not guarantee coverage. Workers in formal jobs are insured through their employers.

Voluntary insurance is also available but the migrant women’s organization Mujeres Raíz said its lowest monthly payment, about 32,000 colones (about $72), is out of reach for many refugees and it asked UNHCR and the government for an option matched to their incomes. Some groups keep their access.

Children, adolescents and pregnant women are entitled to state-covered care whatever their nationality or migration status, once they are enrolled through the Caja. People living with HIV can continue antiretroviral treatment without interruption. No special transition has been announced for other patients who need permanent treatment. UNHCR said it will keep working with the government to inform refugees and asylum seekers about their rights and the options open to them.

The change comes three months after Costa Rica reopened an immigration category for 10,000 rejected asylum seekers. Requirements for each type of insurance are published by the Caja, and applications are handled in person at local health centers.

World.title: Who Would Pay Costa Rica’s Proposed 10% Tax on Airbnb Platforms
World.content:
A proposal to tax short-term rental platforms in Costa Rica has opened a dispute over who would end up paying, the companies or the people who book through them. The bill carries the signatures of Frente Amplio’s José María Villalta Flórez-Estrada and six party colleagues, and targets what short-stay platforms collect in commissions and service fees with a special 10% charge. Where a company is domiciled makes no difference, as long as the property is in Costa Rica.

The charge is aimed at the intermediary’s earnings, not at the full price of a stay. On a booking where the platform keeps 15%, the tax would equal 1.5% of the total, if the company passed all of it on. The Asociación de Consumidores Libres expects exactly that. Its president, Juan Ricardo Fernández, argued that guests would absorb the cost directly, and noted that it would sit on top of the 13% value-added tax while leaving other kinds of lodging untouched.

The group called the plan protectionism in favor of competing lodging sectors and warned of fewer listings and higher rates. Among those it says would be hurt are Costa Rican families on vacation and patients or students who travel to San José from outside the metropolitan area. Villalta has said the aim is to bring order to the business, not to prohibit it. His explanatory statement cites a 2025 OECD report in arguing that short-term rentals have pushed up rents and squeezed housing access, above all on the coasts.

Half of the revenue would go to municipalities, 30% to the national housing bank Banhvi and 20% to the Costa Rican Tourism Institute. Banhvi’s share is earmarked for housing and affordable rental programs in cantons under heavy tourist pressure. The tax is only one part of the text. Local governments could limit how many short-term rentals operate in a district, neighborhood or building, provided technical studies support the limit.

An owner renting out a single apartment would have to meet seven requirements to register with the tourism institute, and operators could be fined up to 20 base salaries, about 9.2 million colones ($20,600). Platforms would also have to hand host and guest information to state institutions, a clause the consumer group says lacks explicit data protection safeguards.

The debate has not started and the Legislative Assembly has been in extraordinary sessions since Nov. 1, and the Executive Branch, which sets the agenda in that period, has not included the bill. Until it does, the proposal cannot advance, and any change to what a rental costs or how many can operate remains months away at the earliest.

World.title: Route 1 Traffic Costs Commuters 38 Days a Year as Costa Rica Pledges a Fix
World.content:
A driver who commutes on Route 1 between La Uruca and La Garita loses about 907 hours a year to congestion, the equivalent of 38 days, according to the State of the Nation 2026 report. On Sunday the government answered Costa Rica traffic complaints with the largest budget in the history of the public works ministry and a rebuilt highway that it says will take more than 40 minutes off the trip.

The report puts the added travel time on that stretch at about 216 minutes a day. That is 57 minutes in the morning and 112 in the afternoon, plus a buffer of roughly 23 minutes each way that drivers allow for the unexpected. It prices the lost time and the extra cost of running a vehicle at 1,687,233 colones a year (about $3,780) for a person who works a standard weekday schedule.

That equals 2.8 times the monthly gross salary of about 600,000 colones used as a reference, or 21.7% of annual gross income. In 2019 the cost was about 1.1 million colones, or 15.9%. On the Circunvalación beltway, Route 39, the added time between Zapote and Calle Blancos is about 26 minutes a day. The report estimates the annual cost there at 220,000 colones (about $490).

Both roads were widened in recent years and the report concludes that the relief was temporary. Luis Vargas, an economist and researcher with the State of the Nation Program, said congestion eased after the works and during the pandemic, began rising again in 2023 and by 2025 was above its 2019 level.

Vargas said no road can keep pace on its own. He said infrastructure investment has to come together with public transport, urban planning and a smaller vehicle fleet. The report notes that only 52% of the national territory has a current zoning plan and that about 110,000 vehicles use the Route 1 corridor, a number that could grow by as much as 7% by 2032.

In a pre-recorded national broadcast yesterday, President Laura Fernández said the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT) will have 550,000 million colones (about $1.23 billion) in 2027. She attributed the congestion to decisions postponed by previous administrations. The broadcast did not explain how the money will be divided among projects.

Public Works Minister Efraím Zeledón said work on the central section of the San José–San Ramón highway expansion will begin in 2027 with earthworks, drainage and a bridge over the Cañuela River. He said the Coyola interchange will start in February. Zeledón said the finished project will cut travel times by more than 40 minutes for people who live in the west of the Central Valley. He did not present data to support the estimate. The expanded highway is also expected to carry four tolls.

The government also said the widening of the Barranca–Limonal highway will be finished in 2027 and that 10 overpasses will replace roundabouts on the route between Guápiles and Limón. It gave no cost or start date for the overpasses. The tender to design and build a metropolitan train is to be published in the first quarter of 2027, according to the broadcast. No route, cost or financing model was given.

The San José–San Ramón contract went out in October Fand the start dates announced on Sunday are the government’s own projections. The report’s figures describe the corridor as it is today.

World.title: Thousands of Costa Rica Teachers Could Lose Pay After Court Rules Strike Illegal
World.content:
A San José labor court has declared illegal the Nov. 11 strike called by five education unions, a ruling that allows the Ministry of Public Education (MEP) to deduct pay for the time workers missed. The ministry counted 36,994 staff members absent that day. Judge Carolina Muñoz González of the Labor Court of the First Judicial Circuit of San José issued the sentence on Friday and the decision became public last night. The case was brought by the State through the Attorney General’s Office.

The ruling covers the Secondary School Teachers Association (APSE), the National Association of Educators (ANDE), the Costa Rican Educators Union (SEC), the National Union of Guidance Professionals (Sinapro) and the Patriotic Education Union 7 de Agosto (Sinpae). The court found that the unions did not meet the legal requirements for a lawful strike. According to the ruling, the stoppage went ahead without the plan the Labor Code requires to keep basic school services running, including cleaning, security and care for students with disabilities.

The judge also found that staff from MEP school cafeterias took part in the strike. The court treated school meals as an essential public service, in which strikes are prohibited. The ruling further cited defects in the strike notices and in the proof of the minimum level of worker support.

Under the Labor Code, a declaration of illegality allows employers to deduct wages for time not worked. Workers who prove a justified absence through the ministry’s administrative process are exempt. The ruling also leaves the ministry the option of ordering that lost time be made up instead, through a reasoned resolution copied to the Comptroller General’s Office and the Ombudsman’s Office.

The decision is a first-instance ruling. The parties have three days to appeal before the same court and it comes after the government moved to dock pay for education workers who joined the strike earlier this month. Education Minister Leonardo Sánchez Hernández said at the time that the 36,994 absences represented about 35% of the ministry’s staff. The ministry also reported that 175 school cafeterias did not open and that about 800 schools had problems with cleaning or security.

An earlier ministry count, taken on the day of the strike, showed 13,074 officials absent and 58 cafeterias closed. A certified court record cited in the case put the number of closed cafeterias at 50. During the proceedings, ANDE, APSE and Sinapro argued that school closures could not be attributed to the protest without proof for each individual worker. The judge found that the timing of the absences and closures established an objective link between them.

The unions did win on one point. The government had argued that the stoppage was a dispute over employer obligations. The judge instead classified it as a protest against public policy, covering the education budget, salaries and pensions, a type of strike the Labor Code allows without prior conciliation.

The court also noted that neither the ministry nor the unions sought dialogue to agree on a basic-services plan before the strike, and it exempted both sides from paying legal costs. The one-day strike, which included a march from Parque La Merced to the Legislative Assembly, was called to protest cuts to public education in the 2027 national budget. Those cuts had already drawn warnings that the National University could stop round-the-clock tsunami monitoring on Jan. 1.

The budget fight has since moved to the courts on several fronts. The Constitutional Chamber has ordered lawmakers to strip conditions from the 2027 budget bill, including restrictions on funds for the Judiciary. Whether the unions appeal will determine how soon the ministry can act on the deductions. The broader dispute over education funding will continue as lawmakers finish work on the 2027 budget, which the Constitution requires them to approve by the end of November.

World.title: Costa Rica Will Co-Host the 2031 Women’s World Cup After FIFA Approval
World.content:
Costa Rica will co-host the 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup after FIFA’s member associations approved on Monday the joint bid it shares with the United States, Mexico and Jamaica. It will be the first time matches of a senior World Cup, men’s or women’s, are played in Costa Rica.

The decision came at an extraordinary FIFA Congress held by videoconference. The four-nation proposal was the only bid for 2031, and FIFA said the hosts were appointed by acclamation. The same Congress awarded the 2035 tournament to England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.

Osael Maroto, president of the Costa Rican Football Federation (Fedefútbol), said the tournament is a chance to put Costa Rica’s name before the whole world and thanked FIFA’s members for backing the bid. He said a long road of preparation lies ahead and that the event should leave a legacy for future generations.

FIFA President Gianni Infantino said the 2031 and 2035 tournaments should reach beyond the pitch, with more women and girls playing, coaching, refereeing and leading in the sport.

The 2031 edition will be the first with 48 teams and the first played across four countries. The bid calls for 104 matches from mid-June to late July in 20 stadiums: 14 in the United States, four in Mexico, one in Costa Rica and one in Jamaica.

Costa Rica’s venue is the Estadio Nacional in La Sabana, San José, which opened in 2011 and holds about 35,000 people. FIFA’s evaluation report gave the stadium 3.8 out of 5 and said it appears to meet most requirements. The bid as a whole scored 4.4 out of 5 in the technical evaluation.

Fedefútbol also put forward the Ricardo Saprissa stadium in Tibás, which is not among the 20 recommended venues. With a single stadium, Costa Rica may host the matches of only one group. How many games come to San José has not been decided.

The same report identifies transport as the weak point. FIFA wants better ways to move fans from Juan Santamaría International Airport to San José and to the stadium. It noted a heavy dependence on cars and, so far, no formal commitment to free public transport on match days.

Hotels, telecommunications and government support met FIFA’s requirements, according to the report. The airport recently opened a single pickup hub for taxis, shuttles and rental cars, but the road into the capital remains one of the most congested in the country.

Costa Rica has staged two FIFA youth tournaments, the U-17 Women’s World Cup in 2014 and the U-20 Women’s World Cup in 2022. The United States hosted the senior women’s tournament in 1999 and 2003, while 2031 will be a first for Mexico, Jamaica and Costa Rica.

Monday’s decision was the last formal step in a process that saw FIFA inspectors visit Costa Rica in February and the bid clear FIFA’s technical evaluation on Nov. 11. The match schedule, the final list of stadiums and ticket details will be announced later.

World.title: Nicoya Towns Got 10 Minutes of Tap Water a Day as El Niño Dried Their Wells
World.content:
Residents of Iguanita, a rural community in Nicoya, received piped water for about 10 minutes a day through most of October, after the springs that feed the local aqueduct came close to running dry. It is one of several cases of water rationing in Guanacaste, where community-run systems are cutting service or relying on tanker trucks as El Niño reduces their supplies.

Luz Marina Villegas, vice president of Iguanita’s community water association (ASADA), said recent rain has partly restored the springs. The association still fears the shortage will return. It has begun the process of asking the national water utility, AyA, to take over the system because there are no nearby sources to fall back on.

In Moracia, also in Nicoya, the association’s main well dried up on Oct. 31 after its flow had been falling since May 20. Homes there now get piped water every second day, from 8 p.m. to 11 p.m. A tanker truck arrives from Santa Cruz on Mondays, Wednesdays and Saturdays. Gabriela Fonseca, the Moracia association’s administrator, said anger over the rationing has led to confrontations with residents.

The association is working with the Costa Rican Electricity Institute (ICE) to drill a new well. It has also asked AyA for a hydrogeological study to determine whether the existing wells can be deepened. Elsewhere in Guanacaste, the Pilangosta association, which also serves Marbella and Pita Rayada, has been supplying water for about 12 hours a day for the past two months.

Pita Rayada is the worst affected. Its springs are low and its well cannot meet demand, so the association is drawing water from a stream, chlorinating it by hand and building a new well. Association president Emel Rodríguez said rain raised the levels for a time. He expects the shortage to deepen as the rains stop. The dry season began in Guanacaste earlier this month.

AyA executive president Lourdes Sáurez said several associations have reported that their sources have dried up. Systems run directly by AyA have lost flow, she said, but none has run dry. Guanacaste has 304 community water associations, and the effects of El Niño vary from one community to the next.

The utility has assigned two tanker trucks to community aqueducts and announced two more. It has also bought 16 tankers, with deliveries scheduled for November and December. From about Dec. 15, AyA plans to place storage tanks of up to 22,000 liters (about 5,800 gallons) at fixed points, so residents can collect water without trucks stopping at every home. It will also distribute pipe to replace damaged and leaking sections.

The pressure is not limited to rural systems. AyA has already asked households to cut their water use, and the World Meteorological Organization expects El Niño to peak in December. Rationing schedules on community systems are set by each local association, which is the first place to check for changes.

World.title: Costa Rica Starts the Week at 35°C With a Cold Push Due by Thursday
World.content:
Pack for heat if you are heading to the Pacific coast. Costa Rica weather this week starts hot and dry, with Monday’s high reaching 35.4°C (96°F) in Liberia and clear skies over most of the country, according to the National Meteorological Institute (IMN). Nicoya and Puntarenas are close behind at about 35°C (95°F). There is very little moisture in the air, so few clouds form, and that is why temperatures are climbing on both coasts and in the center of the country.

In the Central Valley, expect a clear, warm morning and a few clouds in the afternoon. San José tops out at 27.5°C (82°F) and drops to 19°C (66°F) overnight. Alajuela reaches 30.7°C (87°F). You will feel the trade winds in the morning over the valley and Guanacaste, where they blow at moderate strength. They ease after midday, which is when the heat is hardest to escape.

You only need a rain jacket in two areas. The mountains of the Central Pacific get scattered showers in the afternoon, and the South Pacific sees brief, isolated ones. Golfito still reaches 33°C (91°F). The Caribbean and the Northern Zone stay mostly clear all day. Limón reaches 31.6°C (89°F), Sarapiquí 33°C (91°F) and Upala 34°C (93°F).

This follows a hot, nearly rainless weekend, and it marks a turning point in the calendar. The Central Valley finishes its shift from rainy season to dry season on Monday, the IMN says. The Central Pacific follows by Nov. 30, when the change begins in the South Pacific, and the western Northern Zone starts around Dec. 3.

Conditions change later in the week and the IMN expects a weak cold push to influence the weather between Thursday and Friday. Cold pushes usually strengthen the wind and bring rain to the Caribbean side, but the institute has not yet given details for this one, so check the forecast again midweek if you have weekend plans.

One thing you can stop watching for is a tropical storm. The Atlantic hurricane season ends on Nov. 30, and the IMN does not expect any more systems in its final week. Until the cold push arrives, the sun is the main thing to plan around. With almost no cloud cover, midday exposure is intense at any elevation, so carry water, use sunscreen and take your breaks in the shade.

World.title: El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo Finishes Runner-Up at ATP Finals in Turin
World.content:
El Salvador’s Marcelo Arévalo and Croatian partner Mate Pavić fell just short of the ATP Finals doubles title Sunday, losing 3-6, 7-6 (2), 10-6 to France’s Théo Arribagé and Albano Olivetti in Turin. Arévalo and Pavić took the opening set 6-3 but could not hold off the French pair, who won the second-set tiebreak 7-2 and carried that momentum into the deciding match tiebreak at Inalpi Arena, played in place of a full third set.

Arribagé and Olivetti won 10 consecutive points across the two tiebreaks to turn the match around, then closed out the decider 10-6 to claim their seventh title of the season. The defeat ended Arévalo and Pavić’s run at the season-ending tournament, which brings together eight of the year’s leading doubles teams. It was their second appearance together in the ATP Finals title match. They also finished as runners-up in 2024.

The fourth-seeded pair arrived at Sunday’s final unbeaten in Turin, including a group-stage victory over Arribagé and Olivetti. Arévalo and Pavić had reached the final with a hard-fought semifinal win over American Christian Harrison and Britain’s Neal Skupski. They came through that match 7-6 (10), 6-7 (7), 10-7.

The final also marked the end of Arévalo and Pavić’s three-year partnership. Together, they won nine tour-level titles, including the 2024 French Open and four ATP Masters 1000 tournaments. Their 2026 season included a title at Queen’s Club in London and a run to the Wimbledon final. They also reached the finals of the Masters 1000 events in Monte Carlo and Canada.

For Arribagé and Olivetti, the win capped their first appearance together at the ATP Finals. The French pair began playing together in October 2025. In the singles final, Carlos Alcaraz beat Alexander Zverev to win his first ATP Finals title.

World.title: Fi Wi Land: The fight to save Jamaica’s dying lignum vitae
World.content:
A symbol of Jamaica’s natural beauty and national identity, the lignum vitae holds a special place in the island’s heritage. But despite its significance as Jamaica’s national flower, this treasured species is facing growing threats to its survival, raising concerns about the future of one of the country’s national symbols.

Renowned for its exceptionally hard and durable wood, the lignum vitae has faced years of overexploitation, habitat loss and land degradation, contributing to a decline in its population.

With the species subject to international trade restrictions under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), protecting and restoring its population is an important conservation priority.

In this week’s episode of Fi Wi Land, Environmental Officer for Flora at the National Environment and Planning Agency (NEPA), Ashleigh Sanderson, sheds light on the threats facing Jamaica’s national flower and the efforts being made to safeguard its future.

From population surveys revealing concerns about its decline to conservation action plans and environmental protection measures, discover how NEPA is working to preserve the lignum vitae and other threatened plant species across the island.

Catch the latest episode on the Jamaica Observer’s YouTube channel and other digital platforms.

World.title: Calls to rename Catherine Hall main road in honour of late Deputy Mayor
World.content:
Late Deputy Mayor of Montego Bay Dwight Crawford's widow, Reninho signs a condolence book dedicated to her husband at a special sitting of the St James Municipal Corporation on Monday, November 23, 2026.

ST JAMES, Jamaica — Councillor Michael Troupe (People’s National Party, Granville Division) has indicated his intention to move a motion to cement the legacy of the late Deputy Mayor of Montego Bay, Dwight Crawford, by renaming the main road through Catherine Hall in his honour.

Paying tribute to Crawford during a special sitting of the St James Municipal Corporation (SJMC) on Monday, Troupe said he intended to bring the proposal before the Council early next year.

“I am going to move a motion in the future, maybe the first part of next year and I am sure you will agree with me to make sure that the road that runs across Catherine Hall be named in his honour,” he declared.

Crawford represented the Spring Gardens Division in the SJMC, with the Catherine Hall/Westgreen area forming a significant part of the division.

Troupe, who serves as minority leader within the Council, shares a political boundary with Crawford’s former division. Both divisions fall within the St James West Central constituency.

“That road is fitting for the honour that we are saying here today,” he added.

The proposal received support from fellow councillors, who indicated that renaming the road would be a fitting way to immortalise Crawford’s legacy.

In a further tribute, attorney Maurice McCurdy, who was among those in the gallery, called on the Corporation to write to the relevant authorities recommending that Crawford be posthumously awarded the Order of Distinction for his service as a councillor.

That proposal also received signs of approval from members of the Council.

Throughout the special sitting, Crawford was remembered as a man who served everyone, regardless of political affiliation. Fellow councillors spoke of his kindness, camaraderie and genuine commitment to people, highlighting his ability to make everyone feel welcome.

They also recalled his efforts in the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa, when he worked tirelessly to assist residents of Catherine Hall and Westgreen as they grappled with the effects of one of the worst flooding disasters to affect the communities.

Mayor of Montego Bay, Councillor Richard Vernon, described Crawford as “a colleague, friend and a brother”. Crawford was elevated to the position of deputy mayor at the same time Vernon assumed the political leadership of the St James Municipal Corporation.

“In the aftermath of Hurricane Melissa, Spring Gardens suffered substantial devastation particularly in Westgreen and Catherine Hall. I joined Dwight on the ground as we worked side by side to restore some measure of normalcy for affected residents,” the mayor recalled.

Members of the business community and civil society were among those gathered in the gallery for the sitting. Crawford’s family, including his wife and two children, as well as several friends, were also in attendance.

Speaking on behalf of the family, Robin Russell expressed gratitude to the Council and others for their support during the period of grief.

“We could not not say thank you to everybody here. One thing I know about Debo, you all will miss him because he shared the DNA of my father which is, he gave himself to everyone,” he said.

“Everybody here has a personal story to Debo and when I hear members on the opposite side advocating for a road to be named after him, when I see his friends, his colleagues here, we just want to say thank you, his kids, his wife, Jason, all of us, thank you,” he added.

World.title: Commander Gayle should resign as ODPEM boss, says Golding
World.content:
Opposition Leader Mark Golding (left) is calling for the resignation of ODPEM boss, Commander Alvin Gayle.

Opposition Leader Mark Golding has called for the resignation of the Director General of the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM), Commander Alvin Gayle.

Golding made the call Monday during a press conference hosted by the People’s National Party (PNP) to draw attention to the damning findings of the Auditor-General’s report into ODPEM’s management of Hurricane Melissa relief donations.

READ: ODPEM audit finds expired food, insect-infested supplies and millions in unaccounted donations

The audit that was made public last Tuesday shows that a significant number of container houses cannot be accounted for, that donated funds were used for other purposes than originally intended, and that food held in storage has since spoiled, having gone past their best-before-date.

Insisting that someone should be held accountable, Golding said Gayle, who was seconded to the post from the Jamaica Defence Force in November 2025, should do the honorable thing and tender his resignation.

World.title: Jamaica to co-host 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup alongside US, Mexico and Costa Rica
World.content:
Fédération Internationale de Football Association (FIFA) President Gianni Infantino.

KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaica has been selected to co-host the 2031 FIFA Women’s World Cup alongside the United States, Mexico and Costa Rica, marking a historic milestone for the country and Caribbean football.

The announcement was made at the FIFA Congress in Zurich, Switzerland on Monday.

Jamaica’s selection as a co-host will also guarantee the country’s automatic qualification for the 2031 tournament, which will be the first FIFA Women’s World Cup to feature 48 teams.

The development marks the first time a Caribbean nation will play a role in hosting a senior FIFA World Cup tournament.

While the region has previously hosted several FIFA competitions, including the men’s and women’s Under-17 World Cups in Trinidad and Tobago, the Beach Soccer World Cup in The Bahamas and the 2024 FIFA Under-17 Women’s World Cup in the Dominican Republic, Jamaica’s selection represents a new chapter for Caribbean football.

President of the Jamaica Football Federation (JFF), Michael Ricketts, welcomed the announcement, describing the opportunity to host the global tournament as a major achievement for the country.

“We are truly delighted with the opportunity to welcome the world to our shores in 2031 to play a part in hosting a FIFA Women’s World Cup. I would like to thank the entire team at the JFF for their hard work in aiding us have a successful bid. Every department played a significant role and I am truly grateful. We now wish our senior women’s national team all the best later this week versus Costa Rica so that hopefully come Friday we can say that Jamaica will be at four FIFA World Cup tournaments in a row,” Ricketts said in a release on Monday.

Concacaf President Victor Montaglianni also offered his congratulations to Jamaica.

“This is a historic moment for women’s football and a tremendous achievement for our entire Concacaf family. I want to congratulate Costa Rica, Jamaica, Mexico, and the United States. Hosting the first-ever 48-team FIFA Women’s World Cup across four nations is an extraordinary opportunity to showcase the strength and unity of our region, inspire millions of girls, and create a lasting legacy for women’s football across all 41 of our Member Associations. Together, we are committed to making 2031 a defining moment for the growth of our game,” Montaglianni said.

The 2035 FIFA Women’s World Cup will be hosted in England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

World.title: ‘Bad apples’
World.content:
St Ann North Eastern Member of Parliament Matthew Samuda (centre) speaks during the funeral for Kenise Dunn, with St Ann’s Bay Mayor Michael Belnavis and Lime Hall Division Councillor Genevor Gordon-Bailey.

MEMBER of Parliament for St Ann North Eastern Matthew Samuda has expressed anger over what he described as a lack of empathy and respectful communication towards the family of Kenise Dunn following her death.

He noted that, while Jamaica has some of the best doctors and nurses, there are “bad apples” in the health system whose treatment of patients and relatives must not be tolerated.

Speaking at Dunn’s funeral at Exchange Seventh-day Adventist Church in St Ann on Sunday, Samuda said his concern was not to judge the medical treatment she received, but the way patients in pain and their relatives are treated by hospital staff.

He said the family’s grief had been made worse by what he described as a lack of care and consideration, adding that no family should have to endure such an experience while dealing with the death of a loved one.

“Now, Mayor Belnavis would have spoken to the fact that, yes, the matter is under investigation, but one thing is clear — a family is hurting and that hurt was made worse because of the lack of empathy, lack of care, and the decency of respectful communication, and that gives me concern, real concern. And I don’t want this to be mistaken because Jamaica has, in all things — whether you talk about sports or music and even in health care — you have some of the best doctors and best nurses in the world in this country, but you do have bad apples,” he said.

“And this is not an assault on those who work in that sector; this is, I want to be very clear, an acknowledgement that there are those in the system who are not showing their humanity in how they speak to people, how they treat those who visit the hospitals. And, certainly, I am deeply concerned,” he added.

Samuda, who said he was “admittedly angry”, made it clear that he was not qualified to determine whether the medical care provided to Dunn was appropriate. Instead, he said health-care workers must show compassion to people experiencing physical pain, and communicate with their relatives in a respectful manner.

Dunn, who died at age 33, passed away on August 14, five days after giving birth, according to previous reports. Her death prompted concern from relatives, who called for answers about the circumstances surrounding her treatment at St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital.

Her uncle, Kirk Hall, had previously told the Jamaica Observer that Dunn was admitted to the hospital on July 29, while eight months pregnant. He said she had been experiencing severe stomach pain and difficulty passing stool. Hall also said she underwent emergency surgery and that doctors reportedly found a tumour in her colon and a ruptured bowel.

Following her death, the hospital said an internal investigation was underway, while the North East Regional Health Authority said a comprehensive investigation and clinical review had been launched into the circumstances surrounding her death.

At Sunday’s funeral, St Ann’s Bay mayor and chairman of the St Ann Municipal Corporation Michael Belnavis pledged that the investigation would be thorough.

“When this happened… it was really a traumatic experience for all of them. I was there, and I’m here to tell you publicly that no stone will be unturned… and there will be full investigation into the situation that caused her demise,” Belnavis said.

Samuda also welcomed changes to the hospital’s management, saying further changes were expected. He said Minister of Health and Wellness Dr Christopher Tufton had tabled a report examining the hospital’s operations in Parliament on Tuesday.

He said the wider health system must ensure that families are not left feeling mistreated when they are already dealing with loss. He also pointed to increased staffing and improved pay for doctors and nurses, arguing that these developments should be matched by respectful treatment of patients and relatives.

“We’re putting the system on notice that what took place should never happen. The communication after, and the way the family feels, no family should feel like that again, and that is why I’m happy with the fact that there have already been management changes at the hospital and that there are more to come,” he said.

World.title: ‘The system failed her’
World.content:
Family members Jamal Hall (left) and his father, Kirk Hall, stand in front of Kenise Dunn’s casket during her funeral service.

KIRK Hall, uncle of Kenise Dunn, who died following complications during her stay at St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital, has warned that the hospital cannot continue with business as usual, insisting that his 33-year-old niece was treated wrongly and vowing that he will never rest until justice is done.

Hall, speaking at Dunn’s funeral on Sunday, said he had made up his mind to pursue the matter until those responsible were held accountable, declaring that nothing would distract him from seeking justice for his niece.

“I’m in no joking mood when it comes on to St Ann’s Bay hospital… Sandra (Kenise’s mother) died and I took it, my mother died and I took it, my father died and I took it. But this little girl, I will never rest until justice is done for her in any way, shape or form. It must be done,” he told mourners.

He said his determination had affected his ability to work, as he remained focused on the circumstances surrounding Dunn’s death and the future of her children. Hall said he believes the hospital had failed his niece and rejected the suggestion that staff had done all they could for her.

“We are saying goodbye to her today, [but] we shouldn’t be here saying goodbye to this young soul. No man, the system failed her. The system failed her!” Hall expressed.

He said that when he raised concerns with senior hospital personnel about the way Dunn’s care had been handled he was told that staff had done everything possible. The uncle said his concerns stemmed not only from the outcome, but also from what he described as a lack of proper communication and empathy towards the family during the ordeal.

Hall recounted that Dunn had gone to the hospital with bowel difficulties, and would call or send him messages about what was happening. He said she eventually told him that nobody was attending to her.

He said he visited the hospital on a Sunday and was unhappy with how a nurse handled the situation. He tried to contact the hospital’s chief executive but was unable to reach him. He then contacted another person, who asked him to submit a report the following morning.

Hall said Dunn was later transferred and that he subsequently received information that she had given birth and was being taken for surgery, after doctors reportedly found air on her diaphragm.

He recalled waiting several hours for an update before asking a relative to check on her. He said the relative later told him that Dunn did not look well, after which the family was asked to meet with a doctor.

Dunn died on August 14, five days after giving birth, according to previous reports. Hall had previously told the Jamaica Observer that she was admitted to St Ann’s Bay Regional Hospital on July 29 while eight months pregnant, after experiencing severe stomach pain and difficulty passing stool.

Hall said he had initially trusted the health system to provide the care she needed, but her experience had shaken that confidence.

He called for changes at the hospital, saying he had noticed some developments, but expected more to be done.

“St Ann’s Bay [hospital] has to change. It has to change. It can’t be business as usual,” he said.

Hall also issued a pointed warning to St Ann’s Bay Mayor Michael Belnavis, who is chairman of the St Ann Municipal Corporation, saying that their friendship would not prevent him from demanding accountability if the mayor came under scrutiny over the matter.

“And if he comes under the radar or under my attack, I’m sorry, my brother, justice must be done. So if you’re at the end of it and you’re going to face the bullet, so let it be. It has to happen; it can’t be business as usual,” Hall said.

The North East Regional Health Authority previously said a comprehensive investigation and clinical review had been launched into the circumstances surrounding Dunn’s death. The hospital also said an internal investigation was under way.

World.title: Consultation clash
World.content:
BUNTING... I know you met with the JHTA and the big representatives of the big hotels, but when and where did you meet with the small operators?

THE Government says it has consulted stakeholders on its plan to impose General Consumption Tax (GCT) on short-term rental accommodations, but when pressed in Parliament last Tuesday to identify who was consulted, when and where, Finance Minister Fayval Williams had no immediate details to provide.

The exchange has intensified questions about how prepared the Government is to introduce the measure on April 1, 2027, with Opposition Members of Parliament warning that property owners are still uncertain about the rules they will be expected to follow.

At the centre of the dispute is whether small property owners and managers, many of whom use platforms such as Airbnb to rent rooms, apartments, and houses to visitors, have been properly involved in shaping the tax arrangements.

Williams, who was responding to questions tabled by Manchester Southern Member of Parliament (MP) Peter Bunting, told the House on Tuesday that the Government had spoken with representatives of the tourism industry, accommodation providers and other interested parties. However, she did not name any of the organisations involved or state when the meetings took place.

Bunting and Opposition spokesperson on finance Julian Robinson questioned the account, saying they had spoken with people in the short-term rental business who told them they had not been consulted.

Bunting challenged Williams to identify the representatives of the smaller operators with whom the Government had met, arguing that discussions with large hotels and tourism groups would not necessarily mean that the concerns of small property owners had been heard.

“I know you met with the JHTA [Jamaica Hotel and Tourist Association] and the big representatives of the big hotels, but when and where did you meet with the small operators?” Bunting asked.

Robinson later repeated Bunting’s concern.

“You stated here that you had consultations with the persons. Please state when, where, and who you met with, because in every discussion I’ve had nobody, I don’t know one person who has been consulted about this in the short-term rental market,” he asked.

In her response, Williams said she would obtain the details of the consultations and report back to the House.

The disagreement over consultation comes as several important parts of the proposed system remain unsettled, including whether the existing $15-million annual GCT registration threshold will apply to short-term rental operators and who will be responsible for collecting and paying over the tax when bookings are made through overseas platforms.

Williams said the application of the threshold is still under consideration, with a decision to be announced once finalised. This means some smaller operators do not yet know whether they will be required to register for GCT.

The minister also said the final arrangements would determine whether responsibility for collecting and paying over the taxes rests with the accommodation provider or the booking platform.

Under the general rule outlined by Williams, a registered taxpayer providing a service is responsible for accounting for the tax. However, she noted that the GCT Act makes the operator responsible in the case of tourist accommodation. She added that the Government is also working on arrangements to collect tax through non-resident digital platforms.

Williams also said GCT would apply to the full amount paid by the guest for the accommodation service, rather than only the money received by the property owner after a booking, platform deducts its commission.

She further indicated that cleaning, property management, booking and other mandatory fees would generally be included where they form part of the accommodation service.

Bunting argued that the combined effect of platform charges and the proposed tax could place a heavy burden on small Jamaican investors, particularly at a time when the tourism industry is facing pressure.

He told the House that

Airbnb had moved to charge hosts a 15.5 per cent fee, which he said was previously shared between hosts and guests. He argued that adding GCT and other charges could leave owners with a significantly smaller share of the money paid by visitors.

Bunting also questioned the timing of the measure, saying operators were already accepting bookings for next year without knowing the final tax rules.

“An industry which is under pressure and in recession, this is not the time to add additional taxes to this. This is crazy! Minister, are you willing to reconsider putting this tax on at this time?” he asked.

Williams did not indicate that the Government would delay the measure, instead she defended the policy.

“It is common practice in many, many countries to collect taxes from those who are in the Airbnb sector,” she said.

World.title: Mojo Morgan’s Right Now single debuts at #5 on iTunes reggae chart
World.content:
Mojo Morgan

GRAMMY-WINNING artiste, songwriter, and producer Mojo Morgan is enjoying a significant moment in his musical journey as his latest single, Right Now, makes an impressive impact on the international music scene.

The single debuted at #5 on the iTunes Reggae Chart on November 21, while its accompanying music video has amassed more than 3.6 million views, marking a remarkable achievement ahead of the official audio release on Friday, November 20.

Beyond the numbers, the growing success of Right Now speaks to the power of music to transcend borders, cultures, and generations.

The song’s message has resonated with audiences across various territories, with the video generating considerable attention in Prague, further underscoring reggae’s enduring ability to connect people through shared experiences.

Morgan’s achievement is particularly noteworthy given his hands-on involvement in the creation of the record. In addition to delivering the vocals, the accomplished musician wrote and produced the track, bringing his creative vision to life through a deeply reflective and socially conscious body of work.

The song’s growing international appeal is also clear in the response from fans, with listeners already expressing interest in collaborations. Among them are fans in Zimbabwe, who have taken to YouTube to request a remix featuring their country’s celebrated artiste, Winky D.

RobsonKudakwashePfunda, shared: “We here right now for the remix ft Winky D,” reflecting the enthusiasm surrounding the possibility of a cross-cultural musical collaboration.

The Right Now music video takes viewers on a compelling cinematic journey through Jamaica, Brooklyn, Brixton, and beyond, offering a poignant glimpse into the realities faced by families and young people navigating economic hardship, social inequality, and uncertainty.

Through striking visuals and authentic portrayals of everyday life, the production captures the resilience, dignity, and unwavering hope that continue to define communities across borders.

Its narrative is firmly rooted in reggae’s rich tradition of social commentary, using music and visual storytelling to highlight the challenges confronting society while celebrating the strength found in unity.

At its heart, Right Now reflects the times — a reminder that despite the differences in geography and circumstance, the struggles of ordinary people are often remarkably similar.

Mojo Morgan shared: “As the single continues to gain traction internationally, it is proving once again that meaningful music can speak a universal language. With its powerful message, cinematic presentation, and growing global audience, Right Now is positioning itself as a compelling addition to reggae’s contemporary catalogue.”

World.title: Finland summons Russian ambassador over suspected helicopter incursion
World.content:
Several other European countries have criticized Russia over air incursions with helicopters and drones in recent months. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk warned on Sept. 17 that Russia could launch drone or missile strikes against countries that support Ukraine, and try to pass them off as accidents.

Finnish Defense Minister Antti Häkkänen said the suspected incursion may have been related to “rescue or monitoring operations” involving the Russian cargo ship Sparta II, which was damaged by a Ukrainian drone attack in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday morning.

The Finnish Border Guard said it had towed the ship from Finnish waters to Russia Sunday afternoon.

“Ukraine has the right to defend itself against Russia’s illegal aggression,” the foreign ministry added in the statement alongside Monday’s statement.

Moscow has not yet publicly responded to Finland’s summoning of its ambassador.

World.title: Britain’s runaway Brexit debate is back
World.content:
That will give way to an “informal brainstorm” with the EU ahead of a summit in late 2027, with Burnham only promising to forge further ahead — if indeed he does — in Labour’s next general election manifesto, due by mid-2029.

“There will be no banging on about Europe from this side, or a running commentary. Instead, just a calm, constructive, and pragmatic consideration of what is in Britain’s interests in the long term,” Burnham told MPs.

The prime minister appeared to suggest that his personal enthusiasm for rejoining the EU in his lifetime could wane if, for example, the far-right politician Marine Le Pen wins the French presidency. “Europe could change again in the next year, 18 months, and we’ll have to obviously watch how life changes,” he said.

At a CBI breakfast Burnham attended with 40 executives, a large chunk of the conversation was about his upcoming (mostly domestic) 10-year plan for Britain, according to one person in the room, granted anonymity like others in this piece to speak freely. But existential questions about Britain’s future in Europe were everywhere — and everyone had their own answers.

To Burnham’s many supporters in his Labour Party, he has taken ownership of a debate that dominates British politics anyway, and in doing so has improved Labour’s standing in seats where Labour is battling the pro-EU Lib Dems and Green Party.

One Labour MP said: “It was not going to be possible for us to avoid talking about our future relationship with Europe, and Andy has got out ahead of some of it.”

World.title: Spain turns against Sánchez, POLITICO poll finds
World.content:
The prime minister had already come under pressure over his government’s handling of the Ceuta migration crisis over the summer and corruption cases involving his family, but he finally called a snap election in early October following nationwide protests about unaffordable housing.

A survey pollster PF Global carried out for POLITICO last week shows housing remains a vulnerable area for Sánchez. In the poll, it topped the list of the prime minister’s failures, slightly ahead of migration and the Ceuta crisis.

While PP and Vox voters were more likely to say migration had been Sánchez’s biggest failure, the prime minister’s own support base was more likely to list housing.

Some 40% of people who said they’d vote for the Socialist Party and over half of those backing the leftist alliance Broad Front said he’d fallen short on housing.

Across the board, about one-third of Spaniards in the poll said cost of living would drive their vote. But different parties’ voters had different priorities: For PP and Vox voters, migration was a key factor in their choice, whereas Socialist Party voters said housing and healthcare would steer their vote more.

At the same time, all parties are struggling to convince voters they are well placed to tackle key campaign issues.

World.title: Rejoining EU without referendum is ‘unthinkable,’ says Andy Burnham
World.content:
It is the first time the prime minister has ruled out the prospect of returning Britain to the bloc without holding a special vote on the matter.

Burnham was speaking days after negotiating three new international agreements to ramp up ties with the bloc at a summit in Brussels.

Addressing MPs during Monday's debate, the prime minister accused his critics of being “stuck in the past” by refusing to reopen the issue.

Burnham argued that Britain’s Conservative Party needed to “face up” to mistakes it made on Brexit after several former Tory prime ministers warned him away from reversing the decision.

“They’ve brought out a line-up of former prime ministers, one after another, to say that we shouldn’t even begin to talk about Brexit,” he told the House of Commons.

“Those who say we shouldn’t talk about Brexit risk leaving Britain stuck in the past with a substandard set of arrangements. Instead, we are putting Britain back on a better path and bringing back the hope that has been missing for too long.”

World.title: Lib Dem leader claims he could negotiate EU single market access ‘within a year’
World.content:
Davey said Britain has been through the process before and rejoining existing frameworks would be easier than negotiating a bespoke deal.

The economic benefits would start flowing even before Britain was back inside the single market and customs union, he added.

Davey’s comments came days after Andy Burnham’s Labour government secured deals on agrifood, energy and a youth mobility at a landmark U.K.-EU summit in Brussels on Friday.

The Lib Dem leader said his party had been calling for such a deal “five years ago,” but he argued that the world has since moved on.

“We need a lot more growth, and a lot of growth comes from trade, and I think actually this is quite a timid deal,” he said, adding that it remains within the confines of Boris Johnson’s Trade and Cooperation Agreement.

Burnham has pledged to set out possible options for even closer ties to the EU next month, with rejoining the customs union or single market — or even holding another referendum to rejoin the bloc — among the options floated.

Asked about the possibility of a second referendum, Davey said it would not be so easy.

“We need to explain to British people the huge benefits of Europe before we get to that point,” he said. “I think the Europeans will need a bit of persuading, given the awful history of the last few years.”

World.title: EU targets Russian ex-soldiers, banks and sports in new sanctions push
World.content:
One major measure would restrict visas for former Russian soldiers. The EU agreed on a legal framework for the restrictions in its previous sanctions package over the summer but has yet to put them into effect.

“Russian ex-combatants pose a security risk to Europe. They cannot be allowed to wander freely across our countries,” von der Leyen said, citing a recent escalation in covert Russian operations in Europe.

The Commission also wants to add 70 vessels to its sanctions list targeting Russia’s so-called shadow fleet, which Moscow uses to export oil and other commodities.

European companies would also be barred from repairing Russian refineries damaged by Ukrainian drone attacks. EU citizens would no longer be allowed to sit on the boards of Russian companies.

On sports, the Commission is proposing to bar Russian teams and athletes from competing in the bloc, a move that would prevent Russia from returning to next year’s ice hockey world championship in Germany.

“We propose to ban the display of official Russian symbols. We will also restrict financial flows from Russian sponsors to European based sports and cultural associations,” von der Leyen said.

World.title: Ukraine takes the war against Russia far from its borders
World.content:
In another attack, a cargo ship sailing under the Russian flag was damaged by a drone attack in the Gulf of Finland on Saturday morning, the defense ministry in Helsinki said. Finnish authorities said that Ukraine carried out the attack in international waters; however, Kyiv has not admitted responsibility.

Broadly, Ukraine has expanded its attacks against Russian targets well outside the war zone in an effort to exert more pain on Moscow, said Mykola Bielieskov, research fellow at the Ukrainian National Institute for Strategic Studies.

"Given the fact that frontline operations and strikes against oil refineries and the defense-industrial complex are insufficient to compel the enemy to end the war immediately and unconditionally, Ukraine is seeking additional tools of pressure," he said.

The Libya operation is the first time Ukraine has claimed credit for such a distant strike, but there was little point in denying it after the Benghazi government posted videos of the attacks.

There are also accusations that Ukrainian forces have long been active in other theaters.

Earlier this year, Greece said it would launch an investigation after a naval drone carrying explosives was discovered in the Ionian Sea. Greek and Ukrainian media identified it as likely a Ukrainian-made Magura drone.

World.title: Badenoch: Rejoining EU won’t fix Britain’s economic woes
World.content:
“The last thing this country needs is another five years of division, distraction and arguments about Brexit,” she added.

The Tory leader echoed several former prime ministers, including Tony Blair and Theresa May, who in recent days cautioned Burnham over reopening Brexit. Badenoch said Burnham is opening a "Pandora's box" and noted that "five prime ministers, not just Conservative ones ... have told him that the rejoining the EU conversation he's opening is not the right one.”

Friday's discussions with the EU focused on deals on food and drink, emissions trading and a youth visas scheme. Burnham has said he wants Britain to rejoin the EU in his lifetime but has not committed his government to pursuing membership.

Badenoch said the U.K. should work with the EU on issues including defense, security and trade, but argued renewed membership of the EU "is not going to solve our recurring problems," including lower projected growth and the government spending more than £100 billion servicing its debt.

"Something bad is happening in our economy, and rejoining the EU is not going to fix it. Nor will staying outside the EU automatically fix it either. Britain needs to be more ambitious than just changing our relationship with Brussels," she said.

Instead, Badenoch said the U.K. should continue looking to the rest of the world rather than “locking yourself into one market,” adding that “Europe will always remain an important market, but it is not the market of the future.”

World.title: Visegrád Four leaders voice concerns over EU budget proposal
World.content:
The prime ministers of the Visegrád Four (V4) countries voiced concerns over the European Union's next seven-year budget proposal at a meeting in Bratislava on Monday, questioning spending priorities and plans to include funding for Ukraine.

 

The leaders were meeting with the Austrian chancellor in Slovakia to discuss economic cooperation, migration and the draft of the budget.

Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar said his government did not consider the proposal an acceptable starting point for negotiations.

He said he had therefore written to European Council President António Costa to explain that he saw little point in holding a special council meeting scheduled for later in the week as "there is no point spending two days in Brussels not agreeing on anything."

Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš also signalled his concerns over the proposed budget, saying he had expected the European Commission to show at least some sign that it wanted to save money.

He argued that maintaining a European Parliament in three locations was unnecessary and costly, while also voicing concerns over member state contributions.

Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico, who hosted the meeting, said the leaders had not adopted a joint position on the budget during Monday's meeting, as this had not been the purpose of their discussions, although he noted that they were broadly aligned on the subject.

Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar gestures as he is greeted by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen prior to a meeting at EU headquarters in Brussels. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. All rights reserved

Funding for Ukraine

For his part, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk spoke mainly about security, saying that Poland was committed to peace but that recent events showed the impact of Russia's invasion of Ukraine on Poland.

Tusk underlined the importance of continuing support for Kyiv, arguing that the country's ability to defend itself was of strategic significance for Europe's security.

However, his Hungarian counterpart, Magyar, warned that "support for Ukraine should not be included in the EU budget."

Magyar said there was no question that Ukraine deserved solidarity and noted that Hungary was already providing various forms of assistance to the Ukrainian people and government.

But he argued that financial support for Ukraine should not be incorporated into the bloc's budget in a way that would make contributions mandatory for all members.

On the same issue, Tusk said he did not think it was a good idea for the EU to finance support for Ukraine through joint borrowing - something the Hungarian government has already made clear that it would not take part in.

Tusk, left, speaks with Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy during a bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the EU summit in Brussels, Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026. AP Photo

At a press conference after the meeting, the leaders stressed that regional cooperation was not only important but also achievable, given their shared positions on a number of key issues.

Fico said the V4 countries and Austria broadly agreed on key issues affecting the region, including cohesion policy, migration policy and agricultural strategies.

One of the main topics was how to deal with illegal migration. All the leaders called for strict rules and their consistent enforcement, while Fico also praised a plan for some EU member states to establish immigration return hubs in Rwanda.

Austrian Chancellor Christian Stocker said it was in Austria's interest to cooperate with its neighbours and that he wanted the country to be an ally of the V4.

He added that closer cooperation would also help ensure that the rest of the EU better understood developments in central and eastern Europe and the strategic priorities shaping the region.

World.title: Tanzania: Towering flames engulf beachfront hotels in Zanzibar
World.content:
Thick black smoke rolled over the white sands of Nungwi Beach on Zanzibar’s northern tip after an afternoon fire at Makofi Hotel, whipped along by strong winds and thatched roofs, swept into adjacent resorts, restaurants and shops. Eyewitness mobile footage recorded buildings roaring with flames as tourists and locals scrambled down the beach, some hauling suitcases, others pitching in to help, until firefighters drawn from three stations subdued the blaze after approximately three hours. Although several hotel staff sustained injuries, officials confirmed that every one of the 183 tourists escaped unharmed, with more than 20 hotels in Mchangani and Matemwe stepping in to house displaced guests free of charge.

 

Across the six affected hotels (Makofi, Z Hotel, Nungwi Garden, BR, Pasha and Sand Beach), four restaurants and about 40 shops, the scale of the damage poses an acute challenge for local businesses and workers in the semi-autonomous Tanzanian archipelago, where tourism is an economic mainstay. On Monday, investigators were still working to confirm whether the fire started in a bread-baking oven, as early accounts suggested, while Tourism and Antiquities Minister Nasra Nassor Omar urged patience ahead of an official inquiry and promised a rapid assessment to guide the government’s response.

World.title: German-Ukrainian interceptor shoots down Russian jet-powered drone, company says
World.content:
A German-Ukrainian company said on Monday that its SPYS interceptor UAV had shot down a Russian jet-powered drone in Ukraine.

 

Quantum WIY Industries announced that it had successfully intercepted a Russian Geran-5 K5-K attack drone during combat testing in Ukraine, according to a press release shared by Quantum Systems, a German defence firm that launched the joint venture alongside Ukraine's WIY Drones.

“We need to keep developing and scaling interceptors to protect Ukrainian cities and critical infrastructure. Russia keeps adapting its attack systems, so we work closely with Ukrainian brigades to adjust our systems accordingly," Sven Kruck, co-CEO of Quantum Systems, said.

"You can never stand still," he added.

According to WIY Drones, the SPYS system is a high-speed interceptor UAV that can be deployed to defend against aerial targets.

It is designed to counter both attack and reconnaissance drones and to protect military positions, mobile units and critical infrastructure, the company says on its website.

The SPYS interceptor can reach speeds of up to around 450 kph and has a flight ceiling of 4 km, according to WIY.

The GUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency, said in early November that Russian forces had begun using the K5-K variant of the Geran-5 in attacks on Ukrainian cities at the beginning of autumn.

The agency said that "based on its aerodynamic scheme and tactical-technical characteristics," the K5-K "can already be classified as a compact cruise missile."

It added that the drone can hit speeds of more than 450 kph and can reach an altitude of 6 km.

Unlike conventional attack drones such as the Geran-2, which use propeller engines, jet-powered drones can hit significantly higher speeds, making them harder for Ukrainian air defences to deal with.

World.title: Belgium: Workers march against spending cuts as living costs rise
World.content:
Carrying placards warning that "Rent is eating into our wages" and "The rich earn more, the workers pay more", demonstrators rallied in Brussels to oppose around €10 billion in proposed spending cuts before clashes broke out with riot police, who responded with tear gas, water cannons and charges as a car burned and officers made arrests amid plumes of smoke. For protesters already squeezed by high energy costs, inflation and shrinking purchasing power, the planned savings threaten to place an unfair burden on the lowest-paid while undermining social security, employment support and help for families.

 

The street anger spilled over on the very day Prime Minister Bart De Wever met King Philippe to update him on strained talks over Belgium’s 2027 budget. Having set a year-end deadline for coalition partners to sign off on the cuts, and warned that the government could collapse if negotiations fail, De Wever now faces sharpening resistance both inside parliament and on the streets as he seeks to reconcile fiscal discipline with demands to protect living standards.

World.title: What went wrong at the COP31 climate talks? Europe Tonight breaks it down
World.content:
Despite becoming the longest UN climate conference in history over the weekend, the COP31 talks failed to produce a deal after the European Union and a number of countries rejected a final proposal over the omission of fossil fuels.

 

Across Europe, frustration is growing and questions are being raised about the future of international climate diplomacy. Is the COP process still capable of delivering meaningful results, or has it reached a breaking point?

To explore what went wrong in Turkey, what the failed negotiations mean for Europe and for the future of global climate action, Euronews' Felicia Pochhammer spoke with Chiara Martinelli, the director of Climate Action Network, on Europe Tonight.

Watch the video above to catch the full interview.

World.title: NATO warns of intensifying threats as Ukraine peace proposals face key questions
World.content:
The NATO Parliamentary Assembly has been holding its annual session in Berlin amid a fresh wave of security incidents across Europe, including hybrid attacks and airspace violations.

 

Speaking at the meeting, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warned of "intensifying malign activities targeting our nations."

Henri Vanhanen, a senior fellow with the Transatlantic Security Initiative at the Atlantic Council’s Scowcroft Center for Strategy and Security, joined Euronews’ new show Europe Tonight to discuss the growing security concerns and the prospects for peace in Ukraine.

Watch the video above to catch the full interview.

World.title: Merz says it was a 'mistake' not to admit Ukraine into NATO in 2008
World.content:
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz described the decision not to admit Ukraine into NATO in 2008, following a proposal by then-US President George W. Bush, as a “mistake.”

 

Speaking alongside NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte at a press conference in Berlin, Friedrich Merz told reporters: "I think we all see today, at least from the point of view of what a mistake it was, not to follow the American proposal in 2008 at the NATO summit in Bucharest."

He added that the full-scale invasion of Ukraine would have been 'prevented' had the alliance opened up membership back then.

"If Ukraine had become a member of NATO, this war would have been likely to be prevented," said Merz, in comments that were translated from German.

The meeting came amid ongoing US-led negotiations to end the war in Ukraine, with Rutte visiting the German capital for the NATO Parliamentary Assembly's annual meeting.

Rutte struck a cautious tone on the prospect of reviving discussions about Ukraine's NATO membership, stressing that successful peace negotiations would need to come first.

The remarks came in response to recent comments by French President Emmanuel Macron, who called for the debate over Ukraine's membership of the alliance to be reopened.

Kyiv's potential NATO membership has resurfaced as part of a potential final resolution to ending the war.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has reportedly indicated he would be willing to end the war in Ukraine, provided NATO agrees to return to its 1997 posture. This would effectively mean reversing the alliance's subsequent expansion by withdrawing membership from countries that joined after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

However, NATO membership for Ukraine remains a distant prospect, according to Rutte. He noted that while "it's a long-standing position that Ukraine should be a part of NATO," there is no unanimous agreement among alliance members on its accession.

Rutte also rebuffed the notion that the Kremlin could have any say in the current or future makeup of the NATO alliance. "What cannot happen is we are forced to roll back NATO to the 1997 borders," he said.

"It's only the 32 allies deciding who is in NATO and who is not in NATO".

Rutte was also addressing ongoing tensions in Europe over increasing Russian hybrid attacks, including last week's incursion into Poland, when two Russian cruise missiles and a drone landed on Polish territory, according to Polish officials.

He attributed Russia's increased aggression to mounting battlefield casualties, claiming that Russian forces are losing up to 50,000 soldiers each month in Ukraine. He contrasted this figure with Soviet losses in Afghanistan and US casualties during the Vietnam War.

"Ukraine is rolling back the frontline in the direction of Russia and striking deep" into Russian territory, Rutte told journalists.

Rutte reiterated NATO's position that the best solution to growing hybrid attacks is doubling down on support for Ukraine.

"Most importantly, we need to keep our military support for Ukraine going," said Rutte.

"For every incident in Europe - more support for Ukraine," he added.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered the strikes following what he described as “weak meetings” with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

“Russia is trying to compensate for its military and diplomatic impotence with precisely this kind of terror," Zelenskyy wrote in a post on "X" last Friday.

Separately, NATO ambassadors met in Brussels Monday to discuss the Russian incursion into Poland. The alliance is now considering deploying more assets to the region in response.

NATO's chief military officer, the Supreme Allied Commander (SACEUR) is now "examining the deployment of additional assets as he continues to assess our deterrence and defence posture in Poland and elsewhere," a NATO official confirmed to Euronews.

World.title: 'Don't waste those talents': GTA VI hacker released on licence
World.content:
A 21-year-old man was sentenced to seven years in prison in the United Kingdom on Monday after a string of cyberattacks targeting major companies including Grand Theft Auto VI maker Rockstar Games.

 

Arion Kurtaj, who was released on licence after already having spent years in custody, pleaded guilty last Monday to a series of hacking attacks that he carried out between 2021 and 2022 as part of the Lapsus$ hacking group.

"You are obviously a very talented young man," the judge said.

"Don't waste those talents by spending the rest of your life in and out of prison," he continued, adding that the sentencing decision required "balancing the seriousness of what you did with, on the other hand, your young age" and medical diagnoses.

Prosecutors said Kurtaj had caused "serious disruption to major international business" and put sensitive information at risk with the hacks.

In one incident, Kurtaj managed to obtain 90 gameplay videos from Rockstar's much anticipated and at the time unfinished GTA VI game before leaking them online under the pseudonym "TeaPotUberHacker." He also threatened to release the game’s source code, according to prosecutors.

Kurtaj is said to have used just a mobile phone, a hotel TV’s Wi-Fi and an Amazon Firestick to carry out the hack.

He also targeted neobank Revolut and ride-hailing firm Uber.

Kurtaj was initially arrested in September 2022 but was deemed not fit to stand trial following a medical assessment.

In 2023, he was handed an indefinite restricted hospital order. A court ruled in January 2026 that the hospital order could be lifted, and his case was scheduled for trial.

World.title: Turkey seizes control of last major independent news channel amid fraud scandal
World.content:
Turkey's last operating independent TV news channel has fallen under state control, as President Recep Tayyip Erdogan scrambles to contain a wave of public fury over a $20 billion investment fund scandal that has swallowed the life savings of hundreds of thousands of people in the country.

Advertising

Sozcu TV vanished from the airwaves before dawn on Tuesday as police enforced a court order installing a state trustee, cutting the channel's transmission as it was broadcasting a programme on the latest revelations in the investment fraud scandal.

The move echoes a similar state takeover last month of Halk TV, another major independent broadcaster.

The silencing of Turkey’s two largest independent news channels has drawn sharp condemnation from opposition parties and human rights groups. While the government maintains that the judiciary operates independently, critics argue the court orders are politically motivated.
