A baby who fell from a third-storey window in Amsterdam survived the incident, police have revealed.

The one-year-old boy was found lying on the ground on the evening of October 30 by a passer-by on Amstelveenweg.

Police are still investigating how the child fell and have appealed for witnesses or anybody in the area with video footage to contact them.

The boy was taken to hospital after the incident. Police did not disclose any details of his condition.

World.title: NL sends delegation to India over abducted Amsterdam girl
World.content:
The Dutch government is sending a delegation of officials to India this week to push for the return of Insiya, a girl from Amsterdam who was abducted on her father’s orders 10 years ago.

Foreign minister Tom Berendsen, who happens to be on a working visit to India, told broadcaster NOS that officials from the foreign and justice ministries will discuss what legal options are available, including the Netherlands’ request to extradite her father, Shehzad Hemani.

He said he hopes the delegation can take the first steps towards restoring contact between Insiya and her mother, Nadia Rashid, who has not seen her daughter since 2016.

Insiya was two years old when she was taken from her grandmother’s home in Amsterdam-Oost in 2016 by a group of men hired by her father. They took her to India via Germany using false documents. She is now 12.

A Dutch court sentenced Hemani in absentia to 8.5 years in prison. Several of his accomplices were jailed for up to four years. India has not extradited Hemani and has not signed the international treaty on child abduction. Indian courts do not treat a child’s removal as abduction if the child lives with one of the parents.

The delegation’s trip follows a video message to Insiya that Amsterdam mayor Femke Halsema posted on social media on Sunday. The video is an attempt to get round an Indian court order that has hidden hundreds of articles about the case from users in India.

Since October 30, Google has blocked publications about Insiya for users in India, following an order by a court in New Delhi, NOS reported. The case was brought in the girl’s name by her father and grandmother, who cited safety concerns.

The block covers Dutch and international media reports, Dutch court press releases, government documents and Rashid’s social media accounts, which she had used to try to reach her daughter.

Halsema put out a video message while on a trade mission in Mumbai last week, in which Insiya’s mother tells her daughter that she misses her. Halsema encouraged people to share the video widely.

World.title: PvdD marks 20 years in parliament fighting factory farming
World.content:
Animal rights party PvdD celebrated its 20th year in parliament yesterday, two decades after it became the first political party on earth to gain such power under the banner of improving livestock welfare and banning factory farming.

Party leader Christine Teunissen addressed a crowd of members in Nieuwegein, Utrecht, saying that the group has grown to be “the thorn in the side of the ruling powers”, according to broadcaster NOS.

She drew attention to the leverage the PvdD achieved during the recent cabinet crisis, in which the Jetten government managed to pass its tax plan with essential support from the party, who lent its backing in return for (among other things) funding for alternatives to animal testing.

Teunissen said it she was proud that the PvdD could “break through the VVD’s power politics”, and had shown “what is possible when the VVD is not in control”.

The right-wing liberal VVD voted against its coalition partners, centrist D66 and Christian Democrat CDA, after they agreed a new tax proposal with left-wing opposition parties. This sparked a crisis that many feared would collapse the government.

The PvdD originally refused to support the plan, but its 3 seats in parliament became pivotal amid the dispute.

A bill on livestock farming, which addresses the party’s founding purpose, is due to be voted on in December. It would effectively ban factory farming by 2040, ensuring that all animals are kept in conditions that respect their natural behaviours.

There is already a government act in place that seeks to ensure the same ends, but the PvdD maintains it is too weak to be realistic. A separate bill on banning cruel slaughter methods is also in the works.

World.title: Prosecutors ask for 30 years and treatment for Erasmus shooter
World.content:
Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Prosecutors have demanded a 30-year sentence on appeal for a medical student who shot dead two of his neighbours and a teacher in a fit of “uncontrollable rage”.

Faoud L., from Rotterdam, was given a life sentence for the triple murder at his original trial in February last year.

The public prosecution service said a fixed term was more appropriate because it would allow L. to be given a compulsory treatment order. L. is also appealing against the sentence.

The trial judge said therapy was unlikely to be effective after 30 years in prison, whereas a prisoner on a life sentence can apply for parole after 25 years.

L. shot his next-door neighbour, a 39-year-old woman named as Marlous, and her 14-year-old daughter, Romy, in September 2023, before setting his own flat on fire.

He then rode his motorcycle to Rotterdam’s Erasmus Medical Centre where he shot dead 43-year-old Jurgen Damen as he was giving a lecture to a class of students.

L., now 35, was studying medicine at the university, but became enraged when the exams committee refused to let him sit for his diploma unless he underwent a psychological assessment.

He told an earlier court hearing that he originally planned to kill several students in the classroom, but persuaded himself to target only the lecturer after an “internal conflict”.

Researchers at the Pieter Baan Centrum, which carries out psychological assessments on criminal suspects, concluded that he had a type of autism that made it difficult to process and recognise emotions.

World.title: How much Dutch do you need to get hired in 2027?
World.content:
“Native Dutch” in every vacancy? Here’s how to get hired anyway:

New year, new job hunt! But two little words keep stopping internationals in their tracks. Here’s why they don’t have to stop you.

“Is it even worth trying?” Jamila Vriesman, founder of Amstel Dutch, hears it all the time. Her Dutch language & culture school in Amsterdam has one simple belief: you can’t really learn Dutch without understanding the Dutch. So her students learn both.

Lately, many of them share the same story. Months of lessons. A shiny new CV. Then they spot “native Dutch” in a vacancy and close the tab faster than you can say gezellig.

“I get it,” says Jamila, a born Amsterdammer. “But please don’t give up. The market has changed. So your strategy needs to change too.”

Harder, not hopeless

Short answer: it’s not just you. Since autumn 2025, job seekers in the Netherlands have outnumbered vacancies. The latest CBS figures show 92 vacancies for every 100 job seekers.

“When employers can choose, language often tips the balance,” Jamila explains. Every month you wait, the pile of CVs next to yours grows. And more of them say “some Dutch”. The good news? This is a tiebreaker you can train for.

“Native” is a signal, not a stop sign

“Native Dutch” tells you how important the language is in the job. “Honestly, ‘native’ is an unfortunate requirement,” says Jamila. “Most employers mean professional fluency: you can follow a fast meeting and write a clear email. That is something you can learn. Being born here is not.” Tick the other boxes? Apply. Be honest about your level and show how you are working on it.

And “Dutch is a plus”? “That is not a wall,” Jamila points out. “That is an open door. Walk through it!”

Show what you’ve got

For many other jobs, you don’t need to be fluent to stand out. “Imagine 200 people apply and 15 of them speak some Dutch,” Jamila suggests. “Who do you think gets noticed? Even A2 tells an employer: I’m planning to stay.”

And A2 is closer than you think. With a busy job and one lesson a week, many people get there in about 12 months. More time? You’ll go even faster.

So show it off. Write your LinkedIn summary in Dutch. Add a short Dutch paragraph to your cover letter. Start your interview with a warm goedemorgen (good morning). “Nobody expects you to discuss tax law in your first sentence,” Jamila laughs. “But that one word already does a lot of work.”

Know your world

Every sector sets its own bar. According to Indeed, Dutch is a must in healthcare, education and law, while many tech teams mostly work in English. Know which world you’re walking into, and learn the Dutch it speaks.

Survive your first Dutch meeting

An interview follows a script. A team meeting does not. Suddenly you are in a room full of jokes, shortcuts and half sentences, nodding along and hoping nobody asks you anything. Sound familiar?

“And when a Dutch colleague calls your plan interessant, it’s not always a compliment,” Jamila smiles.

Her tip: train your ears, not just your mouth. Pick two lifesaver phrases and use them this week: Kun je dat nog een keer zeggen? (Could you say that again?) and Wat bedoel je precies? (What exactly do you mean?). Small sentences, big difference.

Find your crew

Can you do all this on your own? Partly. Apps are great for words. But they won’t tell you why your colleague went quiet after your feedback. “A teacher hears the mistakes you no longer notice,” Jamila believes. “And a group gives you a safe place to get things wrong before you do it in a meeting.”

Her last tip: stop comparing yourself to native speakers. “Compare yourself to who you were a year ago. Every level opens more doors. Companies don’t just want someone who can do the job. They want someone who’ll stay and feel at home. Language is the door. Culture is the room behind it.”

Ready to stop nodding along? Jamila and her team at Amstel Dutch teach you the language and the unwritten rules of Dutch working life. No boring drills. No stuffy classrooms.

During the Dutch City Experiences, you explore Amsterdam with your group, use your Dutch where it actually happens and end with a drink in a bruin café. Think of it as a dress rehearsal for your first coffee break at a new job. And to keep the conversation going, join the free monthly taalcafé and practise your Dutch in a relaxed setting.

In a hurry or ready to immerse yourself? Amstel Dutch also offers intensive weeks that take you through a full level in one week (coffee included, sleep optional): A0 to A1 from 14 to 19 December and A1 to A2 from 11 to 16 January 2027. More dates follow throughout the year.

Not sure where to start? Book your free 20-minute intake: you’ll know your level, the level your next job asks for, and the quickest realistic route between the two. Your way into Dutch life starts here.

World.title: Dutch households turning down gas as global unrest stokes prices
World.content:
Dutch households are using less gas for heating and more electricity in response to the steep rise in energy prices, according to figures from energy supplier Essent.

The company said gas consumption dropped by 10% year-on-year at the start of November, despite the cold start to the month, while electricity use was up by 40%.

Essenty said there was a clear trend towards switching to electric heating systems such as infrared panels and air conditioning units, which can also be used for heating.

Households are still using gas as their main source of heating, but electric heaters are being used as a top-up supply, with a surge in demand in the early hours of the evening as people come home from work and school.

Most homes are still connected to the gas mains, but the Dutch government is committed to switching off the supply completely by 2050.

“Under normal temperatures we saw the same gas use as normal, but op November 3, when it was 1 degree below the normal temperature, we saw 4% less gas use,” Essent energy market specialist Denise van Zon told NOS.

Earlier surveys by Essent found that a quarter of households are planning to use electric heating devices as gas prices are expected to remain high through the winter because of the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which is restricting global supplies.

“I think the unrest is the reason for the increase,” Van Zon said. “We’ve heard about the gas reserves, the conflict in Iran and we have seen another significant increase in prices.”

The average household gas price has risen by 35% since October last year and many energy companies are offering lower prices for multiple-year contracts in an attempt to encourage customers to fix their prices for the long term.

World.title: Dutch man who spent 42 years in US prison for murder dies
World.content:
A Dutch man who spent 42 years in prison in the US for murder has died of leukaemia, eight months after being repatriated to the Netherlands.

Jaitsen Singh, 81, spent his final months in Scheveningen after the appeal court in The Hague ordered the government to bring him home because of his age and ill health.

His death on Sunday was confirmed in an online post by his lawyer, Rachel Imamkhan, who represented him since 2011. He was the longest serving Dutch prisoner in foreign custody.

“Those who knew him will mainly remember the man behind the case,” she wrote.

In August the appeal court ordered him to be transferred from the US to the Netherlands, following years of campaigning by his family and lawyers.

He was born in Suriname when it was still a Dutch colony and held a Dutch passport, even after moving to the US in 1970. The Dutch attorney general opposed his repatriation, arguing he had insufficient ties to the country.

Denied guilt

Singh was jailed in 1986 for “56 years to life” for arranging the murder of his wife and stepdaughter, but he has always denied committing the crime.

Their bodies were found in the boot of their car in Los Angeles two years earlier. A key piece of evidence was a statement by a serving prisoner who was later found to have been bribed.

Imamkhan said his case was “seen by many as a miscarriage of justice in the United States and remained a subject of debate for years.”

But the family of his wife and stepdaughter said they believed he was responsible for their deaths and his “‘continued denial and lack of remorse have only deepened the family’s suffering”.

In a statement released through the family support organisation Namens de Familie, they said Singh was being portrayed as a victim “while two innocent lives that have been taken away are once again fading into the background.”

Last August the appeal court ordered the state to request Singh’s transfer from the US to a Dutch prison, following years of campaigning by his family and lawyers. He flew into the Netherlands in March this year.

He was born in Suriname when it was still a Dutch colony and held a Dutch passport, even after moving to the US in 1970. The Netherlands opposed his repatriation, arguing he had insufficient ties to the country.

World.title: US turtle invasion: exotic species spreading through NL
World.content:
An “invasive exotic species” in spreading through the Netherlands – the yellow-bellied slider turtle – which has been brought from the US and can now survive in an increasingly warm environment, according to radio programme Vroege Vogels.

The species has long been imported from America and sold as pets but until recently could not survive in the cold Dutch climate.

This has changed and last Spring someone spotted a group of young turtles by a pond in Zuid-Holland, and contacted Faunawatch, an organisation dedicated to abandoned turtles.

After inspecting the site, sixteen empty eggs and two young turtles were found, both of which have been taken to a rescue centre in Limburg.

Tim Huijsmans, a researcher from Faunawatch, told the radio programme that climate change is making it possible for these turtles to breed in the Netherlands for the first time.

“If it is too cold, the hatchlings die in the egg. So now, for the first time, young water turtles have been born. After hatching, they burrowed into the ground during the winter and went to the water in the spring,” he explained.

An estimated 200,000 freshwater turtles have been dumped in the Dutch wild, he said, and the government now needs to allocate funds to monitor their spread and the risks associated.

The Netherlands will become the latest country to purchase Poland’s Piorun man-portable air-defence systems, which have been increasingly in demand following their successful use during Ukraine’s defence against Russia. On Monday, their Polish manufacturer, Mesko, which is part of state-owned defence group PGZ, signed an agreement adding the Netherlands to a list of countries that will buy Pioruns with funds from the European Union’s SAFE mechanism for financing defence spending. 🇵🇱🇳🇱⚡ HOLANDIA DOŁĄCZA DO DRUŻYNY PIORUNA! W @PGZ_MESKO_SA w Skarżysku-Kamiennej podpisano aneks do umowy ramowej, umożliwiający Holandii dołączenie do wspólnych zamówień zestawów PIORUN. ✍️ Dokument podpisali gen. dyw. Artur Kuptel, Szef @AgencjaUzbr, oraz Krzysztof Marwicki… pic.twitter.com/lVH0QgdD0t — Polska Grupa Zbrojeniowa🇵🇱 (@PGZ_pl) November 23, 2026 Piorun (meaning “thunderbolt” in Polish) is a shoulder-mounted system that fires air-defence missiles capable of destroying aerial vehicles, such as helicopters, drones and low-flying planes, at short range. In 2022, Pioruns were among the large quantities of military equipment that Poland provided to Ukraine to help its eastern neighbour defend itself from Russia’s full-scale invasion. The systems have been successfully used to take down Russian aircraft. Since then, they have been in high demand, with Mesko receiving orders from the United States, Norway, Belgium and Sweden, as well as Ukraine itself. In August this year, Mesko signed an 8 billion zloty (€1.8 billion) agreement to supply further Piorun systems to Poland, Norway, Lithuania and Latvia, with the deal financed through SAFE funds. Precise details were not revealed. However, the agreement was said to involve the supply of “several hundred” launchers and “several thousand” missiles, with over 80% of the equipment going to Poland’s own armed forces. Now Mesko has signed an addendum to that deal, adding the Netherlands to the list of countries that are jointly ordering Pioruns. Deputy defence minister Magdalena Sobkowiak-Czarnecka, who has overseen Poland’s participation in the SAFE programme, said after attending Monday’s signing ceremony that the Netherlands would not be the last country to join the procurement of Pioruns. “We promised that the list of Mesko’s buyers from all over Europe would grow, and today we have living proof of that,” said Sobkowiak-Czarnecka. “And I can reveal a secret: it’s not over yet.” She noted that Mesko has stepped up its production volumes in response to demand. Last year, it could produce “several hundred” systems annually; that has now risen to 1,500, and is set to grow even further. Last week, PGZ and the state assets ministry signed an agreement to support Mesko’s expansion with around 370 million zloty from the state Capital Investment Fund (FIK). It will help bring production capacity to around 2,500 per year. 🗣️ "Obiecywaliśmy, że lista kupujących z całej Europy będzie się powiększać i mamy tego żywy dowód. A mogę zdradzić sekret, że to jeszcze nie koniec. Dzisiejsza umowa to umowa w ramach zakupów w mechanizmie SAFE"@magdasobkowiak o zestawach Piorun dla Holandii ⤵️ pic.twitter.com/sTxG5SwnbZ — tvp.info 🇵🇱 (@tvp_info) November 23, 2026 Growing demand for Pioruns resulted in Mesko last year posting the best financial results in its 100-year history. The firm’s revenues of 2.3 billion zloty in 2025 were up 33% year-on-year. The EU’s SAFE programme is providing a total of €150 billion in loans at preferential rates for member states to use on defence-related spending. Poland, with around €44 billion, is the largest single recipient. While most SAFE purchases are conducted individually by member states, some are also carried out jointly. Such joint procurement can also involve certain non-EU countries, such as Norway. World.title: Public astronomical observatory opens in Warsaw
World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Warsaw’s first astronomical observatory open to the public and run by a local municipal institution launched on Sunday. Its organisers say the facility, with two telescopes allowing safe observation of the Sun and photography of the cosmos, is aimed at astronomy enthusiasts as well as children and young people, who will be able to watch the night sky and participate in recording data without needing their own equipment. The new observatory, which is located on the roof of the Gocław Culture Terminal in the Praga-South of Poland’s capital, was created in response to growing public interest in astronomy, science and new technologies, says city hall. “Under the three-metre-high dome, specialised equipment awaits, allowing for observation of the sky, including safe viewing of the Sun,” said mayor Rafał Trzaskowski, who visited the facility last week ahead of its official opening. “Anyone who is interested can come here and learn about space through observation, photographing the sky and hands-on activities,” he added. The observatory will be free to use but only accessible during organised events, owing to limited space and the expensive equipment it contains, reports newspaper Super Express. “The dome houses very expensive equipment. For most of the year, it will function as a broadcasting station, and images from the telescopes will be projected onto screens in the main hall of the terminal,” Jacek Białek, head of Gocław Culture Terminal, told the newspaper. “We will invite people inside the dome as part of programs, the dates of which will be published on the cultural centre’s website,” he added. Participants in workshops and events will also be able to help collect and analyse data, with Białek noting that the centre will be working closely with scientists from the University of Warsaw The new facility cost around 500,000 zloty (€111,000), most of which was covered from the district budget, with contributions from private donations as well as grants from the state-owned military optoelectronic equipment company PCO and the national lottery foundation. The core of the new facility is a 14″ DO-GSO (Ritchey-Chrétien) telescope with a mirror diameter of approximately 35 cm and a focal length of approximately 2,850 mm, placed on an EQ8-RH equatorial mount with automatic sky tracking. This setup, along with a QHY268M Pro monochrome camera, a filter wheel and an electronic focuser, will be used for astrophotography and targeted photometric measurements, producing images suited to Warsaw’s atmospheric conditions. The observatory also boasts a specialist Sky-Watcher Heliostar 100 H-Alpha telescope, which is used for safe and detailed observation and astrophotography of the Sun, allowing viewers to see structures in the solar atmosphere invisible through an ordinary telescope. The telescope allows solar prominences – large, bright features extending out from the Sun’s surface – to be observed and compared with images produced on other days. The telescope is protected by a three-metre dome that automatically opens and rotates. Warsaw has been chosen as the location for a new European Space Agency security centre, as Poland takes another step in its ambitions to become a bigger player in the space sector The facility will be the @esa's first outside its 11 founding member states https://t.co/WnHIbrW3ze — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 13, 2026 The observatory also features a computer coordinating its measurements, a camera showing almost the entire sky, and a weather monitoring system. Observations will depend on atmospheric conditions and visibility. “Examples of how this telescope might be used include photographing the cosmos and conducting simple research, such as measuring changes in the brightness of stars and producing graphs illustrating these changes,” explained Ewa Konarzewska from Gocław Culture Terminal. Poland has placed great emphasis on developing its space industry in recent years, with the aim of becoming a major European player in the sector. Last year, the country launched its first national military satellite. A Polish firm, Creotech Instruments, signed Poland’s largest-ever contract with the European Space Agency, a €52 million deal to build and launch a constellation of Earth observation satellites. Meanwhile, 2025 also saw astronaut Sławosz Uznański-Wiśniewski become the second-ever Pole to travel into space, as part of an ESA mission to the International Space Station. Earlier this year, Warsaw was chosen as the location for a new ESA centre focused on civil security and resilience, with the agency’s head declaring that “Poland has rapidly become one of the driving forces in Europe’s space sector”. World.title: Poland confirms three objects that struck its territory were all Russian missiles
World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! We cannot do what we do without your support. Prosecutors investigating three objects that landed in Poland last Friday morning have confirmed that they were all Russian Kh-101 cruise missiles. They added that preliminary findings indicate the missiles were recently manufactured at a plant in Dubna, Russia. The objects struck at three different locations in southeastern Poland – Nowy Lipowiec, Rudnik and Mołodycz – not far from the Ukrainian border. The incidents took place amid large-scale Russian attacks on Ukraine. No injuries or damage to infrastructure was reported as a result of the strikes on Poland. Prokuratorzy wojskowi oraz Żandarmeria Wojskowa ustalili, że w Nowym Lipowcu, Rudniku i Mołodyczu spadły rosyjskie pociski manewrujące Ch-101. Wyprodukowano je w IV kwartale 2026 r. w zakładach w Dubnej pod Moskwą. W dwóch miejscach oględziny już się zakończyły. Dziś rano,… https://t.co/nNfkvx4FAq — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) November 23, 2026 Initially, on Friday, Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, identified one of the objects as a Kh-101 cruise missile – the same type as one that entered Polish airspace and exploded in eastern Poland in July this year. He said another was also likely a missile while the third was probably a jet-powered drone. However, in a statement issued on Sunday, the district prosecutor’s office in Lublin, which is leading the investigation, confirmed that all three objects were Kh-101 cruise missiles. Analysis is still underway, but “preliminary findings indicate that all the missiles were manufactured in the fourth quarter of 2026 at a plant in Dubna (Moscow Oblast, Russian Federation)”, said the prosecutors. Dubna is home to MKB Raduga, the Russian aerospace firm that produces Kh-101 missiles. “Kremlin trolls will once again try to convince Poles that these are not Russian missiles,” wrote Waldemar Żurek, the justice minister and prosecutor general, “but the evidence nips those lies in the bud.” Ireneusz Nowak, the operational commander of the Polish armed forces, revealed on Friday that the three missiles were in Polish airspace for around three minutes before hitting the ground. Two Swedish Gripen fighter jets, which are helping patrol Polish skies as part of a NATO air policing mission, had attempted to intercept the missiles. They received authorisation from NATO’s Combined Air Operations Centre to fire upon the objects if certain conditions were met. However, the pilots were unable to confirm the identity of the objects in time, largely because of “extremely difficult weather conditions”, said Nowak, quoted by the Rzeczpospolita daily. Komunikat szwedzkich Sił Zbrojnych w związku z naruszeniem polskiej przestrzeni powietrznej: "Szwedzkie myśliwce JAS Gripen w misji obrony powietrznej nad Polską Szwedzkie Siły Powietrzne uczestniczyły minionej nocy w operacji obrony powietrznej z wykorzystaniem samolotów JAS… pic.twitter.com/oq9WXW3vXO — Ambasada Szwecji (@AmbSzweWarszawa) November 20, 2026 Poland’s NATO allies have expressed support for and solidarity with Poland in the wake of Friday’s incident. “I can guarantee that NATO will defend every ​inch of Polish territory,” said the alliance’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, on a visit to Warsaw on Saturday. Later that day, Kosiniak-Kamysz announced that, “in the near future, we will receive strong support from our NATO allies to strengthen the protection of our eastern border”. He revealed that an extraordinary meeting of the North Atlantic Council, NATO’s main decision-making body, would take place on Monday, at which Poland will present specific proposals for action. W najbliższym czasie otrzymamy od sojuszników z NATO silne wsparcie wzmacniające ochronę naszej wschodniej granicy! W poniedzialek w Kwaterze Głównej NATO odbędzie się nadzwyczajne spotkanie Rady Północnoatlantyckiej, na którym przedstawimy konkretne propozycje i określimy nowe… — Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (@KosiniakKamysz) November 21, 2026 Russia has so far not commented on its missiles hitting Poland. It remains unconfirmed whether they were deliberately directed into Polish airspace or veered off course during the large-scale attacks on Ukraine. However, in recent months, the Polish government has warned of intelligence suggesting the likelihood of “provocations” by Russia, including airspace and border violations. In September this year, a Russian helicopter briefly crossed the border from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Earlier this month, Poland claimed to have foiled a ground operation around the border with Kaliningrad. In September 2025, around 20 Russian drones crossed Poland’s eastern borders in an unprecedented violation that prompted Poland to trigger NATO’s Article 4. World.title: FedEx-led consortium completes €7.8bn takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. A consortium led by FedEx has completed its €7.8 billion (34.5 billion zloty) takeover of Polish delivery giant InPost. The deal will see InPost remain headquartered in Poland, with founder and CEO Rafał Brzoska staying at the helm. Friday’s announcement brings to a close a process that was first announced in February and received European Commission approval in August. InPost’s shares have now been delisted from the stock exchange. The takeover follows years of rapid growth for InPost, which pioneered the use of parcel delivery lockers in Poland before spreading rapidly in major western European markets, including France, Spain and the UK. A consortium of Advent, FedEx, A&R Investments and PPF has completed its takeover of Poland's InPost, which is now private. InPost has delisted from Euronext Amsterdam. Founder Rafał Brzoska stays on as CEO, and the company remains headquartered in Poland. pic.twitter.com/HWigKVPC3w — IPO Newsroom (@IPONewsroom_) November 20, 2026 Under the deal, FedEx and Advent, an American private equity firm, each hold 37% of InPost. A&R Investments, Brzoska’s own investment vehicle, has 16% and PPF, a Czech investment fund founded by the late billionaire Petr Kellner, 10%. PPF, A&R and Advent were previously already stakeholders. The consortium acquired InPost at a price of €15.60 per share, valuing the company at approximately €7.8 billion. In a statement published on Friday, Advent confirmed that InPost would retain its name, branding, Polish headquarters and operational independence following the takeover. Brzoska, who founded his business in 1999, will continue as CEO alongside the existing management team. “InPost’s home market of Poland will remain the blueprint for new innovations, which will then be scaled across InPost’s wider European network,” said Advent. They added that the new consortium would now “accelerate investment” in InPost’s operations, helping the firm “extend its reach further”. FedEx and InPost would also “explore opportunities” to cooperate with one another. “InPost has built a leading position in Europe’s out-of-home delivery segment,” said FedEx’s CEO and president, Raj Subramaniam. “Connecting our global network…with InPost’s last-mile capabilities gives both businesses a potential springboard for profitable growth.” Brzoska, who is one of Poland’s wealthiest individuals, said that the new partnership would “deliver the long-term capital, global reach and deep technology expertise we require to build on what we have already achieved together as a leading European e-commerce enabler”. President Macron has thanked Polish delivery giant InPost for its latest investment in France The firm, which already operates over 9,000 parcel lockers in France through its subsidiary Mondial Relay, will now spend a further €500m to expand its presence https://t.co/caOGNQemfm — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 2, 2026 InPost is the largest operator of parcel lockers in Europe, with around 70,000 across the continent. That includes roughly 30,000 in Poland and 16,000 in the UK, including in branches of the British Post Office, with over 23,000 more in the seven Eurozone countries where InPost operates. In the second quarter of 2026, InPost had revenue of 4.18 billion zloty (€970 million), up 18.2% year on year, while its number of parcels handled rose 16% to 380.9 million. The strongest revenue growth came in the eurozone, where sales increased 37.9%, followed by Poland, with 12.7% growth. Revenue in the UK and Ireland rose 9.8%. Poland recently managed to prevent a planned Russian “false-flag operation” at the border that, if it had not been stopped, could have “ended tragically”, says a retired general who acts as an advisor to the defence minister. His statement follows a report earlier this week by a leading newspaper, based on statements by unnamed senior officials, that Poland had foiled an attempt by Russia to carry out a major “provocation” on the border with the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Polish government figures, including Prime Minister Donald Tusk, have confirmed that a Russian operation at the border was prevented, though they have not provided further details. Generał Mieczysław Bieniek o próbie rosyjskiej prowokacji przy granicy z Polską !!! Polskie władze potwierdzają udaremnioną próbę rosyjskiej prowokacji przy granicy z obwodem królewieckim. – Udało się udaremnić, być może tragiczny w skutkach, incydent – przyznał w "Faktach po… pic.twitter.com/raQMfJ4uUp — Andrzej Mitura #Mocnytakżeosobno (@AndrzejekMitura) November 19, 2026 “The public isn’t informed about everything,” retired general Mieczysław Bieniek, who acts as an advisor to defence minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, told broadcaster TVN on Thursday. Bieniek then revealed that, “based on information we received from both our allies and our own intelligence services, we managed to thwart an incident with potentially tragic consequences, because the planned false-flag operation could have ended tragically”. “For example, if a group of people crossed the border and later dressed in uniforms, whether Ukrainian or Polish, but were Russian citizens disguised as others, and carried out an attack on their target, the side whose uniforms were worn would naturally be blamed,” continued the general. “Fortunately, nothing of the sort happened,” he added. “Certainly this preventative action [by Poland] forced the other side to desist from these acts.” Bieniek’s comments followed a report published on Wednesday by the Rzeczpospolita daily, which said it had learned of a planned Russian sabotage operation on the border between Poland and the Kaliningrad exclave. The newspaper, citing unnamed high-ranking figures from the uniformed services, said that the planned incident could have involved Russia mounting an attack on one of its own facilities but blaming it on Ukraine. Such actions are known as false-flag operations. “It was supposed to be reminiscent of the Gleiwitz incident,” said one unnamed source, referring to a false-flag attack in 1939 staged by Nazi Germany, in which German operatives dressed in Polish uniforms. However, Kosiniak-Kamysz did not comment on or provide any specific details of what kind of incident Poland may have prevented on the Kaliningrad border. Later on Wednesday, Tusk himself reiterated to journalists that “we received signals that some unacceptable events could occur near the Polish-Russian border” and that “it seems that the mobilisation of the border guard and police in this place blocked any plans or ideas to carry out any provocation”. Two Russian missiles and what is likely to have been a jet-powered drone struck Poland last night during large-scale attacks on Ukraine, the defence minister has confirmed https://t.co/QM2t2hOwlg — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 20, 2026 Poland’s government has for months been warning that Russia is planning escalatory provocations against eastern NATO states, which could involve border and airspace violations. In June, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski even announced that he was “expecting an attack on Russian territory under a false flag, to which Putin will ‘respond'”. Sikorski pointed to the Gleiwitz incident as an example of such an operation. On Friday morning, two Russian missiles and what is believed to be a drone entered Polish airspace and hit the ground in three locations. Tusk condemned the incident as a further “Russian escalation” and said that it was likely to have been “an intentional provocation”. World.title: Two Ukrainians charged with vandalising Polish monuments on behalf of Russia
World.content: Why are you now seeing adverts on our website for the first time? Click here to learn more. Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. Two Ukrainians have been charged in Poland with working on behalf of Russia to paint slogans praising the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), a nationalist formation responsible for massacring Poles during World War Two, on three monuments in the Polish city of Poznań. Polish prosecutors say that the operation was intended to fuel hostility between Poles and Ukrainians. The incidents in Poznań were part of a seemingly coordinated wave of similar graffiti on monuments in three other Polish cities. Ukraińcy malowali na pomnikach hasła „Sława UPA”. Działali na zlecenie wywiaduhttps://t.co/knLgZzo8ct — Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 19, 2026 In early November, the words “Slava UPA” (“Glory to the UPA”) were painted in red on three monuments in Poznań commemorating World War Two soldiers. While the UPA is remembered by many in Ukraine for fighting for independence from Moscow-imposed Soviet rule, in Poland it is primarily associated with leading the Volhynia massacres, in which around 100,000 Polish civilians, mostly women and children, were slaughtered as part of an ethnic cleansing operation. The history of those massacres, and the continued veneration of the UPA by some in Ukraine, has regularly stirred tension between Poland and Ukraine, who are otherwise close allies. On Thursday, the National Prosecutor’s Office confirmed to the Polish Press Agency (PAP) that two Ukrainians, who can be named only as Nikita S. and Dmytro Y. under Polish privacy law, had been detained and charged in relation to the vandalism. According to prosecutors, Nikita S., “acting on behalf of Russian intelligence and in order to obtain financial benefit of $500”, persuaded Dmytro Y. to “commit an act of sabotage by painting the slogans” with the aim of “publicly inciting hatred based on national differences between the Polish and Ukrainian peoples”. The suspects were identified by police and the Internal Security Agency (ABW), who had analysed surveillance footage of the perpetrator, reports the Gazeta Wyborcza daily. Both were detained in Poznań, according to PAP. In the wake of the Poznań vandalism, Poland-based Belarusian news outlet MOST reported that, a few days before the graffiti appeared, an advert offering $500 for someone to paint pro-UPA slogans on monuments in the city had appeared on messaging service Telegram. When an undercover journalist from the outlet contacted the person offering the job, they were told that similar work was available in other Polish cities. Around the same time, almost identical graffiti praising the UPA appeared on further monuments in the cities of Gdańsk, Gdynia and Warsaw, including one dedicated to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising. Around a dozen monuments in Poland, including one dedicated to the Warsaw Ghetto Uprising, have been defaced with graffiti glorifying the WWII Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA). Ukraine’s embassy in Warsaw has condemned the vandalism and blamed it on Russia https://t.co/iaZb2CyiPx — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 15, 2026 Last week, local police in Gdańsk confirmed that they had detained a 17-year-old Ukrainian suspected of carrying out the graffiti there and in Gdynia. He has been charged with promoting fascist ideology, incitement to violence and hatred based on nationality, and desecration of monuments. The Ukrainian embassy in Poland has condemned the acts of vandalism, calling them a “disgraceful provocation” and “a manifestation of the hybrid war that Russia is attempting to wage by any means in European states”. Poland has been a primary target for Russia’s so-called hybrid actions in Europe, which have included acts of sabotage, espionage, disinformation and efforts to stir hostility towards Ukrainians. Such operations are rarely carried out by Russian operatives themselves. Instead, Russia often recruits people already on the ground, often members of Poland’s large Ukrainian and Belarusian migrant communities, as well as Poles themselves in some cases. In July this year, a Ukrainian teenager was indicted by Polish prosecutors on charges of painting dozens of pro-UPA slogans in public places, including on a monument to victims of the Volhynia massacres. Two Russian missiles and what is likely to have been a jet-powered drone struck Poland today amid large-scale attacks on Ukraine, the defence minister has confirmed. On Friday morning, an image published by Polish media outlet Wirtualna Polska showed a crater in the ground with a fire burning in the middle of it. The website reported that it had been caused by an object landing in a field in the village of Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland, around 60 kilometres from the Ukrainian border. 🔴Tu spadł niezidentyfikowany obiekt. Mamy zdjęcie z tego miejsca… — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) November 20, 2026 At a press conference later on Friday morning, Kosiniak-Kamysz said that the object in Nowy Lipowiec was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile (the same type as one that entered Polish airspace and exploded in eastern Poland in July this year). The defence minister also revealed that another missile had fallen in the town of Rudnik nad Sanem and what is likely to be a jet-powered drone had struck in the village of Mołodycz. Both of those locations are also in southeastern Poland, not far from the Ukrainian border. He added that there were no reports of injuries or any damage to critical infrastructure as a result of the incidents in Poland, which he noted had taken place during “one of the largest Russian attacks on Ukraine since the beginning of the full-scale war”. Kosiniak-Kamysz also suggested that the fact that these incidents had taken place now was “no coincidence”, given that military exercises of the Coalition of the Willing – a group of countries supporting Ukraine – are taking place in Poland not far from where the missiles and drone struck. Addressing the media on Friday afternoon, Prime Minister Donald Tusk declared that Friday represented “another instalment in the Russian escalation”. He said that there was no doubt that the objects which had hit Poland were Russian. “I’m cautious in my wording, but it does seem that we’re dealing with an intentional provocation,” added the prime minister. NATO’s secretary general, Mark Rutte, announced that he had spoken with Tusk about “the grave violations of Polish airspace” and declared that the alliance “stands in solidarity with Poland and will continue to strengthen our ability to deter and defend”. Such communiques have become common in recent months, as Poland has had to scramble its forces in response to Russia’s increasing strikes on targets in western Ukraine, including a passenger train travelling between Kyiv and Warsaw that was hit by a jet-powered drone in September this year. In recent months, the Polish government has warned of intelligence suggesting the likelihood of “provocations” by Russia, including airspace and border violations. In September this year, a Russian helicopter briefly crossed the border from the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad. Back in November 2022, during the early stages of Russia’s war in Ukraine, two people died in Poland after a missile crossed the Ukrainian border and struck the ground. Poland’s consumer protection authority, UOKiK, has fined Allegro, one of Europe’s largest e-commerce platforms, 55 million zloty (€12.3 million) for misleading consumers over a campaign that promised to plant trees in exchange for collecting parcels through its delivery service. The case is one of a series of investigations into so-called “greenwashing” launched by the authority against companies operating in Poland. UOKiK found that two of the Polish e-commerce group’s practices relating to the tree-planting initiative had infringed consumers’ interests. The first involved promotional claims suggesting that collecting 10 parcels through Allegro’s delivery service would result in a tree being planted. In practice, however, Allegro calculated the number of trees to be planted using forecasts prepared the previous year, rather than linking plantings to individual consumers’ parcel collections. This meant that decisions on the number of trees had already been made before customers collected their parcels. 🌳 Greenwashing ma swoją cenę! Blisko 55 mln zł kary dla Allegro – ekologiczne obietnice miały zachęcać do odbioru paczek, ale rzeczywistość nie była tak zielona. Milionów deklarowanych drzew nigdy nie posadzono. ❌ Ekościema nie może się opłacać 🔎https://t.co/yPQznKz0H1 pic.twitter.com/UDcWXWq3LI — UOKiK (@UOKiKgovPL) November 18, 2026 The second breach concerned the conditions attached to the campaign, which Allegro failed to communicate clearly to consumers. According to UOKiK, Allegro’s promotional messages could have led customers to believe that collecting 10 parcels through their delivery was sufficient to trigger tree planting. In fact, customers had to do it within a single calendar year and, from January 2024, submit a dedication for the tree within a specified period. Without a dedication, collecting the required number of parcels did not result in a tree being planted or assigned to the customer. UOKiK also found that the option to submit a dedication was unavailable for extended periods. Between March and November 2024, the feature was disabled for a total of 264 days, the watchdog said. The prolonged interruptions could have led customers to forget about the requirement or abandon their attempts to submit a dedication, meaning they would not receive the promised tree. UOKiK imposed a fine of 29.9 million zloty for the first practice and 24.9 million zloty for the second. Its decision can still be appealed in court by Allegro, which has not yet commented on the decision. “Green claims must be truthful, specific and verifiable; otherwise, they may mislead consumers and constitute an example of greenwashing,” said UOKiK president Tomasz Chróstny. “If a consumer hears, ‘collect 10 parcels, and we will plant a tree,’ they have the right to interpret that literally,” Chróstny said, adding that “several million [trees] – more than half of the total number claimed by Allegro – were never planted at all”. When announcing its decision, UOKiK noted that, according to a 2025 consumer survey conducted by the European Union, 43% of Poles said that the environmental impact of a product or service influenced their choices. The Allegro case forms part of a broader crackdown on suspected greenwashing by companies operating in Poland. Alongside Allegro, UOKiK has brought charges against delivery companies DHL, DPD and InPost, mobility firm Bolt, retailers Tchibo and Zara, and cosmetics firm L’Oréal Polska. World.title: Massive Attack to Headline Colours of Ostrava in 2027
World.content:
British trip-hop pioneers Massive Attack will perform at Colours of Ostrava on July 22, 2027, organisers have confirmed.

The band will take the main stage at the four-day festival, which runs from July 21 to 24 at the former Dolní Vítkovice industrial complex in Ostrava.

The announcement marks Massive Attack’s return to the Czech Republic after a nine-year absence.

The Bristol-born group, formed in 1988, is regarded as one of the most influential acts in the development of trip-hop.

The band is best known for songs including Teardrop, Angel and Unfinished Sympathy. Its music combines electronic sounds with elements of hip-hop, soul and dub, creating a distinctive style that helped shape British music in the 1990s.

Massive Attack’s live performances also feature large-scale visual projections, often incorporating political and social commentary.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Colours of Ostrava official 💛 (@colours_cz)

They join an already announced line-up for Colours of Ostrava 2027 that includes Robbie Williams, Ellie Goulding, Martin Garrix, 5 Seconds of Summer and David Kushner.

World.title: Leo Express Opens Prague–Munich Train Tickets From 49 CZK
World.content:
Leo Express has started selling tickets for its new Prague–Munich express service, which will replace České dráhy on the route from December 13.

The cheapest domestic fares currently available start at just 49 CZK for journeys between Prague and Plzeň.

The new service, known as Ex36, will be operated by Leo Express for five years after the company won a public tender. It will take over the route currently served by České dráhy’s Bavarian Express trains.



International tickets are not yet available. Although German stations already appear in the booking system, passengers can currently only book journeys within the Czech Republic. Leo Express says bookings for the full Prague–Munich route will open in the coming days.

The lowest advertised fare between Prague and Plzeň is 49 CZK. The same starting price applies to journeys as far as Domažlice. Business class tickets start at 199 CZK.

Prices will vary depending on demand and availability, so not all seats will be offered at the lowest fares. A second-class ticket between Prague and Plzeň will cost up to 236 CZK, equivalent to the standard OneTicket fare.

For comparison, České dráhy currently charges between 155 CZK and 235 CZK for the same journey, depending on the time of travel. Passengers can also use the cheaper Berounka express service by combining tickets from the Prague Integrated Transport (PID) and Plzeň Region Integrated Transport (IDPK) systems.

According to the booking system, most trains will have six carriages, including two business-class carriages. The operator will use former Deutsche Bahn carriages purchased by Spanish railway company Renfe and leased to Leo Express.

The trains will include both open-plan seating and traditional compartments. Eight services will run in each direction every day, matching the current timetable of České dráhy’s Bavarian Express.

World.title: Prague’s Abandoned Vyšehrad Station Begins Its Transformation Into Apartments
World.content:
Work has begun on the redevelopment of Prague’s historic Vyšehrad railway station, set to become part of a residential complex with 138 micro-apartments, shops and two new buildings.

Developer Karlin Port Real Estate, led by Milorad Mišković and his business partner Miki Goldshtein, began preparatory work at the end of October.

The company plans to start the main renovation and construction works in March 2027.



The developer acquired the station and surrounding land in early 2024 from Cyprus-based company Miquelira Limited, which has been linked to businessman František Savov. The deal followed months of negotiations and extensive checks, as the listed historic building was in a serious state of disrepair.

The plans include the restoration of the original station building and construction of two additional buildings. The development will offer 138 micro-apartments, around 50 underground parking spaces and up to 13 retail units on the ground floor.

The apartments will be sold rather than operated as rental accommodation. According to Mišković, they could appeal to students, young professionals, investors and families looking for temporary accommodation for children studying in Prague.

The developer also wants to improve the wider neighbourhood, including the streets connecting the station with Albertov and the Vltava riverfront.

More projects planned across Prague

Karlin Port Real Estate is also preparing other residential developments in the capital. In Hostivař, the company plans to start construction of the Výhledy Košík project in 2027. It will include 228 apartments and approximately 1,500 square metres of retail space.

The company is also exploring opportunities involving former railway properties and preparing to enter Prague 9, where it plans to focus on the redevelopment of former industrial sites.

Mišković said brownfield regeneration remains his main interest, although the company is now considering projects across Prague rather than concentrating exclusively on the city centre.

World.title: 9 Czech Castles and Chateaux to Visit During Advent 2026
World.content:
Christmas markets are not the only way to enjoy the festive season in Czechia.

Across the country, castles and chateaux are preparing special Advent programmes, with decorated interiors, traditional markets, candlelit tours and activities for families.

Here are nine places worth visiting in the weeks leading up to Christmas and during the holiday season.



1. Loučeň Chateau

Located in Central Bohemia, Loučeň Chateau is hosting a Christmas exhibition titled The Story of the Christmas Tree until January 17, 2027.

Visitors can also explore the illuminated Labyrinths of Light in the castle park. One of the main highlights will take place on November 28, when the country’s largest Advent wreath will be blessed in the courtyard.

Special Advent tours and children’s programmes will run throughout December.

2. Karlštejn Castle

One of Czechia’s most famous castles will also welcome visitors with Christmas decorations.

From November 27, 2026, to January 3, 2027, selected tours of the Imperial Palace will include festive decorations and an introduction to Christmas traditions associated with the court of Charles IV.

The castle will be closed from December 21 to 25.

3. Sychrov Chateau

Sychrov Chateau in the Liberec Region will host its traditional Advent Market on November 28 and 29.

The market will feature Christmas decorations, seasonal products and food stalls in the castle courtyard.

Visitors planning a trip during the Christmas holidays can also explore the decorated interiors through self-guided tours from December 27 to January 3, 2027.

4. Křivoklát Castle

Křivoklát Castle, one of the most important medieval castles in Central Bohemia, will host its traditional Royal Advent event on December 5–6 and 12–13.

The programme includes an Old Bohemian Christmas Market, with artisan stalls selling traditional products, dried fruit, Christmas biscuits, sausages and mulled wine.

Visitors will also be able to explore the castle interiors at their own pace.

5. Hrádek u Nechanic

Built in the Windsor Gothic style, Hrádek u Nechanic will open its doors for Advent visits on selected weekends between November 28 and December 13.

The decorated interiors will feature Christmas trees, traditional ornaments, nutcrackers and nativity scenes. Guided tours will also explain how Christmas was celebrated in the past.

Special candlelit evening tours are scheduled for November 28, December 4 and December 11, while Advent concerts will take place on December 5 and 12.

The castle kitchen will also serve traditional English punch.

6. Dětenice Castle

Dětenice Castle in the Jičín area will offer a festive programme throughout December.

On December 5, children can take part in a St. Nicholas celebration in the medieval tavern. Visitors can also see Krampus performances on December 4, 5 and 12.

The castle’s medieval entertainment programme runs daily from 7 p.m. to 10 p.m.

More Advent Destinations Across Czechia

Other places organising seasonal events include Třeboň Chateau, which will host Advent markets on December 5 and 6, and Jindřichův Hradec Castle, where a weekend programme of theatre, music, dance and traditional crafts is planned for the same dates.

In South Moravia, Valtice Chateau is displaying 30 Christmas trees decorated with more than 2,500 handmade glass ornaments. The exhibition runs until December 23.

Villa Stiassni in Brno is also offering special Christmas tours, featuring period decorations and an exhibition of historical toys.

World.title: Looking for a Team Challenge in Prague? This Venue Has 25 Different Tests
World.content:
Looking for something to do in Prague beyond the usual sightseeing?

TEPfactor offers an indoor adventure combining physical challenges, puzzles and teamwork, just a short walk from Wenceslas Square.

Located at Vodičkova street, the 1,500-square-metre venue takes inspiration from the TV show Fort Boyard.



Its main attraction features 25 challenges testing participants’ strength, logic, dexterity, patience and ability to work together.

Visitors compete in teams of two to six people, tackling a series of tasks that require both physical effort and problem-solving skills. The main game takes approximately three hours, making it an option for groups of friends, families and visitors looking for an alternative to traditional tourist activities.

For those seeking something more intense, TEPfactor also operates Fear House, a horror-themed attraction with several levels of difficulty. Options range from group experiences to more demanding individual challenges.

The most intense version, Hardcore + Kidnapping, includes a staged kidnapping scenario and must be arranged in advance.

The venue also caters to organised groups. Schools can book activities designed to encourage communication and cooperation, while companies can use the challenges for team-building events. Birthday celebrations, stag and hen parties and private gatherings are also among the available options.

Beyond the adventure games, TEPfactor offers event space for larger gatherings. Facilities include a theatre-style room with a stage, sound equipment and the option to arrange a DJ and catering.

Additional entertainment can include pub quizzes, stand-up comedy, mobile casino activities and theatre performances.

Reservations can also be made through its online booking system.

World.title: Prague Pride to Host Studio 54-Inspired New Year’s Eve Party
World.content:
Prague Pride will celebrate the arrival of 2027 with a Studio 54-inspired New Year’s Eve party at Slovanský dům, bringing disco music, drag performances and LGBTQ+ matchmaking.

The event, titled Disco Royale, will take place on December 31, 2026, from 8 p.m. until 4 a.m. at Empire Hall in Slovanský dům, Prague 1.



Organisers are promising a night inspired by the legendary New York nightclub Studio 54 and the disco era of the late 1970s.

Guests are encouraged to dress accordingly, with sequins, satin, colourful suits, platform shoes and extravagant accessories all part of the suggested dress code.

The programme will combine live entertainment with music and activities throughout the evening. A queer and drag cabaret will feature performances by Radek Horáček, Hugo Seneši, Lukas Illusion, Rudy Daddy, Melancholia Blackbile and Barbora Elz.

Music will be provided by DJ Jan Witek, who will play a mix of disco classics by Donna Summer, ABBA, the Bee Gees and Chic, alongside modern disco-house and contemporary party tracks. DJ Koko will also join the line-up.

Beyond the dance floor, visitors can take part in LGBTQ+ matchmaking activities, including a Traffic Light Dating System and an interactive game designed to help guests meet new people. A Studio 54-themed photo booth and a New Year’s raffle are also planned.

A dedicated chill-out area will offer a quieter space away from the music, while the bar will serve a signature New Year’s Eve cocktail.

Tickets are available in two categories. Basic admission costs 890 CZK and includes a welcome drink, a complimentary snack and access to open seating in the main hall and lounge area.

VIP tickets cost 1,390 CZK and include guaranteed table seating, access to a second-floor balcony and the same welcome refreshments.

Tickets are available through December 30, or until the event sells out. Proceeds from ticket sales support Prague Pride’s work with LGBTQ+ people in Czechia.

World.title: Black Friday in Czechia: When to Shop and How to Spot Fake Discounts
World.content:
Black Friday will officially fall on November 27 this year, but shoppers in the Czech Republic will not have to wait until the final Friday of November to find deals.

Major retailers have already turned the traditional one-day sale into a weeks-long campaign, with promotions appearing in several rounds throughout the month.

While stricter consumer protection rules have made misleading discounts harder to advertise, shoppers still need to be careful. Some retailers continue to use pricing strategies that make reductions look more attractive than they really are.



When does Black Friday 2026 start in Czechia?

Black Friday 2026 takes place on Friday, November 27. Originally an American shopping tradition held the day after Thanksgiving, the event has gradually become one of the biggest retail campaigns in Europe.

In the Czech Republic, however, the sales period now extends well beyond the official date. Many retailers begin advertising discounts in early November, gradually introducing new offers under campaigns commonly marketed as Black Week or Black Month.

The extended shopping period also serves a practical purpose. Spreading orders across several weeks helps online retailers manage warehouse operations, deliveries and payment systems, avoiding the logistical pressure that would come with concentrating all purchases into a single day.

The country’s biggest retailers are following slightly different approaches.

Alza.cz typically divides its Black Friday campaign into several stages, with different product categories and limited quantities of discounted items introduced throughout November. The final round is expected to coincide with the week of November 23–29.

Datart also rotates its promotional selection during the month. Its offers cover everything from large household appliances to smaller electronic devices, with discounts available both online and in its physical stores.

Allegro, which has incorporated the former Mall.cz into its marketplace, uses a different approach. Its platform features daily promotions from a large number of independent sellers, with special offers continuing throughout November and reaching their peak on November 27.

Notino focuses its Black Friday campaign on selected brands and promotional discount codes. Its broader offers are concentrated around the main Black Friday shopping period.

Black Friday or Cyber Monday when should you buy?

The official Black Friday date is not necessarily the best opportunity to make every purchase.

Cyber Monday, which falls on November 30 in 2026, follows the Black Friday weekend. Originally introduced as an online equivalent of traditional in-store sales, it has become another important date for retailers, particularly those selling electronics and IT equipment.

For some products, waiting until Monday could pay off. Retailers may review their weekend sales figures and introduce additional reductions on items that have not performed as expected. Televisions, laptops, monitors and computer components are among the categories worth monitoring.

How to recognise artificial discounts

Although Czech consumer protection legislation has introduced stricter rules on how retailers advertise price reductions, promotional labels do not automatically mean a product is being sold at its best price.

Under the European Omnibus Directive and the related amendment to the Czech Consumer Protection Act, retailers must generally display the lowest price charged during the 30 days preceding a price reduction.

This requirement is intended to prevent sellers from temporarily increasing prices before a sale and then advertising a seemingly substantial discount against the inflated amount.

Nevertheless, consumers should not rely exclusively on the percentage displayed next to a product.

Independent price-comparison services and historical price-tracking tools can help establish whether an offer represents a genuine saving. Checking how much an item cost in the weeks before Black Friday is often more useful than comparing its current price with the original recommended retail price.

World.title: Prague Has 2,600 Homeless People, but Shelters Cannot Keep Up
World.content:
Around 2,600 people are living on the streets of Prague, according to estimates by the non-profit organization Naděje.

While the city and its municipal districts provide various forms of assistance, social workers say existing shelters and day centres are struggling to meet demand.



Prague’s support system includes overnight shelters, emergency accommodation, low-threshold day centres, professional counselling and temporary housing programmes. The city also operates hostels, provides grants to municipal districts for homelessness-related projects and works with non-profit organizations.

One of the main forms of assistance is provided by social curators, municipal employees who work directly with people living on the streets. Prague 1 and Prague 2 both employ their own teams.

Prague 2 established a food bank distribution point in the courtyard of the New Town Hall (Novoměstská radnice). People in need can collect food and basic hygiene supplies there.

Social services struggle to meet demand

Despite these initiatives, the capacity of Prague’s existing facilities remains a major concern.

Aleš Strnad, head of services at Naděje’s Prague branch, said the number of places available in day centres and overnight shelters was insufficient.

According to Strnad, opposition from local residents is one of the main obstacles to opening new facilities. He pointed out the contradiction between resistance to new centres and public complaints about the growing number of people living in poor and unhygienic conditions on the streets.

The city also introduces additional measures during the winter months. From December until the end of March, its humanitarian programme allows people experiencing homelessness to spend the night in heated facilities free of charge.

World.title: Foreign minister: Hungary to host next Friends of the Western Balkans meeting
World.content:
Hungary will host the next meeting of the Friends of the Western Balkans group, Foreign Minister Anita Orbán announced on Monday following talks in Athens. The initiative focuses on supporting the region’s European integration, with Budapest arguing that the Western Balkans’ stability has a direct impact on Hungary.

Orbán attended the group’s meeting in the Greek capital, where participants discussed the EU accession prospects of Western Balkan countries. In a Facebook post, the foreign minister said Hungary supports bringing countries closer to EU membership as soon as they meet the necessary conditions.

She stressed that accession requires economic and institutional readiness, the rule of law, free elections and strong democratic institutions. However, she added that the EU itself must also prepare for enlargement and ensure that new member states do not end up in a second-tier position.

“Hungary consistently supports the European integration of the Western Balkans,” Orbán wrote.

Hungary joined the initiative in July

The minister described Monday’s meeting as an important milestone, noting that Hungary joined the Friends of the Western Balkans group in Rome in July and has been actively supporting the region’s EU integration since then.

The group brings together countries that support the Western Balkans’ European perspective. Hungary’s decision to host its next meeting signals its intention to remain involved in the enlargement process.

Talks with Greece, Kosovo and North Macedonia

During her visit to Athens, Orbán also held several bilateral meetings with regional counterparts, according to a statement from the Hungarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs.

In talks with her Greek counterpart, she discussed EU accession for the Western Balkans, the preservation of agricultural and cohesion funding, the diversification of energy sources and the protection of the EU’s external borders.

Her meeting with Kosovo’s foreign minister focused on regional security and the NATO-led KFOR peacekeeping mission. Hungary is the mission’s third-largest contributor, according to the ministry.

With North Macedonia’s foreign minister, Orbán discussed opportunities for Hungarian companies and transport links. One of the topics was a potential corridor connecting the Budapest–Belgrade railway line with the Aegean Sea.

Security and EUFOR also on the agenda

Orbán’s talks with Bosnia and Herzegovina’s foreign minister covered the situation following the country’s elections and the EUFOR mission, the EU’s military operation in the country.

Hungary is one of EUFOR’s largest contributors, and a Hungarian officer currently serves as deputy commander, the ministry said.

World.title: How much will one euro cost in Hungary in 2027? Here’s what analysts predict
World.content:
The Hungarian forint is expected to remain relatively close to its current level against the euro next year, according to a survey of financial analysts. Their forecasts suggest an average exchange rate of HUF 366.5 per euro in 2027, although one institution warns that the currency could weaken significantly under less favourable conditions.

The figures were compiled by Világgazdaság, which asked experts from five financial institutions for their outlook on the forint. Most expect relatively limited movement, with their forecasts clustering around the current exchange rate.

What exchange rate do analysts expect in 2027?

The five institutions surveyed predict the following average euro-forint exchange rates for 2027:

Equilor: HUF 365

HUF 365 Erste: HUF 367.5

HUF 367.5 CIB Bank: HUF 365

HUF 365 ING Bank: HUF 362.5

HUF 362.5 Akcenta: HUF 372.5

This produces a consensus average of HUF 366.5 per euro. The figures suggest that most analysts do not expect a dramatic change in the forint’s value over the coming year.

If you missed it: Hungarian forint weakens further as euro approaches pre-election levels and dollar keeps marching on

Geopolitical tensions and energy prices remain key factors

According to Orsolya Nyeste, chief analyst at Erste, the forint’s performance will continue to depend heavily on geopolitical tensions, energy prices and movements in the euro-dollar exchange rate. Hungary’s strategy for adopting the euro could also influence the currency.

Following recent volatility, Erste expects the forint to strengthen below the HUF 360 level again in the medium term, provided global energy prices ease. The bank forecasts an exchange rate of HUF 360 in the first half of 2027 and HUF 355 in the second half.

Equilor, meanwhile, expects the euro to cost HUF 370 at the end of this year and HUF 365 at the end of 2027. Its chief analyst, Péter Aradványi, highlighted the interest rate policies of the Hungarian National Bank (MNB) and major central banks, geopolitical tensions and their impact on oil and gas prices as important factors.

Hungary’s economic growth, credit rating outlook, budget implementation and progress towards meeting the euro adoption criteria could also affect the exchange rate, he told Világgazdaság.

ING sees the forint as an attractive regional investment

ING’s latest currency outlook for 2027 is relatively positive about the Hungarian currency. The Dutch bank considers the forint the most attractive investment prospect among the three main Central European currencies it follows, ahead of the Polish zloty and Czech koruna.

ING expects the MNB to keep its base rate unchanged at 5.5 per cent over the next nine to 12 months. Although inflation trends could theoretically create room for interest rate cuts, geopolitical risks, energy prices and high global yields are expected to encourage caution.

The bank forecasts that the euro-forint exchange rate will fluctuate within a range of HUF 350–370 over the coming quarters. It expects HUF 360 by the end of 2026, HUF 365 in the first half of 2027 and HUF 360 in the second half.

According to ING, a stronger forint could bring the exchange rate down towards HUF 350, but this might prompt markets to anticipate earlier interest rate cuts, limiting further appreciation. On the other hand, if the forint weakened sharply towards HUF 370, the central bank could intervene verbally or through market measures. An interest rate increase would be a last resort, the analysts suggest.

CIB expects gradual economic recovery to continue

CIB Bank’s analysts also anticipate a relatively stable exchange rate, despite uncertainty in the global environment. They expect Hungary’s gradual economic recovery to continue in 2027, with GDP growth reaching 2.3 per cent, compared with a forecast of 1.7 per cent this year.

Annual inflation could remain around 3 per cent, while the euro is expected to trade at approximately HUF 365 by the end of 2027.

The bank’s outlook reflects the view that domestic economic developments will continue to be shaped by external risks, even as growth gradually picks up.

Akcenta warns that the euro could reach HUF 400

The Czech financial company Akcenta is the notable outlier among the five institutions. It expects the euro to trade mostly between HUF 365 and HUF 380 in 2027, but warns that the exchange rate could exceed HUF 400 under unfavourable conditions.

According to its analysts, the budget deficit, the central bank’s interest rate policy and energy prices will be among the main factors determining the forint’s performance.

Overall, the forecasts point to a relatively narrow range for the Hungarian currency next year. However, the differences between the institutions show that the outlook remains sensitive to both international developments and domestic economic policy.

As Világgazdaság notes, traders will be paying particular attention to monthly budget figures and whether the disinflation process continues steadily.

World.title: Hungary’s guest worker U-turn: What happens next for foreign employees?
World.content:
Nearly six months after Hungary restricted guest worker recruitment, the future of foreign employment remains uncertain. While the government is considering a new regulatory framework, employers are warning about labour shortages, and trade unions are demanding stronger protections for Hungarian workers. So has the policy achieved what it promised, and what could happen next?

In June 2026, Péter Magyar’s Tisza government suspended new applications for a specific guest worker residence permit category, marking a major departure from the recruitment policies of the previous Orbán administration. The decision particularly affected nationals of the Philippines, Georgia and Armenia, although it did not amount to a complete ban on foreign employment.

Existing permit holders were not automatically required to leave Hungary, and other employment-related residence permit categories remained available. However, alternative procedures can involve considerably longer waiting times, creating new difficulties for both employers and prospective employees.

Guest workers are still an important part of Hungary’s labour market

Interestingly, the restrictions came at a time when the number of foreign employees in Hungary was continuing to rise. Approximately 112,300 guest workers were employed in the country in June, with the figure increasing to around 112,900 in July.

These numbers include workers employed under different residence categories, so they do not demonstrate whether the suspended permit system succeeded or failed. Nevertheless, they highlight the complicated relationship between immigration policy and the country’s labour needs.

Employers and unions disagree on the way forward

The government has since started discussions about restructuring Hungary’s employment-related immigration system, which currently includes around 24 different legal categories and procedures.

Employers want simpler administration and more predictable recruitment, arguing that certain industries cannot fill vacancies with domestic applicants alone. Trade unions, meanwhile, are pushing for stricter controls, better working conditions and stronger priority for Hungarian jobseekers.

The disagreement raises a difficult question: can Hungary reduce its dependence on foreign labour without making it harder for businesses to operate and attract investment?

What does this mean for guest workers?

For thousands of international employees, the debate is about more than government policy. Their ability to renew permits, change employers and continue working in Hungary depends on the rules applicable to their particular residence status.

The government has yet to complete its proposed overhaul, leaving important questions unanswered.

What changes are employers demanding, what do Hungarian trade unions want, and could the new rules put existing foreign workers at risk?
