World.title: Filipino Nationals Get Busy Learning Croatian Language
World.content:
November the 22nd, 2026 – Filipino nationals are getting busy learning the Croatian language as new rules loom next year. They are by far the most numerous foreign workers actively learning the language at the moment.

Just over six months separate Croatian employers and foreign workers from the 4th of June 2027, when the legal obligation to prove basic knowledge of the Croatian language and Latin script (level A1.1) comes into full force as a condition for extending residence and work permits. As Marija Brnic reports for Poslovni, as the deadline approaches, employers are increasingly focused on organising classes, which is most clearly confirmed by figures from the Croatian Employment Service (HZZ).

filipino workers are the most numerous language learners

Since the start of shorter informal Croatian language learning programmes for foreigners in April 2024, a total of 2,312 vouchers have been awarded. This year their number has grown many times over compared with previous years. While only 102 vouchers were awarded in 2024 and 259 in 2025, as many as 1,951 vouchers have been approved during 2026. According to the HZZ, interest has been more or less constant throughout this year, with around 200 vouchers awarded each month. The structure of the awarded vouchers shows in which sectors employers are most counting on the long-term retention of foreign labour. Since seasonal workers are legally exempt from the language exam requirement, the greatest interest unsurprisingly comes from activities with year-round operations. The processing industry leads with a share of 34.5 percent, followed by construction with 22.9 percent, hospitality with 21.8 percent and the food industry with 15.5 percent.

Viewed by country of origin of the participants, the vouchers are most often used by workers from the Philippines, who make up more than a third of all users (36.9 percent). They are followed by citizens of Nepal with a share of 29.5 percent and India with 15.7 percent, which together account for more than 82 percent of all approved vouchers for learning Croatian. The regional distribution of users brings another interesting piece of data that explains the dominance of the processing industry. The county with the largest number of voucher users is not the most populous and economically strongest City of Zagreb, but Međimurje County with 437 participants.

In general, the largest share of users is concentrated in the northwest of the country – in addition to Međimurje, Varaždin, Zagreb and Krapina-Zagorje counties stand out, i.e. the regions with the most developed manufacturing and processing base and a constant need for the long-term retention of workers. At the very bottom of the ranking is Vukovar-Srijem County, where only two users of vouchers for learning Croatian have been recorded so far.

the financial data speaks volumes

How much this year’s wave of applications has surpassed the previous two years is also visible from the financial data. Since the start of the voucher scheme for learning Croatian for foreigners, a total of €612,909 has been reserved, of which €342,792 has so far been paid out to educational institutions. The overwhelming majority of the funds were contracted precisely in 2026 – this year €527,784 has been reserved, while €260,527 has so far been paid out for completed classes. The difference between the reserved and paid amounts also shows that a significant part of this year’s participants are currently in the process of learning and that payment for the programmes is expected after the courses are completed.

Co-financing via vouchers, depending on the conditions and the size of the employer, can amount to between 30 and 70 percent of the education costs. The average value of a voucher awarded so far has been €283, with the cost varying depending on the activity and the specialisation of the vocabulary. The highest average amounts were recorded in the healthcare sector (€340) and construction (€321), while in the most used processing industry the average voucher amounted to €278. That employers are increasingly viewing the learning of Croatian not only as a pure administrative obligation but more and more as a strategic part of human resources management and worker retention is also confirmed by the Croatian Chamber of Economy (HGK). This trend is supported by the results of its EDUkarijera 2026 survey, conducted among 572 employers from various economic activities.

Among companies that already employ or plan to employ third-country nationals, as many as 81 percent highlight learning Croatian as an important measure for the easier integration of workers. At the same time, 62 percent list difficulties with their adaptation within the organisation itself as one of the main challenges of employing foreigners, which is why investment in language skills is becoming key both for productivity and for safety at work.

the language programmes are designed by sector

Anita Stipić, head of the Labour Market Department at the HGK, explains how the system works in practice, emphasising that the model is well organised, but that the right to a voucher is not automatic and depends on meeting the prescribed conditions. The submission of applications itself is fully digitalised through the Moj vaučer system, and the HZZ is obliged to assess a complete application within 10 working days.

As a particularly positive aspect, Stipić highlights the fact that Croatian language learning programmes are designed according to the specific needs of individual activities, including construction, tourism and hospitality, processing and food industry, healthcare and social care, transport, telecommunications and personal services. Such sectoral orientation is key because language needs are not the same for all occupations – a worker in hospitality needs different communication situations and professional terminology than a worker in production, construction or healthcare. Within the HGK, she notes, there is also a Community for Lifelong Learning, which brings together adult education institutions and actively works on connecting the education sector with the concrete needs of the economy.

World.title: Where Will the Snow Fall in Croatia Next Week? New Map Published
World.content:
November the 22nd, 2026 – Snow is set to fall in Croatia next week, but there are areas far more likely than others to turn into a winter wonderland.

In the middle of next week, a noticeable change in the weather is expected, bringing snow and lower temperatures. Index reports that according to the latest forecasts, on Thursday the 26th of November, snow should fall across a large part of the interior.

snow or rain?

The Croatian Meteorological and Hydrological Service (DHMZ) has published a forecast map showing the expected precipitation for Thursday. Areas marked in pink are those where more than one centimetre of snow is predicted, covering the interior and mountainous regions. On the coast and islands, marked in green, rain will fall.

colder temperatures

In addition to the type of precipitation, continental and coastal areas will also differ in temperatures. Although it will be colder everywhere than this week, the biggest drop is expected in the interior, where temperatures will fall below zero. The Meteorological Institute, in its forecasts up to the 28th of November, predicts that the lowest temperature in Zagreb, Osijek, Karlovac and Varaždin will be –4 °C. In Gospić –5 °C is expected, in Vukovar –3 °C, and in Rijeka –1 °C.

World.title: Ille Nakurt-Murumaa: Everyone wants a hand in entrepreneurs' pockets, including private health care
World.content:
Estonian entrepreneurs are facing growing pressure from both labor unions seeking minimum wage increases above economic growth and private health care providers pushing for expanded occupational health requirements that would increase employers' costs, argues Ille Nakurt-Murumaa.

The Ministry of Social Affairs is currently drafting occupational health policy guidelines through 2035 and candidly acknowledges the system's problems: uneven or inadequate quality, health checks that do not reflect actual workplace risks, and limited access to occupational health physicians outside major cities, where services are often available only at high cost.

The Estonian Association of Occupational Health Service Providers (ETTOL), which strongly supports mandatory occupational health services and their expansion, proposes the opposite approach: turning occupational health into an expanded primary health care service that would assess employees' general health and broader public health risks. Employers, or partly the Health Insurance Fund, would be expected to pay for these additional services.

The association claims that a working group reviewing occupational health policy reached a consensus on the idea and that the ministry has since moved away from it. In reality, no such consensus ever existed within the working group. It remains a business objective of ETTOL's members, one that neither I, as a field expert, nor the Estonian Association of Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises (EVEA), which represents small businesses, can support.

A business model, not health policy

Neither the current occupational health system nor the expansion advocated by ETTOL represents health policy. It is a business model. If the law requires every employer to purchase increasing amounts of services, a small number of providers are guaranteed a stable revenue stream. There are few occupational health physicians in Estonia, and nearly 80 percent of the market is controlled by a handful of major providers.

"EVEA's proposal is straightforward. Mandatory health checks should be tied to actual workplace risks."

Given the already excessive requirements, entrepreneurs would be forced to pay even more for services that should be covered through social taxes and family physicians, or through a well-organized primary care system partially funded by employers. Larger occupational health providers may welcome growing revenues guaranteed by legislation, but that should never be the purpose of regulation.

This has happened before. Since 2023, employers have been required not only to arrange regular health checks but also to purchase a "comprehensive occupational health analysis" every three years. For employers, this has meant another bill rather than healthier employees. As a consultant, I see these assessments every day and must admit that most are completely worthless for both employer and employee.

Employers have a responsibility to ensure safe working conditions, but they cannot be expected to manage or finance employees' overall health and well-being. Those responsibilities should primarily rest with individuals themselves and, when specialist help is needed, with family physicians and the Health Insurance Fund, which we already finance through social taxes. Estonia does not need two parallel systems, and it is time to acknowledge that we lack both the money and the doctors to support one.

Service in Tallinn, bills in Võru County

According to the Ministry of Social Affairs, Estonia had 68 occupational health physicians in 2025, 28 of whom were at least 65 years old. This year, only two residency positions were available in the specialty.

With resources this limited, occupational health physicians cannot begin duplicating the work of family physicians and nurses, nor is there any need for such duplication. In fact, providers are already operating in a way that conflicts with the law. Although the Occupational Health and Safety Act states that health examinations must be carried out by occupational health physicians, most employees never actually meet one. The necessary procedures are performed by general practitioners or nurses, while occupational health physicians simply sign off on the results.

We should finally admit that the current occupational health system does not work and never will in its present form. Occupational health physicians are specialists whose expertise should be reserved for determining whether a person's health issue is work-related.

The expanded service sought by providers would be significantly more expensive and would drive the remaining small occupational health providers out of the market. As a result, employees in places such as Sõrve, Sõmerpalu, Tõrva and Tahkuna could lose practical access to occupational health services altogether.

Large companies and government agencies in Tallinn might enjoy comprehensive services because they have both money and providers nearby. A small auto repair shop in Raudoja or a store in Laadla would, at best, receive minimal services through a mobile clinic or be forced to transport employees dozens or even hundreds of kilometers to larger centers while paying far more. Waiting times for even basic services could stretch to six months or longer.

Many local entrepreneurs provide jobs out of responsibility to their communities rather than in pursuit of large profits. Every new mandatory expense pushes them closer to the point where they may have to close their doors. And as noted, they receive obligations rather than meaningful value in return.

Current law already requires health checks for office workers. In Tallinn, such examinations cost at least €75 per employee. In rural areas, transportation costs and lost work time must be added when employees need to travel to a larger center.

Those who don't pay the bill make the decisions

Private health care is not the only group reaching into entrepreneurs' pockets. At the same time, negotiations are underway on the 2027 minimum wage, and the Estonian Trade Union Confederation, which represents only a small share of employees, is once again shaping economic realities for all businesses.

Most Estonians work in small and medium-sized enterprises, yet those businesses have no representative at the negotiating table. If the minimum wage rises faster than economic growth, the consequences will be severe: jobs will disappear in rural regions and regional inequality will deepen. In both debates, the pattern is the same: decisions are made over the heads of small business owners.

Family physicians first, occupational health physicians as specialists

EVEA's proposal is straightforward. Mandatory health checks should be tied to actual workplace risks. Employees exposed to noise, chemicals or night work should receive targeted monitoring. General health care should remain the responsibility of family physicians.

For example, computer screen use today is primarily a public health issue rather than a specific workplace hazard. Eyeglass compensation or massage treatments should not have to be routed through occupational health physicians and charged to employers.

Occupational health physicians are specialists much like neurologists or orthopedic surgeons. Family physicians should refer patients to them when expert advice is needed or when a diagnosis requires specialized evaluation. Rather than measuring blood pressure or prescribing adjustable desks and ergonomic computer mice, occupational health physicians should serve as specialists advising primary care doctors.

Before imposing any new requirement, the state should calculate the cost to employers and the Health Insurance Fund and weigh it against the actual health benefits.

Neither employers nor the Health Insurance Fund have bottomless pockets. The purpose of occupational health care is to protect people from work-related harm, not to guarantee revenue for service providers.

World.title: Government greenlights new Pelguranna tram corridor
World.content:
Infrastructure Minister Kuldar Leis has approved the revised Pelguranna tram line project, allowing Tallinn to move forward with construction. The new tram line is expected to be completed in 2029.

The project has an estimated cost of €27.9 million, of which up to €19.5 million will be covered by the European Regional Development Fund, the Ministry of Climate said.

"Although the previous route would have served more residents, an expert assessment of the project confirmed that building the tram line is justified in light of the area's long-term development. Põhja-Tallinn needs good public transportation connections that offer people an alternative to traveling by private car," Leis said.

The infrastructure minister added that it is now up to Tallinn to move the project quickly from the design phase to construction and complete it by the end of 2029.

The original Pelguranna tram line plan underwent an assessment in 2024. However, because Tallinn subsequently changed the route, the state had to reassess the entire project. The project received approval from the evaluation committee and was deemed to meet the funding requirements.

As the design process continues, Tallinn must pay particular attention to ensuring that stops are accessible and to preserving the Pollinator Highway's (Putukaväil) green spaces and recreational areas or mitigating the project's impact on them.

The new tram line, approximately 1.9 kilometers long, will be built as a branch of the existing Kopli tram line. The route will branch off near the Krulli stop, cross the Kopli freight yard and the Ristiku tänav viaduct and continue along Pollinator Highway across Sõle tänav to Kolde puiestee. It will end at a planned turning loop around the property at Puhangu tänav 45, with a terminus on Kolde puiestee.

Under the city's approved schedule, the tram line is expected to be completed in October 2029. To qualify for European Union funding, the project must be completed by the end of that year.

World.title: Opposition stalls 2027 budget and climate law debates
World.content:
The Riigikogu's opposition parties on Monday blocked approval of agendas in both the Finance Committee and the Environment Committee, delaying discussions on the 2027 state budget and the climate law.

The Finance Committee agenda received five votes from members of the Reform Party and Eesti 200, while five opposition lawmakers voted against, the Center Party said. Because the vote ended in a tie, the agenda was not approved and the committee's regular meetings scheduled for this week were canceled.

According to Finance Committee Vice Chair Andrei Korobeinik of the Center Party, the opposition cannot remain silent while the governing coalition attempts to push through a budget that fails to address Estonia's most pressing economic and social problems.

"The government wants to move a state budget to its third reading that will not help Estonia emerge from the economic crisis but will instead deepen insecurity among residents. The coalition has rejected proposals that would reduce everyday expenses for families, stimulate the economy and distribute the tax burden more fairly," Korobeinik said.

As a result, the 2027 state budget cannot yet be sent to a third reading and final vote. Next week is a recess week in the Riigikogu, leaving only two sitting weeks remaining this year afterward.

The opposition used the same tactic Monday in the Environment Committee, where the agenda also failed to win approval, preventing regular meetings from being held.

Center Party lawmaker Lauri Laats said the climate law would undermine the competitiveness of Estonian businesses, particularly in the industrial and energy sectors.

"The opposition and stakeholders have clearly signaled that there is no point in passing this law during the current Riigikogu term," said Environment Committee Vice Chair Andres Metsoja of Isamaa.

World.title: Social Affairs Minister Karmen Joller resigns
World.content:
Social Affairs Minister Karmen Joller of the Reform Party announced in parliament Monday that she is stepping down from her post after acknowledging a legal violation involving a company board position.

Just hours earlier, Joller had said on social media that she intended to remain in office and would not resign.

Addressing the Riigikogu, Joller said she had learned she was in breach of the law and had informed Prime Minister Kristen Michal of her wish to resign.

"This morning, I said I would not resign because I had not broken any law. Thanks to a letter sent to me by one person, I learned that I had in fact done so. Unintentionally and without my knowledge, but I did," Joller said.

She explained that she has owned a company established in 2008 that carried out translation work. Although the company has been inactive for the past decade, she remained a member of its management board and disclosed the position annually in her declaration of economic interests.

"However, the law does not allow members of the government to sit on the board of any company. There are no exceptions. A minister must not break the law, even if they have gained no benefit and no one has suffered harm. Therefore, I informed Prime Minister Kristen Michal today of my intention to resign," Joller said.

She stressed that no one had been harmed and that she had received no personal benefit.

"Failing to remove myself from the patient list in time and replacing myself on the board of an inactive company would both have been simple administrative actions. I admit that it simply did not occur to me. I believe no one doubts my good intentions. But the mistake is mine, and I take responsibility for it. This was the final straw that broke the camel's back," she said.

Joller also accused one Estonian media outlet of conducting a campaign against her.

She argued that systematic attacks from the outlet began shortly after an EMOR poll showed her to be the government's second most popular minister.

Earlier Monday, opposition parties said they were collecting signatures for a no-confidence motion. Center Party parliamentary group leader Lauri Laats said 51 lawmakers had indicated they would support Joller's removal.

The Riigikogu agenda, which listed Joller's political statement as its first item, was approved by a vote of 45–44.

Opposition parties announced last week that they planned to initiate a no-confidence vote against Joller, citing her failure to give up her family physician patient list on time. Questions were also raised about whether she may have used her ministerial position to pursue legislative changes that would have allowed her to retain it.

World.title: Estonia launches multinational exercise with UK and French forces
World.content:
Exercise Pikne 2026 begins in Estonia on November 23, bringing together the Estonian Defense Forces, the Estonian Defense League and allied troops from France and the United Kingdom for three weeks of training.

The exercise, led by the Estonian Division, runs through December 11, with most activities taking place in northern Estonia. Around 1,000 personnel from Estonia and allied countries are participating.

According to Division Commander Maj. Gen. Indrek Sirel, the exercise will focus on strengthening cooperation between Estonian and allied units, training reservists on new weapons systems and improving command-and-control and communications capabilities.

The first two weeks will center on assembling and training reserve personnel from the Division's Artillery Regiment, culminating in live-fire exercises at the Central Training Area. French troops will also conduct live-fire drills there during the final phase of the exercise.

Field training exercises involving Estonian, British and French units will take place in Harju County from December 4–7.

The exercise is defensive in nature and includes the use of blank ammunition and other simulation devices. The Defense Forces warned residents to expect increased military traffic on roads in northern Estonia throughout the exercise.

NATO multinational battlegroups are deployed in Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania and Poland. At present, British and French units contribute to Estonia's defense as part of the Allied forces deployed forward.

World.title: Court rejects early release request of woman who killed her baby
World.content:
Harju District Court has denied early release to Kairi Kuusemaa, who is serving a prison sentence for killing her newborn child, despite acknowledging her good behavior and progress in prison.

Harju District Court has rejected a request for early release from Kairi Kuusemaa, who is serving a prison sentence for killing her child. Although the court found that Kuusemaa had made positive changes in her behavior, it did not consider her release justified.

Kuusemaa was sentenced to three years and nine months in prison for killing her child during or immediately after childbirth. She began serving her sentence on March 9, 2024, and is scheduled to remain in prison until December 9, 2027.

On Monday, Harju District Court issued a ruling rejecting Kuusemaa's request for early release from prison.

The court identified several factors supporting Kuusemaa's early release: she has behaved appropriately during her imprisonment, has received no disciplinary penalties and has completed the programs and interventions assigned to her. Since July, she has been held in an open prison and has been permitted to spend time and work outside the prison.

If released, she would have a place to live, employment opportunities and support from her family and friends. Tallinn Prison and the Prosecutor's Office also support her early release. The court did not identify a risk of reoffending that would, in itself, rule out early release.

However, the court considered it important to assess whether Kuusemaa's attitude toward the crime she committed had changed substantially since her previous early release proceedings.

Although Kuusemaa expressed remorse over her child's death during the court hearing and stated that she accepted responsibility for what happened, the court found her explanations insufficiently convincing to conclude that her attitude toward the crime had fundamentally changed.

The court also took into account the need to protect public order. After considering all the circumstances, it concluded that Kuusemaa's positive progress during her imprisonment did not currently outweigh the circumstances of the crime or the court's assessment of her attitude and outlook. It therefore found no grounds to grant her early release on parole.

The ruling is not yet final and may be appealed to Harju District Court within 15 days.

World.title: Ants Nõmper: How to legalize euthanasia in Estonia?
World.content:
I believe there are no credible arguments against holding a referendum on whether euthanasia should be permitted. Just as a competition is a celebration for athletes, a referendum is a celebration of democracy, writes Ants Nõmper.

The Riigikogu is considering a proposal by Eesti 200 to hold a referendum on euthanasia. As usual, there are differing opinions and criticisms.

Broadly speaking, the criticism directed at the proposal can be divided into three categories. The first consists of arguments based on the Constitution. Is it even permissible to put such an issue to a referendum? Can the referendum be held alongside parliamentary elections?

The second category covers criticism rooted in medical law. Is the question sufficiently clear? Is it asking about euthanasia, assisted suicide or limiting medical treatment?

The third category includes broader ethical and societal objections, such as whether Estonian society is ready. Are our other systems functioning well enough?

All these criticisms will have to be addressed individually in the Riigikogu. Let us assume that a referendum is held and the outcome is positive, meaning that the public supports legalizing euthanasia. How, then, should Estonia go about legalizing it?

What is euthanasia?

Before regulating something, we must understand what it is we are regulating — in other words, what constitutes euthanasia and what does not.

Euthanasia means the termination of a person's life by a physician on humanitarian grounds. Euthanasia is permitted in some countries and prohibited in others. Each country must decide for itself whether to allow euthanasia at all and, if so, under what conditions.

But what does not constitute euthanasia? A patient dying from complications of medical treatment is not euthanasia. For example, administering painkillers to a patient in doses that cause death as a side effect is not euthanasia, but rather the realization of a knowingly accepted risk. Every medication is a poison and potentially life-threatening, even when administered in accordance with treatment guidelines.

Nor is it euthanasia when a physician refrains from acting because there is an obstacle to providing treatment. One such obstacle may be the patient's wishes, meaning a situation in which treatment is not initiated or treatment already underway is discontinued at the patient's request.

Another obstacle may arise when a physician refuses to initiate treatment or discontinues treatment already underway for medical reasons. Thus, a physician may allow a patient to die because consent to treatment has not been given or to avoid providing futile treatment.

Neither situation constitutes euthanasia, which involves an act intended to bring about a patient's death at their request and out of compassion. Death does occur, but it is not the objective of the action; rather, it is an inevitable consequence. The patient is not killed but allowed to die. Medical care is provided during the dying process, not for the purpose of causing death. Providing medical care during the dying process is entirely lawful and requires no additional regulation.

Centuries-old debate

When is the right time to regulate a particular aspect of society? No one disputes that any regulation must be preceded by public debate. But how long, extensive, substantive and so on must that debate be? I know of no specific criteria for determining when there has been enough debate and when there has not. What I do know, however, are the statistics on the euthanasia debate.

According to DIGAR, a database that catalogs Estonian publications, the word "euthanasia" first appeared in the Estonian press in 1935. Even then, legalizing euthanasia in Estonia was considered to require legislation allowing people to make an advance declaration of their end-of-life wishes.

The newspaper even published the text of such a declaration:

"I am … years old and suffer very severe pain from … disease. As I have been informed, my illness is incurable and already at a very advanced stage. I have spoken with my relatives and put my affairs in order as far as I could. I have consulted my physician, Dr. …, and authorized him, in accordance with legal requirements, to grant me a quicker and more peaceful death. I know that in doing so I am shortening my life, but also my suffering. I authorize my physician to hasten my death."

In the first years following Estonia's restoration of independence, the debate over euthanasia was largely dormant. According to DIGAR, an average of six articles on euthanasia appeared annually during that period. A significant increase in press coverage came in the mid-1990s and by the end of the decade, nearly 50 articles on euthanasia were being published each year.

The peak year for coverage of euthanasia was 2013 when 119 articles appeared in the Estonian press. Interest subsequently waned somewhat, with an average of approximately 60 articles published annually. In total, the subject has been covered 1,758 times in the Estonian press. This figure excludes social media, television, radio and online media whose content has not been reproduced in print, including all coverage by Estonian Public Broadcasting.

In addition to the mainstream media, opinions have also been expressed in professional publications. Professor Jaan Sootak, the grand old man of Estonian criminal law, initiated a legal debate on euthanasia in the journal Juridica in 1995. Physician Dr. Rait Lobotkin brought the discussion to the medical journal Eesti Arst in 1998. The Estonian Council of Churches published its position in 2006 and the Estonian Bioethics Council organized a conference on euthanasia in 2010.

The journal Juridica subsequently brought all stakeholders, except patients, together again in 2017, organizing two roundtable discussions on euthanasia. Physicians, ethicists, lawyers and theologians participated in these discussions. Thus, all the relevant professionals have had an opportunity to express their views. Everyone except the public.

What do the people want?

The first attempt to gauge public opinion in Estonia was a survey conducted by Eesti Päevaleht in 1996. Asked whether euthanasia should be permitted when a person has no hope of recovery and can survive only in a hospital bed connected to life-support equipment, 60 percent of the 254 respondents answered yes, 27 percent said no and the remaining 13 percent had no opinion.

Since the issue of euthanasia frequently arises in connection with cancer patients, the views of this group were also examined. Asked whether a patient with incurable cancer should have the right to request medical assistance in ending their life with dignity, 5 percent of the 110 patients surveyed at Tartu University Hospital answered no, 58 percent said yes, 22 percent were undecided and 13 percent could not say.

The will of the people can also be expressed through citizens' initiatives. In fact, the bill introduced by Eesti 200 is not the first attempt to seek public input on euthanasia.

The first proposal, which collected 2,246 signatures, was submitted by the Estonian Greens in 2020. Reading the proposal, however, it is unclear what exactly its supporters were signing, as it conflated euthanasia with advance declarations of end-of-life wishes. The Riigikogu's Social Affairs Committee did not support the citizens' initiative, citing the need to first regulate advance declarations of end-of-life wishes and improve access to palliative care.

Is the time right now?

The current Riigikogu has successfully dealt with advance declarations of end-of-life wishes. Starting next year, adults with full legal capacity will be able to specify, either on paper or electronically, what healthcare professionals may or may not do to them. So half the job is done. But what about the other half — palliative care?

"Since 2020, hospice care has been included on the Estonian Health Insurance Fund's list of healthcare services, meaning it is publicly funded."

Palliative care, which includes hospice care, does not cure illness but alleviates symptoms and improves the well-being of patients with serious illnesses that diminish their quality of life. Access to palliative care in Estonia has improved significantly in recent years. Since 2020, hospice care has been included on the Estonian Health Insurance Fund's list of healthcare services, meaning it is publicly funded. A two-part clinical guideline on palliative care has also been in place since then.

There is no doubt that palliative care needs more funding, but isn't the same true of cancer treatment, cardiology, dental care, child psychiatry and most other areas of medicine? Limited treatment options are undoubtedly an important consideration when determining the substance of any regulation, but they are not a reason to avoid public debate. I would therefore argue that the other half of the job has also been done and the time is ripe for a substantive debate on regulating euthanasia in Estonia.

What needs regulating?

Looking at euthanasia regulations in different countries, the requirements can be summarized as follows: Anyone reading the law should be able to find answers to the following questions:

Who may request euthanasia? It would be advisable to restrict eligibility to Estonian residents who are adults and have legal capacity and decision-making capacity.

Under what circumstances should euthanasia be considered? It would be advisable to take both an objective approach based on diagnostic codes and a subjective approach that considers the severity of suffering. A decision must be made on whether eligibility should be based solely on physical illness or also include mental illness and how close a patient must be to the end of their life.

How should the patient's wishes be established? It would be advisable to require consultations with physicians, consideration of alternatives, repeated expression of the patient's wishes after a waiting period, written documentation, notification of family members and so on. Safeguards must be put in place to prevent undue influence by family members and inappropriate motives on the part of the patient, such as a desire to avoid becoming a financial burden.

What medical safeguards should be in place? A medical review by a panel of physicians should be required, a humane method of ending life must be agreed upon, physicians must be guaranteed the right not to participate in euthanasia and documentation requirements must be established.

What oversight should be in place? Euthanasia should not be available at every medical facility and law enforcement authorities should be notified when a patient requests euthanasia. It may also be reasonable to establish a role for an ethics committee and create a registry to analyze the effects on society.

Lawful act or lack of prosecution?

If Estonia decides to introduce legislation regulating euthanasia, the main legal question will be whether euthanasia is a lawful act or remains an unlawful act for which no one is nevertheless convicted.

Estonian criminal law recognizes several circumstances that exclude the unlawfulness of an act. These include self-defense, necessity, conflicts of duties and so on. Euthanasia could be added to this list, thereby establishing that euthanasia is a lawful termination of life. However, countries generally do not choose this approach.

Instead, they usually take a second approach based on procedural law. In a state governed by the rule of law, only a court can convict someone of a crime. A court can hear a case only if prosecutors bring it before the court. Prosecutors, in turn, receive cases from the police. However, if the police or prosecutors are authorized under certain conditions to discontinue an investigation or refrain from bringing charges, the result is a situation in which no one is convicted in court for ending a person's life.

The conditions that must be met would constitute the substance of euthanasia regulations. If a physician deviates from these conditions, they risk criminal liability for intentional homicide. There is therefore no reason to assume that physicians would engage in euthanasia lightly, since the risk of criminal liability would always remain.

In place of a summary

I believe there are no credible arguments against holding a referendum on whether euthanasia should be permitted. Just as a competition is a celebration for athletes, a referendum is a celebration of democracy. We have not had too many such occasions.

If the public rejects the proposal, the issue should be off the table for about 10 years. If the public supports regulating euthanasia, it could still take another 10 years for the legislation to finally take effect, as the points of contention are virtually endless.

Of course, we can continue to bury our heads in the sand and avoid dealing with the issue. That is what happened with assisted suicide until one individual came along and demonstrated that assisted suicide is legal in Estonia even without specific legislation.

I believe a similar situation could arise with euthanasia. Even now, it is possible to interpret existing laws in such a way that a physician who ends a patient's life at their request to relieve their suffering in a hopeless medical situation could be acquitted in court. However, the law should be made by the legislative branch, not the judiciary. Hopefully, lawmakers will have the sense of responsibility to address the issue.

World.title: Estonia's defense minister: The Gulf of Finland has not become more dangerous
World.content:
Defense Minister Martin Herem said recent drone attacks on Russian ships have not made the Gulf of Finland more dangerous, adding that cleaning up the aftermath of Ukrainian strikes can be seen as part of supporting Ukraine.

"In my assessment, it has not. These attacks have taken place mainly in the eastern part of the gulf and have clearly targeted vessels linked to the Russian Defense Ministry. I see no indication that the threat has increased in any way. Although the situation does not look good, I cannot say that the risk to passenger or commercial shipping in the Gulf of Finland and the Baltic Sea has increased at this point," Herem told ERR.

Ukraine first attacked a Russian warship on the night of November 10–11, striking a missile corvette belonging to Russia's Baltic Fleet. According to Col. Aron Kalmus, deputy commander of the Estonian Defense Forces' Division, the warship was hit several times and there were fatalities. An escort vessel eventually helped the corvette head toward St. Petersburg.

The second incident occurred Saturday when Ukraine launched a drone attack on the Sparta II, a Russian cargo ship used by the Russian Defense Ministry, in the Gulf of Finland. The ship was struck in Estonia's exclusive economic zone and subsequently drifted into Finnish territorial waters where the Finnish Border Guard launched a rescue operation. The crew was evacuated and efforts began to extinguish a fire aboard the vessel, with Estonian and Russian rescue ships also arriving at the scene. Russian rescue vessels eventually towed the ship from Finnish waters into Russian waters.

According to Martin Herem, Finland and Estonia acted in accordance with international maritime law.

"This is done even during wartime, when an enemy vessel has been hit and sailors are in the water. There is an obligation to help them; they are not left there. That is also required under the laws of war. We, however, are not a party to this conflict. International maritime law defines the areas where we are required to provide assistance, just as our sailors receive assistance in other areas. There is really no question about that," Herem said.

"Another matter is an oil spill or some other hazard resulting from Ukrainian attacks that affects our waters or coastline. But we have to deal with that, just as we would if it were a civilian accident," he added.

Ukraine defending itself

Herem said he had not spoken with Ukrainian officials about Saturday's incident in the Gulf of Finland. "I haven't spoken with them. But what should they have to tell us?"

"We provide Ukraine with more than €100 million annually in direct support for its war effort. Cleaning up some of the aftermath of its military operations costs a relatively small fraction of that and I don't think it's an issue," Herem said.

"It is not Ukraine that has put us in this situation, but Russia. These are Russian warships. Russia invaded Ukraine and these are its targets. Ukraine is defending its country and if we are prepared to support it with ammunition or anything else it needs to fight the war, we should certainly be prepared to provide support on a much smaller scale through other activities, especially those that are already our obligations under international law," Herem said.

"Frankly, I see no problem with supporting Ukraine in this way as well — if you can even call it support — by dealing with some of the consequences of its attacks," he added.

ERR asked Herem whether the attack would have been more successful from Ukraine's perspective if the ship had sunk.

"This ship has been transporting supplies for the Russian Defense Ministry. Whether those were weapons, vehicles, ammunition or something else, even uniform pants, I really don't know. Nor do I know what was on board this time. The fact is that they now have one fewer ship available for use. I can't say whether the cargo was destroyed. Would it have been better if the ship had sunk? That's where my concern for the environment comes in and I would say that a ship on the seabed is certainly worse than one in a Russian port being repaired or written off. I think it was a successful attack," Herem said.

Ukraine not coordinating its attacks with Estonia

Herem said Ukraine has neither coordinated its attacks in the Gulf of Finland with Estonia nor provided information about them and that the country should not be expected to do so.

"What would they coordinate with us? If they were to coordinate anything significant with us, first of all, that would effectively amount to cooperation. But we are not cooperating with them in attacking these targets. Second, they keep these attacks secret even from their own people. The more people who know a secret, the easier it becomes for the enemy to obtain that information. All these communication channels are vulnerable in one way or another. I don't think they should have to coordinate anything with us, but they must take into account that we have not made our airspace or waters available for their use," Herem said.

Herem added that Ukraine has not requested permission to use Estonian airspace or waters either.
