World.title: MCD works against legal hurdles to clear Ghazipur landfill, meet 2027 deadline
World.content:
The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) is currently navigating a Supreme Court order on stay on a tender owing to which work on the third phase of biomining operations at the Ghazipur landfill site is on hold. According to government data released in October, at Ghazipur, 69 lakh Metric Tonnes (MT) of legacy waste was still left to be cleared.



According to a report published by the Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) on Sunday, the progress in legacy waste processing at Ghazipur is the slowest among all major landfill sites in Delhi, with the commission rating it ‘unsatisfactory’.

Reason: stay on tender

The Supreme Court had last month stayed the tender for the work at the site, awarded to Greentech Environ Management. The Rs 249-crore project for the third phase of biomining and reclamation of the land was awarded to the agency, which was the lowest bidder. The Standing Committee of the MCD had also approved awarding of the tender at a meeting held last week. The tender was issued last year.

World.title: Pune traffic changes in place for Guru Nanak Jayanti November 24
World.content:
Traffic restrictions will be in place in parts of Pune on Tuesday, November 24, in view of Guru Nanak Jayanti celebrations at the Gurdwara Guru Nanak Darbar in Pune Camp, where devotees are expected to visit in large numbers for satsang, keertan and community service.

The Pune City Traffic Police announced diversions on three approach roads to the Gurudwara. The restrictions will be in force from 6 am to 11 pm on Tuesday, according to a press note issued by the traffic branch following a notification by DCP Traffic Sandeep Bhajibhakre.



While Guru Nanak Jayanti is marked at various Gurudwaras in the city, the main events will be held at Gurdwara Guru Nanak Darbar in Pune Camp, locally known as Hollywood Gurudwara.

World.title: Naqvi complicated provinces debate by 'irrelevant speech at irrelevant forum', says Rana Sanaullah
World.content:
PML-N Senator Rana Sanaullah on Monday said Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi “complicated” the matter of creating new provinces by making an “irrelevant speech at an irrelevant forum”.

In his fresh remarks, Sanaullah stood by his criticism of the interior minister’s choice to start the debate on provinces while addressing the Pakistan Economic Summit in Islamabad in July. Naqvi had whipped up a political storm by calling for creating new administrative units in the country to “reset” the current “system” of governance.

Following recent remarks by his predecessor, Naqvi, without naming Sanaullah, warned, “The day I comment on this minister, he will not be able to show his face.”

Subsequently, appearing on Geo News programme ‘Aaj Shahzeb Khanzada Kay Sath’ on Monday, Sanaullah said it was his right as a colleague and as a political worker to express his opinion on Naqvi’s work.

Sanaullah, also the prime minister’s political adviser, contended that Naqvi’s decision to make the remarks at the business forum “complicated this issue, and today this matter is in such a state that it has become extremely controversial”.

“And now if it comes to Parliament, it will arrive in a controversial state,” the senior politician observed, affirming that his party will make all possible efforts to build a consensus.

“There should have been a very healthy discussion on this issue. [But] he chose the wrong method, the wrong procedure, the wrong forum, and then made such a speech right at its inception that the whole system collapsed,” Sanaullah said, observing that those remarks had diverted attention away from the actual debate of new provinces.

In a noteworthy observation, Sanaullah seemed to back PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari’s stance that the system was “made to collapse”.

Asked about his comments from Aug 1, Sanaullah said: “No, this is not a personal matter. When he said that the system has collapsed, I do not accept this notion. I believe that the system did not fail or collapse; it has been made to fail, it has been collapsed.

“In making it fail, politicians, political parties, the establishment, our worthy judges and the judiciary, [and] bureaucratic circles have played a part. All of us together have made it fail. There is no flaw in the system, nor has it collapsed [on its own]; it has been made to collapse.”

The PML-N leader clarified that it was his “version”, adding: “If someone has another version, that’s fine, let them hold it, but I also have full right to present my stance and speak about it.”

Sanaullah maintained that he never commented on Naqvi’s “personality and thoughts” and never will do so.

“Is he Quaid-i-Azam that for two and a half to three years, I have supposedly been commenting on his personality and thoughts, and it just doesn’t seem to end?” he quipped.

“Whenever I have expressed an opinion, I have done so while keeping his respect and honour in mind. I have never addressed him as anything less than the worthy interior minister,” Sanaullah said, reusing the term from his previous interview.

Upon the programme host asking if he meant “worthy” — following chatter on social media about Sanaullah’s remark — the PML-N leader responded in the affirmative: “Definitely, worthy as in English.”

Expressing his opinion on Naqvi’s July speech, Sanaullah said the interior minister made “completely irrelevant remarks regarding the prime minister”.

He claimed that later, Naqvi also made indirect remarks about the military chief: “Field Marshal is a national asset and a national hero; [but] attributing this kind of talk to him indirectly, that he is a red line and that he does not want to cross it, so I objected to these things.”

The PML-N leader reiterated his stance that the matter of creating new provinces has to come before the Parliament sooner or later.

The PM’s adviser stressed the importance of building consensus among political parties, expressing hope that an agreement could be reached when the matter is debated in the Senate and the National Assembly.

On whether there were still chances for a consensus considering PPP’s objection, Sanaullah said the interior minister “mishandled” the matter and that he should have taken the PPP on board first.

Responding to Naqvi’s reported remarks from a day earlier, Sanaullah questioned what the need was to be “so short-tempered” and issue “threats”.

Asked about other federal representatives, including Khawaja Asif, Tariq Fazal Chaudhry and Tallal Chaudhry, voicing their support for new provinces, Sanaullah said each minister was entitled to their opinion.

“Nothing has been achieved from [discussing] this at forums and seminars, apart from making this issue controversial,” the PML-N senator said.

Sanaullah also commented on Bilawal’s stance that neither he nor his father, President Asif Ali Zardari, had been approached by the government about the matter after the debate began.

“Then what have you (Naqvi) been doing for four months? At the place where you are present all the time, and he (President Zardari) is your benefactor as well and he holds you so dear; if you could not even take him on board, then this is your total failure,” he asserted.

Asked whether his calling Naqvi a “son” of President Zardari was a personal comment, Sanaullah said, “I have personally heard, with these very ears of mine, Zardari sahib say more than once that ‘Mohsin is my son’.”

The programme host said Naqvi was invited to present his response on the show if he wanted to.

World.title: Petrol price reduced by Rs3 per litre; diesel remains unchanged
World.content:
The government on Monday reduced the price of petrol by Rs3 per litre while keeping that of diesel unchanged at Rs357 per litre, after snapping a 12-day streak of consecutive reductions in the rate of petrol the previous week.

Following the revision, petrol will retail at Rs319 per litre on Nov 24 (Tuesday), according to a notification by the Oil and Gas Regulatory Authority (Ogra).

The government continues to levy Rs114 per litre in taxes and duties on petrol and Rs100 per litre on diesel.

Under an arrangement announced on Nov 2, for 30 days, oil refineries will contribute to the petroleum levy by bearing a cumulative impact of Rs15 billion, according to the government. This allows a Rs14.71 reduction in the petrol price at the consumer end.

On Sept 17, the government rolled out the Prime Minister’s Fuel Relief Scheme across the country to ease the public’s burden amid rising fuel prices due to the Middle East situation.

The subsidy scheme applies to owners of motorcycles, rickshaws and vehicles of up to 800cc.

Rise in fuel prices

The price of HSD has come down from a peak of Rs520.35 recorded on April 3. Its price had started rising from Rs281 per litre after the US-Iran war broke out on Feb 28.

The petrol price had peaked at Rs458.41 on April 3 after beginning its upward trajectory from Rs266 in the first week of March.

Meanwhile, the government has reintroduced a raft of austerity measures in response to rising fuel prices amid the ongoing Middle East conflict. Under these measures, markets are required to close by 9pm, and fuel allocations for official vehicles have been cut by 50pc for three months.

Since July 17 , the government has been revising fuel prices on a near-daily basis due to fluctuations in international market prices following renewed hostilities between Iran and the US.

The petroleum minister stated that the cabinet and the prime minister had decided to give Ogra the responsibility of deciding fuel prices on a daily basis based on international market trends.

Prior to this, the government had been announcing weekly revisions to fuel prices since early March, alongside measures for the conservation of fuel amid possible oil supply disruptions due to the conflict. The federal government had also announced targeted relief measures in April to provide subsidised fuel.

Petrol is mainly used in private transport, small vehicles, rickshaws and two-wheelers, and changes in its price affect the middle and lower-middle classes.

Similarly, changes in diesel prices also impact the public at large, as it is mainly used in the heavy transport sector, power plants and large generators.

Petrol and HSD are the major revenue earners, with monthly sales of about 700,000 to 800,000 tonnes, compared to just 10,000 tonnes of monthly demand for kerosene.

World.title: 'No national security risk': Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO after affair scandal
World.content:
Nvidia on Monday reinstated Jensen Huang as chief executive after input from senior US government officials left its board confident he posed no national security risk, less than two weeks after the co-founder resigned due to an alleged spy scandal.

The board voted unanimously to bring Huang back as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately, after a series of meetings left directors satisfied with his “candour and ability to lead,” the company said in a statement.

Nvidia did not name the government officials it consulted or say what they told the board.

Nvidia shares surged on the news, jumping more than 25 per cent in premarket trading.

The decision came three days after US President Donald Trump publicly urged Nvidia to take Huang back, calling him “one of the truly most brilliant minds in the world” and saying he would “love to see Jensen be given a second chance”.

Trump described Huang as “a good man” who “made some bad decisions,” and said the company should rehire him “if they were smart.” Huang had offered to return, but the board initially refused.

Board chair Harvey Jones had said on an earnings call last week that directors had unanimously accepted his resignation and did “not intend to reinstate Jensen as CEO”.

“I take this responsibility with the greatest humility and renewed commitment,” Huang said, thanking the board, staff, shareholders and his family.

“I can’t wait to get back to work.”

Huang, 63, stepped down on Nov 12 following reports that he had a relationship with Alice Huang — no relation — a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, a company that bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia.

US intelligence services reportedly concluded she passed information to Beijing, which has denied the allegations.

Board chair Harvey Jones said Monday that directors now believe Huang “is the right person to lead Nvidia” and that his return serves the interests of shareholders, employees, partners and customers.

Jones, a former Synopsys chief executive who was named Nvidia’s first-ever board chair during the crisis, will stay in the role. Chief financial officer Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO, will continue as CFO.

Nvidia said a committee of independent directors set up earlier this month to investigate whether Huang was targeted by a foreign intelligence effort will see its probe through to the end. Huang supports the investigation and has committed to cooperating, the company said.

Trump, who had previously called on the AI giant to reinstate Huang, congratulated him in a post on Truth Social.

“The Nvidia board of directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO. The country needs Jensen’s leadership at Nvidia in order to ensure the success and prosperity of not only the company, but the American economy,” he wrote.

The US president clarified that the US government had “no reason” to believe that Huang’s reinstatement posed risks to national security, adding that the US attorney general had confirmed that the government did not possess evidence against Huang.

Trump further said that he had gotten to know Huang, describing him as a “great patriot and national treasure”. Trump directed that Nvidia should continue its internal investigation into compliance with US export controls.

Trump told CNBC on Monday that Huang “didn’t know about” advanced Nvidia chips going to China.

The US president described him as a “genius” and a “brilliant guy”, adding: “Losing the brainpower of somebody like Jensen — to me, that would be a far bigger threat than anything we’re talking about.“

“As far as the woman is concerned, every time you have a Chinese woman that’s good-looking or beautiful, they say she’s a spy. Now with Swalwell, she probably was a spy — but with Jensen, I don’t believe that’s true,” Trump said.

Jack Gold of J. Gold Associates called the reinstatement “a big mistake”, noting that the investigation into whether Huang was compromised by the alleged spy was still under way.

“This action further amplifies the notion that big ‘tech bros’ don’t need to play by the rules like the rest of us do,” Gold said, adding that the board’s decision appeared “driven more by financial influences than ethical practices”.

US Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer vowed to investigate potential wrongdoing surrounding Huang’s reinstatement, accusing Trump of putting personal financial interests ahead of national security.

“Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump Administration, Jensen Huang, other Nvidia executives, and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain,” said the veteran New Yorker, who is seen as likely to remain in his position when Democrats take control of Congress in January.

Alice Huang had contact with China spy agency: NYT

Alice Huang, the alleged spy at the centre of the Nvidia scandal, was in touch with an official from China’s top spy agency during an affair with the chip giant’s former chief executive, the New York Times reported on Sunday.

She was in contact with an officer of China’s Ministry of State Security from the spring of 2025 until the fall of this year, the Times reported, citing people with knowledge of the intelligence.

According to the Times, Alice Huang’s contacts with the Chinese spy agency correspond to the affair as well as a period when Megaspeed was acquiring large amounts of advanced Nvidia chips.

The Times also reported that US intelligence agencies have gathered evidence that Alice Huang’s business partner Kang Wei — who the newspaper said was often introduced as her husband — worked with the same Chinese spy agency.

He is to be questioned by US lawmakers on December 1 over national security concerns.

World.title: Peshawar to host opening ceremony, inaugural match for 12th edition of PSL: PCB chief
World.content:
PESHAWAR: Pakistan Cricket Board (PCB) Chairman Mohsin Naqvi said on Monday that Peshawar will host the opening ceremony and the inaugural match for the 12th edition of the HBL Pakistan Super League (PSL) scheduled for next year.

Naqvi made the announcement while addressing a press conference alongside Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Governor Faisal Karim Kundi in Peshawar.

“The biggest announcement today, for which I congratulate both the governor and Peshawar Zalmi, is that after 12 years, PSL will hold its opening ceremony and first match in Peshawar,” the PCB chief said.

He added that multiple matches will be held in the provincial capital, with the schedule to be finalised later by PSL.

The 12th edition of the cricket tournament will be held from March 18 to May 2, 2027.

The announcement by Naqvi came shortly after Kundi — whose administration now runs the province under governor’s rule — said the name of Arbab Niaz Stadium would be restored, reversing the PTI government’s decision to rename it to Imran Khan Stadium.

In its press release, PCB stated: “The announcement marks a defining moment for cricket in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and for the thousands of supporters who have followed the league, and their team, from afar since the very first season in 2016.”

The board noted that fans in Peshawar “have filled stands, packed streets and carried their colours across the country for more than a decade, without once watching an HBL PSL match in their own city”.

“That changes with HBL PSL 12. Peshawar’s supporters will finally experience the league’s electric atmosphere at home, with the world’s best T20 talent on show in front of a crowd that has earned its moment,” the statement declared.

“This is a moment the league, and above all the fans of Peshawar, have been looking forward to for 12 years,” PSL Chief Executive Officer Salman Naseer was quoted as saying.

“Peshawar’s love for cricket is unmatched, and HBL PSL 12 will finally give that passion the stage it deserves. Adding a sixth venue is a major step in the growth of the league, and we look forward to delivering a memorable experience for every fan who walks into the stadium.”

Speaking to the media, the PCB chairman noted that Peshawar Zalmi and its owner Javed Afridi had also been wishing for the tournament to come to the city.

Naqvi, also the interior minister, stated that matters related to law and order in the province were “improving very rapidly”.

He recalled that Governor Kundi would call for “reviving cricket in KP” whenever the two met, even before the imposition of governor’s rule and emergency in the province on Oct 11.

“This province has produced amazing stars for the cricket team, and I strongly believe that with some promotion and streamlining, […] along with joint efforts, we will see positive results from here in months, not years,” the PCB chief said.

He also announced holding a week-long cricket tournament between the U-19 team, Pakistan Shaheens and the national team.

Peshawar was supposed to host a PSL match on March 28 in the previous edition, but matches were restricted to Karachi and Lahore as part of austerity measures after the US-Iran war broke out.

Asked about that, Naqvi maintained that “best efforts” were made so a match could be staged in Peshawar, but it could not happen due to “purely administrative issues and some concerns”.

He clarified there was no “political reason” for not holding the match, adding that Peshawar was an option for one of the venues but it was not announced as such.

Responding to a query, Naqvi said that there were plans underway to build an academy for tribal districts, with the specifics of its location and construction timeline to be finalised in the next two weeks.

“Those districts are also very important for us,” he affirmed. The merged districts are among the 12 districts where special emergency measures were imposed on Oct 11 as the areas were deemed to face intense security challenges.

Speaking on district-level cricket grounds, Naqvi said the PCB planned to work in collaboration with the government to maintain grounds at “whatever level possible”.

‘Preserving Peshawar’s history’: Kundi on reversing stadium name change

Announcing his administration’s decision to restore Arbab Niaz Stadium’s name, Kundi said on X: “In 13 years, despite KP’s immense sporting talent, the PTI could not build a single new cricket stadium, even though the Pakistan cricket team boasts a significant number of Pathan players. Yet, they were quick to rename the one we already had.”

He contended that the decision was about “preserving Peshawar’s history, respecting its heritage and honouring those who have genuinely contributed to the province’s sporting legacy through their work and achievements”.

The stadium was named after Arbab Niaz, a former federal minister for sports. In Feb 2025, the PTI government in KP, led by then-chief minister Ali Amin Gandapur, renamed it after PTI founder and ex-premier Imran Khan.

Speaking on the matter during Monday’s press conference, Kundi termed the renaming of the stadium as a “huge injustice to the people of Peshawar”.

The governor highlighted that Niaz had the cricket ground built in the 1980s, stating that putting one’s plaques on past projects completed by others was inappropriate.

“If they had built it themselves and named it after him, that would have been fine,” the PPP leader said, adding that the name would be restored within a few days.

Speaking about provincial matters, Kundi reaffirmed that countering terrorism remained the top priority.

He stated that 70 per cent of a Rs160 billion package announced by the federal government will be allotted to the 12 designated districts, while the remaining 30 per cent will go to the rest of KP.

He also highlighted his administration’s crackdown on encroachments and illegal placer gold mining, and a cleanliness campaign.

World.title: Pemra bans ads, promotions for commercial infant formula on electronic media
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: The Pakistan Electronic Media Regulatory Authority (Pemra) on Monday banned s and promotional activities for commercially manufactured infant formula milk on electronic media with immediate effect, directing television channels and other regulated broadcasters to stop airing such s.

The ban will remain in force until the required legal compliance and no-objection certificate, approval or permission is obtained from the concerned department or health regulatory body.

According to an order issued by Pemra, the decision was taken following a letter from the Ministry of National Health Services, Regulations and Coordination dated Nov 18, regarding implementation of the Protection of Breastfeeding and Child Nutrition Ordinance 2002.

The order said that Pemra’s committee deliberated on sections 7, 8 and 9 of the ordinance, which prohibit certain s, promotional activities, distribution of free samples and direct marketing of designated products.

The committee also reviewed relevant provisions of the Drug Regulatory Authority of Pakistan Act 2012, the Pemra Ordinance 2002 and the Pemra Electronic Media (Programmes and s) Code of Conduct 2015.

Invoking Section 27 of the Pemra Ordinance 2002, the authority declared that “(s) of infant formula products (commercially manufactured formula powder milk) shall be prohibited forthwith”.

The authority has also referred the matter to its Council of Complaints for recommendations in accordance with the provisions of the Pemra Ordinance.

Pakistan is among the 118 countries that voted in favour of adopting the International Code of Marketing of Breast-milk Substitutes during the World Health Assembly in May 1981.

It enacted a national breastfeeding law in October 2002 in the shape of a presidential ordinance to enforce the code, which also envisaged a National Infant Feeding Board.

The Senate Standing Committee on National Health Services called on Federal Health Minister Mustafa Kamal earlier this month to enforce the ordinance, warning that weak implementation undermines child health. The committee chairman, Senator Amir Waliuddin Chishti, expressed concern over the law’s lack of enforcement despite being in place for over 20 years.

The Sindh government in August launched World Breastfeeding Week with a renewed commitment to strictly enforce the province’s law against the promotion of infant formula.

Sindh Health and Population Welfare Minister Dr Azra Fazal Pechuho said breastfeeding remained one of the most effective interventions for protecting newborns, improving child nutrition and reducing infant mortality.

World.title: AB de Villiers makes new claim about Australian 'Sandpapergate' ball-tampering scandal
World.content:
Former South African batsman AB de Villiers has alleged that Australia engaged in ball-tampering from the first match of their 2018 “Sandpapergate” tour of South Africa.

De Villiers alleged in a post on his YouTube channel that the ball-tampering, which culminated in Cameron Bancroft being caught using sandpaper in the third Test in Cape Town, actually began in the first Test in Durban.

He also said the Australian bowlers, who have denied any involvement, must have known what was going on.

A fierce debate about the eight-year-old events was triggered in Australia this month when Usman Khawaja claimed the whole team knew about the plot to alter the flight of the ball.

Bancroft, who was banned along with captain Steve Smith and David Warner after the incident, said in a recent article that sandpaper was first used in the second Test in Port Elizabeth.

But De Villiers said: “It started in Durban, by the way, not in PE. I’m very happy for people to quote me on that.

“I see everyone is sort of admitting that in Port Elizabeth it also happened. I can very much tell you Durban was no different, in the first Test.

Go look at the footage. Absolutely no doubt in my mind.”

He added: “We lost that first Test match in Durban with the ball reversing at a very, very interesting time. Way too early for anyone to reverse a ball at Kingsmead. Trust me, I’ve played a lot of cricket there.”

De Villiers added: “So whatever they did there, whether it was sandpaper or [a] nail, I don’t care. The fact of the matter is they were caught and everyone knew. Just stand up and say ‘we were wrong’. A lot is at stake now because they lied.

“The bowlers in particular knew because the ball doesn’t just reverse. It’s not your first Test match for Australia. So just stand up and say, ‘guys, we were wrong’.”

De Villiers was a central figure in a bad-tempered series. He was run out in Durban and Australian bowler Nathan Lyon appeared to drop the ball on him — one of several incidents that inflamed tensions during the series.

The then-South African captain Faf du Plessis revealed in his autobiography that he had persuaded the normally mild-mannered De Villiers to lead an aggressive response in the second Test to what Du Plessis saw as bullying tactics by Australia.

“I spoke to AB and said that the only way we were going to win the series was if he was willing to lead the fight against the Aussies with me. ‘You and I will fight fire with fire. The rest of the team will follow, but only if the two of us lead the charge’.”

Du Plessis wrote that his former schoolmate took up the challenge, not only by aggressively “sledging” Smith but by scoring an outstanding century, which helped South Africa win the match and go on to win the series.

Cricket Australia on Saturday threw its “unanimous support” behind Pat Cummins to remain the current Test captain, rejecting any suggestion his integrity had been compromised by the lingering “Sandpapergate” scandal.

Cummins has been under huge pressure since Khawaja claimed the whole team knew about the ball-tampering plot, but he strenuously denied being aware of what was going on in a press conference last week.

World.title: Bilawal calls for restoring supremacy of Parliament and trust in judiciary, electoral system
World.content:
PPP Chairman Bilawal Bhutto-Zardari on Monday called for restoring the supremacy of Parliament as well as trust in the judiciary and the electoral system.

He made the remarks while addressing the inauguration ceremony to mark the launch of the Sindh Youth Card in Karachi.

“To restore the trust of Pakistan’s youth, if any reset is to take place, it must be a democratic reset,” the party leader said.

“If a democratic reset happens, then the people’s stake will remain, and through that reset, we must restore the supremacy of our Parliament. We must restore confidence in our judiciary, and the election system we have, we must restore trust in it now.”

Bilawal’s remarks come as the debate over a “system reset” in the country has intensified over the past few months. In July, Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi stirred a political storm by calling for the creation of new administrative units, arguing that the current system of governance had “collapsed” and needed a “reset”.

Last week, in a hard-hitting speech, the PPP chairman asserted that the governance system had not collapsed, but was rather “made to collapse”.

“Every child in this country hates corruption. The youth [of Pakistan] want to see a country where there is no corruption. They want it, and we also want to join together and build such a Pakistan,” he said on Monday.

According to Bilawal, to achieve that objective, two things needed to be done: the first was to use modern digital technology, whether it was the Youth Card or Kissan Card, to build systems that shut down avenues for corruption.

“Along with that, we have to build a system that functions without discrimination,” he added.

“Instead of taking revenge, [the system] works to fix our situation.”

Bilawal stressed that the restoration of trust would have to be a “joint effort” — to restore the opposition’s trust in the government and vice versa, and the public’s trust in the country’s system, its parliament, judiciary and media.

He said if such conditions were created, Pakistan could achieve unity for the first time, enabling it to confront economic hardships, terrorism and climate change-related disasters.

“I know that a Pakistan that is united, [will] have the ability to face any crisis, any disaster, any catastrophe.”

“At the same time, I fear that if we keep fighting among ourselves and remain divided further, and [spread hatred] in society instead of hope, then we will not have the capacity to face any crisis,” Bilawal added.

“Then whatever happens to Pakistan, whatever negative consequences occur, the youth will hold us accountable, asking, ‘You were there, what did you do to save us from this trouble?’ And at least I want when that question is asked, I can proudly, with my head held high, say that my intentions were good,” he said.

The Bhutto scion claimed he had poured his blood and sweat into resolving the nation’s issues.

“I made this effort so conditions would be created in this country enabling us to serve you,” he said.

“And if I succeed, then it will be for the benefit of Pakistanis, for the benefit of our country. Even if I fail, history will remember that a young man stood up and tried.”

At the outset of his speech, Bilawal said he had been a part of Pakistan’s politics for 20 years, during which he maintained ties with all political parties and politicians.

“Given the circumstances we face today, and the position we are in, if I myself am disillusioned, one can only imagine how the people of Pakistan, especially the youth, must feel,” he said.

The inauguration ceremony was attended by Chief Minister Murad Ali Shah, Sindh Sports Minister Sardar Mohammad Bux Khan Mahar, and other PPP leaders.

Speaking at the event, CM Murad said the Sindh Youth Card would establish an “effective means of direct engagement” with young people and create a database.

He said that the card had been initially launched for 100,000 young people, with the programme’s scope to be expanded over time.

“With Sindh’s youth population estimated at approximately 13 to 14 million, further measures are being taken, including youth development centres and public-private partnerships, to secure young people’s futures while providing them with better opportunities for growth and a supportive environment,” the CM said.

World.title: ‘Rights at stake, not privileges’: Opposition leaders write to SC, FCC, IHC chief justices on Imran, Bushra’s health
World.content:
ISLAMABAD: National Assembly and Senate opposition leaders, Mahmood Khan Achakzai and Allama Raja Nasir Abbas, on Monday wrote to the chief justices of the Federal Constitutional Court (FCC), the Supreme Court (SC) and the Islamabad High Court (IHC), urging them to take notice of the health condition of PTI founder Imran Khan and his wife Bushra Bibi.

Imran has been in prison since August 2023. The IHC has allowed him twice-a-week meetings — on Tuesdays and Thursdays — with his family, lawyers and other associates. But despite multiple court directives, the PTI founder has been restricted from meeting visitors. Concerns about his health have also arisen in the past year, with the PTI demanding he be given medical treatment by his personal physicians, a demand as yet unheeded by the government.

In an open letter to the same three judges last week, Imran appealed for medical treatment for himself and Bushra Bibi.

Advocate Khalid Yousuf Chaudhry, counsel for the incarcerated PTI founder, told Dawn on Monday that the letter by Achakzai and Abbas urged the SC to convert the application into a petition and hear it as a case of basic human rights.

Chaudhry said the joint letter was written by the opposition leaders in their constitutional capacity by invoking the high judiciary’s jurisdiction and requesting that the letter be treated as a petition for the enforcement of fundamental rights.

It also demanded that a writ of mandamus be issued regarding the non-implementation of the SC’s Aug 18 order for shifting Imran to Shifa International Hospital, and the concerns regarding Imran and Bushra Bibi’s health and detention.

In the seven-page letter, seen by Dawn, the two opposition leaders argued that Imran’s life was in danger in state custody.

“An order of the SC made to protect that life has been flouted and ignored for three months now,” it said.

“The threat to Imran’s life has increased, not diminished.”

Recalling the PTI founder’s open letter on Nov 16 from Adiala jail in which he described being denied fundamental rights and the impact on his health, they demanded that his plea be answered “through a writ of mandamus that compels the state to do what the Constitution and the SC already require of it”.

It said that Imran suffered from cardiac and blood pressure issues, loss of sight and solitary confinement with access largely denied to his lawyers and family and medical recommendations to improve his well-being ignored. In particular, it pointed out that solitary confinement of over 15 consecutive days was prohibited under the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners.

Imran, the letter said, had been held in these conditions for nearly 11 months.

The letter added that Imran’s case was “no longer a domestic matter that the government can wish away”, as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk had taken notice of the issue and called for Imran’s release and proper treatment, as well as defusing of political tensions around the case.

It also recalled that Pakistan, as a party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights as well as the Convention against Torture, had made these commitments to human rights in its own name and was bound to uphold them.

“The high commissioner’s statement is a warning to the government. It is also a reminder to all of us that the reputation of Pakistan’s institutions, including its courts, is now being judged by how this case is handled.”

The opposition leaders said that the Aug 18 order by the SC was “defeated” within 72 hours: the PTI founder was instead taken to the state-run Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (Pims), then returned to the jail before dawn, while the ordered medical board was never constituted.

“The hospital and the independent doctors were the substance of the order,” the opposition leaders argued.

“An order to provide independent care is not implemented by providing care that is not independent.”

Now, three months after the order was made, they said, it remained “unimplemented in every essential respect” while Imran’s condition had grown worse, the letter said.

It also highlighted that Bushra Bibi needed a second eye operation to prevent permanent loss of sight and her access to her doctors was being restricted.

“The rights at stake are not privileges of a prisoner. They are guarantees the Constitution makes to every person, which no conviction and no executive convenience can suspend,” the letter stressed.

The letter demanded that the chief justices, within their respective constitutional jurisdictions, “treat this letter as a petition for the enforcement of fundamental rights and issue a writ of mandamus, or such directions as are necessary”, to the federal government, the Islamabad chief commissioner, the Punjab inspector general of prisons and the superintendent of Adiala jail.

They asked that the writ of mandamus direct these authorities to move Imran to Shifa International Hospital within 24 hours and keep him there as long as the medical board advised; to constitute this board “exactly as ordered” and carry out the treatments and investigations it recommended without delay; and to place his examination and treatment under the supervision of his own physician, Dr Faisal Sultan, as well as his sister Dr Uzma Khan, with continuous access and complete medical records to be provided within 24 hours.

In addition, it called for his solitary confinement to be ended immediately and his rights to weekly meetings, regular calls with his family, unhindered access to his lawyers, and access to “books, newspapers and recreation” to be restored, and transferring Bushra Bibi to a specialised eye hospital for her second operation under specialists of her family’s choice and the release of her full medical record to her family and counsel.

The letter also urged that a court officer or local commission be appointed to oversee and report on compliance within seven days; that the pending contempt petition, appeals and applications be fixed for urgent hearing while holding those who “defeated” the Aug 18 order to account; and that the federal government be directed to bring Imran and Bushra’s detention conditions into conformity with Pakistan’s obligations under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights as well as the Convention against Torture.

“Every day that the court’s order remains unimplemented diminishes the authority of the court and the promise of Article 9 and every day it is noticed far beyond our borders,” the letter stressed.

“If harm comes to Imran or to Bushra Bibi in state custody, the responsibility will rest on the state, but history will also ask what the courts did when they were told, in plain words, by the elected representatives of the people in both Houses of Parliament, that a life was at risk.”

Imran and Bushra Bibi’s health

Imran has been in prison since August 5, 2023 , while his wife was arrested on January 17, 2025, in a separate case in which the couple were sentenced.

Imran’s eye ailment — right central retinal vein occlusion — came to light in late January, following which he has been taken to hospital multiple times.

On Aug 18, the SC directed the government to shift the jailed ex-premier to Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad, a day after the superintendent of the Adiala jail — where Imran is imprisoned — submitted a report to the court on the ex-premier’s health condition.

However, the government took the PTI founder to Pims and subsequently transported him back to prison. At the time, Information Minister Attaullah Tarar had blamed “the security situation created by PTI workers on the way to and outside” the hospital for the diversion. The PTI has denied the allegations and accused the government of deliberately flouting the court’s orders.

Meanwhile, Bushra Bibi suffered a retinal detachment in April and was taken to the hospital for surgery. She has since approached the courts seeking an immediate medical examination by an ophthalmologist and permission to receive treatment from doctors of her choice at her own expense amid concerns over her deteriorating eyesight.

According to the former first lady, doctors who examined her had diagnosed her condition as a “mature cataract” and advised that another eye surgery would be required.

World.title: Ramisa rape and murder: Sohel Rana mentions new name as charges framed
World.content:
A new name has surfaced in the Ramisa rape and murder case, with prime accused Sohel Rana telling reporters today that a man called "Dollar" was responsible for the rape and murder of the eight-year-old girl.

However, no further details about the person were immediately available.

Sohel made the claim while being escorted to the courtroom of the Dhaka Metropolitan Children Violence Suppression Tribunal.

"I am at fault, and Dollar is also at fault. I am not the only culprit," he told reporters.

Standing in the courtroom's dock, he shouted at the lawyers present in the courtroom after the hearing, and said, “I did not commit the rape; I only dismembered the body. A man named Dollar committed the rape. I have sinned, so punish me for that sin.”

At that time, Sohel further claimed that Dollar had promised to pay him Tk 2 lakh if he could bring the girl to him.

However, police officers present immediately stopped him from speaking further.

Sohel also claimed that his wife, Swapna Khatun, was innocent.

Earlier in the day, Sohel and Swapna were brought to the lock-up of the Metropolitan Sessions Judge's Court in Dhaka.

Later, Judge Masrur Salekin of the tribunal framed charges against the couple in the case over the rape and murder of Ramisa in Dhaka's Pallabi area.

Both accused pleaded not guilty after the charges were read out, said Bench Assistant Pankoj Peter Gomes.

The judge also fixed tomorrow for the start of the trial, with the victim's father, Abdul Hannan Mollah, scheduled to testify first, he added.

On May 24, Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station submitted the charge sheet before the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate's Court in Dhaka, accusing Sohel of rape, murder and destruction of evidence, and Swapna of destruction of evidence and providing false information.

Several hours later, the CMM Court transferred the case to the Children Violence Suppression Tribunal for trial.

Ramisa, a second-grade student of Popular Model High School, was found beheaded on May 19 in the house of her neighbour, Sohel.

The following day, Ramisa's father filed a case with Pallabi Police Station, accusing the couple and an unidentified person.

According to the case statement, Sohel lured Ramisa into his room and raped her. Investigators said he later slit her throat and attempted to dismember the body to conceal the crime.

On May 20, police produced Sohel and Swapna before a Dhaka court, and court sources said Sohel agreed to give a confessional statement before a magistrate. The third and unidentified accused was on the run. Dhaka Metropolitan Magistrate Aminul Islam Junaid recorded Sohel's confessional statement after police brought him to the magistrate’s chamber, said a court staff member.

Sub-Inspector Ohiduzzaman of Pallabi Police Station told The Daily Star that day, the prime accused had already admitted to the crime during primary interrogation.

On May 22, the Dhaka Bar Association decided not to provide legal assistance to the accused following an emergency virtual meeting of its executive committee, citing the gravity of the allegations.

The next day, the government appointed Supreme Court lawyer Musa Kalimullah as a state defence counsel to represent the accused to ensure a fair trial.

This report has been corrected at 4:43pm. In the earlier version, Sohel Rana’s comment was misreported. We regret the error.

World.title: Why Bangladesh must pivot to renewable energy now
World.content:
There are moments in a nation’s history when a crisis does more than create hardship. It reveals the weakness of an old system and opens the door to a better one. Bangladesh is now standing at such a moment.

The country is facing an energy crisis that no longer centres on power cuts. It is affecting factories, farms, schools, offices, exports, foreign currency reserves, and the daily life of ordinary people. What we are seeing today is not just a temporary shortage of gas or fuel. It is a signal that our energy system has become too dependent on imported fossil fuels.

More than 60 percent of Bangladesh’s energy demand is met through imports. LNG, coal, oil, and other fossil fuels have kept the country running for years, but this dependence has become risky and expensive. Global fuel markets are unstable because of geopolitical tension, supply chain disruption, and price volatility. For a country like Bangladesh, this creates double pressure: fuel supply becomes uncertain while fuel costs keep rising.

The government is now spending more than BDT 200 crore per day in energy subsidies. Annual energy import expenditure remains around USD 12 billion, putting serious pressure on foreign currency reserves. Nearly 70 percent of Bangladesh’s LNG imports come from Qatar. If supply is disrupted, Bangladesh can quickly face a severe shortage. In the power sector, daily gas demand exceeds 2,500 mmcfd, but supply sometimes falls to 850–900 mmcfd. This can create a power generation shortfall of 1,500–1,800 MW. Overall, the daily gas shortage exceeds 1,100 mmcfd, and peak-time electricity shortages may reach nearly 2,000 MW.

Bangladesh also has a weak Strategic Petroleum Reserve. The current reserve capacity is sufficient for only about 35–40 days, well below that of countries such as China and Japan. This makes the national energy system even more vulnerable.

Visual: Teeni and Tuni

The impact is already visible. In the readymade garments sector, gas shortages and load shedding are reducing productivity by 25–30 percent in many cases. This threatens export earnings, foreign currency reserves, and economic stability. The crisis has also reached ordinary households. Although Bangladesh declared 100 percent electrification in 2022, many rural areas still experience 10 to 20 hours of load shedding every day during summer. This affects education, small businesses, agriculture, and people’s dignity.

We have also seen long lines at fuel stations, schools moving online, and offices shortening working hours because of fuel shortages. These are not isolated events. They show how deeply energy insecurity can disturb national life.

Over the last 15 years, electricity tariffs in Bangladesh have been increased on many occasions, including more than 10 rounds of increases at both bulk and retail levels. This path is not sustainable. Fossil-fuel-based electricity depends on imported fuel, global prices, the availability of the dollar, subsidies, and repeated tariff adjustments. Solar power offers a different path. With a one-time investment, solar can provide stable energy for 15–20 years. Once installed, its fuel cost is almost zero.

The economic comparison is clear. A 1 MW HFO-based power plant produces electricity per year at a cost of nearly BDT 190 crore, with much of the cost paid in foreign currency. In contrast, a 5 MW solar project requires a one-time investment of around BDT 25 crore, after which fuel costs are practically zero. Each 1 MW of solar power can save around USD 325,000 per year in foreign currency.

This is why renewable energy should not be discussed solely in technical terms like decarbonisation, emissions, and sustainability. For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Despite Bangladesh’s potential, renewable energy contributes less than 5 percent to power generation, far below the global 30 percent target by 2030. Clear, measurable goals and timelines are essential for effective policy planning and investment decisions.

Renewable energy equipment imports face around 50–60 percent in duties and taxes, hindering local manufacturing growth. Policy reforms that reduce import duties and support local industry can accelerate renewable deployment and reduce dependency on imports.

For Bangladesh, renewable energy means jobs, fuel independence, savings in foreign currency, industrial competitiveness, agricultural protection, and economic strength. Policymakers and stakeholders can lead this transformation, inspiring confidence in a sustainable future.

Import duty is usually imposed to protect the local industry. But where local production is not yet significant, a high duty only increases project costs, reduces investment returns, and slows renewable energy expansion. Policy reforms can unlock this potential, making stakeholders feel their efforts directly contribute to progress.

India, Pakistan, Vietnam, and China have expanded solar and wind power by offering low or zero import duties, tax exemptions, and low-interest financing. Many countries have also reduced duties on lithium-ion batteries and energy storage systems. Bangladesh should learn from these examples.

The barriers are clear: high duties and VAT, high financing costs of 10–12 percent or more, limited access to easy loans, slow approval processes, net metering delays, high LC margin, weak Merchant Power Policy, lack of clear policies for rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, floating solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage, weak local manufacturing, and insufficient grid digitalisation. Addressing these collectively can accelerate Bangladesh's renewable journey, uniting stakeholders in a common goal.

One urgent reform is customs assessment. The current weight-based assessment system does not reflect the actual value of solar equipment. It can create artificial overvaluation and raise duties by three to four times. Bangladesh should shift to transaction-value-based assessment using pro forma or commercial invoice values, in line with international practice and WTO customs valuation principles.

The second urgent reform is the elimination of customs duty on renewable energy equipment. This should apply to Solar PV Module, Photovoltaic Cell, Solar Inverter, DC Cable, Data Logger, Aluminium Mounting Structure, Battery Pack, Battery Cell, BMS Circuit Board, PV DG Controller, Hybrid Controller, Solar Plant Safety Aluminium Walkway Mesh, Safety Accessories, and related components.

Current TTI rates are high. Solar PV Module carries 26.90 percent, Photovoltaic Cell 25.75 percent, Solar Inverter 28.73 percent, DC Cable 58.40 percent, Data Logger 37.25 percent, Aluminium Mounting Structure 58.40 percent, Battery Pack and Battery Cell 58.40 percent, BMS Circuit Board 31.50 percent, pack materials 37.25 percent, PV DG Controller or Hybrid Controller 89.08 percent, and Solar Plant Safety Aluminum Walkway Mesh 37.25 percent. These should be reduced to zero percent for renewable energy expansion.

The third reform is a tax holiday. Rooftop solar power producers and project companies should receive benefits comparable to those of utility-scale renewable energy producers. A practical structure could be a 100 percent tax holiday for the first 10 years, 50 percent for the next 3 years, and 25 percent for the next 2 years. This should apply to CAPEX, OPEX, IPP, and MPP models. A broader 10–20 year tax holiday for renewable energy projects should also be considered.

Bangladesh has a remarkable solar opportunity already waiting on its rooftops. About 7 percent of the country’s land is covered with concrete or other built structures. This means more than 10,000 square kilometres, or about 10 billion square meters of built surface. If only 30 percent is usable, that would give around 3 billion square meters. At 10 square meters per kW, this can create nearly 300 GW of solar potential. Bangladesh’s peak demand is only around 16–18 GW. The opportunity already exists on rooftops, factories, warehouses, schools, hospitals, government buildings, and commercial establishments.

Rooftop solar should therefore be relaunched nationwide with a clear business model. Utility-scale solar also needs support through unused khas land, transparent tendering, and grid readiness. Floating solar, river-based solar, agrivoltaics, solar irrigation, and hybrid solar-storage should receive separate policy attention.

The suspended solar projects must also be revisited. A total of 31 solar power projects, with a combined capacity of more than 3,000 MW, were previously suspended or cancelled. Many were being developed by foreign investors, with more than USD 200 million reportedly already invested. If implemented, these projects could save around BDT 10,800 crore annually in energy import costs. They should be reassessed and revived quickly.

Energy storage is another missing pillar. Solar and wind need storage support to become more reliable. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and other storage systems should be reduced to zero. This will help stabilise renewable power and support future grid flexibility.

Electric vehicles can also become part of the solution. In China, Japan, and the United States, EVs are increasingly seen as mobile energy storage systems. A typical EV battery has a capacity of 40–70 kWh, enough to power an average household for 1–2 days. If Bangladesh had 1 million EVs, the country would have 40–70 GWh of distributed storage. This is several times higher than the daily peak demand gap. Solar-powered EV charging, vehicle-to-home, and vehicle-to-grid systems should be included in future energy planning.

If Bangladesh had 30–40 percent of the grid powered by solar, along with solar-powered EVs, the country would be far less exposed to global fuel market shocks. Long fuel lines, online schooling, shorter office hours, and industrial disruption could be reduced. Solar, storage, and EVs should now be planned together.

Finance will decide how fast this transition happens. Renewable energy projects cannot grow at interest rates below 10–12 percent. Long-term financing should be available at an interest rate of 3.5–4.5 percent. A 10–15-year financing facility at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent should be introduced. Bangladesh Bank’s green refinancing fund should be expanded. Rooftop and residential solar customers should be eligible for collateral-free loans. The LC margin for renewable equipment should be limited to 5%.

Net metering must be simplified. Approval should be completed within 15–30 days through a one-stop service. Approval, interconnection, inspection, billing adjustment, and utility coordination should all be simple and time-bound. Wheeling charges for renewable energy should also be kept reasonable and low. The Merchant Power Policy should be clear, simple, and investment-friendly so that industries and commercial consumers can directly procure renewable electricity.

Agriculture should also be included in the solar transition. Bangladesh can set a target to convert 1.5 million diesel irrigation pumps into solar pumps. This will reduce diesel imports, lower farmers’ production costs, and protect the environment. The program should include duty-free facilities, low-cost loans, investment support, and local service networks.

Waste-to-energy should also receive policy support. City corporations need clear rules, easy financing, and private-sector participation to enable urban waste management and distributed power generation to work together.

Bangladesh now needs a phased national roadmap for renewable energy.

In the short term, within 0–6 months, customs duty, VAT, and taxes on renewable energy equipment should be reduced to zero. Duties on lithium-ion batteries, BESS, and energy storage should be withdrawn. Approval for net metering should be obtained within 15–30 days. Industrial and commercial solar installations should be eligible for special incentives. The 31 suspended solar projects should be reassessed. Wheeling charges should be rationalised. Solar, storage, and EV charging should receive urgent policy support. Collateral-free lines of credit should be introduced for rooftop solar. NBR should quickly implement assessment reform and a 0 percent duty.

In the medium term, within 1–3 years, renewable energy financing should be available at a maximum interest rate of 5 percent for 10–15 years. The LC margin should be limited to 5 percent. Land banks and grid infrastructure should be developed for utility-scale solar. Merchant Power Policy and MPPA should be simplified. Rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, and hybrid solar-storage projects should receive a 10–15-year tax holiday. A national program should convert 1.5 million diesel pumps into solar pumps. Rooftop solar should be made mandatory or incentive-based for government buildings, industrial zones, EPZs, economic zones, and large commercial buildings. EV solar charging and distributed storage policies should be developed. Renewable energy skill development and employment programs should also be launched.

In the long term, within 3–10 years, Bangladesh should aim to reach more than 10,000 MW of solar power by 2030. Offshore and onshore wind should be developed. Floating solar, river-based solar, and agrivoltaics should be implemented. A National Energy Storage Strategy should be prepared. Smart grid and power sector digitalisation should be accelerated. Local assembly and manufacturing of solar panels, inverters, mounting structures, battery packs, BMS, and EV charging equipment should be encouraged. Regional power trade should be expanded. The Renewable Purchase Obligation should be introduced. Fossil fuel subsidies should be gradually redirected to a renewable energy transition fund.

Image Visual: Anwar Sohel

The benefits can be large. Energy import costs will fall. Pressure on foreign currency reserves will decline. Industrial production costs will reduce. Export competitiveness will improve. The subsidy burden will decrease. New investment will grow. Renewable energy can create 20–25 jobs per MW through rooftop solar, utility-scale solar, solar pumps, EV charging, battery storage, smart grids, manufacturing, installation, operation, and maintenance.

The government may worry about revenue loss from tax and duty exemptions. But this should be seen as an investment. In the short term, there may be a limited impact on revenue. In the long term, Bangladesh can save far more by reducing fuel imports, lowering subsidies, saving foreign currency, strengthening industries, and attracting new investment.

Bangladesh’s energy crisis is a major challenge but also a historic opportunity. The crisis is not only a supply problem. It is a policy framework problem. Renewable energy, especially solar power, storage, and EV integration, can be among the most practical solutions for the country.

The question is no longer whether Bangladesh should adopt renewable energy. The real question is how quickly, how systematically, and how boldly the country can complete this transition.



Mohammad Ataur Rahman Sarker is a renewable energy entrepreneur and the secretary of the Bangladesh Sustainable and Renewable Energy Association.

Md. Tanvir Siraj is a renewable energy researcher.

World.title: The forgotten art of Bengali advertising
World.content:
I have never seen someone at a rustic village market, anklets jingling, shouting slogans for "Khol Company’s Ringworm Ointment." No smooth-talker has ever leaned in, fanning out thin booklets like a deck of cards, whispering rhythmically, "Here are the mysteries of Gopal Bhar, and here—the secret love letters."

I never hid colourful s of a reclining Gauhar Jaan, cigarette in hand, between the folds of shirts in my drawer. I did indeed rummage through my grandfather’s pockets to collect old tram tickets, but none of them bore that curious notice for "Ashtavakra Toothpowder." Perhaps the elders of the house witnessed a tram tearing through the heart of a half-awake city, bearing the Khadi Pratisthan’s pledge for cow protection—but there was no question of me witnessing such a sight.

An iconic early 20th-century  for Bukhsh Ellahie & Co., featuring classical maestro Gauhar Jaan holding a cigarette to promote their brand

Someone’s great-grandfather might have known which drummers came beating the kara and nakara to announce, "Tonight at seven, the Chaitanya-lila folk play commences." I never heard the name of a young "lad" like Dhiren Bal, who reportedly painted the  for "Himkalyan Hair Oil" at a three-way junction in Dinajpur.

While searching the Panjika (almanac) for the auspicious moment of a wedding, I never had the chance to chuckle at the suggestive illustrations for "Libido-Enhancing Tablets." On a morning shortly after Mahatma Gandhi’s assassination, I didn't sit with a newspaper wondering which artist, known only as "Munshi," had used swirling brushstrokes to sketch a portrait as a final tribute on behalf of some bankrupt cotton mill.

I saw none of this because I hadn't been born yet. Most of those who witnessed it are now gone forever. Yet, even without being born in that era, I have managed to 'see' it all. The old, withered newspapers and digital archives acted like Alibaba’s cave, revealing to me a lost jewelry box. To me, those vintage s were not just pages of history; they were the precious Sita-har, the Jhumko, and the Nak-chabi themselves. I saw those 'ornaments'—the lost illustrations—and through them, I glimpsed a world that has otherwise vanished.

Actually, on a sudden whim, I spent a long time digging through ancient newspapers and periodicals. My eyes kept getting stuck on the bizarre s still surviving on the faded, brownish-yellow newsprint of yore. I was looking, most of all, at the illustrations.

As I tasted this history, I remembered a book I read long ago: The Lost Tribes of Israel by Tudor Parfitt. Many believe that since the foreign invasions of Israel in the 8th century BC, at least twelve tribes went missing. Mr. Parfitt scoured the planet in search of them—a search that reportedly continues today. Some even believe the signs of those lost people are visible in the Afghans.

Looking at the drawings for old s, I felt I found a resemblance between those legendary lost tribes and these forgotten illustrators. That is why the book came to mind. It also felt as though there was no such mismatch that could prevent us from linking these unknown artists’ ghosts to their successors, even without a DNA test!

The connection might be clear, but can we not grant them even a small corner in the history of Bengal's illustrative arts?

Renowned figures like the artist Raghunath Goswami continue to say—no, those  drawings or ideas are not even worth considering. They claim it is a "mindless and indiscriminate simplification of art objects." They say the expression has neither grace nor form. Artistic value? Far from it!

For some reason, despite respecting the scholars' verdict, I grew stubborn. As I weighed the pros and cons, even the "ugly" artworks of those who drew s for ringworm cures or hair-growth tonics began to pull at my eyes. I saw in them plenty of humour, and plenty of heartache too. Nevertheless, I began looking for a way to have a long conversation with those early advertising artists.

A representative of a "vanishing species" like O.C. Ganguly (Arun Kumar Gangopadhyay) introduced me to a certain "madman." He had a crow's nest of hair. His lower garment was draped over his chest like a shawl. He wore a striped vest. His hands were shackled in massive iron rings.

It is precisely these kinds of s that art critics have referred to as brainless and ugly art. The  regarding the cure for insanity, however, dates back to 1952. Yet, long before that, a group of young artists from agencies had completely transformed the face of Bengali ads.

Apparently, such a madman would no longer need to be restrained. Why? Because the illness would be cured simply by administering "ABD Pills" and "Dutta Oil." Such was the claim of the "Bengali Asylum" of Dutta Nagar, Dum Dum, whose head office was at 29-A Vivekananda Road (Phone: Jorasanko 5220).

Seeing the address "Jorasanko" in that illustrated ad, I was immediately reminded of the Tagore family—specifically, their members who struggled with mental health. One was Birendranath Tagore, the fourth son of Maharshi Debendranath. He was brilliant at mathematics but suddenly fell victim to "wind-disease" (mental instability). The other was Somendranath, another brother of Rabindranath.

The Nobel laureate poet knew well which medicines helped the "insane." I learned of another —not for the ABD Pills of Dum Dum, but a special notice from "S.C. Roy & Co." at 167/3 Cornwallis Street. They advertised Dr. Umesh Chandra Roy’s world-famous "Great Cure for the Mad," priced at five rupees per bottle. The ad claimed that for over 70 years, this medicine had cured "millions of violent madmen and all kinds of nervous patients." This  would appear with a quote from the poet himself, saying: "...I have been aware of its efficacy for a long time." Was the "Great Cure for the Mad" then used on Birendranath or Somendranath? I know bringing up Rabindranath's name is somewhat irrelevant, but seeing these old drawings makes my mind wander in a thousand directions!

The illustrated  I mentioned was published in 1952—the day I saw the picture of the shackled madman in the paper. That drawing was made several years after legendary artists had already begun to dominate Bengali advertising. By then, Bengalis had seen hundreds of fantastic drawings for various products. A legend like O.C. Ganguly was earning forty rupees a month at Calcutta’s "Stronach Advertising" as early as 1937. An agency named "Paradise Advertising" existed in Calcutta in 1928. No one can really speak of agencies in East Bengal (now Bangladesh) before the Partition. We mostly know of the birth of agencies like Bitopi, East Asiatic, or Interspan in the 1960s. Clearly, advertising production in both Bengals (undivided India at the time) was centred in Calcutta. Be that as it may, an agency required an artist—someone to present the matter attractively to lure customers.

But not all sellers went to agencies. Instead, they took "ugly" creations (by today’s standards) made by local artists to make printing blocks for newspaper offices. The madman illustration is a classic example. The calligraphy in that ad was purely amateurish—something no professional agency would ever approve. Whether that ad ran before 1952 or if that was the first, I do not know.

It is undeniable that finding artists from the era before the establishment of agencies (pre-partition) is extremely difficult. Only a handful of artists signed their names on those ads, and even then, it was just a tiny first initial of their name and surname, usually in English. Pranabesh Maity, who drew ads in the 60s and 70s, had a more bitter experience. He claimed that even if artists signed, agency bosses would often erase the signature to imply that the agency was everything and the artist didn't matter.

This makes me think of the "Lost Tribes" and a piece by Premendra Mitra about the Patuas (traditional scroll painters). Premendra once had a great desire to find the lost Patuas of Kalighat. Briefly, the story goes like this—a young boy walking the streets of Kalighat would watch with wonder a specific style of indigenous painting. Ordinary men in dirty clothes sat cross-legged on mats in small roadside shops, painting those pictures. Yet, the walls of the shops were adorned with framed, colourful photographs of gods and goddesses. People coming to the temple preferred to buy the framed photos. Even so, the Patuas would sit down to paint whenever they found a moment’s respite between sales.

Then came a day when not only the scroll paintings but even the expensive printed pictures of deities vanished from those shops. The Patuas disappeared too. I don't know if that young boy was Premendra himself—since his childhood was spent in North India, having been born in Varanasi. But for a creative man like him to imagine that boy while thinking of the Patuas is not far-fetched. When a kind soul eventually went looking for those Patuas, he was utterly disappointed. He learned that they had been pushed out of the city. Their descendants had not become "useless" painters; some took jobs as labourers in jute mills or chose other professions. At most, unable to ignore the "blood connection," some practised their hand at painting the chalchitra (background canopy) of idols. Premendra tracked down a few of these "unfortunate" descendants and asked to see old scroll paintings. He was shocked to find they had almost nothing left. One or two pulled down a bundle of papers tucked into the thatch of their huts. Premendra saw the pathetic state of those soot-stained, discoloured papers—they were ready to crumble at any moment. Calling the insects "connoisseurs of art," a somber Premendra described how those paintings were being destroyed.

The author was accompanied by an art collector. His friend bought some paintings that were in good condition from the descendants for an unexpectedly high price. Later, he and others wrote about them. Premendra noted how his "self-satisfaction" was bruised. He commented that while many were becoming famous artists by adopting the Patua style, and those paintings were selling at major exhibitions to decorate drawing rooms—even impressing Pablo Picasso—the Patua sitting on a dirty mat in a narrow shop and the ordinary customer buying them for a pittance are nowhere to be found today.

Thinking of the early artists of Bengali advertising, I am reminded of Premendra Mitra's essay "Barbar Yuger Pore" (After the Barbaric Age), just as I was of The Lost Tribes of Israel. In it, I found no real difference between the forgotten Patuas and the nameless illustrators from the dawn of Bengali advertising.

The artists whose work I later came to know and appreciate were giants like Annada Munshi—whose ideas and illustrations revolutionised the look and feel of Bengali advertising. But I wanted to see what kind of "ugly and tasteless" creations (as labelled by later critics) Annada and his peers had replaced. Without seeing those, how could I understand the evolution of style?

Here, I must mention the artist Hemen Majumdar. He is never known to have drawn for s. Everyone knows that when art lovers discuss him, his paintings of "drip-wet Bengali women" inevitably come up. Who that woman was, was once a subject of intense speculation. A few know that he often painted while keeping a photograph by his side. Hemen had taken photos of his wife, Sudharani, in various poses as she returned from bathing in the family pond. His wife was his model. When giving the picture its final form, he would simply change Sudharani’s face and paint the face of a relative instead—much like modern-day Photoshop!

Essentially a romantic artist, Hemen Mazumdar never illustrated s himself. Yet, his signature style of depicting women was extensively adapted by other advertising artists.

Though Hemen was skilled at copying photographs, he knew the magic of glorifying them with colour. But that wasn't all. This was a man who was invited to design the gateway for King George V’s visit to India, who was a pioneer in publishing art journals, who painted the landscapes of Kashmir at the invitation of the Maharaja, who was the "Court Artist" of the Maharaja of Patiala, and who gave an artistic form to Mahatma Gandhi at the spinning wheel. He didn't just paint wet clothes!

At the same time, it is true that his skill at painting beautiful women was so popular that other artists, while drawing women for s, often mimicked Hemen’s postures—or those of the women painted by Raja Ravi Varma. Thus, even without drawing for ads himself, Hemen was "present" in this branch of art through the figures of women drawn in his style. Of course, bringing out the "wet-clothed" look or suggestive sensuality in black-and-white newspaper ads was a difficult task!

It’s worth mentioning that Hemen’s own work was occasionally used in advertising. An organisation called "Bengal Autotype" used to run ads featuring a sketch of Rabindranath Tagore by Hemen, accompanied by the Poet’s message. The advertisers even sold prints of that picture. The ad read: "A Wonderful Picture of Poet." Each print cost one rupee, with an additional 50 paise for postage. This ad appeared in the Visva-Bharati journal in the late 1930s, detailing the paper quality and dimensions.

In the eyes of some critics, the work of the "erotic painter" Hemen began to gain popularity in 1926 after a commercial firm in Mumbai bought his paintings to make calendars. The "forbidden" sword of the Hemen-style became a weapon for advertising illustrators too. One could easily call them followers of Hemen’s "voyeuristic" work. However, no matter how they were drawn, it's not as if the artists of the Battala press or the Patuas hadn't used such "swords" long before! Based on the consumer's mindset, this tradition seems never-ending—at home, abroad, and everywhere else.

Sandip Dasgupta has spent nearly three decades working in the editorial offices of newspapers and news portals. He has authored several history-based books, and a subject particularly close to his heart is the illustrations created by Bengali artists.
