World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Judge to deliver summing up to jury after defence closing
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome our live coverage of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s double-murder trial in the NSW Supreme Court in Sydney.

Justice Natalie Adams has predicted the jury will retire for their deliberations on Wednesday. Defence barrister John Stratton, SC, will conclude his closing address this morning, followed by the judge’s summing up.

Beau Lamarre-Condon, centre, is standing trial over the alleged murders of Jesse Baird, left, and Luke Davies, right. NSW Supreme Court, Supplied, Stephen Kiprillis

Lamarre-Condon, a former NSW police officer, has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder over the deaths of Jesse Baird, 26, a former TV presenter, and Luke Davies, 29, a Qantas flight attendant, on February 19, 2024.

Both men died of gunshot wounds from the accused’s police-issued Glock pistol. The Crown case is that Lamarre-Condon plotted to kill Baird after their casual relationship ended, and that he killed Davies to eliminate a witness.

The defence case is that he acted in self-defence and that Davies grabbed the gun and shot himself in a struggle.

During his closing address yesterday, Stratton said:

Forensic and ballistics evidence alone was “enough to raise a reasonable doubt” about Lamarre-Condon’s guilt, including DNA found on the accused’s gun.

The court has heard that a partial DNA profile matching Davies was detected from a swab inside the barrel of Lamarre-Condon’s gun. Stratton said the jury might conclude that “the DNA was found in many locations on the gun because it was in the hands of Mr Davies when the final shot was fired”.

Tests recovered DNA from at least three people on the grip and trigger of the gun, the court has heard. Davies was identified as a major contributor, while the accused was matched as a minor contributor. The third person was not identified. Stratton submitted that it was “powerful evidence that it was his [Davies’] finger on the trigger when the third shot was fired”.

Stratton submitted that the jury might think that if his client had been planning to kill someone, he “wouldn’t have waited” to buy cleaning products, as he did after Baird and Davies died. This was a powerful piece of “negative evidence” that was inconsistent with the Crown’s hypothesis of a premeditated murder, Stratton said.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732), the Rainbow Sexual, Domestic and Family Violence Hotline (1800 497 212) and Lifeline (13 11 14).

World.title: Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as chief executive after direct lobbying by Trump
World.content:
Updated WorldNorth AmericaAI Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as chief executive after direct lobbying by Trump Michael Koziol Updated November 24, 2026 — 10:48am ,first published 1:10am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Washington: Nvidia has reinstated chief executive Jensen Huang in a shock reversal just 11 days after he was forced to resign amid revelations he had an affair with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy. Nvidia’s board of directors said it unanimously voted to reinstate Huang as chief executive, president and a director of the company after receiving “input” from senior levels of the US government reassuring them that his return would not pose a risk to national security. Nvidia’s board of directors said they unanimously voted to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO, president and a director of the company. Getty US President Donald Trump, who counts Huang as a confidant and adviser, revealed that he personally lobbied Nvidia’s board to reinstate the ousted chief executive, saying the US had to protect its geniuses. “I spoke to them, let me just put it that way. And I convinced them,” Trump told CNBC television on Monday morning (US time). “It was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago.



“I felt very strongly about it. I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company … I think the company’s going to do fantastically, and without Jensen, I don’t think it would be possible to do.” Asked whether it was appropriate for the president to be directly involved in choosing the chief executive of a public company, Trump said it was a good question, but he did it for the country. “If I didn’t get involved, you’d probably have a very sad Nvidia for a long time to come.” Huang has been a close adviser to Donald Trump, and the president publicly argued for his return. NYT Vice President JD Vance was also heavily involved in the machinations over the weekend. Trump named Vance among the people he was engaged with on the matter, and the Associated Press reported that the vice president acted as an “emissary” to ease concerns on Nvidia’s board. Nvidia shares closed more than 31 per cent up on Monday, as other technology stocks climbed. The tech-heavy Nasdaq finished 6.5 per cent higher, and the S&P 500 rose 4.7 per cent.



The board of directors said it was satisfied with Huang’s candour and ability to lead the multitrillion-dollar company, following a series of meetings and discussions. On Truth Social, Trump said the US government had no reason to believe Huang’s return to Nvidia posed a risk to national security. Trump posted this meme of Huang – a reference to a photo of the president taken after an assassination attempt in 2024 – on social media shortly after the Nvidia decision was announced. TruthSocial Attorney-General Todd Blanche – who is Trump’s former personal lawyer – “confirmed that the US government does not possess evidence that [Huang] has engaged in any unlawful conduct”, the president said. Asked to confirm that the president called into Nvidia’s board meeting, White House communications director Steven Cheung told this masthead that Trump was “totally involved” and that the board made a great decision.



In a statement released shortly before markets opened in New York on Monday, Huang said he was honoured to return to Nvidia and took the responsibility with “the greatest humility and renewed commitment”. He thanked interim chief executive Colette Kress, chairman Harvey Jones and executive staff. “I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support,” Huang said. “Above all, I am grateful for the love and support of my family. I can’t wait to get back to work.” Alice Huang seated next Jensen Huang in June 2024. Huang founded Nvidia in 1993 and built it into the world’s biggest and most important producer of advanced chips, and a crucial player in the artificial intelligence boom. As such, it is a critical company in the US’ artificial intelligence arms race with China. The revelation that Huang, 63, had developed a close relationship with Alice Huang (no relation) – a Chinese citizen who ran a Singapore-based data centre company and whom US intelligence suspected of funnelling information to Beijing – stunned the industry and the national security community.



Nvidia’s board announced two weeks ago that it would initiate an investigation into reports that Huang was the target of a foreign intelligence effort. Days later, amid intense public pressure and media reports about other infidelities, he resigned and admitted to cheating on his wife. The board said on Monday it would proceed with the investigation until its conclusion, indicating it was incomplete. Huang supported the investigation and would co-operate fully, it added. Flowers outside Nvidia headquarters in Santa Clara, California on the day Jensen Huang resigned. AP The board has also established a National Security and Export Control Committee to “oversee trade compliance and national security risks”. Trump encouraged Nvidia to continue its investigation into compliance with US export controls, but made no mention of the unfinished probe into whether Huang was compromised by foreign intelligence.



Jensen Huang’s return came just hours after The New York Times reported that Alice Huang had been in contact with an official from China’s top spy agency, the MSS, for more than a year while in a secret affair with Jensen Huang, citing people with knowledge of US intelligence reports. Related Article Trump's America ‘Vibes have definitely shifted’: The perfect storm that changed how America sees big tech Trump was dismissive of that report when he called into CNBC television on Monday. “Who wasn’t in contact?” he said. “I just left China. I had a great summit; it was at the top of the line. President Xi respects our country greatly again … He met me at the plane, which is something they’ve never done. “As far as a threat is concerned, I think probably China speaks to everybody. They speak to me, they speak to everybody. That doesn’t make them bad.”



Trump added: “The bigger threat would be losing the brainpower of someone like Jensen. That would be a far bigger threat than anything we’re talking about.” Related Article Analysis

Trump's America National security has been sacrificed for the stock market – and that’s a scandal The president also said that Xi heaped praise on Huang when they discussed the matter at their meeting in Shenzhen last week. “We have to protect our geniuses – and he’s certainly a genius,” Trump told CNBC. “We don’t have enough of them. Frankly, he went through hell.” But Huang’s reinstatement, and the president’s direct intervention, come amid a push for far greater scrutiny over Nvidia and chip exports to China and Chinese-linked entities.



On Monday, the US Commerce Department added cloud computing company Megaspeed – where Alice Huang was once an executive – to its entity blacklist. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was criticised for failing to blacklist the company despite pressure from other parts of the bureaucracy. A notice published to the federal register said Megaspeed was added to the list because of “the significant risk of these entities being or becoming involved in the diversion of advanced computing commodities to unauthorised end uses or end users”. Chuck Schumer, the leader of the Democrats in the Senate, said the party would wield the full power of Congress to investigate the matter. AP Huang and Lutnick have been summoned to testify before congressional committees, and Democratic Senate leader Chuck Schumer said Huang’s return on Monday underscored the need for Congress to act. “Trump is putting his own financial interests and the needs of his billionaire buddies before our national security, emphasising that he’s learned nothing from his resounding election defeat,” Schumer said.



“Democrats will wield their full power to investigate any wrongdoing by the Trump administration, Jensen Huang, other Nvidia executives and anyone selling out our national security for financial gain.” Related Article Opinion

Xi Jinping Everyone’s talking about the Chinese spy. Everyone’s missing the bigger story Parnell Palme McGuinness Columnist and communications adviser Republicans also queried the series of events leading to Huang’s return. John Curtis, a Republican senator from Utah, said he wanted to know what had changed since last week, when Nvidia’s board said it did not intend to reinstate Huang. Rick Scott, a Republican senator from Florida who sits on the Senate’s homeland security and foreign relations committees, said the reinstatement of Huang “looks terrible on its face” and the federal government owed the American people answers. “[This] drives home the need for Congress to be informed on the full impact of Jensen Huang’s actions on our national security and economy. Congress needs to be fully briefed on this as soon as possible, so we can take appropriate action if need be,” Scott said.



Video posted to social media by Nvidia employees on Monday showed staff at the company’s Santa Clara headquarters cheering and applauding as Huang returned to the office. “Let’s get to work,” one person yelled. View post on X Huang’s fellow AI leaders generally rallied around him during his 11 days in exile. “The mistake has been corrected,” SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk, the world’s richest person, posted on Monday. “Everyone I know at Nvidia wanted Jensen back and it shows.” Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: WA news LIVE: Uni merger business case leader speaks publicly for the first time since appointment
World.content:
The person heading the probe into whether to merge three of WA’s universities into one is making his first public address since the business case was announced.

Mark Barnaba is the chair of the steering committee overseeing the project, which has received backlash from Curtin and Murdoch university leaders.

It’s expected he will tell an industry breakfast this morning that Western Australia has “a higher education problem” that needs to be addressed, and that people need to remain open-minded as to what the solution is.

Yesterday, higher education minister Tony Buti said 15 per cent of WA’s students were now heading east to study, compared to the 1 or 2 per cent coming the other way.

He said the figures showed WA was losing its “brightest and best” to other Australian universities.

“I don’t think the situation now is actually a really good situation, so let the business case take its course, and we’ll see what happens after that,” he said.

World.title: ASX jumps after Wall Street roars higher on Huang’s shock return to Nvidia
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX jumps after Wall Street roars higher on Huang’s shock return to Nvidia Staff writers Updated November 24, 2026 — 10:11am ,first published 5:18am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket jumped at the open after a thunderous rally on Wall Street following the surprise return of Jensen Huang, the charismatic and flawed booster for the entire artificial intelligence industry, as Nvidia’s CEO. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 109.50 points, or 1.3 per cent, at 8680.10 at about 10.10am AEDT. It’s a step change from the recent market gloom, which saw the ASX suffering its worst weekly fall in six years last week as mounting AI anxiety sparked a massive sell-off. The bourse slipped 0.3 per cent on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US66.29¢. Tech stocks surged as Wall Street clawed back more than half of their brutal loss from last week. AP The newly created AFR Real Economy index – which tracks 500 companies that mirror the ABS’ composition of the actual economy– was up 1.6 per cent, and so was the AFR Global 50, which tracks Australia’s top 50 companies with majority revenue from offshore. Overnight on Wall Street, US stocks recovered just over half their brutal loss from last week, which was one of their worst since the 2008 financial crisis.



The S&P 500 surged 4.7 per cent in a demonstration of how much the US stock market depends on just one industry. Rallies for beaten-down AI stocks sent the Nasdaq composite up a market-leading 6.5 per cent, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average jumped nearly 3 per cent. Even before Wall Street opened for the day, trading in the futures market suggested US stocks were set to halt the seven-day losing streak that dragged the S&P 500 more than 10 per cent below its all-time high set last month. Then came the bombshell about Huang’s return to Nvidia, even though its board is still investigating whether he was the target of a foreign spy and created any national-security concerns. That kicked the rally into overdrive. Related Article Health insurance ‘Young people cross-subsidise older people’: Health insurance battle revs up Nvidia’s stock surged 31.5 per cent and finished just shy of its best day since 2000, close to when the dot-com bubble peaked. That followed its plunge of nearly 23 per cent last week, though it’s still below where it was before Huang’s scandal initially broke. Stocks closely tied to Nvidia rocketed higher. CoreWeave, a company that buys Nvidia chips and then rents out access to them over the cloud, shot up 22.3 per cent.



Other stocks in far-flung industries that have benefited from the AI boom likewise recovered some of their losses. GE Vernova, which is helping to power AI data centres, rose 8.2 per cent following last week’s drop of nearly 13 per cent. Caterpillar, whose sales of equipment have benefited because of the construction boom around AI, climbed 7.2 per cent after sinking 15 per cent last week. How AI-related stocks do matters incredibly for workers’ pension accounts because Nvidia and other chip stocks have grown into some of Wall Street’s largest and most influential. Coming into the day, a 1 per cent swing for Nvidia’s stock carried more of an effect on the S&P 500 than a 1 per cent move for all but two of the 500 companies in the index. Monday’s rebound for the S&P 500 was its best day since April of 2025, which is when President Donald Trump paused most of his tariffs announced on “Liberation Day” that had sent stock markets reeling. Trump had an influence on this most recent surge as well. He told CNBC in an interview Monday, “I believe my intervention was very important” in convincing Nvidia’s board to reinstate its co-founder. Less than a week ago, Nvidia had rejected an offer by Huang to return as CEO. Trump said his administration assured Nvidia there were no national security concerns about Huang’s return. The US president likely personally benefited from the surge in Nvidia’s shares through his sprawling financial portfolio. At the end of 2025, Trump owned at least $US12 million worth of Nvidia shares, according to his financial disclosure report, and his brokerage accounts have continued to buy and sell Nvidia shares as recently as September, the New York Times reports.



US President Donald Trump told CNBC he believed his intervention was instrumental in the return of Jensen Huang. Bloomberg To be sure, AI stocks and the broader US market have been prone to extreme reversals since mid-year, not only week to week but even hour to hour. The market’s strength overnight easily give way to more losses because of the long list of worries dogging the industry. Beyond general concerns that AI stock prices shot too high and entered into a bubble, worries remain that a Democratic-controlled Congress and statehouses across the country could increase regulations on the AI industry. High interest rates in the bond market are meanwhile making it more difficult to borrow money to pay for the AI build-out. Related Article Updated

AI Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as chief executive after direct lobbying by Trump ”Markets have been badly bruised by the turmoil of recent weeks, but we do not think the underlying cycle is broken,” Barclays’ Ajay Rajadhyaksha and Amrut Nashikkar wrote in a research report. “Earnings remain strong, global growth is holding up and even if the AI build-out slows a little, it is not collapsing. The risks are real, but for now we think they are manageable.”



Oracle rose 12.3 per cent after making a pre-emptive announcement that it had in place all the funding needed to fulfil its deal to provide computing power to OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT. In other international markets, European indexes climbed more than 1 per cent following a weaker finish in Asia. South Korea’s Kospi fell 3.3 per cent due in part to drops for its big stocks tied to the AI economy, but those moves came ahead of Huang’s return to Nvidia. In the bond market, the yield on the 10-year Treasury inched up to 4.93 per cent from 4.92 per cent late on Friday. Yields got an upward push as investors felt less need to herd into investments seen as safer. At the same time, they felt a downward push due to falling oil prices. Brent oil fell 3.6 per cent to $US86.68 per barrel. It’s been yo-yoing between $US72 and $US114 since the Iran war started at the end of February. with AP, Bloomberg The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Albanese stands by Bowen after failed COP amid global recriminations
World.content:
PoliticsFederalParis Agreement Albanese stands by Bowen after failed COP amid global recriminations Natassia Chrysanthos and Nick O'Malley Updated November 24, 2026 — 9:50am ,first published 7:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has maintained it was in Australia’s national interest for Energy Minister Chris Bowen to co-host this year’s COP31 in Turkey, despite the summit’s negotiations collapsing without a final outcome. The Coalition hammered Labor over Bowen’s role on Monday as the energy minister travelled home from Antalya, where the climate talks reached a stalemate on Sunday night for only the third time in the conference’s 32-year history. Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen. Getty Images The central sticking point was whether the final document should specify phasing out fossil fuels – oil-producing nations led by Saudi Arabia wanted to scrub those references, while nations seeking more ambitious action, including Europe and the Pacific, said they must be included. The deadlock has cast a shadow over both the future of the UN’s climate summit and the role of Bowen, who campaigned for his role as president of negotiations when Australia lost its bid to host the talks in Adelaide.



The Coalition on Monday called for Bowen to resign, with opposition energy spokesman Dan Tehan telling question time the minister had wasted “$150 million of our money on his big COP flop, including $30 million on a pre-COP [event in the Pacific that] no-one went to.” Albanese defended Australia’s involvement, saying climate change was making weather events more extreme while the countries least responsible stood to lose the most, including Pacific neighbours. Opposition MP Dan Tehan has led the argument against Bowen’s joint COP presidency. Dominic Lorrimer “The government believes that we have responsibility to this and future generations to act. [Critics argue that] one country acting alone won’t make a difference. We agree with that. We need to bring other nations with us on the journey,” Albanese said, to jeers from opposition MPs who asked how that was going. The prime minister also said there were links between environmental security and national security, referencing the interests of the Pacific. “I don’t think [the prime ministers of Fiji, Tuvalu, Samoa, Tonga and the Solomon Islands] thank the member opposite for the nature of that question, in which he said no-one was there at the pre-COP meeting held in the Pacific,” he said.



Tehan, however, argued Bowen had embarrassed Australia on the world stage. “The [COP] model as it currently stands is completely and utterly broken,” he said. “Chris Bowen should have known that, and then he would have spared Australians the expense of $150 million for an exercise, which became a vanity project for him.” There was jeering in Monday’s question time as Albanese stood by Australia’s investment in this year’s COP. Dominic Lorrimer Consensus approach the ‘root of the problem’: Bowen In the aftermath of the calamitous result, summit delegates are debating whether the joint co-hosting arrangement between Turkey and Australia, proposed by Bowen, backfired by muddying authority and slowing discussion in the conference’s final days.



Some critics questioned Bowen’s strategy of insisting all 198 parties agree to a final cover decision. The cover text, which captures the COP’s headline aims, is negotiated throughout the summit to achieve consensus, and sinks if any country objects. The death knell this year came when Irish climate minister Darragh O’Brien, on behalf of the European Union, rejected the text on Sunday night because it “does not even mention fossil fuels”. Photo: Matt Golding Bowen said he tried to strike a balance: instead of using explicit language, the draft text referred to previous agreements on fossil fuels. “It was good faith attempt. It wasn’t enough,” he said. The Australian Greens were scathing of Bowen’s approach. “At the end of COP 31, we have the Albanese Labor government choosing to side with Saudi Arabia and Trump, and not mention fossil fuels, rather than back in Europe and our Pacific neighbours,” said leader David Shoebridge.



“This is worse than disappointing.” Others argue that the requirement for consensus is a problem. The United Nations’ climate chief, Simon Stiell, said he was asking for advice on reforming the system on Sunday night. Bowen said the consensus rule was “the fundamental root of the problem”, not the joint presidency. Chris Bowen, president of COP31 negotiations, during the closing session at the climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. AP Photo/Khalil Hamra “When positions are so strong, that’s a very big challenge for any presidency – joint or individuals – to come to the global context,” he said in Turkey after the talks finished.



“Australia left nothing on the field, trying to find solutions to reach what I now see as unbridgeable red lines. The situation coming into this COP was the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory. Related Article Updated

Paris Agreement ‘Abject failure’: Coalition demands Bowen’s head as COP31 ends without a deal “Unfortunately, we’re unable to reach agreement on a cover decision, and that’s disappointing ... I take my share of responsibility. Ultimately, you know, people can judge what could have been done or couldn’t have been done. Ultimately, it’s a party-driven process.” Bowen pointed to positive outcomes, such as more than 90 countries signing an electrification pledge. “People of goodwill worked very hard. I haven’t slept in the last three nights. We’ve been negotiating all the way through,” he said. Fiji’s environment minister, Lynda Tabuya, said the failure to agree on a cover text was not Bowen’s. “It is a collective responsibility that rests with all parties. Consensus requires compromise, courage, and political will from all of us,” she said.



Failed COP talks create hope for better forums The stakes were raised at this year’s conference given the United Nations’ environment program had warned just weeks before that the world would overshoot the Paris Agreement of limiting global warming to 1.5 degrees. Former president of Ireland, Mary Robinson, said that should have shaken leaders into action, but “instead COP31 saw a shameful lack of urgency and leadership from the co-presidencies Turkey and Australia”. Former United States vice-president Al Gore, however, blamed the failure on a “handful of petro-states [who] have veto power over any mention of fossil fuels”. Other climate change advocates praised the EU and its allies for choosing to play hardball, including former UN climate change executive secretary Christiana Figueres, who said COP31 showed progress could be achieved without consensus.



“Let’s be clear about what happened in Antalya: more than 130 countries refused to sign a deal that would have belied the true state of our crisis,” she said. Related Article Analysis

Climate policy There is no getting around the scope of this failure – both for Chris Bowen and the world Matthew McDonald, a professor of international relations at the University of Queensland, said the longer-term legacy of this year’s talks could be a “recognition of the limits of this consensus-driven approach to climate negotiations, and the development of alternative sites for climate action.” Tuvalu’s climate change minister, Maina Talia, said the island nation would next year co-host with Ireland the second conference on transitioning away from fossil fuels, alongside “a growing coalition of doers”. “Tuvalu cannot accept this as the final scenario. So we are putting our resolve where we can make an impact,” he said. “It is moving beyond debating whether fossil fuels are simply mentioned in a text, to creating detailed plans for a global transformation.”

World.title: Sinner in doubt for Australian Open
World.content:
Sinner in doubt for Australian Open

After reports of Jannik Sinner's knee surgery have gone public just twp months before the event, the Italian is now in doubt to play the 2027 Australian Open.

World.title: The insider’s take on Newcastle, NSW
World.content:
InspirationLocal Knowledge The insider’s take on Newcastle, NSW Laura Agnew November 24, 2026 — 9:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

For a truly quintessential Newcastle stay, book the Merewether Beach Shack on Airbnb. The 1960s blue weatherboard home is owned by Silverchair’s Daniel Johns and home to arguably the best view in town. Seafood restaurant and bar Scottie’s in Newcastle East is an institution for good reason. It has exceptional food, an excellent natural wine list and an idyllic seaside location. Frenchie, in the heart of town, is an intimate spot with an unmissable cheeseburger. Merewether Ocean Baths, Newcastle. For coffee, specialty drinks, baked goods and very good panini, Sunnyboy is a local go-to (it has two locations at Dixon Park and Foreshore Park). No trip to Newy is complete without a swim in Merewether Ocean Baths. Bonus: the shallow, sandy bottom pool is perfect for little kids.



The 1970s heritage-listed Tower Cinemas screens new releases as well as classics. Find beautifully curated items – think Thonet, Maison Balzac and Cultiver Linen – at Monsoon Living, which is housed in a beautiful terrace on King Street. For something you can keep forever, head to Artefact in Cooks Hill, which specialises in fine handmade jewellery. Nab one of its signature welded bracelets for the perfect Newcastle souvenir. The Bogey Hole is Australia’s oldest purpose-built ocean pool, dating back to 1819. Tucked away below King Edward Park, this pool is the perfect place to cool off and soak up local history. Done all that? It’s less than an hour’s drive to Shoal Bay. 



The Lass O’Gowrie pub – alias “The Lass” – is always a vibe; I’ve been to many birthdays in its beer garden. Little French Cafe is our regular for coffee and pastry. You won’t regret a trip to The Lock-Up – cutting edge contemporary art in an old police station. It’s amazing. The walk up to Nobbys Lighthouse stretches your legs and offers spectacular views. For a retail fix, Newcastle Art Gallery shop has pieces by local artisans and plenty of art books. Nearby is Blackbird Corner, the perfect shop to find a gift for yourself or a friend. Stock is sourced from artists all over Australia, plus a few special house-made items, too. A walk up to Nobbys LIghthouse offers terrific views. If you want to get out of town, visit MAC yapang, a beautifully located art gallery on the shores of Lake Macquarie in Booragul, with a sculpture park to picnic in.



My first choice of hotels is QT Newcastle. Request some rock oysters and champagne to your room on arrival, then head up to the rooftop bar for sunset views. It’s in the East End, so you’re a short walk from beaches, bars and, of course, Humbug. Starting the day with a coffee from Floozy is a good shout. It is a roastery where you can get a world-class filter or espresso. The owners are legends and have such a high level of care for their product and a strong commitment to ethical sourcing. Then do brunch or lunch at Equium Social. If you like books, records and clothes with a post-punk flavour, head to Abicus in Cooks Hill. Its approach to a modern cafe menu is considered, unique and ultimately nourishing. Get a long black and the Nordic plate with pumpernickel, gravlax and lots of fresh and pickled things. Abicus on Darby Street has a curated collection of records, books and fashion leaning heavily into post-punk, indie rock and vintage. Newcastle City Farmers Market on Sunday mornings will give you that locals-only feeling. Related Article New South Wales Australia’s second-oldest city has entered a bold new era While there, browse Cuchillos Tigre for rugged and stylish locally made knives from recycled materials – and maybe get a quote on a custom piece. Or you could grab a meal at Bangkok Nights or Hokkaiya in Hamilton before you hit up Hamilton Station Hotel for a local punk or metal show. Nothing beats the Hunter Valley for a day out. Two-hatted restaurant EXP is a must-do if you can get a booking.

World.title: Non-religious pilgrims? Why secular travellers are flocking to sacred spaces
World.content:
Travel newsCulture holidays Non-religious pilgrims? Why secular travellers are flocking to sacred spaces Kate Cray November 24, 2026 — 9:12am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

At the start of 2025, Ben Pages found himself feeling burned out and, in his words, “like I had lost my North.” He needed a chance to clear his mind and break out of his routine — so he booked a room at a local Catholic monastery. While there, he spent his days in silence — working out, walking around the snowy garden, and peering through a door at the city life beyond the monastery’s walls. He read the Bible. He napped. He tried to guess what time it was. (He’d chosen to go without a phone or watch.) The Church of Saint Martin of Tours, in Fromista, Spain, lies along the Camino de Santiago pilgrimage route. iStock At first his inner monologue overwhelmed him. “I had never realised how auditory I am,” he wrote in his journal on the first day. But as his stay continued, the voices in his head quieted. Eventually, he reached “this beautiful, blissful state,” he said. “It was like I had hit ‘inbox zero,’ and I could hear my being, what’s really underneath all these thoughts.” For Pages, a 35-year-old mindset coach in the Czech Republic, the experience was sacred, but not necessarily religious. Although he’d sought out a monastic retreat, he doesn’t identify as Catholic or as a member of any organized religion, and he’s not sure he believes in God.



‘A wider array of spiritual resources’ 



Those less keen on walking are dousing themselves in holy water at healing sites, like the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, in France, and staying at convents and monasteries, which have become destinations unto themselves. After a video on TikTok about one girl’s convent vacation went viral, many convents now have waiting lists. Brother Luis Cortez, the guest-master at the Abbey of Our Lady of New Clairvaux in Vina, California, said that its rooms book out months in advance during the spring and fall. The Sanctuary of Our Lady of Lourdes, in southwestern France. iStock For those who conceive of religion as a commitment to a set of beliefs, the proliferation of nonbelievers booking monastery stays and walking pilgrimages might seem surprising. But ways people choose to interact with faith have always been much broader than their adherence to a single creed, said Elizabeth Drescher, a professor of religious studies at Santa Clara University. Especially now. As formal churchgoing is dropping, people are instead “engaging a wider array of spiritual resources” and creating a new type of what Drescher calls “liminal religiosity.” In practice, this might look like going on a pilgrimage while using the time to reflect on questions in your own life rather than pondering the Immaculate Conception. Or visiting a monastery and appreciating “the beautiful surroundings, the community, the singing and the sense of reverence,” without wanting to convert, said Brian Smith, a former priest and the author of “Reaching the Religiously Disaffiliated.” In the process, visitors are transforming these experiences from rare acts of worship, taken on by the most intense devotees, to practices that can offer small doses of spirituality to people of all beliefs. After all, many people could benefit from a period of silence to calm their thoughts, or a conversation with a nun or monk about what they believe. Long-distance walking “elevates your endorphins into a rolling high that lasts for days and even weeks,” said George Greenia, the founder of William and Mary’s Institute for Pilgrimage Studies.



Spiritual trips are often affordable, too. Pilgrimages tend to be budget-friendly, and many monastic retreats operate on a donation-only basis. For those that charge (or include suggested donations), fees can hover about $150 a night, with meals included. Travellers on the Via Francigena pilgrimage route. iStock Spiritual transformation, of course, can be a lot more taxing than enjoying a cocktail on the beach or museum-hopping in a new city. But for millennials and members of Generation Z, who see a link between travel and personal growth, immersion is part of the allure. Many tourists now put a premium on trips that feel authentic and unique. “We want to experience a culture from the inside,” Greenia said, “rather than just gawking from the outside.” Studies show that people are especially likely to pursue these trips at life transition points. Greenia has seen people walk to process job loss, deaths, breakups and post-traumatic stress. But even in less dramatic moments, many still appreciate the digital detox and break from daily distractions. Cortez has been struck by how frequently guests at the Abbey use their retreat time to sleep. “You don’t realise how tired you are until you get into an environment where you have permission to rest,” he said. Revelations and transformations



Agatha Dirosa decided to spend a week at a convent in the Catskills after she’d seen a video on TikTok posted by someone who’d done the same. She was particularly intrigued by the possibility of staying with nuns, whom she felt an affinity for, as “women who separate themselves from society to live communally and for the common good,” she said. Related Article Europe One of the world’s greatest walks can now begin in an unusual place A 27-year-old aesthetician and Reiki practitioner, Dirosa had a varied spiritual background. Her extended family was Roman Catholic. As she grew older, she explored other traditions: She had practiced Wicca as a teenager and later read tarot cards and collected crystals. She went into the convent with an open mind. She found that she appreciated how unstructured the days were, anchored only by Mass in the morning and vespers in the evening. She enjoyed listening to the nuns sing, and in between she read, and explored the grounds. “It was the most at peace I’ve ever felt in my life,” she said. A few days in, she decided to take psychedelic mushrooms and had a revelation. She’d never believed in God as “a literal big dude in the sky,” but she finally understood how she did see him: as nature embodied, as “a way to humanise the universe.” On her final afternoon, she lay outside on a rock, listening to the woods and “feeling everything,” she said.



Since the retreat, Dirosa’s relationship with religion has transformed. She has been going to Mass and is considering completing the Order of Christian Initiation of Adults to get confirmed in the Catholic Church. Related Article Travel tips The mid-life bucket list: 20 extraordinary trips to do after 50 After his stay at a Catholic monastery, Pages still doesn’t consider himself religious. He found it hard to maintain the blissful state he’d reached there. Similarly, on the Camino, which he’d done two years earlier, he began his walk with lots of questions about his identity and his purpose in life and left without much resolution. Although the journey didn’t offer easy answers, it did push him in ways he hadn’t expected, he said. “I got to deal with a lot of my fears. I got to deal with things that frustrated me. I got to deal with people that get under my skin,” he said. In the process, he said, he had grown more mature, and had realized he had to leave behind some of the childish ways he had been living. He hadn’t come back with a new religion, but had come back changed all the same. This article originally appeared in The New York Times.
