World.title: 'Toughen it up': David Seymour wants answers on RNZ by Christmas
World.content:
Ministers are pushing for a tougher and faster inquiry into RNZ's financial failures, with David Seymour hopeful it will be wrapped up by Christmas.

But Labour is asking why it has not been consulted on such matters, given it's still not clear who will form the next government.

Two weeks ago, RNZ's board promised an independent inquiry into the public broadcaster's shock $11.8 million loss, more than 25 times worse than what was forecast for the last financial year.

Chair Brent Impey said at the time he wanted it completed by "the early part of next year".

Seymour - who has shareholding responsibilities for RNZ - said he and Media Minister Paul Goldsmith had requested changes to the draft terms of reference after receiving them late last week.

"Our overall feedback was: let's toughen it up," he said. "I would hope that it will be wrapped up by Christmas."

David Seymour. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

Seymour described the draft terms as "pretty good" but wanted closer scrutiny of individual responsibility and particular transactions, not just RNZ's wider systems.

"Sometimes, actually, the process is not the problem. It's the people who are involved in it, and that's called accountability.

"And sometimes we don't have enough of it in New Zealand."

Asked whether responsible executives or board members would or should be named, Seymour cautioned against "vindictiveness".

But he said the review needed to keep open the possibility that "somebody had a job and they didn't do their job".

Seymour said the failure at RNZ was "clear and demonstrable" and further evidence of "low standards everywhere" in the wider public service.

He warned against letting the inquiry drag on: "You do have to give people the time to do it properly. But we also don't want paralysis by analysis."

Seymour wanted RNZ's incoming chief executive Jason Winstanley to "hit the ground running" next year, informed by feedback from the next government's ministers.

Labour wants job cuts put on hold until review's findings are back

Labour's media spokesperson Reuben Davidson said the ministers should have sought other parties' feedback on the draft terms given the election's outcome remained uncertain.

"I've not been provided with the draft terms of reference. I've had no contact from the caretaker minister."

He said a Christmas deadline seemed like "a pretty quick turnaround" but it was hard to assess without having more details.

"Any review needs to provide an assurance that all of the right questions have been asked ... so that we can ensure that there isn't a repeat of this in the future."

Davidson also questioned whether the same people who had overseen the "significant crisis" should be deciding which staff lost their jobs.

"They're making those calls prior to having the results of a review," he said.

Alongside news of the budget blowout, RNZ announced a plan to cut 58 staff by March to get operational spending back under control.

Davidson called for a halt on all job cuts until after the investigation had concluded and its results were made publicly available.

Approached for comment, an RNZ spokesperson said the budget, which had been approved by the board, showed a need to reduce current staffing levels.

"It is for RNZ to consult with staff and the unions to determine the potential roles and redundancies," RNZ said.

"Any proposals will be guided by our Charter, audience needs and strategy, with a focus on protecting audience services as far as possible."

World.title: 'Heartbreaking setback': Fire closes Auckland bakery for foreseeable future
World.content:
An Auckland bakery says it's heartbroken after a fire destroyed its building.

Fire and Emergency (FENZ) northern shift manager Nadine Davies said at about 12.30am on Tuesday, it received several reports about the fire, which was contained to the first level of a bakery on Waiapu Lane in Onehunga.

She said the fire was extinguished and crews had since left the scene.

A fire investigator had been notified to establish the cause.

In a Facebook post, Angkor Bakery confirmed the fire was at its premises.

"It is with incredibly heavy hearts that we share the devastating news that our bakery has been destroyed by fire.

"We are still trying to process what has happened, and our priority right now is working through everything and doing all we can to put things right.

"Unfortunately, this means we will be closed for the foreseeable future while we assess the damage and work out the next steps."

The bakery said the fire was particularly frustrating after just having celebrated its new customer car park a few days earlier.

"Having only just recently reopened our car park after a week of work, this is an incredibly heartbreaking setback, and something none of us could have anticipated.

"We know this news will be upsetting for our wonderful customers and community, and we are truly sorry for the disappointment and inconvenience this will cause."

World.title: Guam secures $10.3 million US grants for infrastructure, healthcare, energy
World.content:
[author_mark_rabago]

Guam has secured nearly US$10.3 million in federal funding for 16 projects aimed at improving infrastructure, emergency services, healthcare, and energy security across the island.

The government announced the US$10,272,937 funding package on 19 November, with the largest allocation of just over $3 million going toward repairs and improvements to the Talofofo Boat Ramp.

Another $2.35m will support architectural and engineering work for a planned cybersecurity and data science building at the University of Guam.

The Guam Power Authority will receive nearly $1.3m for energy infrastructure initiatives, while the Guam Fire Department has been awarded more than $1.17m to expand its ambulance fleet and emergency response capabilities.

The Guam Memorial Hospital Authority will receive $800,000 for workforce pay planning and healthcare accreditation efforts.

Funding also includes $400,000 for critical roof repairs at the Southern Region Community Health Center and $370,000 for heavy equipment purchases.

Guam Legislature generic RNZ Pacific / Eleisha Foon

Governor Lou Leon Guerrero said the grants would help strengthen essential services and improve the island's resilience.

"These federal dollars translate into safer neighborhoods, stronger infrastructure, and better public services for every family on Guam," she said.

The grants are being provided through four federal programmes covering capital improvements, technical assistance, maintenance, and energy development in island communities.

World.title: Police seek sightings of missing Wānaka hiker
World.content:
Police are seeking sightings of a hiker who has been missing near Wānaka for 10 days.

Shaun Gilbert, described as an experienced tramper, had been staying at Roses Hut on the Te Araroa trail north of Arrowtown on November 13 and 14.

Police said he was expected to walk north and meet friends in Wānaka but he had not contacted them.

"Shaun is believed to be on the Te Araroa trail, but may have gone off trail, or pack rafting in the area. Enquiries so far have not located him," a spokesperson said.

"Police and Shaun's family would like to see him return home."

World.title: Kiwi stocks rebound after Jensen Huang's return to Nvidia
World.content:
The New Zealand share market rebounded strongly in trading on Tuesday morning following the Wall Street rally sparked by Jensen Huang's return to the helm of Nvidia.

Huang's reinstatement as chief executive saw shares in the AI chipmaker Nvidia surge 31 percent, regaining nearly a trillion US dollars of the market value it lost following his resignation.

All three Wall Streets index's rose sharply with the tech heavy Nasdaq up 6.5 percent.

In trading this morning, the NZX was up more than 1.5 percent at 13,955.

The gains mean it has recovered some of the ground lost from Monday's sharp fall of over 2.5 percent.

The Kiwi dollar, however, has continued to come under pressure against the US currency, falling further in trading this morning to around 54.48 US cents.

World.title: Auckland could save up to $17 billion over 10 years by planning energy use - report
World.content:
A new report says Auckland could save up to $17 billion over the next decade by planning ahead for its energy use.

The report, commissioned by the council, said that as domestic gas supplies dwindle and the fuel crisis highlights uncertainty, the supercity needs to get ready.

It said the council, businesses and residents could together save billions by compact city growth and infrastructure planning.

The report said improved public transport, more solar power and managing the load on the electricity network would help to build long-term resilience.

It said a 'business-as-usual' approach would cost $14 billion more by 2035.

Chair of the council's policy and planning committee, councillor Richard Hills, said the plan laid out the cost of an ever spreading city, reliant on fossil fuel.

"It's not just about roads and pipes, we actually have to think about how we're planning our energy future, and the fact that a lot of money has got to be spent on lines and the infrastructure of energy into the future," he said.

Hills said the data had pointed the city in the right direction.

"Hopefully, people can see it as a business opportunity to reduce costs long-term by investing in the right types of energy, the right type of infrastructure, and hopefully closer to consumers, closer to residents as well."

Much of the city's energy came from overseas, Hills said.

"How do we make sure we're cushioned from these shocks, and that is by about electrifying our fleet, that is about introducing solar, reducing our gas use, or even not investing in more gas-aligned energy and trying to live closer together."

Councillor Richard Hills. LDR/SUPPLIED

Vector group chief executive Chris Blenkiron said there was opportunity in electrification.

"If you think about the fuel sources of electricity in New Zealand, that's rain at the hydro-dams, whether that's the South Island or the central North Island, that's wind in the turbines, or even the sun on the roofs here in Auckland or across New Zealand," he said.

"The more we can electrify, the more resilience we build into the energy system itself, and that's, as proven, a very good thing."

The council's economic development general manager, Pam Ford, said it was important that all electricity players coordinated and worked together.

Vector group chief executive Chris Blenkiron. Supplied

Audio player for " Auckland growth question offers $31 billion swing " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/business/2755657%2Fauckland-could-save-up-to-17-billion-over-10-years-by-planning-energy-use-report

Auckland growth question offers $31 billion swing Nine To Noon Download MP3 14m

She told Nine to Noon that included Vector, which she said was very important.

"That's why we've worked with them closely on this report, and you're seeing that across the country with so much more emphasis on energy and all of the players," Ford said.

"Certainly, I was at an event, or a hui, if you like, with all of the economic development CEs in June. And without fail, all of those regions talked about energy as one of their top three issues or challenges. So this is an issue I think we're going to hear a lot more about.

"We saw it through the election, all the policies that came out. So I think it's a good thing that we're talking about how we can be better coordinated around such an important issue, such as, you know, how we keep the lights on, how we move around the city and how we keep warm."

The report also suggested that household power bills would be significantly lower than now - with inflation adjusted - and back to 2010 levels.

Ford said that talked to more efficiency in the whole system, smart metering, people using electricity more efficiently, and the networks providing it more efficiently.

"The report authors worked with the suppliers and worked with Vector and projected the different costs that are coming through," she said.

"The better use of technology was a bigger factor. We're not short of energy. It's more about how it's distributed."

Ford said there were many aspects to energy efficiency and how that could be achieved.

"If you're thinking about transport, it's about reliance on liquid fuels. If you're thinking about buildings and homes, it's how you might incentivise insulation, how you might incentivise better uptake of solar.

"When we're talking about households, that's when you start thinking about equity. We've got to make sure that this is an equitable transition for all. So people on higher household incomes are better probably placed to transfer to an $8,000 heat pump.

"But how do you make sure that other people, renters are also an important aspect, probably don't have as much access to influence over their energy choices, and that's why this report is pretty important, because it's kind of recognising all of those different elements and how all the different players have got a role to play."

Wayne Brown. RNZ / Marika Khabazi

Meanwhile, the city's mayor, Wayne Brown, had described energy as an economic issue, not just an energy-sector niche.

"Everything we want for the city runs on reliable, fairly-priced energy - this includes jobs, new industries, affordable homes, investment and our way of life," he said.

"We need a practical path that will make the most of the infrastructure and resources we already have, to avoid unnecessary costs and deliver more value for Aucklanders."

New Zealand Green Building Council chief executive Andrew Eagles. Supplied / NZGBC

New Zealand Green Building Council chief executive Andrew Eagles said the findings were further evidence that New Zealand needed to prioritise energy efficiency in planning.

"Every piece of new research is leading us to the same conclusion: energy efficiency is a crucial part of the solution. This new report from Auckland Council is an important addition to this work," he said in a statement.

"It's pleasing to see some of the report's 'quick-win' recommendations draw on trusted, independent and internationally recognised accreditations such as Green Star, Homestar and NABERSNZ energy efficiency ratings."

Eagles said options presented in the report included investigating preferential consenting for Homestar certified homes, stronger disclosure of commercial building performance and successful implementation of the Ratepayer Assistance Scheme to encourage low-income households and rental properties.

Those were popular, respected tools already in use across the sector, he said.

"Better-performing buildings lower bills and emissions while also reducing pressure on the electricity grid - saving potentially billions of dollars needed on expansion and modernising," Eagles said.

World.title: New research explores kapa haka as tool for improving Māori health
World.content:
A Māori researcher is looking at how cultural practices like kapa haka could help support Māori health, as Aotearoa marks Diabetes Action Month this November.

Lincoln University lecturer Dr Hoani Smith (Kāti Mamoe, Kāi Tahu) said kapa haka can support several dimensions of Māori hauora, bringing together physical activity, cultural connection and whanaungatanga.

Smith is one of four researchers to receive funding through the Diabetes New Zealand Research Foundation's 2026 Small Research Grants. Smith's project, Kapa Haka for Metabolic Hauora: A Māori-Led Feasibility Study for Type 2 Diabetes Prevention, will explore how regular participation in kapa haka could support metabolic health and type 2 diabetes prevention.

Māori and Pasifika communities continue to carry a disproportionate burden of health inequities, including type 2 diabetes.

"Kapa haka is something that already exists in our whānau," Smith told RNZ.

"It's deeply embedded in our culture and it's much more than just movement. It's whakapapa, identity, whanaungatanga."

"And we can all strive to be better by doing something that our whānau are enjoying, rather than force it in our communities."

Dr Hoani Smith told RNZ kapa haka is also an opportunity to support physical activity, strengthen connections between generations, and improve overall hauora. Supplied / Dean Mackenzie

Smith, who specialises in sport, exercise and health research, said a lot of whānau, when they get told what to do without any buy-in, tend not to stick to it.

"And so those habits end up kind of on the wayside after that 21-day cycle.

"So if we can prescribe something that's already been done and we can connect with our people and our culture, it's a win-win for everyone.

"And it also would save long-term down the track inequities that currently exist, because Māori and Pasifika, we carry the heaviest burden. And if we can do something that already exists, mean Māori mean."

Smith draws on the Māori concept of kaitiakitanga - or guardianship - which was announced as this years most beautiful word by international language learning app Babbel.

"So now all of the 'tanga's' can be incorporated and connected to your community."

Muriwhenua in full haka mode. RNZ/Peter de Graaf

He said the physical demands of kapa haka were something he wanted to explore further, alongside the social and cultural connections that came with participating.

"When you actually go to kapa haka practice, they're doing HIIT. They're doing high-intensity training, followed up by waiata, followed up by movements, followed up by playing guitar and then connecting with one another.

"And it goes for many hours. It's not just necessarily go to the gym and exercise for 30, 40 minutes. You're physically and mentally active.

"And the meanest thing is that while singing waiata, you're fatigued as well as having to maintain posture. So it's something rare that I don't think has been researched that well."

Smith said the benefits of kapa haka go beyond just physical health. Haka practices can bring together people of different ages, allowing them to learn from one another while strengthening their connections to their whānau and communities, which he said has an important role to play in supporting the different dimensions of hauora.

"I can be with my elders as well as my grandkids can be with my elders, all at the same time, learning together."

Varron Armstrong steals the show with Ōtiria Marae Kapa Haka. RNZ/Peter de Graaf

Using the te ao Māori view of health and wellbeing, Te Whare Tapa Whā, Smith said kapa haka could contribute to several aspects of a person's health, strengthening all pillars.

"You've got the social aspect of it. Socially, we're connecting with one another because we like being with ourselves, with our own groups that are in the community.

"You've got your physical. You've got your general well-being. You've got your grounding.

"It's also educational as well. It's also singing and being present and being spiritually connected."

From seasoned performers like five-time Te Matatini champions Te Waka Huia (pictured) to haka-loving tamariki taking the stage for the first time – Hakangāhau brought together a full spectrum of talent. Supplied / Te Matatini Enterprises

He said traditional exercise options can be difficult to access for some whānau, with factors such as cost, transport and where people live influencing their ability to stay active.

The feasibility study will bring together researchers with expertise in exercise science, Māori health and general practice. The team hopes to assess participants' metabolic health, including HbA1c levels and insulin sensitivity, over a period of six weeks or more.

Participants will continue taking part in their kapa haka practices, Smith said, allowing researchers to explore what happens through an activity already established within their communities.

The research could also help inform other forms of community-led physical activity, including waka ama and other forms of tākaro (sport).

Te Kapa Haka o Ngāti Whakaue at 2025 Te Matatini Festival at Pukekura/Bowl of Brooklands in New Plymouth Supplied / Te Matatini Enterprises

With Te Matatini approaching, Smith said there was also an opportunity to highlight the wider role kapa haka played in people's lives.

"We can build in our strengths and walk alongside our whānau to ensure Māori knowledge and values and aspirations and ways of being can help shape the world that we live in."

Thousands of performers and supporters will come together through the national kapa haka festival, providing a platform to celebrate the practice and its place within Māori communities.

Smith hopes the research will help bring more attention to the health benefits that can come from activities whānau are already passionate about.

"Let's actually look at how we can improve our own wellbeing, then we can improve the community and the world.

"If we focus on what's in front of us and help to grow those around us, we'll be much better off."

He said changing the way people talk about diabetes is also important, particularly when it comes to reducing stigma and encouraging whānau to seek support and get checked early.

World.title: Police investigate unexplained death in west Auckland
World.content:
Police are investigating an unexplained death in west Auckland.

Emergency services were called to Rimu Street in New Lynn at around 10.20pm on Monday after a body was found at a home.

Do you know more? Email: iwitness@rnz.co.nz

They are treating the death as unexplained, and forensic staff could be seen at the house early Tuesday morning.

"A post-mortem examination will take place in due course as part of our enquiries," Detective Inspector Chris Barry said.

"Residents can expect to see an ongoing Police presence in the area while a scene examination is carried out."

World.title: Hobart's stadium and precinct costs rise to $1.54b
World.content:
The total estimated cost of the Macquarie Point stadium precinct has risen to $1.54 billion, the Tasmanian government has revealed.

The 23,000-seat roofed stadium, which is a condition of Tasmania's AFL deal, was approved by the Tasmanian parliament last December.

A new estimate revealed today has put the cost of stadium delivery at $1.23 billion.

But that figure does not include the wider precinct infrastructure costs needed to support the project that the government also announced today.

A car park and power supply for the precinct was budgeted at $132 million, while project delivery costs add another $183 million.

This brings the total to $1.54 billion.

The government had previously estimated the stadium cost at $1.13 billion. (Supplied: MPDC)

Contingency costs not included

There is also a "client contingency" amount, which has not been revealed or included in costs.

It will cover any potential rise though the final stage of procurement negotiations and, if needed, would bring the project cost even higher.

Until today, the most recent stadium cost estimate had been from September, when the government priced the stadium at $1.13 billion, however this figure included project costs and contingencies.

Last week, the lower house of the Tasmanian parliament passed a motion calling for the "current estimated cost" of both "stadium delivery", and "the broader Macquarie Point precinct-enabling infrastructure", including power upgrades and a centralised car park.

In order to win over the votes needed for the approval order to pass the Legislative Council, the government made a number of commitments, including to limit the state's contribution to $875 million.

Treasurer and Minister for Macquarie Point Urban Renewal Eric Abetz said the government would cover the shortfall from state funds, breaking the promised state contribution cap.

He said the state would then "look to what opportunities there are to gather the funding, and as a result reduce the borrowings that are necessary".

The stadium will have a roof, which was a requirement of the agreement with the AFL for a state team. (Supplied: MPDC)

The federal government is chipping in $240 million, and the AFL $15 million.

Despite the US–Iran war pushing up construction costs worldwide, the government has only recently admitted the stadium would likely cost more than estimated last year.

Oil, material and labour costs blamed for price increase

Premier Jeremy Rockliff called the increases "unavoidable", pointing to high oil and materials prices, higher labour costs and the "complexities driven by the parliamentary-driven order".

He said the state was in conversation with its funding partners about them making larger contributions.

While some MPs had been calling for the parliament to be required to tick off any cost increase, Mr Rockliff said it would not be doing so.

"The parliament had its say last year in early December," he said.

He remained committed to the project.

"Every generation gets a handful of opportunities to shape the future, and the stadium is one of those opportunities," he said.

The independent member for Clark, Kristie Johnston, told 936 ABC Hobart the state would be "on the hook" for significant amounts of borrowing.

"We will be borrowing $1.29 billion to cover the cost of the stadium … that's a significant impost onto the state's finances, particularly when we are in a budget crisis," she said.

" That's taxpayer's money that will need to be paid back and remembering that the stadium will not be generating sufficient income to even cover the interest payments, let alone the principle. "

She said the government needed to explain the different contingencies regarding the estimated costs of the project.

"The job of parliament over the coming days will be to try and understand what those figures represent, what the value for money is, what they are including in those cost deliveries and what the contingencies might be, what risk sharing components they have between both the contractor and the government and indeed what's the break down of those costs?"

Final contract negotiations

The Macquarie Point Development Corporation (MPDC) is in the final stage of negotiations with preferred tenderer BESIX Watpac, and hopes to sign a contract for the build by Christmas.

It submitted its final price to the government earlier this month.

MPDC chief executive Anne Beach said a "intensive, rigorous process" had been run to sign a contract this year.

"There are some risks that are carried by us, and some by the builder," she said of the contract.

She said about $100 million had been saved through value management already, and that MPDC would keep looking for efficiencies.

Our Place Hobart, a community group opposed to the stadium project, said the $1.54 billion project figure was not the full picture.

"That's not including a massive interest bill, the northern access road and contingencies," the group's Roland Browne said in a statement.

He said the government was hundreds of millions of dollars above the maximum state funding figure it promised parliament's upper house.

"This is extraordinary. The government and MPDC have lost control of this project," he said.

World.title: Legal battle looms over potential Russian return to international sport
World.content:
Russia's return to international sport after being excluded over its invasion of Ukraine is facing mounting opposition in Europe, drawing the world's biggest sports organisations into a legal quagmire.

The International Olympic Committee barred Russia from Olympic and international competitions following Moscow's February 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine. It lifted the ‌suspension in July this year and several sports federations are now allowing Russians to compete.

With qualifiers across dozens of sports for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles kicking off in earnest next year, the IOC's recommendation to allow Russia's return to international competition is now being put to the test, with some European countries putting barriers in front of Russian athletes' renewed participation.

Russian athletes were permitted to compete at the 2024 Games as individuals. (Getty Images: Raemon Haazen)

Spyros Capralos, president of the European Olympic Committees umbrella body, said there were concerns the stand-off with Russia could affect key LA 2028 qualifiers, including the European Games in June 2027.

The multi-sport event in Istanbul will offer places at the Olympics across several sports and will likely be the biggest test of how Europe will react.

"It is a massive problem facing Europe because Europe is divided on this matter, with governments which sometimes forget the autonomy of sport," Capralos said.

"They forget that ⁠the most important thing is for all athletes to take part."

The dispute is already before the Court of Arbitration for Sport, the sporting world's top arbitrator. CAS said that the Russian Olympic Committee had filed an appeal against the EOC over conditions on Russian athletes' participation in the Winter European Youth Olympic Festival, to be held in Romania in February.

Russian athletes competed as Individual Neutral Athlete at the 2024 Olympics. (Getty Images via Xinhua: Sun Fei)

Russian athletes were told to compete under their national Olympic committee's logo rather than with their flag and anthem, amid strained relations between Romania and Russia.

Romania, a European Union and NATO member, shares a land border of more than 600 km (370 miles) with Ukraine. President Nicușor Dan, a centrist, has said his country is the target of a hybrid war waged by Russia to destabilise nations that support Kyiv. Russia denies these accusations.

CAS said both parties had agreed to an accelerated procedure, with a ruling expected by December 15 at the latest.

The IOC is eager to have Olympic powerhouse Russia fully back in the games after its athletes competed at the Paris 2024 Summer Games and the Milano Cortina 2026 Winter Olympics as neutrals, without their flag or anthem.

Some international sports federations, such as World Athletics, which oversees a showpiece Olympic discipline, still have restrictions in place.

Furthermore, with the war in Ukraine, Europe's biggest conflict since World War II, about to enter its sixth year, many European ‌nations are ⁠not eager to facilitate Russia's sporting return.

The IOC has recommended Russian athletes be allowed to return to competition. (Getty Images: Kadir Caliskan)

Norway, Sweden and Poland have denied visas to Russian athletes, while some national teams have refused to play them.

Some have said they will not compete against Russia even in junior events, as Norway's ice hockey team has done. Event organisers, meanwhile, are weighing the costs of hosting Russian competitors.

Next year's ice hockey World Championships in Germany are already in focus after CAS ruled that Russia was eligible to compete, overturning an International Ice Hockey Federation decision to exclude the team.

German organisers have said a Russian presence would require heightened security arrangements that could stretch budgets.

Russia, however, is not planning to back down. After briefly considering a switch from the European to the Asian sports federation system several ⁠years ago to give its athletes better access to competitions, it is now taking cases to CAS to secure places in events.

Earlier this year, it succeeded at CAS in securing places for some of its winter sport athletes at the Milano Cortina Winter Olympics.

Russian athletes were permitted to compete at the 2026 Winter and Winter Paralympic Games. (Getty Images: Alex Grimm)

Russia's sports minister and national Olympic committee president Mikhail Degtyarev has criticised restrictions on Russian athletes, saying his country would consider all legal options.

"We are waiting for a legal statement to proceed with all our complaints to authorities. The [Russian} Hockey Federation follows its own ⁠line, and we would go through the IOC," Degtyarev told Russian television on November 12.

The IOC, which says entry visas are a sovereign responsibility, wants Russia back in the fold.

"Athletes' access to international competition should not be limited by the passport they hold or affected by the involvement of their governments in a war or conflict," an IOC spokesperson told Reuters.

However, it has made clear that outside the Olympic Games, it is for international sports federations to ⁠deal with the issue of Russian participation at their events.

"The international federations have to navigate the complex and evolving reality — and concrete consequences — of the current geopolitical context, in particular for events they have already awarded and planned," the IOC said.

Those consequences could, however, end up affecting the IOC's own events, including the Olympic Games.

"There is, of course [concern]," Capralos, who is also a member of the IOC Executive Board, said, when asked whether the arguments could affect Olympic qualifiers.

"One of the reasons we wanted to have Russians competing was to allow them to qualify for the Games," he said.

Reuters

World.title: W Award winner Georgie 'not anymore' in older sister Maddy's shadow
World.content:
With the league best and fairest medal around her neck, Georgie Prespakis looked down at her sister Maddy from the stage.

"To think that she's been up here and been able to achieve this. I'm full of emotion and trying to hold back some tears for sure," the Geelong star said into the microphone.

"I've always wanted to follow in Maddy's footsteps, and at times, I probably felt a little bit in her shadow."

The camera then panned to Essendon's Maddy, who mouthed "not anymore" with a face wet with tears. The room erupted with laughter before focusing back on Georgie.

Georgie presented Maddy with the W Award in 2020. (Getty: Michael Willson/AFL Photos)

"It's obviously a hard game. It's a hard game at times, so to be able to lean [on] and support one another is something that's meant a lot to me, particularly this year," she said, after the Cats finished in the top two but exited the finals in straight sets.

When asked what made the pair so good, Georgie replied: "Certainly some good genes. I'll take those for sure.

"[But] no, no doubt my family, my parents particularly, are feeling super proud, and yeah, I can't wait to obviously share this moment with them."

The Prespakis pair became the first sisters in AFLW history to both win the league's highest honour, the W Award.

When Georgie and Maddy play each other, it's subbed "the Prespakis cup". (Getty: Daniel Pockett/AFL Photos)

The only brothers to win the men's equivalent, the Brownlow, were Albert and Harry Collier, back in 1929 and 1930 respectively.

Maddy won it back in 2020. With the awards held via Zoom due to the COVID-19 pandemic, Maddy was presented with the medal by Georgie in their shared backyard.

A year later, Georgie was drafted to Geelong.

In her early years at the Cats, Georgie was constantly being compared to her older sister. When Geelong and Essendon (or Carlton when Maddy was still there) played each other, it was referred to as "the Prespakis cup".

As the years went on, Georgie burst out of that shadow, as she does from stoppages, and began to represent a new era of AFLW talent.

Inaugural player Jasmine Garner was the favourite on Monday to take out the W Award, a medal that has eluded her over her career despite long being regarded as the best player in the competition. She earned her ninth All Australian blazer this week, the most of any player in the history of the competition.

Garner polled 24 votes, falling behind the other two frontrunners, Charlie Rowbottom (28 votes) and Georgie (30 votes).

Georgie Prespakis is the first Geelong player to win the AFLW W Award. (Getty: Morgan Hancock)

Charlie and Georgie were drafted in the same year, with picks one and two respectively. They are the first players not to have played in the first two seasons of the competition to poll so high.

"I've always set really high standards for myself," Georgie said.

"And I've always wanted to be the best that I can be, and I will always work incredibly hard to kind of get myself in that position. And no doubt, my first season of AFLW was a real eye-opener just as to how difficult it is.

"That was something that I really struggled with, and knew that off the back of that, I had to lose a little bit of chubby, baby fat and get to work, and that was something I did.

"It was really difficult to move out of home and go up to Geelong and start a life down there. And I think that's why I feel so grateful to have landed at such an amazing club… [that} allowed me to become not only a better person but a better footballer."

World.title: Steve Smith labours on return from injury in Sheffield Shield
World.content:
Steve Smith has fallen cheaply in his batting comeback, making a laborious 12 for New South Wales against Queensland in their Sheffield Shield clash.

Smith had not played a innings since October 22, when he battled a neck injury in Australia's second Test in South Africa.

The star batter returned for NSW ahead of Australia's first Test against New Zealand starting on December 9 in Perth.

In reply to Queensland's 278 all out, the Blues were 7-195 at stumps at the SCG on Monday.

Smith's knock in tricky conditions was cut short by fringe Test paceman Michael Neser.

Smith struggled for touch on a rain-affected day and, with stadium lights on in the last session, faced 59 balls.

Smith was adjudged LBW when trapped on the crease to an in-dipping Neser delivery, though replays showed the ball perhaps would have missed leg stump.

The ex-Test captain, who has maintained a public silence amid the renewed furore over Australia's sandpaper scandal, cut Bulls spinner Mitchell Swepson (3-45) for four early and was six runs from eight balls.

He then was scoreless from his next 24 deliveries. His next run came when he almost chopped a Cameron Gannon short ball onto his stumps.

Steve Smith rarely displayed his fluid best shot-making. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

Smith came to the crease to replace NSW opener Sam Konstas, who did no harm to his claims for a Test recall, making 42 from 86 balls.

Konstas, who has been in fine touch in the domestic season, struck a six and five fours before being dismissed in strange fashion.

Facing Swepson, Konstas attempted a half-hearted push to the leg-side but got a leading edge to pop a simple return catch to the Queensland tweaker.

Konstas fell after a 79-run opening partnership with Josh Philippe, who also departed when within reach of a half-century. He edged to keeper Jimmy Peirson from the bowling of Neser (2-28) when on 46.

The most remarkable dismissal of the day though came when Charlie Stobo was caught by Hugo Burdon at wide long on off the bowling of Marnus Labuschagne.

Stobo could have been caught on the rope by Burdon, only for the Queensland opener to put his hands up and acknowledge that he trod on the boundary rope in his attempt to throw the ball back in to himself.

Despite that reprieve, the very next ball Stobo went to hit Labuschagne to the exact same spot, where he was caught.

Earlier, Queensland were bowled out for 278 with Test spinner Nathan Lyon claiming a wicket in his first over on Monday. He finished with 1-86 from 29 overs.

Charlie Stobo (3-45) and Liam Hatcher (3-55) were the most successful bowlers.

AAP

World.title: Giddey's historic triple-double rewrites 60-year Chicago Bulls record
World.content:
Josh Giddey has broken his own NBA record and rewritten 60 years of Chicago Bulls history with a remarkable triple-double in an overtime loss to Denver.

The point guard improved his own assist high for Australians in the NBA with 22, while adding 23 points and 14 rebounds in the Bulls' 151-145 loss to the Nuggets.

No Chicago player had notched more than 20 assists since 1985, and Guy Rodgers in 1966 was the last Bull to record at least 20 points, 20 assists and 10 rebounds in a game.

Giddey, who hit 10 of 17 field goals and scored seven late points to force overtime, recorded his 33rd NBA triple-double to move to 14th on the all-time list — equal with countryman Ben Simmons.

Remarkably, it came after he managed just two points and was benched by coach Tiago Splitter in the fourth quarter of a loss to Washington.

He had combined 18 points, 14 rebounds and nine assists in the game before that, rebounding from a four-point effort in the game prior to sum up a rollercoaster season for the battling 4-12 Bulls.

"He [Splitter] can relate to us. He was good about it and doesn't sugar-coat it. I wasn't surprised or confused as to why I wasn't out there," Giddey said post-game of his recent struggles.

"You appreciate it a lot more after the fact. During the moment, you don't want to hear those things.

"I have learnt you've got to be able to move on. I can't come into practice still pissed off and dwelling on things."

Nikola Jokić had 37 points, 18 rebounds and 11 assists for the 202nd triple-double of his career — closing the gap on NBA leader Russell Westbrook (209) — while Jamal Murray scored eight of his season-high 45 points in overtime.

Nikola Jokić (right) also registered a triple-double in a high-scoring game. (Getty Images: Jayden Mack)

Giddey's stat line came without their two leading scorers, the injured Norman Powell and Caleb Wilson (fractured metacarpal), who are averaging a combined 39.7 points per game this season.

"He played extremely well," Splitter said.

"We've got to give them flowers when they deserve and last game they didn't have it. Tonight they brought it."

Earlier on Sunday (Monday AEDT), Giddey's Boomers teammate Dyson Daniels put the brakes on Detroit star Cade Cunningham to hand Atlanta a fourth-straight win.

Daniels had 14 rebounds to go with eight assists, five steals and five points in his 39 minutes on court in the 107-97 win.

He kept Cunningham (five points) under wraps — the All-Star failed to hit double figures for the first time this season.

The 23-year-old leads the NBA in steals at three per game through 17 matches this season, and also tops the league in deflections and loose balls recovered.

The Hawks are now perched in third place in the Eastern Conference with an 11-6 record.

The Pistons led 85-74 at the start of the fourth quarter before the Hawks took a 92-85 lead with 18 unanswered points. Isiah Joe's three-pointer with 4 minutes and 52 seconds remaining ended Detroit's scoreless streak.

Nickeil Alexander-Walker posted 27 points, while Corey Kispert scored a season-high 18 points and Lu Dort 16 for the Hawks, who were without CJ McCollum (left calf strain) and Australian Jock Landale (right big toe ⁠strain).

AAP

World.title: Australia beats France in Billie Jean King Cup tie
World.content:
Sam Stosur's Australian team will be back for a crack at the Billie Jean King Cup crown next year after "unreal" Maya Joint joined the party with two victories to seal a crushing 4-0 win over France in their play-off tie at Le Portel.

Joint had watched her teammates Storm Hunter and national number one Talia Gibson give the visitors a convincing lead in the French seaside town after the first day on Saturday, but was thrust into the action alongside Hunter to try to seal victory in the key doubles rubber on Sunday, local time.

Even on the Le Chaudron clay court chosen by the hosts, the Aussie duo were in a different league to the home pairing of world number 38 Diane Parry and world No.8 doubles player Kristina Mladenovic, racing to a tie-sealing 6-2 6-4 victory.

Joint, who produced some spectacular tennis in that win, then got in on the singles action, swiftly outplaying Elsa Jacquemot 6-1 6-3 in under an hour. Victory in that "dead" rubber underlined the triumph before organisers scrapped the last scheduled match between Hunter and Clara Burel.

"Maya was unreal today. It was a really tough match against quality opponents," said Hunter, whose own game always seems to go up a notch when she wears the green and gold.

"We're really happy with the result."

Joint, delighted to be returning to her best at the end of a season when her Wimbledon triumph over Serena Williams proved the absolute highlight, added: "The vibes were high all week, we were just really happy and excited to all be here."

The three Australians, between them, had blasted through their four matches without dropping a set, and conceding just 20 games over the whole weekend of one-sided fare.

It was also a moment of revenge for captain Stosur, who played in the 2019 final, which she lost 3-2 on home soil in Perth against a French team that included Mladenovic.

If they had lost the tie, she knew Australia would have been condemned to relegation to its regional group next year, thus ruling it out of a chance to shoot for the 2027 title.

Instead, they will be back in April's qualifiers amid what looks like a renaissance in the Australian women's game, looking to seal a place in the week-long finals in Shenzhen where they could pursue a first title since 1974, when the World Cup of women's tennis was known as the Federation Cup.

"It's a fantastic feeling for us right now; we put in a lot of hard work to try and make this result happen," Stosur said.

"We put on these jackets in the green-and-gold, and it really does bring out the best in a lot of our players. If we can keep building the way we are, for sure we want to try and lift that trophy one day again."

The seven-time champions are looking to bounce back from a disappointing early exit in 2026 when they lost 3-1 in a home qualifier against Great Britain in Melbourne in April.

It's now four years since Australia last reached the final, losing 2-0 to Switzerland in Glasgow.

AAP

World.title: New Zealand rearguard holds India to draw first Test
World.content:
Australia have moved up to join leaders and reigning champions South Africa in the 2025-2027 World Test Championship top two after New Zealand and India drew at Basin Reserve in Wellington.

New Zealand fought a battling rearguard on Monday to deny ‌India in the first Test, but drop out of the top two in the WTC standings due to the draw, while India remain in fourth.

The tourists ended five wickets short of converting their mammoth ‌first-innings lead into a victory, after India entered the final day requiring eight dismissals to take a 1-0 lead in the series.

New Zealand were 5-239 in their second innings, still trailing India's first-innings 9-720 declared by 113 runs, when the captains shook hands to end the contest.

Daryl Mitchell and first-innings centurion Glenn Phillips put on 63 for the sixth wicket on a Basin Reserve track that had been all but lifeless since the ‌opening session and a bit of the ‌match.

The pair stayed together for 43 overs, Phillips scoring 26 from 126 balls and Mitchell 49 not out from 186 balls before the teams shook hands and stumps were drawn with an hour remaining in the day.

"As you look back over the five days from that first innings to where the game ended up, the wicket changed throughout but I thought it was a great Test match," Nicholls said.

"Both teams gave it everything.

"For us to get a draw from where we were was a pleasing result."

Daryl Mitchell was not out on 49 when the captains shook hands. (Getty Images: Hagen Hopkins)

India will take ⁠some confidence from their batting performance heading to Christchurch for the start of the second Test ​on Friday after six players scored half centuries or better in their single, record-breaking innings of 9-720.

KL Rahul and Rishabh Pant both grabbed centuries in contrasting styles, while skipper Shubman Gill fell two runs short of the milestone.

Pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah impressed on his return to Test cricket after a year out as he helped reduce New Zealand to 5-70 on the opening day, although he was used sparingly as India chased the result on Monday.

New Zealand's match was the tale of two sixth-wicket ‌stands.

The first was ​of 216 runs between Henry Nicholls (175 not out) and Phillips (118) that enabled the hosts to post a respectable 368 in their first knock.

The ​second between Phillips ‌and Mitchell on Monday was never going to be about the tally of runs but more about how long they occupied the ​crease.

They came together in the sixth over after lunch when Tom Blundell departed for 15 via DRS review off the bowling of Anshul Kamboj to leave New Zealand at 5-176.

In the opening session, spinner Washington Sundar had made ‌the first breakthrough by removing Devon Conway for 65, after the ball popped up off the opener's bat and pad for Pant to collect with an athletic catch.

Rachin Ravindra, the other overnight batter, followed for 37 with a miscued shot off the bowling of seamer Prasidh Krishna that flew to Rahul in the slips.

India will rue a few missed chances to make further inroads into the New Zealand batting order, most notably ​a potential run out that would have sent Mitchell back early in his innings.

"We knew it was going to be a challenge to get 10 wickets on that pitch," India captain Gill said.

"We had a couple of chances and a decent day in the field. I think we challenged them in all areas."

AAP/AP

World.title: Devastating injury blow for Adams days after making Socceroos debut
World.content:
New Socceroo Eli Adams faces nearly a year on the sidelines through a horror knee injury.

Adams made his first appearance for Australia off the bench in last week's 3-0 friendly win over Qatar, but was injured at training and had to leave camp before the Socceroos' 2-0 loss to Jordan.

His Japanese club Gamba Osaka confirmed today that Adams had ruptured the ACL in his left knee, along with injuring his MCL and suffering a lateral meniscus tear.

The 24-year-old will return to Australia to start his rehabilitation.

The Queenslander will have a knee reconstruction and faces at least several months — if not up to a year — on the sidelines.

It is a shocking blow for Adams, who earned a move to Japan off the back of stellar form at the Newcastle Jets.

Between 2024 and 2026, Adams scored 20 goals in 52 A-League appearances for Newcastle.

He has since notched two goals in 15 appearances for Gamba Osaka.

AAP

Tech.title: The hacker behind early GTA VI leaks has been sentenced — and released
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

GTA VI: all the news on Rockstar’s next entry in the Grand Theft Auto series

Arion Kurtaj, who pleaded guilty last week to hacking Grand Theft Auto VI developer Rockstar Games and other companies, including Uber and Revolut, was sentenced to seven years in prison but released on license, the BBC reports. After hacking Rockstar, Kurtaj leaked 90 videos of GTA VI in 2022, years before the game’s public release last week.

Prior to his sentencing, Kurtaj had already spent time in a hospital because of his autism and in prison.

“You are obviously a very talented young man,” the judge in the case said, according to Sky News. “Don’t waste those talents by spending the rest of your life in and out of prison.” Kurtaj cannot use platforms Telegram and Discord as part of a five-year Serious Crime Prevention Order, the BBC says.

Rockstar launched GTA VI last week to positive reviews. The studio said the game made $3.79 billion in its first day of sales.
